title: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
description: Voters are turning away from the centre in Germany as fears grow about the economy and migration.
body: Friedrich Merz has led Germany since 2025 A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance. Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis. But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years. It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities. Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again. A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more. A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story. A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time. Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity. And the question of what next is, as yet, unanswered. That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party has made strong gains in recent local elections In the last fortnight, Friedrich Merz's party was beaten to first place in Berlin, pummelled in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and pushed out of parliament altogether in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. A lifeline for Merz is that no-one, within his own centre-right CDU party, is yet willing to challenge the chancellor openly despite persistent rumours of a Kanzlertausch (chancellor swap). But he is on thin ice, with record low approval ratings among voters who often describe him as arrogant and out of touch. It is a problem that in government circles is sometimes more politely referred to as a "communication" issue. Those who back the Chancellor say it is time to double down on much-needed reforms, alongside its centre-left SPD coalition partner, and find a better way of talking to people. Swapping chancellors is not the answer as anyone would face the "same challenges", argues Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson in parliament for Merz's CDU and its sister party, the CSU. Hardt pointed out that the CDU/CSU fared far better in other regional elections earlier this year, when we spoke minutes after Merz addressed party lawmakers at a closed-door meeting in the Bundestag. "I think Friedrich Merz knows about his deficits," says Hardt. "He will work on him and we will work on us as (a) party. And hopefully we will convince the people in the next months that we are on the right way." Merz came to power in 2025, promising to get tough on immigration and boost Germany's ailing economy. He appeared to offer a dynamism that might act as an antidote to the former dull, unhappy drumbeat of centre-left leader Olaf Scholz's bickering three-way coalition. Olaf Scholz and his three-way coalition struggled in power, and he was ousted in 2025 And Merz's allies would claim he has had some success. This week, leading economic institutes raised the country's growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 above 1% while illegal entries into Germany – and Europe – are down year on year. But that will not eliminate public anxieties, on either issue. Households and businesses continue to endure high energy costs while fears persist that China is cannibalising German industry, including its iconic car sector. It is a brutal reversal of Germany's old recipe for success: cheap Russian gas that powered a booming export-driven economy. And when it comes to immigration, the focus is now less on new arrivals and more on concerns about public safety, welfare costs and integration. While there are local exceptions, voters appear to be losing faith in Germany's two principal governing parties (CDU and SPD). Enter the rising force in German politics, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD): a party that alarms security officials with its Russia-friendly stance and contains regional branches that are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence. Smears and misrepresentations, argues the AfD, as it claimed its third victory ever in a state election last Sunday in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania. Its co-leader, Alice Weidel, told me this week that Friedrich Merz's days were numbered. The AfD are a divisive force, with their recent local election wins sparking protests The AfD has survived numerous scandals in recent years to now top the polls nationwide, at around 28%. It carries the swagger of a party making the political weather. It has capitalised on a nostalgia for the past alongside an anxiety in the present as it consolidates its strongholds in the former communist east. An AfD placard I saw in Berlin read "Berlin braucht Ordnung" (Berlin needs order). It is the as yet untested promise that this party can bring back a lost sense of stability. But in Germany's capital it was in fact Die Linke (the Left) that topped the polls last Sunday in a further blow to the country's traditional "big tent" parties. The victory has put fresh scrutiny on Die Linke, as it faces allegations of antisemitism. The party leadership has insisted it is committed to protecting Jewish life. This round of regional elections has encapsulated the country's fault lines: the eroding support for Germany's political centre, and a polarising debate on the AfD. Rarely in post-war Germany has a set of local polls generated so much upheaval at home and interest abroad. title: Drumcree parade decision to be challenged in High Court
description: Residents are applying to the High Court in Belfast to overturn the decision to allow a planned Orange Order on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown.
body: The parade (pictured above in 2018 on a 20th anniversary protest) will be allowed to march on the Garvaghy Road on Sunday A legal challenge to the Parades Commission's decision to allow the Orange Order to march on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown is take place on Saturday morning. The commission announced that a the parade can go ahead on Sunday, for the first time in almost 30 years, with restrictions in place. Rather than start at 13:00 BST on Sunday as intended, the commission has said the march can depart no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested. No bands or supporters are allowed. The decision is facing the legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, which opposes the march. A detailed document known as a determination, which was published on the commission's website, external on Friday afternoon said: "This decision is not, and should not be perceived, as a victory for one side or a loss for another." The five-person commission, led by Prof Evelyn Collins, held face-to-face talks with the Orange Order earlier this week, and held a separate meeting with the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition. Senior police officers were also consulted about the planned parade. Within the 31-paragraph determination by the Parades Commission, details were revealed of conversations held with the PSNI. The document stated: "The police made both written and oral submissions, indicating that they, at the time of making them, had no information indicating that the parade would result in disorder or violence." The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said it had activated "mutual aid arrangements to support contingency planning for a policing operation" in Portadown on Sunday. It is understood about 200 officers are coming from Scotland. Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, gathered with others outside the High Court in Belfast on Friday On Friday, a residents' group on the Garvaghy Road said they were ''furious'' over the decision, adding that the community were "fearful about what will happen over the weekend". Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, said: "The feelings of people in the local community here, you can describe them as shock, and you can also describe them as anger. "After 28 years of this community being able to avoid confrontation, the parades commission by their decision is creating the grounds for a confrontation." DUP MLA Carla Lockhart said residents have "nothing to fear" and asked them not to get "caught up in hysteria". "Thirty-five men walking down a road silently with no bands in an orderly fashion. "These men work, live and do business in this community," she added. She said Sinn Féin should "show political leadership and ensure calm remains across the community". However Sinn Féin President Mary-Lou McDonald said the decision to allow the parade was "utterly reckless" adding that it shows a "complete disregard" for the rights of the community of the Garvaghy road. "This is a grave situation, recklessness of this scale of course has implications and consequences." She called for anyone that can intervene, including the prime minister and taoiseach, to "put this right". British soldiers erect a security fence at Drumcree Church in July 2002 The Parades Commission has been in the political spotlight since its previous Drumcree determination was quashed in the High Court in August. A review of the commission has since been ordered by the Northern Ireland Office. The Drumcree parade dispute began in the mid-1990s and it almost derailed the peace process at the time. Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders. When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years. The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches. Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order over the past three decades. What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? title: Inside the FBI hack: Agents fearful and angry after 'dangerous' data breach
description: Current and former agents speak to the BBC about the devastating impact of the FBI hack.
body: Current and former FBI agents have spoken to BBC News of their shock, fear and anger following a hack that appears to have exposed the private and personal information of the agency's entire workforce. "This is really bad for our undercover agents," says one former FBI agent, who fears for the safety of his colleagues. The former cyber investigator is in a group chat with current agents who are worried their personal information could soon be freely available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers. He says staff fear they could be targeted, or that criminals could use the data to create highly convincing phishing attempts, scams or demands for bribes. The hacking group ShinyHunters is threatening to publish the stolen databases and documents within four days unless its demands are met. Some agents are also concerned about the risk of physical attacks from cyber criminals they have investigated. "One of the things we are discussing in the group chat is 'violence-as-a-service' attacks from young online gangs," says the former worker. "They could use this information to harass an FBI agent who has worked on their cases." Groups similar to ShinyHunters - believed to be an English-speaking gang - have in the past been linked to swatting incidents, and even petrol bomb attacks against law enforcement officers and rivals. The group claims it breached FBI systems on Monday and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site. The FBI has not responded to requests for comment. However, on Wednesday the agency acknowledged the breach - saying it was "aggressively investigating" how it occurred. For Michael McPherson, a former FBI agent who is now senior vice president of security operations at cyber firm ReliaQuest, the hack presents "a security threat which cuts to the core of agent safety, particularly their families". He says agents understand the "inherent risks" that come with the job. "But this incident reportedly includes personal data such as home addresses and contact information, which could expose family members who are normally insulated from the threats associated with such a career," McPherson says. ShinyHunters shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand. The samples appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses. The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors. The criminals also appear to possess highly sensitive medical information relating to thousands of special agents. BBC News has seen samples of stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations containing information such as blood and urine test results, along with doctors' notes mentioning conditions including a "shellfish and banana allergy". Agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical issues including "blood in the urine" and "high cholesterol" are now in the criminals' hands. Cynthia Kaiser, who was the Deputy Director of Cyber at the FBI and now leads the Research Centre at Halcyon says ShinyHunters appear to already have lost control of some of the data which is circulating in various online groups of cyber researchers and could lead to harm even before the main tranche is published. "A lot of the damage may already be done, and as we have seen in past FBI data breaches, that information continues to circulate the dark web years later," she said. There are also concerns about the breach's national security implications, such as staff becoming targets for recruitment efforts by hostile foreign intelligence services. Alongside fear, many of those who spoke to the BBC expressed anger at the FBI for allowing the data to be stolen. The hack is particularly embarrassing from a technical perspective because ShinyHunters is not generally regarded as a highly sophisticated hacking group. One former cyber agent said FBI staff were furious about the "sloppy and lazy security failures" that allegedly enabled the breach. There is also confusion about how to handle any fallout if data is published next week, as threatened. The FBI appears unlikely to comply with the extortion demands, and the hackers have indicated they intend to post the information on their darknet site. Unusually, the group is not demanding money. Instead, it wants the FBI to retract an advisory published in May, which it claims "offended" them. "The agency leadership is lost," the former cyber investigator tells me. He says staff have been advised to sign up to a service called DeleteMe, which helps remove personal information from data broker websites - a response he feels is inadequate. The hack may raise further questions for FBI director Kash Patel, whose leadership has already faced scrutiny According to another former agent, there is widespread shock that such a breach could happen at one of the world's best-resourced law enforcement agencies. "You would think this information would not be internet-exposed. It's disturbing, actually," he says. There is also embarrassment that a prolific group of young cyber criminals has repeatedly managed to evade law enforcement while carrying out a string of high-profile hacks. ShinyHunters has been linked to numerous extortion attacks, including on Rockstar Games and the education platform Canvas. The group regularly communicates with reporters via Telegram, where members often boast about their activities. "The bureau doesn't know what to do with teenage cyber criminals," one former agent says. McPherson says there is no doubt the FBI is taking the incident extremely seriously. He expects the agency to draw on its extensive network of partners and resources "to make this group suffer the consequences for this brazen and taunting attack". title: 'It's a brutal adjustment': How to cope when your child goes to uni
description: This new stage of parenthood is emotional - but learning how to let go can help you cope.
body: Luke felt overwhelmed with both pride and grief after dropping his son off at university for the first time. "It feels like a brutal adjustment," he says. "After 18 years of seeing him every day and taking care of him, I miss him so much and I don't really know what to do with myself." Like other parents we have spoken to, Luke (not his real name) and his wife have felt compelled to regularly check a Facebook group for parents and carers with children living in the same halls of residence, as well as a university-wide version with more than 2,000 members. At first, being in these groups felt helpful for practical information, particularly in the weeks before his son headed to university, Luke says. But now they're feeding his anxiety. "People will post things like: 'Is it normal to spend so much time in your room?'; 'I'm worried my daughter is struggling to make friends'; 'My child isn't replying to messages - how often are people hearing from theirs?'" There have also been questions about Amazon parcel logistics, requests to borrow cereal bowls and what tog duvet other people's children were given. Luke thinks these kinds of social media groups have fuelled his temptation to keep checking his son's location on a tracking app "to make sure he is going out enough and finding friends". Because his messages and calls go largely unanswered, Luke will also watch videos posted on the university's social media accounts, hoping to catch a glimpse of his son among the throngs of Freshers. Other parents have sheepishly confessed they're doing the same. Across universities, some enterprising parents have set up the sort of WhatsApp group chats you'd more typically find being used when children are at school. Only rather than asking after lost jumpers and what day PE is, these groups might be used to try to parent long-distance. Some parents say they feel compelled to regularly check a Facebook group for parents and carers "Sometimes parents send their child to university and they're not even worried, but then these group chats create a worry that something might be wrong," says Rayyah Uddin, 20, a third-year student at the University of Nottingham. She knows of WhatsApp group chats being set up by parents of first-year students at her university and has also seen parents use TikTok to share their worries about their child not making friends, and asking other parents for their help. "These are issues the students should really be figuring out for themselves, and it is better if parents try and talk to their child rather than immediately jump to other parents," she says. Not hearing from your child all the time isn't necessarily a cause for concern - "they might just be having a really good time and are getting absorbed into university life," Rayyah adds. Parent social media groups can be useful, according to psychologist Charlotte Armitage, but not when they are used to share private difficulties, track movements or ask questions that the student is capable of asking themselves. "Constant checking, tracking or intervening may soothe the parent in the short term, but it can inadvertently communicate to the young adult: 'I am not sure you can cope without me.'" "Of course, where there is a credible safeguarding concern, a significant change in behaviour, or a known risk to their wellbeing, parents should act." A big part of going to university is about being independent, says Manchester University student Archie Forde, 19, who has heard stories of parents "pinging phones at 3am and calling their kids 12 times a week". He thinks parents turning to social media groups have "mostly fair concerns" but are going about things in the wrong way. The groups can be "echo chambers where everyone just spins each other out about their kids", he says, and suggests having a proper conversation with your child about boundaries, before university starts. Every family will have different ideas about what is overbearing, but a student shouldn't have the worry of choosing between "cutting back parents' communication and ruining that relationship, or responding to a flurry of texts at pre-drinks and detaching yourself from the social situation". Archie Forde, 19, says parents turning to social media groups are going about things in the wrong way Writing a letter or sending a parcel - without the expectation of a getting a response - could be a good way to let your child know you're thinking of them, "without it feeling like a demand", says child psychologist Laverne Antrobus. Perhaps negotiate a time to check in with them, "and be prepared to not always have long conversations," she says. And when you do speak to your child, "make sure your curiosity is genuine, rather than half-informed by the surveillance you've been doing". "Already knowing where they've been and what they've been up to makes for an unrewarding conversation with them and children are bright - they will know." Rayyah says she looks forward to properly catching up when she goes home. "If you've spent months being closely monitored it might feel as if you haven't really been away or gained any independence; it could feel frustrating." Having seen three children off to university, Nichola McClellan wants to reassure parents that it does get easier. Based in Cheshire, she shares her experience of being an "empty nester" on social media. "It's a huge emotional adjustment after years of your life revolving around your children, so we need to give ourselves time and permission to miss them. "I think back to how lost I felt. I didn't know who I was without the kids. "They're learning how to leave," she says, "but we're learning how to let go." Rather than expect constant contact, Nichola sends "little no-pressure messages" on their family WhatsApp group. "'Love you', 'proud of you' - thing

title: E-bikes seized by police sold on at auction, BBC finds
description: Thousands are confiscated annually because they are suspected of being driven illegally or used in a crime - most are destroyed, but last year police sold at least 161.
body: Two of the bikes recently listed on an auction website used by police E-bikes seized by police forces in the UK are being sold on at auction, despite some fears they could end up back in the hands of criminals, the BBC can reveal. Thousands are confiscated annually because they are suspected of being driven illegally, or used in a crime - most are later destroyed, but a BBC investigation has found some are sold on to members of the public in online auctions. Across the UK, police sold 161 e-bikes last year and 54 in 2024, although the real number could be higher because not every force responded to the BBC's Freedom of Information request. Some of the forces said they had now ended the practice, but others defended it as a way of putting "money back into policing". Six forces responded to say e-bikes they had seized had been sold, including large forces such as West Midlands Police and Police Scotland. The figure includes electrically-assisted pedal cycles, which look similar to bicycles and have a motor that kicks in as a rider pedals, as well as electric motorbikes, which are usually more powerful and are propelled only by their motor. E-bikes have become controversial because some think they are linked to crime and anti-social behaviour. Recent BBC reporting has highlighted cases across the country of balaclava-clad young men riding illegally on footpaths and intimidating residents. There have also been a number of pedestrian deaths, including 86-year-old grandmother Gloria Stephenson, who was struck at a zebra crossing in Sunderland last year by an illegal e-motorbike. The BBC found listings of e-bikes "sold at direction of police" Police Scotland, which covers the whole country, says it sends seized e-bikes to an accredited recycler who may then decide to auction them, with money going back to the force. Last year 93 e-bikes seized by Police Scotland were sold, more than any other force. Two e-bikes seized by West Yorkshire Police last year were sold at auction. The force said any money raised from the auctions was split between the force and the West Yorkshire Combined Authority, and said some cash went to "local good causes". All of those sold were "legally compliant", they added. West Midlands Police, which sold 12 e-bikes last year, said the "vast majority" of seized bikes were destroyed, with a "small number" sold "via an independent auction company so that the money can be put back into policing". The BBC found some forces had also sold e-scooters. It is illegal to use a privately-owned e-scooter on public property, although owning an e-scooter is not illegal. Durham Constabulary sold three of them last year, and West Mercia Police sold one. West Mercia's force also sold 24 e-bikes. Both forces told the BBC they have recently reviewed their policy and they will no longer sell e-bikes or e-scooters. Clive Grunshaw, the Police and Crime Commissioner for Lancashire said: "There's nowhere apart from [a] back garden that these scooters can be legally used, so it's a confused message," he said. He urged police forces to stop selling e-bikes, which he said have become the "transport of choice for drug gangs" because they are "so difficult to catch". He suspects that some criminals whose vehicles are seized simply try to buy them back from auction websites. Grunshaw worries some criminals are buying legally compliant e-bikes from police and then giving them illegal modifications. Legal electric pedal bikes are restricted so they cannot drive faster than 15.5mph, but criminals can buy "tuning kits" online, often from eastern Europe, allowing some to travel faster than 40mph. Durham Constabulary, which sold 29 e-bikes last year, told the BBC they had recently reviewed its policy, and they "will now be crushed without exception". Greater Manchester Police sold one e-bike last year. Police tend to sell the vehicles through commercial auction websites like Raw2k, a company listed by several forces. The website regularly advertises e-bikes as "sold at the direction of police", including a Chinese-manufactured electric dirt bike that it says was auctioned from Falkirk earlier this month, with an opening price of £250 (much less than the £3,295 listed as the retail price for a new model). title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
description: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.
body: Only small patches of snow remain on Papua's Sudirman Range The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries. The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history. They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it. But now, nearly all the snow is gone. A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks. But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two. Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime. "There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow". She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas. Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history. Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool. But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it. The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936 The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall. El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace. The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says. A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds. The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape". Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systems At least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations. The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow". "Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity." According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live. Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts. "How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed." The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribe For many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event. The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape. Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys. Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded. The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment. "Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people." This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows where ice used to be in light blue As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left. Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains. From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts." Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change. "When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains. title: Warrington edge past Leeds to reach Grand Final
description: Warrington Wolves reach their first Super League Grand Final in eight years with a thrilling victory against Leeds Rhinos.
body: Luke Yates' try just before half-time was pivotal in Warrington's win Betfred Super League play-off semi-final Tries: Hall, Connor Goals: Connor 2 Tries: Bentley, Yates Goals: Irwin 3 Warrington Wolves have reached their first Super League Grand Final in eight years with a thrilling victory against Leeds Rhinos at AMT Headingley Stadium. In a tense and topsy-turvy semi-final the sides traded two first-half tries each and were locked at 12-12 at the break, before the Wolves were awarded a contentious penalty which was slotted nervelessly by 18-year-old Ewan Irwin to nudge them ahead. Half-back Jake Connor scored 10 points for an injury-depleted Rhinos, including a first-half try which he inventively created in midfield, and attempted a goal-kick from 62 metres out with the final play of the game but the ball landed short of the sticks. The Wolves will face the winners of either Wigan Warriors or Wakefield Trinity in the showpiece final at Old Trafford next Saturday, as they stand just one win away from a first league title since 1955. Live text coverage of the first Super League semi-final Old hands or new blood? Wigan & Wakefield vie to reach Grand Final Leeds limped into the semi-final missing a number of key players including the league's top try-scorer Maika Sivo, captain Ash Handley, and Man of Steel nominee Lachie Miller. The Rhinos were dealt with a further injury blow moments before kick-off when Chris Hankinson pulled up in the warm-up and had to be replaced by Ned McCormack in the starting line-up. Warrington breached Leeds' inexperienced backline after five minutes as England captain George Williams' pinpoint kick was met by Matty Ashton, who helped find former Rhino James Bentley to slide over for an early score. Brodie Croft's cut-out pass found Ryan Hall to score his 358th career try to draw level with former Wakefield legend Neil Fox in the all-time scorers list, as Connor nailed the extras from touch to drag Leeds level. Connor was then involved at the other end of the field, teaming up with young full-back Fergie McCormack to usher Albert Hopoate into touch as he threatened to score and moments later Arron Lindop collided with team-mate Hopoate as the Wolves again squandered a certain four points. Leeds made the Wolves pay soon later as they raced down field. A delicate kick over the top from Connor bounced kindly for McCormack, and once Kallum Watkins found Connor he was not to be denied by Ashton's scrambling defending, using his momentum to spin and crash down. Jake Connor finished off an excellent first-half try which had put Leeds into the lead Moments before the break, prop Luke Yates pirouetted elegantly past Cooper Jenkins to slide in next to the sticks as Irwin levelled the scores with the boot as half-time approached. The game's decisive moment came after the break when James McDonnell was adjudged to have challenged Williams off the ball under a high ball and Irwin stepped up to the tee to notch Warrington two points in front. A charge down from Keenan Palasia near his own line kept Leeds in the fight but a great tackle from Bentley forced a knock-on as both defences were on top in the second period. Connor's sensational 40/20 with two minutes remaining ultimately was in vain as Palasia's ball-carrying arm had already hit the floor in the build-up. A block off the ball gave Connor the chance to be the hero and force the game into golden point but, at the wire, he was unable to find the distance required and Williams kicked the ball into touch to the relief of the travelling supporters. Leeds Rhinos head coach Brad Arthur said: "I've not whinged or complained the whole time I've been here. I'm extremely proud of our team and our club and players. "I don't know what more we could have really done. We got a couple of bits and pieces wrong but so did they. It just would have been really nice if the game was decided by an individual or a piece of skill. "We're talking about a field goal or something like that rather than a soft penalty to decide such a big game. It is a soft penalty. "Ned got escorted four or five times tonight on kicks and I wasn't expecting penalties for them. But that's a soft penalty to decide such a big game." Warrington Wolves captain George Williams told BBC Radio Merseyside: "Nerve-wracking, mad game, just pleased we've came through the other side. "Credit to Leeds, they gave it a good crack. They've been a great team all year but we rode the waves and the main thing is we're through to the big dance next week. "They were probably dominant for the first 20 [minutes], we came home strong in the back end [of the first half]. It's no good for the nerves but sometimes it's better when you're out there, you can do something about it." [On earning the match-winning penalty] "People think it might be a bit controversial but I was chasing the ball and I got a little nudge. I was off balance and nowadays, with the escorts, they give them. Luckily, it went to us and that was the game." Leeds: F. McCormack; Lumb, N. McCormack, Newman, Hall; Croft, Connor; Oledzki, O'Connor, Lodge, Watkins, McDonnell, Palasia. Interchanges: Holroyd, Jenkins, Smith, Cassell. title: Rodri believes in Man City's 'innocence'
description: Former Manchester City midfielder Rodri believes the club are innocent of any financial wrongdoing and will trust them unless they are proved otherwise.
body: Rodri (right) made 298 appearances for Manchester City between 2018 and 2026 Former Manchester City midfielder Rodri believes the club are innocent of any financial wrongdoing and will continue to trust them unless they are proved otherwise. City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching by the Premier League, although they are set to appeal. Speaking at a news conference before Spain's Uefa Nations League match against England at Wembley the 30-year-old, who joined Barcelona in August, backed City's stance. "They always express the confidence that they never did something wrong and we believe in that," Rodri said. "Until the moment they are proved wrong, we will believe the club. They always tell us the confidence they have on the innocence." City were cleared of separate financial fair play charges by the Court of Arbitration for Sport in 2020, having initially been given a two-year ban from European competitions by Uefa. Rodri cited the case as a reason for the confidence of the club's players. "We had the example of 2020 that the process was the same and at the end nothing happened," he explained. "We have faced something similar, we had a similar judicial process. Different accusation but similar process. "There as well in the first instance we were found guilty, but we believed in the club and the innocence that the club maintained and in the end we ended up acquitted. "So, I believe in the justice system, and I believe in the innocence of the club." The club won eight trophies in the period covered by the Premier League case, including three league titles, three League Cups, one Community Shield and one FA Cup. Rodri dismissed talk of City being stripped of some of the titles they won as part of any punishment against the club. "What we did, they cannot take out of us," he added. "It's something that is not paid by money. It's paid with effort, with the damage, with, you know, being shoulder to shoulder every day. "I can tell you that everything was deserved, and I'm glad that I could live one of the best eras of English football in here." This video can not be played 'What we did, they cannot take from us' Prime Minister Andy Burnham has urged people to "study" the independent commission's report in "some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions" on the charges facing Manchester City. "I would have to look at the report of the independent commission, and people shouldn't jump to those kinds of conclusions," Burnham told ITV Granada. "I know this has been a long process between the club and the Premier League. I think it has been quite a contested process. "So I don't think it's as simple as jumping to conclusions. I think we would all need to study the independent commission's report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions." title: Fury v Joshua fight to provide 'big boost' to city's economy
description: Cardiff is preparing for an influx of fans from across the globe for the 11 December showdown.
body: The British heavyweight boxing clash will take place on 11 December Business owners expect the much anticipated clash between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury to provide a "big boost" to the Welsh economy. The British heavyweights are set to fight on 11 December at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, with fans expected to travel to the Welsh capital from all corners of the globe. A bar manager intends to order triple his usual amount of beer barrels, but some residents have expressed concern about the impact the fight will have on public services. Transport for Wales said it intends to put extra services on to deal with the influx of fans, as hotel prices for that weekend sky rocket due to increased demand. Chairman of Cardiff Night Forum Nick Newman said he was "absolutely delighted" by the announcement, as another "fantastic showpiece" is coming to the city. He manages nine pubs, and said venue owners across the city will be planning, getting beer in the cellar and food in the fridges. Newman said he has "no concerns" about the scale of the event, with planning meetings set to take place in the months leading up. Tyson Fury called out Anthony Joshua to be his next fight after beating Arslanbek Makhmudov He said they have agreed with Cardiff council and South Wales Police licensing that businesses can apply for an extended hours license. "That means we can serve alcohol until 05:30, and then close the premises at 06:00," he added. Newman said this would allow the city to "reset" for any workers in the city centre on Saturday morning. He expects there to be a similar level of excitement to Joe Calzaghe's fight against Mikkel Kessler in 2007, when more than 50,000 fans descended on what was then the Millennium Stadium. "That's great for the economy. That's great for jobs. That's great for the sort of feel-good factor around the city," he added. Twm Jones says the fight will be great for Cardiff's hospitality industry Twm Jones, assistant manager of On the River, a venue opposite the Principality Stadium, says they are "really excited" for the event. The bar opened on the first weekend of the Oasis tour, which kicked off in Cardiff, which gave him a sense of how busy the city can be when big events take place. "We'll probably be buying in triple the amount of barrels that we usually would," he said. They expect to have a couple of hundred people in the venue on fight night and Jones said they intend to stay open until "at least before the fight, and probably after as well". "It gets a bit rowdy but its all good fun," he added. But Sarah Hill, who lives close the Principality Stadium, disagrees and says she "doesn't see the appeal" of the fight. "Why are they doing it? I don't really pay attention to boxing at all," she added. Hill realises that Cardiff is no stranger to hosting big events, but said "every big event at the Principality Stadium is an inconvenience to the people that live here". "Rock concerts, rugby games. Any kind of sporting event is just a nightmare," she added. "The entire city shuts. So if you want to get from the train station to your house, you have to go out of your way just to get a taxi." She said the taxis can "cost a fortune" on event days, due to surge pricing, and the late start time has also left her questioning how Cardiff's infrastructure will cope, with the event feeling like "it's just about money". "The trains only run so late so it's just about selling as much booze before and after the event," Hill added. "If the start time is there to benefit the audience in the United States, why is it even here?" Jack Gower has moved to Cardiff for his university studies Jack Gower moved to Cardiff this month for his university studies and said it has become a "big event city" in recent years. "It's good because any big event in the UK you think London or Manchester. It's good for cities like Cardiff to get the publicity," he added. Jack said he is not much of a sports fan, but admits the event is likely to "impact everyone in some way". He added: "Especially for local bars and tourist places. Uni students moving in will probably be the biggest thing [boost for bars], and this will just boost the economy more for them." Dave Leyshon runs DTL Travel, an online travel business based in Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, and is selling tickets for the heavyweight clash costing between £450 and £12,000. "I know it's not a title fight but it's two former heavyweight champions. It's a fair price when you compare it to other major sporting events such as the football World Cup," he said. Leyshon has called on TfW to "get the travel right" after the fight night rail service was criticised when Joshua fought in Cardiff in 2018. "That's so important and I know some coach firms locally to me and also in west Wales will be running buses in case people fear there'll be an issue with the trains," he added. Gerry Toms says Cardiff is better equipped to host major sporting events than it was in 2007 It has almost been 20 years since Joe Calzaghe defeated Kessler at the stadium. Former stadium manager, Gerry Toms, was in charge then, and said it was a "challenge" putting on a fight in the early hours, but staffing was key. "A lot of the planning is needed with the police, the rail network, the council, hoteliers, and the taxi services," he said. "It all has to be coordinated to provide the best possible service you can." A 22:30 curfew was implemented that night to get the fans into the stadium early, ensuring they would not "descend on the stadium" just before the fight began. "We still had a couple of fights in the stadium, which weren't in the ring, but good stewarding can keep that calm and step in early to defuse it, " he said. title: Murder or medical mix-up? New questions in the case of killer nurse Colin Norris
description: A BBC podcast reveals a scenario in which the nurse's murders may never have taken place at all.
body: Colin Norris has been in prison for 18 years For two decades, Ethel Hall's family believed that staff nurse Colin Norris murdered the 86-year-old by injecting her with insulin while she recovered from a broken hip in a Leeds hospital. After his latest appeal against conviction, some members of Ethel's family are having doubts. "The evidence, it's just not sitting right to me," daughter-in-law Helen Hall told a new BBC podcast, Disclosure Investigates: Killer on the Ward. Norris was convicted in 2008 of killing Ethel and three other elderly patients as well as attempting to murder a fifth. The Court of Appeal rejected his challenge against his convictions last year but the new BBC podcast has reviewed medical records, looked again at police interviews and heard about new scientific discoveries. It reveals a scenario in which the murders may never have taken place at all. Ethel Hall was in hospital recovering from a broken hip The podcast series comes a week after a public inquiry reported on the case of former neonatal nurse Lucy Letby who was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others at a hospital in Chester a decade ago. While the circumstances are very different, Norris' supporters also argue that his case hinges on disputed interpretations of medical evidence. The story begins in 2002 when Norris, a 26-year-old nurse, originally from Glasgow, found Ethel in an hypoglycemic coma as she recovered from a broken hip. Doctors took blood samples to find out what caused her blood sugar to drop so low. The test results seemed conclusive - she had a massive amount of insulin in her blood. She died 21 days later, sparking a murder investigation. A nurse who had been on shift on the night Ethel was found told the police that Norris had predicted the 86-year-old might not last the night. He quickly became the prime suspect. The police operation trawled retrospectively through all the deaths on Norris's wards, looking for potential murders that may have gone unnoticed. They identified three other cases of unexplained severe hypoglycemic deaths and one where the patient recovered. No blood tests had been taken from these cases at the time of their deaths to be able to prove insulin poisoning but experts for the prosecution said in court that their medical charts showed persistent and severe low blood sugar readings. They said that because this was so rare in non-diabetics that it must be murder. When it came to court in 2007, experts called by the defence said four of the five patients had died of natural causes. But after a five-month trial and a deadlocked jury, Norris was convicted by a majority of 11-1 and told he would not be eligible for parole for 30 years. After the verdict, Ethel's son Stuart Hall said: "I don't think he should come out again. He's got the knowledge to commit murder but do it discreetly." Convicted nurse Colin Norris has spent 18 years behind bars. But as Louise Shorter revisits his story, new questions emerge. When I got involved in the case in 2009, Norris, who is now known as Colin Campbell, had just lost his first appeal against conviction. Two years later, new scientific evidence came to light which challenged one of the key assumptions underpinning the prosecution case. It claimed hypoglycemia - low blood sugar - in the frail and elderly is not as vanishingly rare as was once thought, suggesting the jury had been misinformed. This new evidence was submitted for a second appeal, which took another 14 years to be heard. During that appeal last year, experts for Norris argued that the symptoms seen in several of the patients could occur naturally in elderly, frail people. Experts for the Crown maintained the deaths were medically distinct. They said their blood sugar readings were refractory, meaning they kept coming back despite being given glucose, whereas naturally-occurring hypoglycemia can be easily corrected with a treatment such as a sugary drink. They argued this distinction could only be explained by deliberate insulin poisoning. Colin Norris was convicted of four murders in 2008 The ultimate question in this case has always been 'what happened to Ethel Hall?', the woman whose death sparked the investigation. Was deliberate insulin poisoning the only explanation or could she have been given it accidentally? Doctors who first attended Ethel suspected she'd been accidentally given insulin meant for another patient. They looked to see if anyone in the neighbouring beds were due to be given insulin in the hours prior to this discovery. But this mix-up theory was dismissed as no-one next to Ethel was due to receive it during the time frame under scrutiny. However, as part of the BBC investigation, we found there had in fact been a diabetic patient elsewhere on the ward who was being given insulin in preparation for an operation around the time doctors were trying to save Ethel. Norris was found to have injected patients at Leeds General Infirmary and the city's St James's Hospital in 2002 Ethel had been found in a coma at 05:00 and her first injection of glucose to increase her blood sugars was given at 06:15. The syringe was administered by the ward doctor, who had asked Norris to prepare it for them. Our review of witness statements and medical notes shows that immediately after this, Norris was preparing another 50ml syringe of dextrose to be injected via a cannula and a 500ml bag of dextrose for a drip. At the same time, in the same treatment room, another nurse was arranging insulin mixed with saline in a 50ml syringe for the diabetic patient. The nurse, who had gone to another ward to get the insulin, asked Norris to check the syringe dosage and apologised for not having the ampoule they had drawn it from. title: Diesel prices exceed £2 a litre at hundreds of forecourts across Scotland
description: Motoring organisation the RAC says it expects the average UK diesel price to hit a new record high over the weekend.
body: Conflict in the Ukraine and the Middle East have driven up prices on forecourts The price of diesel has exceeded £2 a litre at hundreds of Scottish forecourts, according to analysis by BBC Scotland News. Some of the highest prices can be found at garages in Scotland's islands, where fuel is 50p a litre more expensive than that sold at supermarkets in the central belt. Hauliers have described the cost to their businesses as "devastating" and say it now costs £250 a week more to fill up a lorry. Motoring organisation the RAC said it expected the UK average price of diesel to hit a new record high over the weekend. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war has pushed up the cost of crude oil, leading to higher fuel and energy costs. The UK government said it continued to protect British people and business, and there would not be an increase in fuel duty this year. Dave Neil, who runs a haulage firm in Orkney, said fuel costs were "challenging" Analysis by BBC Scotland News suggests there are at least 226 sites - stretching from the Borders to Shetland - where the price of a litre of diesel is greater than £2. Some of the highest prices are in island and rural areas, including 238.8p and 223p in the Hebrides and 209.0p and 208.9p in the Northern Isles. South Uist-based haulier Norman MacAskill said it cost 32p a litre to fill a lorry's tank when he started in the haulage business 40 years ago, but it was now £2.22. "Anyone who is running a lorry is absolutely devastated when they get their fuel bill at the end of the month. There's no business on earth that can withstand that increase in costs," he said. MacAskill's haulage firm, N D MacAskill & Son, transports livestock around Inverness, Dingwall and Stirling but also further afield. "We do a bit of livestock haulage from the north of Scotland down to the north of England," he said. "It's a devastating cost on a fuel run on that job," he said. MacAskill added: "This has been going on every year for the last 10 years now. The cost of running a haulage business has just gone over the top. "There are dozens of haulage firms that have been established 50-60 years with big numbers of lorries going to the wall. When is this going to stop?" Dave Neil, who runs Sinclair Haulage which serves Sanday, Stronsay and Eday in Orkney, said his business was spending £400 a week more on diesel than it was before the summer. "It's a challenging situation," he said. Neil said he was forced to add an extra fee to his customers' costs. "It's probably the fairest way," he said. "When the fuel price drops we can take that surcharge away." The Road Haulage Association (RHA) said fuel was costing operators roughly £250 a week extra per vehicle. It has called on the UK government to scrap any planned fuel duty rises in January, March and April and to introduce an essential user rebate for coaches, lorries and vans. Managing director Richard Smith said: "It's happening elsewhere. Spain, France and Italy already give commercial vehicle operators a diesel rebate. It's about time we caught up. Crofter Amy Henderson said life was hard enough for people already National Farmers' Union Scotland said rising prices were another unwelcome cost for farmers and crofters. A spokesperson said: "Fuel is a significant input cost for farm businesses and increases feed directly into the cost of producing food. "With many farmers currently working through harvest and other intensive autumn operations, there is no scope to reduce fuel use." Crofter and musician Amy Henderson, from Kiltarlity, added: "It is just deflating. Life is hard enough as it is." She said she was having to make "logistical decisions" around whether to use her car or truck. Henderson added: "I have to take it into consideration when quoting prices for performing." James Dunbar of New Start Highland said rising fuel costs were affecting the families the charity supports Inverness-based charity New Start Highland uses vans to collect and deliver donated items, such as furniture, to people in need. Chief executive James Dunbar said: "Rising fuel prices have a direct impact on us as a charity, as well as the individuals we support. "Transport is core to our operations, from collecting and delivering furniture so those facing crisis and hardship can access essential items, to running our enterprise services like removals and house clearances." He said the charity was in the process of moving to a fully electrified fleet, but he said rising fuel costs directly affected the families it supported. The RAC said the average UK record price of diesel would "almost certainly" be surpassed over the weekend. Head of policy Simon Williams said: "The average UK price of diesel is teetering on the brink of a new all-time high at 198.32p, taking the cost of a 55-litre fill-up for a family car to £109. "The UK now has the most expensive diesel in Europe by 12p a litre - ahead of Finland and the Netherlands." He added: "Petrol is now averaging 173.6p – its highest price in more than four years. Petrol has risen nearly 12p in September and more than 40p since the Iran war began. "Diesel is up 14.5p this month alone and 55p since 28 February." Hauliers have called for an essential user rebate for coaches, lorries and vans The AA said its campaigning had persuaded the UK government to set up pump-price transparency. It said there were now websites and phone apps, external drivers could use to check for the latest pump prices and where to find cheaper fuel. The AA said there should be no scrapping of the Treasury's 5p cut in fuel duty, which was first introduced in March 2022. It added that there was a "good argument" for diesel getting further relief. A spokesperson said: "While many big businesses pass the extra cost of diesel onto their customers, often via a sliding scale of fuel surcharges, smaller businesses don't automatically. title: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged', police say
description: Tasia Fortune's body was found hanging from a tree on the grounds of an abandoned home in Jackson in August.
body: Warning: This story contains distressing details Police in the US state of Mississippi have said that they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" and placed hanging in a tree. The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs. The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree on the grounds of an abandoned home in Jackson in August. The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests. In a news release, police said that the medical examiner had determined after an autopsy that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged". The BBC has contacted the court, the medical examiner's office and Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey. Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging was staged. The medical examiner confirmed earlier this month that Fortune's cause of death was homicide and said there would be a murder charge. Speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday, Fortune's mother described how she knows her daughter fought for her life till the very end. "I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey told reporters. Fortune leaves behind four young children, ages 7, 5, 4 and 1, she added. Dressed in a shirt that reads "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she does not want to see any innocent people going to jail. "I just hope they have the right people," she said. Three people have been arrested in relation to the case, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who was arrested and pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody in without bond. A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in the case this week. A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday. The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country. Representative Ayanna Pressley, Democrat of Massachusetts, cites at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress, external, which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers. The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has been ruled a suicide. title: Russia targeting 'ordinary life' with attacks on Ukraine's data centres, Zelensky says
description: Such strikes aim to disrupt "people's ability to stay connected, study, work", says Ukraine's president.
body: Four people were killed in a Russian drone strike on a business centre in Kyiv, Ukrainian officials said President Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia has widened its attacks to target Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, seeking to cause maximum disruption for ordinary people. "All this affects people's ability to stay connected, study, work," he said. On Friday a Russian drone hit a business centre in the capital Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. A separate attack killed a 14-year-old boy. Israel's foreign ministry said he was an Israeli citizen. Russia confirmed it had targeted a data centre site, saying it was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence. About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages on Wednesday due to strikes. Some firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad. In the north-western city of Lutsk, electronic information boards at public transport stops were not working on Friday, officials said. The city council said this was "due to damage caused by a Russian attack on data centres in Kyiv". In Friday's social media post, Zelensky wrote: "The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centres, internet providers – for Russia, all ordinary life is simply a target. "It is important that the world responds to all of this and that Russia feels the response to its terror." Late on Friday, Zelensky said "additional decisions" had been made at his meeting with Ukraine's top defence and security officials to protect the country's data centres and other critical communications facilities to ensure their continuous operation. Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said that Russia was seeking to disrupt the flow of "life-saving information" by targeting data centres. "Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives. This is critical civilian infrastructure... It is not a military target. It is essential to keeping everyday life functioning," Sybiha said. Zelensky's top adviser on defence technologies on Thursday admitted that "there may be local disruptions" following Russian attacks an the cost of internet services could increase to cover the costs of repairs. But Serhii Beskrestnov stressed that Ukraine's internet network was highly decentralised, so the country "will not be left without internet access". A 14-year-old boy, an Israeli citizen, was killed when a Russian drone hit a multi-storey residential building in Kyiv's central Pecherskyi district The data centre hit by Russia on Friday was run by Datagroup. The company said its specialists were assessing the damage after the daytime attack but all services "continue to operate from backup sites". Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said on Friday evening that seven people had been killed and 59 injured after Russian overnight attacks. Russia's defence ministry later confirmed it had hit the Datagroup site, which it said was being used by the Ukrainian military's intelligence. Footage showing the damaged Inkom business centre that housed Datagroup has since been verified by the BBC. The Russian defence ministry also said that over the past few days its forces have targeted a number of data processing and telecommunications centres in Ukraine, including New-Telco, United DC, Kyivstar and Parkovyi. In recent weeks, Moscow has also intensified its strikes on Ukraine's energy and railway infrastructure – seeking to cause maximum damage as winter approaches. Ukraine's military has been hitting Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, saying they help finance Russia's ongoing war effort. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results will be crucial Speaking to reporters late on Friday, Putin said Moscow would "give careful thought" to the idea of resuming direct peace negotiations with Kyiv, citing last week's "massive" Ukrainian attack on the capital Moscow and other recent strikes. "It's all possible," he said, but stressed that Ukraine "must feel our retaliatory strikes", and that all decisions would be taken "based on the Russian Federation's interests". Zelensky had earlier said he was ready for trilateral talks that would also involve the US. Kyiv and its European allies have repeatedly accused Putin of rejecting any peace negotiations, saying he was seeking to seize more Ukrainian territory. Speaking to the media, Putin also restated his position that Moscow had "no plans" and "no reason" to attack Europe. He had made similar statements about Ukraine, before launching his full-scale invasion almost five years ago. In a separate development on Friday, the European Union agreed to release €6.6bn for Ukraine, the bloc's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said, describing this as "good news for Ukraine and bad news for Russia". This includes €900 million for the EU's Military Assistance Mission for Ukraine, and a €1 billion fund for joint procurement of equipment, she said on X. "Moscow's hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing the opposite." Meanwhile, Poland's prosecutors opened an investigation in what they said was an arson attack on a Starlink satellite station in Wola Krobowska on Wednesday. In a statement, the national prosecutor's office said "there is a reasonable suspicion... that the perpetrators acted on the orders of the Russian special services". Moscow has not commented. The station transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlin

title: Northampton begin title defence with win over Newcastle
description: James Pater and Tommy Freeman score hat-tricks as Northampton kick off their title defence with a 59-26 win over Newcastle.
body: Northampton Saints won a second Prem title in three years in June Tries: Pater 3, Hendy, Freeman 3, Coles, Sleightholme Cons: F Smith 5, Belleau 2 Tries: Wade 2, Jordan, Kok Cons: Connon, Henry 2 James Pater and Tommy Freeman ran in hat-tricks as Northampton Saints kicked off their title defence with a comfortable 59-26 win over new-look Newcastle Red Bulls at Franklin's Gardens. Just three months after securing a second Prem title against Exeter Chiefs at Allianz Stadium, Saints were dominant against a much-changed Red Bulls side who have welcomed 25 new players through the door this summer. Three tries each for Pater and Freeman and one each for George Hendy, Alex Coles and Ollie Sleightholme delivered an emphatic scoreline as Saints, brilliantly conducted by fly-half Smith, ran in nine tries. Yet for all that the scoreline delivered another defeat for Newcastle they still scored four tries and came away with a losing bonus point as they hope that, for the first time in five seasons, they may not be destined for bottom place in the Prem. title: Man City found guilty of majority of 115 financial rule breaches
description: The club, which denies all wrongdoing, is accused of breaching the Premier League's financial rules between 2009 and 2018.
body: This video can not be played Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City Manchester City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching. The Athletic , externalis reporting that the sanctions have not been decided but that the independent panel has reached its decision, finding the club guilty of all but one count. The Premier League declined to comment. Asked if the report was correct, City did not comment either way. Instead they released a statement saying the "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality". "The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence," it added. BBC Sport has also been told that, in the event of being found guilty, City will appeal against the findings. Other Premier League clubs are believed to have been informed about the independent panel's decision and have sought legal advice as to whether they would have a compensation claim. Clubs seek legal advice over Man City charges compensation Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City This video can not be played What do Man City charges mean and what happens next? In February 2023, City were charged with more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules following a four-year investigation. The club was referred to an independent commission over allegations it breached financial rules between 2009 and 2018. The hearing began in September 2024 behind closed doors and concluded that December after around 12 weeks. The Premier League claimed City breached rules requiring the club to provide "accurate financial information that gives a true and fair view of the club's financial position". City strongly denied all charges and have said their case is supported by a "comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence". The club won eight trophies in the period covered by the case, including three Premier League titles, three League Cups, one Community Shield and one FA Cup. The charges cover the mangerial tenures of Roberto Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini, and the first two years under Pep Guardiola, who left the club after 10 seasons at the end of the 2025-26 campaign. A separate case between City and the Premier League was also heard last year. In 2024, an independent arbitration panel found against aspects of the league's Associated Party Transaction regulations (APTs) after City launched an arbitration challenge. A tribunal held in February 2025 found the Premier League's rules governing sponsorship deals from the period between 2021 and 2024 are "void and unenforceable". City and the Premier League reached a settlement in September 2025, with the club accepting the APT rules are valid and binding and both parties agreeing to terminate legal proceedings. The rules were formed by the Premier League to prevent clubs from profiting from commercial deals with companies linked to their owners that are deemed above "fair market value". This video can not be played • 54x Failure to provide accurate financial information 2009-10 to 2017-18. • 14x Failure to provide accurate details for player and manager payments from 2009-10 to 2017-18. • 5x Failure to comply with Uefa's rules including Financial Fair Play (FFP) 2013-14 to 2017-18. • 7x Breaching Premier League's Profitability and Sustainability Rules (PSR) 2015-16 to 2017-18. • 35x Failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations December 2018 - Feb 2023. There have been suggestions by the Times and football finance expert Kieran Maguire the number of charges is as high as 130. BBC Sport has been unable to verify this. title: What is kratom, the 'gas station heroin' alarming officials in the US?
description: Kratom, found during an investigation into the deaths of two college students, has been sold in the US for around a decade.
body: Jeffrey Deaver, a 58-year-old retired timber cutter in the state of Washington, has taken kratom for four years to help with severe chronic hip and knee pain. He discovered the herbal product when he couldn't find relief from doctors and while waiting for surgeries. Scared at first, he "started small", but then took more until his pain went away. "It was like a miracle," Deaver said. "I could sleep. I could function. "I just don't know what I'd do without it." Kratom - an herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over-the-counter and consumed in pill or liquid form. This week, investigators found packaged kratom in the possession of two deceased University of Mississippi students. Although their deaths were not attributed to kratom, officials are now issuing warnings about its consumption. For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it's illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi. Here's what we know about it: Kratom is a tree that is native to Southeast Asia in countries like Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia. It's been used for centuries for its stimulant properties, grounded and consumed similar to tea. As its popularity spread around the globe, it entered the US market as a supplement around 2016. "That's really where the problems began," said Dr Shane Speights, dean of the New York Institute of Technology College of Osteopathic Medicine at Arkansas State University. In the US kratom is mostly sold in highly concentrated forms either via pill, powder or liquid, Speights said. It's also widely available - found everywhere from convenience stores and petrol stations to vape shops. Also, because of the supplement classification, kratom products are not federally regulated. "There's no way to know exactly what you're getting," Speight said. "You could go and create something in your basement, market it as a supplement, and nobody's really going to check and see what's in it." Kratom is often marketed as a safe, natural herbal supplement that helps with pain management, anxiety and depression. In lower doses, its stimulant properties create a "caffeine-kind of buzz", Speights explained. Because of its opioid-like effects, it has also been used with the goal of curbing addictions to actual opioids like fentanyl. Those properties stem from the way the plant's compounds - like 7-Hydroxymitragynine - activate various hormones, including dopamine. "It's almost like taking a narcotic," Speights said. "At higher doses, it can create more euphoria and give you more of a general high." The higher doses also pose greater risk for adverse side effects. That includes central nervous system (CNS) depression - which is "where the deaths come in," Speights said. CNS can result in cardiovascular collapse and loss of breathing. Withdrawal symptoms and addiction are also risks, said Jana Wu, director of clinical integration at the addiction treatment centre Mountainside. "It affects marriages, relationships," she said. "I've seen people lose jobs, spend thousands of dollars a month on it." Because it's easy to develop a high tolerance to the herb, users may need to take an increasing amount to achieve the same effect over time. "I've worked with people that were taking like up to 20 pills a day," Wu said. Experts told the BBC that the biggest dangers come from the fact that kratom is not federally regulated. "Is there a safe dose?" Speights said. "My answer is going to be no because - I'm going to go back to this - we don't know what's in it." Kratom is banned in 11 states: Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Massachusetts, North Dakota, Tennessee, Vermont and Wisconsin. Massachusetts was the last state to make it illegal, issuing a temporary emergency order in August. Ten years earlier, the US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) had moved to classify kratom as a Schedule 1, the most dangerous level for drugs, calling it "an imminent hazard to public safety". But the effort failed a few months later, after the justice department said it received "numerous comments from members of the public challenging" the attempt. That leaves states to take action, like Arizona, which recently sued a company selling kratom beverage products. Groups opposed to kratom want states to do more, saying "gas-station drugs are poisoning our communities". Pro-kratom groups like the American Kratom Association are pushing for bans against synthetics "posing as natural kratom". Internationally, kratom is banned in the UK. In Europe, the laws vary by country. In Malaysia, where the kratom tree is native, consumption and sale are banned under the Poisons Act of 1952.
