title: O'Neill left 'baffled' by refereeing in late NI win in Georgia
description: Michael O'Neill has said he was "baffled" by some of the refereeing decisions in Friday's 1-0 win in Georgia in the Nations League.
body: This video can not be played Highlights: Northern Ireland leave it late to beat Georgia Michael O'Neill has said he was "baffled" by some of the refereeing decisions in Friday's 1-0 win in Georgia. Shea Charles scored a 99th-minute winner in Tbilisi as Northern Ireland picked up their first-ever away win in the Nations League. Before the winner, Pierce Charles had saved a controversial penalty from Georgia captain Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and his brother Shea had an appeal waved away at the other end. O'Neill also fumed at a decision from official Orel Grinfeeld not to award a free-kick after Ceadach O'Neill was brought down late on, and key defender Daniel Ballard was injured in the following phase of play. "In the second half we had to show a lot of resilience," O'Neill told BBC Sport NI. "Not only against the opposition, who were very good in the second half when they got Kvaratskhelia in the game a lot more, but some of the decisions that went against us. "I was really disappointed in that side of things with how the game was refereed." NI win in Georgia after Kvaratskhelia penalty miss After a drab first half, the game picked up after the restart and the first flashpoint came in the 65th minute when Ballard was adjudged to have fouled Luka Lochoshvili when challenging for a cross after a VAR review. Pierce saved the penalty from Paris St-Germain winger Kvaratskhelia, and Northern Ireland had an appeal of their own waved away when Charles appeared to have been caught in the area in the 88th minute. The NI manager was also angry at the lack of a foul on substitute O'Neill, who is now tied to Northern Ireland for three years after he won his third cap, and Ballard was injured when chasing a loose ball as Georgia came forward on the counter-attack in the resulting play. O'Neill said his players were "magnificent" and his team "showed every side of our character tonight". "At times it didn't go our way. I've not seen the incident back but to me it seemed incredibly harsh to give a penalty for that. The guy was nowhere near the ball to head it. "We feel aggrieved that we didn't get one at the other end. The foul on Ceadach when he came on the pitch causes Dan to get injured. "I was just baffled by the quality of the refereeing." O'Neill confirmed that Sunderland defender Ballard had injured his hamstring and would miss Northern Ireland's next three games in the window, against Hungary, Ukraine and Georgia. "You saw the nature of how he pulled up. It's a hamstring," he said. "We'll scan him tomorrow but he's certainly not going to be available for the next three games." title: Trump's plans for massive arch move ahead
description: Opposition to building the 250-foot arch, and using it for military purposes, is growing with one Democrat blasting Trump's plans as "foolhardy".
body: US President Donald Trump's plans for building a massive arch appear to be moving ahead, after a federal advisory council terminated talks on how to handle the 250-foot structure's possible effects on nearby historic sites. The council, led by Trump appointees, announced on Thursday it was ending required consultations on the project, saying historic preservation officers from Washington and Virginia had refused to sign off on harm-mitigation plans. Construction was already expected to begin this month, but opposition has been growing. On Friday, Democratic Senator Tammy Duckworth blasted plans to use the arch for defence as "foolhardy" and called it "yet another Trump vanity project". This video can not be played A look at the design plans for Trump's triumphal arch as proposed in April Earlier this week Trump announced that the proposed "Triumphal Arch" would double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones from the roof and plaza. In a letter to the Pentagon and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Duckworth said they "must reject this foolhardy plan and instead focus on increasing the safety of the airspace". The arch is to be built just outside Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia, and about 4mi (6km) from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, the site of the deadly 2025 midair crash between a military helicopter and commercial plane. "The American people cannot afford to stand witness to Trump's risky plan to place a 250-foot (72m) structure along a busy approach path, especially if he follows through on plans to station snipers on the arch and fly drones," Duckworth wrote in the letter, which was obtained by the BBC's US partner, CBS News. The FAA, however, ruled last week that the massive structure would not pose a risk to flights coming into and out of the airport. On Thursday, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, led by Trump appointees, announced it was ending required consultations with local officials about how the structure might affect 42 historic properties in the area. The council said in the announcement that the National Park Service, which oversees federal landmarks, had proposed a plan for mitigating potential harms to those properties, but local historic preservation officers "raised concerns with the purpose and need of the Triumphal Arch". They also questioned whether the service had adequately identified possible harms and planned sufficient actions to address them. Federal and state officials are not required to reach an agreement on a project's harm-mitigation plans, and those consultations are allowed to be terminated if both sides can't agree. The council expects to submit a final report on the process early next month. Meanwhile, Democratic Virginia Congressman Don Beyer says excavation work on the site where the arch will stand has already begun. Beyer, who is leading congressional opposition to the arch, said he found workers operating heavy equipment when he visited the site on Thursday who told him they were "conducting archaeological work to evaluate the composition of the soil". That is "deeply troubling", Beyer said, particularly because the administration is required to give 48 hours notice before work can begin. "The Administration appears to be pushing ahead with activity at the site even while it still has not done the basic work necessary to understand the consequences of this project," Beyer wrote. A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure. title: PM rules out giving Wales independence referendum powers
description: Andy Burnham told the BBC Westminster should have a “say on an issue of that magnitude”.
body: This video can not be played Andy Burnham said the Welsh government would get a "fair hearing" when it came to devolution The prime minister has ruled out handing powers to hold a referendum on independence to the Welsh government. Andy Burnham said other UK nations do not have such powers and he did not "think we can create a different arrangement for Wales". He added that the decision should be made jointly with Westminster, arguing that the UK Parliament has to have a "say on an issue of that magnitude". Wales First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said last week he would seek powers to hold an independence referendum, although he ruled out staging one before the next Senedd election in May 2030. Burnham also said he was open to looking at the Welsh government's "Cynnal" plans to trial offering £10 a week for 15,000 children aged under six, in households already receiving universal credit. This would require the agreement of the Department for Work and Pensions and HMRC to avoid the payment being taxed or other benefits - paid for by the UK government - being reduced. "I'll certainly ensure that there's a proper discussion about the issue," he said. "I mean, I did things as mayor of Greater Manchester without there having to be any tax implications. "So I'm not quite sure why that arises in this in this instance, but we will have a look at it for certain." An Interview with the Prime Minister Ahead of the annual Labour Party conference, the Prime Minister is in Manchester and talks to our Political Editor Gareth Lewis about independence, the future of devolution, and speculation of an early general election. During a visit to the Tata steelworks in Port Talbot in August, Burnham indicated he was "open" to the idea of giving the Welsh government control over policing. BBC Wales understands that idea faces oppostion from many Welsh Labour MPs, with one calling it "a travesty". In response Burnham said on Friday it was "about looking at the case" rather than taking "a fixed view". He added: "I just need to look at it on the merits of the case. I'm the prime minister of all of the UK, including Wales. "I have to respect the governments in the the nations of the UK, and I will, and give fair hearing to anything that is is put to me." The leaders of Plaid Cymru, the SNP and Sinn Fein met in Cardiff last month Labour's conference will get underway with renewed debate about Wales' constitutional future and whether further powers should be devolved to Cardiff Bay from Westminster. Earlier this week a Reform motion that Wales should remain as part of the UK was voted down by the Senedd. A revised Plaid Cymru motion that the people of Wales should decide Wales's constitutional future was passed. Last week, the leaders of Plaid Cymru, the SNP and Sinn Fein met in Cardiff and signed an agreement stating that Westminster should not undermine the right of the people in their nations to decide their own future. Burnham will address his first Labour conference as Prime Minister next week and is expected to set out his vision for the UK for the next 10 years. The conversations about devolution, powers and funding will not stop after this weekend. Next month the prime minister is scheduled to meet first ministers from all the nations of the UK. title: Two arrested after people seen mysteriously emerging from various New York City sewers
description: The city has seen a string of incidents in which people have climbed out of manholes late at night.
body: New York officials arrested two of three men who they said were seen emerging from a manhole, exiting the city's underground sewer system on Wednesday. The New York Police Department (NYPD) arrested 26-year-old Kevin Rodriguez and 25-year-old Samuel Reveron on charges of conspiracy and trespassing. Three men were seen exiting a manhole near the hotel where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was reportedly expected to stay for the United Nations General Assembly. In a statement to the BBC, the NYPD said it had seen a number of incidents involving people going into the sewer system to look for valuables and scrap metal after a storm. "This incident fits that same criteria, but out of an abundance of caution given the U.N. General Assembly and the sensitivity of the location, the NYPD is conducting additional security sweeps with our federal partners," the police department said in a statement. Rodriguez and Reveron, both from Queens, were arrested on Thursday. They allegedly fled the scene after climbing out of the manhole when officers were called around 4:30 EST (9:30 BST) on Wednesday, police said. During a hearing on Friday morning, the two men pleaded not guilty and were released from custody, according to court records. The arrests follow a string of incidents in which people were seen emerging from pavement manholes in different parts of the city in recent months. In August, surveillance footage showed a person coming out of a manhole in Queens early in the morning. The same month, the NYPD said it was investigating three people wearing overalls and headlamps seen climbing out of a manhole near Penn Station. In May, a group of people were captured on surveillance footage shifting a manhole cover and climbing down into the sewer in South Brooklyn. Going into the New York sewer system is both illegal and dangerous, officials have said, cautioning that there is a risk of toxic gases and flooding in a confined space. "For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole, or outfall," the city's Department of Environmental Protection previously told the BBC. This year, a woman died after she opened her car door and accidentally fell into an open manhole in Midtown Manhattan. title: Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenship
description: Critics have questioned the reliability of the data, warning it could result in US citizens being wrongly removed from electoral rolls.
body: The US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration to use a controversial federal database that uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens. Critics have questioned the reliability of the data, warning it could result in US citizens being wrongly removed from electoral rolls. In June, a federal judge ruled that the system was illegal and violated the privacy rights of Americans. But the top court's conservative majority ruled that the National Voter Registration Act prohibits broad purges of voter rolls in the weeks before an election, which limits any "potential impact" of the decision ahead of the midterms. But states can still check the citizenship of individual voters. The three liberal-leaning liberals on the Supreme Court dissented from the majority decision. One of the dissenting Supreme Court justices, Ketanji Brown Jackson, expressed concern that this could mistakenly revoke the voting rights of eligible voters. "The harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the non-existent harm that the government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take," she wrote. The Department of Homeland Security programme, known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, allows officials to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls. The database was first created in 1986 to help officials verify the citizenship or immigration status of those applying for public benefits. But the Trump administration last year expanded its search capabilities by allowing bulk searches using sensitive information from Social Security rolls. In June, however, US District Judge Sparkle L Soonnan - a Biden-appointee - ruled that the revamped system shows that the federal government "knowingly trampled on the privacy rights" of US citizens "in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote". A federal appeals court allowed her ruling to stand, only to be overridden by the Supreme Court on Friday. The top court ruled that a 1996 law allows DHS to seek citizenship and immigration data from federal agencies, and has "an obligation to respond" to states seeking that information. The use of the Save programme by individual states is voluntary. The previous judge's order, the Supreme Court ruled, "prevents the federal government from using the programme it believes is best suited to the task". Lawyers for the Trump administration have long argued that the system is lawful and necessary to prevent non-citizens from voting. A total of 27 states currently use the system to check voter citizenship. Critics, however, have pointed to a number of cases of the system already having led to mistakes. For example, officials in Travis County, Texas, found that of nearly 100 voters identified as non-citizens, at least 10% of them - and potentially more - were US citizens, according to US media reports. Since the state began checking its voter rolls with the Save system last year, only three non-citizen voters have been charged with illegally voting in Texas. Since returning to the White House in January last year, the Trump administration has sought to reform the US electoral system, a process that has included a bid - rejected by the Supreme Court - to reign in mail-in ballots. In 2024, for example, Texas Governor Greg Abbott announced that 1,930 people with a "voter history" had been removed from electoral rolls out of a total of nearly 18 million registered voters. The figures are far below the hundreds of thousands of non-citizen voters that Trump and the Department of Homeland Security have previously suggested were on voter rolls. title: I'm not tempted to call an early election, Burnham says
description: The prime minister told the BBC an early poll would throw the country into a "backward-looking process".
body: This video can not be played Burnham: 'No election anytime soon' Andy Burnham has insisted he is not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process". During a round of BBC interviews ahead of Labour's annual conference, the prime minister said his focus was on helping people with the cost of living and supporting businesses. Recent polling has suggested Labour's position has improved since Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer in Downing Street in July, although Reform UK and the Conservatives are not far behind. An early general election could give Burnham a mandate of his own and free him from commitments made in Labour's 2024 manifesto. The next general election must be held by August 2029. Asked by ITV Calendar if the next election would be in 2029, he replied: "Yes, that's when the next election will be. "All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead." New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM Burnham heads to his first Labour Party conference as prime minister this weekend, with speculation over the prospect of a snap election likely to be a topic of conversation among some of those attending the event in Liverpool. Labour has been projected to lose its majority but remain the largest party in the House of Commons if there was a snap election, according to recent polling. It comes amid media reports that some of the prime minister's advisers have been weighing up the prospect of an election as early as next year. But Burnham sought to rule out this prospect during interviews with BBC regional political editors ahead of the conference opening on Sunday. Asked by BBC West political editor Paul Barltrop whether he was tempted to call an early poll, Burnham replied: "No, not particularly. No, I'm not. "I see all the speculation and it just races ahead," he said. He added: "No election anytime soon. I'm focused on the job as prime minister, doing what I said I would do." He was later asked by BBC East Midlands political editor Peter Saull if there would be a general election next May, alongside council elections in the area. The PM replied "no" before adding: "Not having a general election." Burnham also said he wants to use the conference to say more about "the direction I want to take the country in", adding: "The focus is on that, helping people with the cost of living, helping businesses with the cost of running a business. "These have got to be the priorities right now, rather than throwing the country into a backward-looking process where we're arguing again amongst ourselves." Burnham said he wanted to ensure people are "feeling a bit of hope in their lives again", adding: "That's what I'm trying to do, and I hope to take it further in the coming period, rather than putting people back into an election cycle." The prime minister was also asked about the number of migrants crossing the English Channel in small boats. It comes after 781 people were recorded arriving in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest total for a single day so far this year. Burnham said his goal was that he didn't "want to see any crossings at all". He declined to put a timescale on the ambition, but said his government would "not stop" working until crossings went "right down". He argued that Brexit had hampered the UK's ability to stop the arrivals, saying it had led to a "loss of collaboration with neighbours". Elsewhere in the series of interviews, he said: He would not do any "special interviews" with The Sun. In 2015, he told the BBC he had not forgiven the newspaper for its coverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster. Tourists would not "begrudge paying a few extra pounds" as a result of his proposal to allow regional mayors in England to charge new tax on visitors' overnight stays The government would "do what we can within the resources that we've got to support people" in the Budget next month Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. title: U2 celebrate 50th anniversary at the school where they formed
description: The rock band go back to their roots, playing a gig in the Dublin playground where they first met.
body: U2 were all pupils at Mount Temple Comprehensive School in the mid-1970s Exactly 50 years after they formed, U2 returned to Dublin to play a gig at the school where they met. ”We‘ve escaped from the lab,” declared Bono, as they quartet took to a stage in the playground. “How’s the experiment working for you?” The pupils of Mount Temple Comprehensive may not have been born when U2 were the world’s biggest band, but they gave them a hero's welcome, waving signs that said, “I love U2“, “It’s a beautiful day - no school”, and, “Bono, my mum says hi!” The group treated them to a career-spanning set that included hits like I Will Follow, Vertigo and With Or Without You, as well as their latest single, Silencio. As they played, teachers pulled down pupils who’d climbed on their classmates' shoulders, before getting swept up in the moment and dancing along themselves. As he looked out from the same stage where U2 made their debut in 1976, Bono became emotional. “Thanks for, er… Yeah... I didn’t… Wow,” said the frontman, temporarily lost for words. The band played their first gig at a school talent competition, covering Peter Frampton's Show Me The Way and Bye Bye Baby by the Bay City Rollers The band played seven songs at the end of the school day: I Will Follow, Vertigo, Beautiful Day, Out of Control, Silencio, One and With or Without You Pupils clamoured to meet the band, who have sold more than 175 million records worldwide The U2 story began in those same halls and corridors five decades ago, when 14-year-old Larry Mullen Jr pinned a handwritten note to the school noticeboard. "Drummer seeks musicians to form band." Auditions were held a couple of days later, on 25 September, 1976, in Larry's parents' kitchen. Among the hopeful "misfits", as their school-friend Frank Kearns called them, were Bono, The Edge and Adam Clayton – who arrived wearing a full-length Afghan coat. Initially called Feedback, and then The Hype, they conquered the world as U2, transforming themselves from a scrappy punk outfit into stadium-conquering rock titans, whose big ideas and big anthems attracted millions of admirers, and almost as many detractors. Speaking to BBC News, Mullen confessed the infamous wanted advert had been his father's idea all along. "I'd been playing on my own, in my house, and my dad was pretty frustrated," he says. "I wasn't very good at many things, and playing the drums was included in that. So I think he, out of frustration, said I should try and play with other people." "And unfortunately," adds Bono, "he got the three of us." The group honed their skills over dozens of gigs in the Dublin venue McGonagles Bono, then known as Paul Hewson, had actually been tempted to skip the audition. He was two years older, and concerned about looking out of place. "I wouldn't be hanging out with second years, and particularly really good-looking ones," he says. Eventually, his friend Reggie Manuel persuaded him to attend, even giving him a lift on his rickety old motorbike. "I can tell myself it was a Harley Davidson," the singer jokes, "but really it was a Yamaha DX100." The first band practice didn't exactly show promise. There was more talking than playing. Clayton, a bassist who couldn't play bass, was selected on account of having "the best hair". And Bono, who wanted to be the guitarist, didn't bring a guitar. "I was never any good with gear," he reflects. "Carrying it, unpacking it, that kind of thing." The quartet have remained friends since 1976, partly due to a decision to split all their earnings equally Even so, there were signs the band would attract an adoring legion of fans. Half-way through the rehearsal, a group of screaming girls tried to climb the garden wall. For Clayton, that was the moment that sealed the deal. "Larry already had a fan club, and we thought, 'Well, if he's got a fan club, that looks pretty good to us. Maybe if we hang out with this guy, it might stretch a little further'." Mullen, forever the band's stoic moral compass, was not impressed by the invasion. "As I recall, Larry Mullen took a hose to the fans," laughs Bono. "I don't know what possessed me," the drummer grimaces, while trying to insist the hosing "was an act of kindness and love because it was a hot day". "They enjoyed it," he protests. "It was playful." Bono jumps in to save his friend's embarrassment…. Well, kind of. "It's been the story of our lives ever since. He doesn't even want to have fans, but we quite like them." The 1992 Zoo TV Tour pushed the boundaries of what was possible in a stadium show, ushering in an era of video screens and multimedia backdrops From that kitchen in Rosemount Avenue, U2 became the world's biggest rock band. Anthems like With Or Without You, One and Beautiful Day have always sounded majestic yet personal; powered by The Edge's cascading guitar tone and Bono's lyrics which, for all their proselytising, remain grounded in a belief in humanity. They made a stylistic swerve in the 1990s, embracing electronics, dance music and irony on the albums Achtung Baby, Zooropa and Pop. Along the way, they reinvented stadium concerts with the Zoo TV tour, whose stage was crammed full of multimedia screens and satellite feeds, while Bono made nightly prank calls to the White House. The Edge, real name Dave Evans, puts their longevity down to a lack of formal training. "It's been a guiding light, in some ways, the limitations of the band," he explains. "We're in this place where, musically, we never know what's about to happen. It can fall apart or it can become something extraordinary. "And that's the beauty of U2.” Back on stage at Mount Temple, Bono paid tribute to his alma matter for allowing the band to flourish. title: How 'largest phone smuggling network' was uncovered
description: Police say up to 40,000 phones were smuggled - the equivalent of around 40% of devices stolen in London.
body: Police arrested Amir Muhammad Khadikhel and Ismat Miakhel in September 2025 It started with a single stolen mobile phone, found inside a sealed parcel, inside a warehouse near Heathrow airport. It ended in police dismantling what detectives believe to be the UK's largest phone smuggling network. The device had been electronically tracked to the warehouse not by officers, but by a victim who had it stolen from them just before Christmas in 2024 and alerted the DHL courier company. "The phone was ringing in the package," explains Commander Andy Featherstone, the Metropolitan police's lead on mobile phone theft. "It was still on. Which is very unusual in these circumstances, because they tend to be wrapped up, so the signal isn't working. But in this case it was." Stolen phones are often wrapped in aluminium foil in order to block wireless signals and prevent the devices from being tracked. When police were called to investigate, they found more than 800 devices, packaged in batches of five, stacked into nine boxes, some wrapped in foil, others in bubble wrap. All were stolen and they were destined to be shipped to Hong Kong. A major inquiry known as Operation Echosteep was launched, with detectives who specialise in investigating armed robberies and drug smuggling brought in to track down suspects. Further shipments were intercepted and officers used forensics on the packages to identify two men, who were placed under surveillance. Police say the investigation began after a victim tracked down their mobile phone to a warehouse and heard it ringing inside a parcel In September 2025, police stopped a car being driven through Waltham Forest and arrested Amir Muhammad Khadikhel and Ismat Miakhel. Inside, they discovered several phones strewn around the back seat, with others on the floor wrapped in foil. Both men were found wearing necklaces featuring pins to remove the handsets' Sim cards. Police say about 2,000 more devices were discovered at properties linked to them. Southwark Crown Court heard that one shop, Roshan Fruit and Nuts, on Lea Bridge Road in Leyton, east London, had been used to store the stolen phones. Police found a trapdoor, leading to a basement where boxes labelled as containing dried goods held packages of phones wrapped up in foil, as well as £44,665 in cash. In another property, the court heard stolen phones had been found stored inside the microwave. Prosecutor Karen Robinson KC said the men had played a "leading role" in a "sophisticated and criminal network" that had seen more than 5,000 phones seized by police, with a value in the UK of around £5.5m. The court heard Khadikhel had fled Afghanistan in 2019 and travelled to the UK as an asylum seeker. A third man, Mansoor Mohammed, who came to the UK from India on a visa in 2019, was also identified as being involved in the handling of devices. From left: Amir Muhammad Khadikhel, Ismat Miakhel and Mansoor Mohammed Khadikhel, 35, from Wanstead, and Miakhel, 33, from Walthamstow, along with Mohammed, 30, from Wood Green, pleaded guilty in April to conspiracy to handle stolen goods and participating in criminal activities of an organised crime group. Khadikhel and Miakhel also admitted to conspiracy to remove stolen goods. On Friday, Judge Adam Hiddleston sentenced Khadikhel to nine-and-a-half years' imprisonment, Miakhel to nine years' imprisonment and Mohammed to six-and-a-half years' imprisonment. The judge said the offending had been on an "enormous scale financially" and the criminality was "highly organised and sophisticated". Commander Andy Featherstone says phone snatchers are being recruited over social media and paid hundreds of pounds for each device The prosecutor added that phone smuggling in London was "prolific" and a "very significant societal problem". Police suspect the network was responsible for smuggling up to 40,000 phones during 2024 and 2025, exporting them to China. It is the equivalent of around 40% of all devices stolen in London at that time. Featherstone says that wider group has "many layers in its hierarchy", with handlers recruiting street thieves via social media and advertising how much they were willing to pay them per stolen device. "So a modern device, or the most recent phone that had been released, would fetch a higher premium - in most cases around the £500 mark," he explains. "This network were collecting phones all across London from street thieves, and then they would take those phones in, and when they had enough they would then package them up and ship them out of the UK into China." Saira Pike, from the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "Phone theft is more than just a financial loss as it involves victims losing personal data, precious pictures or memories and their sense of security. "Amir Khadikhel, Ismat Miakhel and Mansoor Mohammed were at the heart of a sophisticated organised crime operation that profited from the misery of victims who had their mobile phones stolen across London." Police say children are often recruited over social media to steal phones. Featherstone tells me one 14-year-old boy was stopped by officers with around 20 stolen phones on him, something he could potentially receive thousands of pounds for in a single day. "Some of these devices, particularly iPhones, can fetch up to £5,000 in China and Hong Kong. The reason being that they can work on the internet without any type of restriction," Featherstone said. "This was a global operation, millions of pounds involved, because of the value of these devices." Police say the network was responsible for smuggling up to 40,000 stolen phones out of the UK The Met says it has made 14 arrests connected to Operation Echosteep, seized more than £250,000 in cash and recovered more than 10,000 stolen phones, though the number of victims reunited with their devices is lower, at more than 1,000. title: Space museum launched by Britain's first astronaut
description: Helen Sharman officially opened the John Dulcamara Space Flight Museum at Grizedale Observatory.
body: Britain's first astronaut Helen Sharman officially opened the John Dulcamara Space Flight Museum at Grizedale Observatory A new space flight museum has been opened at a Lake District observatory. Britain's first astronaut Helen Sharman visited Grizedale Observatory and Planetarium on Friday to officially open the John Dulcamara Space Flight Museum. The collection was donated by private collector John Dulcamara and includes a piece of the command module from the 1969 Apollo 11 - the first manned mission to land on the moon. Sharman said the collection was "extraordinary". Grizedale Observatory near Ambleside, Cumbria, opened in May 2024, offering public access to telescopes, a planetarium and meteorite laboratory, as well as staging a dark skies festival and other events. The collection includes a piece of the command module from the 1969 Apollo 11 space flight Sharman, who became the first British person to visit space in 1991, said: "It's an extraordinary collection. We've got bits of Apollo 11, bits from the Russian space programme - it's just an amazing collection of artefacts from space flight history. "It tells its own story of space history, but also of the people that went and the items that were important to them. "For it to be on show now in this beautiful way, as part of Grizedale Observatory, what a coup for Cumbria." The museum contains a variety of pieces ranging from autographed photos and signatures of prominent people in space flight to parts of actual space craft. Dulcamara said he first started collecting the artefacts after he attended a shuttle launch in 1996 and kept the ticket. "That's what started my 30 year collection off," he said. "There's thousands of pieces on display, I hope people will come and have a look." Observatory director Gary Fildes said that the collection presented some "fascinating stories". "John asked whether we would be interested in keeping his collection here at the observatory so other people could have the chance to see it. He brought a few samples along and we knew we had to make it happen. "We thought: 'failure is not an option'!" During her visit, Sharman met with local schoolchildren to talk about her time aboard the Mir Space Station, where she carried out scientific experiments and observations of Earth. "To have Helen opening the museum is incredibly special," Fildes said. "What makes this particularly important to us is the opportunity for local children to meet Helen. "You simply don't know where an experience like that might lead." Follow BBC Cumbria on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Cumbria on BBC Sounds. title: Tory ex-ministers face serious questions over migrant centre chaos, inquiry hears
description: The Manston centre in Kent became overwhelmed in November 2022 at the height of the small boats crisis.
body: The Manston centre in Kent, used to hold thousands of migrants, became overcrowded in 2022 An overcrowded migrant reception centre, where a man died, raises "very serious questions" for ministers in the former Conservative government, including two home secretaries and former prime ministers, an inquiry has heard. The Manston centre in Kent became overwhelmed in November 2022 at the height of the small boats crisis, with around 4,000 people held there. Home Office officials knew conditions were unlawful and children were at risk of harm, but had no alternative plan for where to accommodate them, the inquiry heard on Friday. Former Home Secretaries Dame Priti Patel and Suella Braverman shared in preliminary evidence that Number 10 was involved in decisions made at the time. The Manston centre, a former military site near Dover, was converted into an emergency holding facility for cross-channel migrants in early 2022, as small boat crossings began to soar. It was designed to hold up to around 1,000 people at any one time and for no longer than a legal limit of 24 hours. But by November 2022, thousands of people were sleeping in marquees and it was apparent that there was disease, illness and no adequate care for children traumatised by crossing the English Channel. During this critical period, the government was hoping that it could eventually send asylum seekers to Rwanda. As the number of detainees grew, doctors identified diphtheria was present - and that 31-year-old Iraqi Hussein Haseeb Ahmed was suspected of suffering from the highly dangerous disease, the preparatory inquiry hearing heard on Friday. He was not immediately taken to hospital, but died on 19 November at 05:30 after he was admitted to hospital as his condition deteriorated. "He was handcuffed until around 2am," Claire Dobbin KC, the inquiry's lead lawyer, said. "His handcuffing in hospital at a point when he must have been close to death, all require separate examination." At one stage, some 81 families were sharing one toilet with babies, children, teenagers and adults sharing the same space despite clear safety concerns, she said. Some detainees had visible wounds. One person, who was not given medical care, was using a plastic croissant wrapper as a dressing. "The position of children is a matter of great concern," said Dobbin. "Generally the circumstances in which children can be detained in England are very limited indeed." Dobbin added that one senior official at the Home Office told colleagues that the conditions were the worst he had seen in 20 years. He wrote in an email: "Political decisions have forced hard-working officials and suppliers into an impossible position. This will end up as a public inquiry and rightly." Other witnesses have said there was racism, hostility and aggression towards the detainees from some staff, with some accused of threatening to withhold meals from people who wanted to use the toilet. "The body of evidence raises very serious questions for senior officials and ministers as to how the detention of children in these conditions was tolerated on humanitarian or legal grounds," said Dobbin. Two former home secretaries involved in the Manston decision-making - Dame Priti and Braverman - have already provided evidence that will be examined in depth in future hearings. Braverman's personal legal representative - who is paid for by the government - gave no statement on her behalf during Friday's session. But the inquiry heard she had already explained in written submissions that Number 10 had been aware of the situation at Manston and that the decision to pause using hotels had led to the overcrowding. It was also told there had been "prolonged periods of disengagement" from Robert Jenrick, the immigration minister in late 2022, although he had provided a statement. It is not clear yet whether former Prime Ministers Boris Johnson or Rishi Sunak will be asked to give evidence about their roles. The inquiry team will now continue gathering evidence with the date for full hearings yet to be fixed. title: British climber dies after falling 60m on Spanish mountainside
description: The identity of the 28-year-old man, who fell down a vertical gully to his death, is yet to be confirmed.
body: Mountain specialists were lowered by winch to the site of the accident to recover the body A 28-year-old British climber has died after falling about 60m (200ft) from one of the highest mountains in northern Spain. The man fell into a gully while descending from the summit of Torrecerredo in the Cantabrian Mountains on Thursday, the Spanish Civil Guard said. Police and an air unit were deployed to the scene after emergency services were called around 13:27 local time (11:27 GMT). The man's body was recovered by a mountain rescue unit. The UK Foreign Office said it was in contact with local authorities "following reports of the death of a British national in Spain". Spanish emergency services said they initially received a call saying that a person had fallen on the eastern face of the mountain and dispatched a rescue group aboard a medical helicopter. A doctor among them confirmed the man's death at about 14:18 and remained at the scene to guard the body until a Civil Guard helicopter could arrive about an hour and 20 minutes later. Specialist mountain rescuers were then lowered by winch to the site of the accident, where they recovered the man's body and belongings. The identity of the climber, who Spanish authorities said was English, has not been given. The accident occurred when he was about 20 metres from the mountain's summit. His body has been transported to the Institute of Legal Medicine, which provides forensic pathology services, in Asturias, the Civil Guard said. Torrecerredo, which has an elevation of about 2,650m, is in the Picos de Europa, which is popular with climbers and walkers. The region's tourism board describes the route up the mountain as "very difficult" with a demanding ascent, warning climbers to take particular care on steep and exposed upper sections on their way down. Sepa Asturias - the body responsible for emergency services in the region - said it also transported a 54-year-old French woman to hospital after she suffered a leg injury on the mountain range on Thursday afternoon. title: Antonelli 'comes back to earth' with qualifying crash
description: Kimi Antonelli says he is "very mad" about his crash in qualifying at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, which means he will start from 16th on the grid.
body: Kimi Antonelli's qualifying ended early when he hit the wall and broke the suspension on his Mercedes Kimi Antonelli says his crash in qualifying at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix was "stupid" and "a good way to come back to earth" as he pursues his first world title. The Mercedes driver, who has been running away with the championship this season, hit a wall in first qualifying in Baku and will start Saturday's race 16th. Team-mate George Russell, his closest pursuer in the title race, starts from pole after a dominant performance. Antonelli said: "I misjudged with the grip being so different compared to the first lap. I hit the wall. Unnecessary mistake early on. "So it's a good way to come back to earth and to remind myself I need to be on top of it every time because otherwise I do these mistakes and a very stupid one." He added that he was "very mad about it". The 20-year-old Italian has been on the back foot all weekend, fighting to make up for time lost to a reliability problem in practice on Thursday. His Mercedes suffered a hydraulic leak halfway through the first session and the car was not ready for him to go back out on track until halfway through the second session. Antonelli was 0.252secs behind Russell in final practice on Friday, 0.092secs quicker than the Briton after his first lap in qualifying and then made his mistake on his second. Russell takes pole in Baku as Antonelli hits wall Azerbaijan GP Quali Review: Drama for Russell and Antonelli His error brought back memories of last year's grand prix in Baku, which proved to be a turning point in the 2025 championship. McLaren's Oscar Piastri appeared on course for his first world title heading into this race, leading team-mate Lando Norris by 31 points. But the Australian crashed in qualifying, jumped the start and then crashed out of the race on the first lap, and his season came off the rails after that. Antonelli's error gives Russell, who is 81 points adrift in the championship, a second chance in three races to narrow his deficit to the Italian. But the Briton has sounded resigned to losing out on the title for some time and he referred back to Antonelli's stunning drive at the Italian Grand Prix, which he won after starting 19th on the grid because of a penalty. Russell said: "You can't discount Kimi. You know, started 19th in Monza and now he's in 16th, so, yeah, he should be leading by a few laps early this time." Oscar Piastri climbs out of his McLaren after crashing out on the first lap in Baku last year Russell also pointed out that this was the first significant mistake Antonelli had made in a competitive session all year. Asked if he believed Antonelli's mistake was a result of "title jitters", Russell said: "When you look at every championship campaign, even for the winners, there are mistakes along the way. "So, I still keep on believing and keep on fighting until it isn't possible any more. But I don't feel any pressure. "I feel excitement every time I jump in the car now, purely because I feel more confident in myself. "When that confidence starts to build, it's just like this upward cycle. "On the flip side, when you're on the back foot, you start losing that confidence and then you start pushing the limits more, and that's when mistakes happen. "But he's been flawless this season. It's the first mistake he's made in a qualifying or race this whole year." Russell's pole margin was a massive 0.837secs, with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc second and Piastri third. The Baku street circuit has a long straight that affords good overtaking possibilities and has a reputation for producing incident-packed races. Saturday, 26 September at 12:00 BST Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live with build-up from 11:00; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app Asked about potential challengers in the race, in addition to Antonelli, Russell said Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who qualified eighth after a difficult session, "is going to be a threat". Verstappen, who was quickest in final practice just ahead of Russell, suffered a string of problems that he said had stopped him taking a place on the front row alongside the Mercedes. "The whole qualifying was not how it should be," he said. "Already from Q1 the engine was 0.5secs down on the straight compared to my team-mate and they can't explain or understand why. So you're on the back foot. "Then in Q3 on my middle lap my battery didn't charge to 100% so I had to abort the lap which means you lose tyre temp and around here that's killing. "I tried to push... but being down on top speed and I had a yellow flag from Lando in front of me, [which] meant that's where we are." The Dutchman added: "The whole weekend we were running really well and then we run into so much trouble in qualifying. It's not good enough. "Looking at George's lap, I don't think we would have fought for pole but there is a big gap behind and we should have slotted in to that easily. "But when you have that many issues you also don't deserve to be there. We need to be more robust and we need to be on top of these things." title: Ex-GTA developer's studio faces closure after debut game flopped
description: Build A Rocket Boy, founded by Leslie Benzies, has gone into administration after its debut game flopped.
body: MindsEye, released in June 2025, was Build A Rocket Boy's debut game A video game studio founded by a former senior Grand Theft Auto developer is facing closure 15 months after the disastrous release of its debut game. Edinburgh-based Build A Rocket Boy (Barb) launched MindsEye in June 2025 to a string of bad reviews and player complaints, with some calling it "the worst game" of the year. Former workers said development of the game was chaotic and accused its boss, Leslie Benzies, of mismanaging the studio. Barb has now gone into administration - a process which could result in it being sold to a new owner or closed down. BBC Newsbeat has contacted Barb for a response. Leslie Benzies, pictured at the 2025 Bafta Game Awards, is regarded as a key figure in the development of Grand Theft Auto Benzies set up Barb in 2016 - the same year he left Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar Games after a legal row over unpaid royalties. It began work on Everywhere, intended to be a multiplayer role-playing game set in a futuristic city, before pivoting its focus to action-adventure MindsEye. The project attracted a lot of interest and, according to company documents, external, Barb had managed to attract more than £233m of investment by 2024. Former staff previously told BBC Newsbeat the development process had "no coherent direction" and accused senior managers of failing to listen to their concerns. Following the game's turbulent launch, between 250 to 300 members of staff were made redundant. Shortly before this, during an all-staff call, Benzies alleged "internal and external" forces had conspired to hinder MindsEye's release, and vowed to root out "saboteurs" within the company. When Newsbeat asked Barb about this, it released a statement saying: "Leslie and the entire senior management team take full responsibility for the initial launch [of MindsEye]. "The version of the game that was released did not reflect the experience our community deserved." Since its release, the company has failed to attract a bigger audience to the game with a series of fixes and content updates. After further layoffs, reports last week suggested the remaining workers at the studio had also been let go. A company goes into administration when it can no longer pay its bills - referred to as insolvency. Any payments to creditors - people or companies they owe money - are put on hold while proposals to restructure the business are drawn up. An administrator from a qualified accountancy firm is put in charge while this process takes place, and one of their main jobs is to keep the business running, usually until a new owner can be found. They must also make sure creditors are paid back as much money as possible. This is usually done by selling off assets such as equipment, furnishings and anything else that can be sold to raise cash. Administration can take months and, in the worst-case scenario, a company can be put into liquidation and shut down if it has no way of making any more cash. According to Barb's most recent accounts, for the period up to September 2025, it incurred a £36.2m loss and had £10.5m in net assets. title: Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered
description: It has taken more than two years, but a judgement finally appears to have been made on the financial rule breaches levelled against the club. Here's what it means.
body: This video can not be played Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City It has taken more than two years, but a judgement finally appears to have been reached on the 115 charges levelled against Manchester City over breaches of Premier League financial rules. Following a four-year investigation, City were charged and the hearing finally got under way on 16 September 2024. BBC Sport has now learned a decision has been made, after the Athletic reported City had been found guilty on all almost of the charges. We are not at the end of this process, however. Far from it. But what does this mean for City's titles? What about their Premier League status? Will there be an appeal? And how long will it be before this saga does come to an end? Man City found guilty of majority of 115 financial rule breaches - sources tell BBC In February 2023, City were charged and referred to an independent commission over alleged breaches that were said to have taken place between 2009 and 2018. The charges - relating to Premier League financial rules - are: 54 x failure to provide accurate financial information from 2009-10 to 2017-18. 14 x failure to provide accurate details for player and manager payments from 2009-10 to 2017-18. 5 x failure to comply with Uefa's rules including financial fair play (FFP) 2013-14 to 2017-18. 7 x breaching Premier League profit and sustainability (PSR) rules from 2015-16 to 2017-18. 35 x failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations from December 2018 to Feb 2023. City have always denied wrongdoing and BBC Sport has been told they would appeal were they found guilty. German newspaper Der Spiegel published leaked documents, including emails purportedly sent between top City executives (some of whom remain at the City Football Group), across several seasons following the club's Abu Dhabi takeover in 2008. It alleged these showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from state-owned airline Etihad and state-controlled telecoms firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from their holding company (Sheik Mansour's Abu Dhabi United Group, or ADUG) as sponsorship income by channelling the funds through the companies' accounts. This, it was alleged, was a means of meeting FFP rules introduced by Uefa in 2011 - and PSR brought in by the Premier League in 2012 - limiting clubs' permitted losses. There then followed further allegations of misreporting financial information centred on documents that claimed to show secret 'off-the-books' payments to then manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi. It is also alleged the club gave players more money than was officially going through the accounts so recorded spending was less than it actually was. City, who have always maintained ADUG is a private fund rather than an arm of the state, refused to comment on any of Der Spiegel's revelations, saying the leaked emails were obtained illegally, and they were an "attempt to damage the club's reputation". City - along with the companies involved - strongly denied breaking any financial rules. But that did not stop both Uefa and the Premier League launching investigations as a result. Manchester City won seven domestic trophies during the period of the alleged offences November 2018: Football Leaks allegations emerge with Der Spiegel publishing claims Manchester City breached financial fair play rules. March 2019: Uefa launches a formal investigation off the back of Der Spiegel's findings. May 2019: City criticise the investigation and launch an appeal process. November 2019: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) deems City's appeal inadmissible. February 2020: Uefa announces a two-year ban for City from European competitions and a €30m fine. July 2020: City's European ban is overturned after an appeal to Cas. July 2021: City lose a jurisdiction ruling that allows the media to report the Premier League is continuing to investigate the champions for alleged financial breaches. April 2022: Der Spiegel publishes a fresh report claiming the Premier League has been investigating the club for three years, providing detailed claims. February 2023: The Premier League charges City with 115 financial breaches. September 2024: The start of a 10-week hearing between the Premier League and City on the 115 charges. February 2025: City manager Pep Guardiola says the club expect to learn the verdict "within one month". Guardiola left the Etihad at the end of last season. September 2026: Reports emerge that a verdict has been reached, with sources telling the BBC that City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the charges. It was never expected the verdict would come complete with the sanctions. We now face a waiting game for even that verdict to officially be made public by the independent panel. We don't know who was on the panel that heard and ruled on the case, and that will only come once a written judgment is released. All options are open to the disciplinary commission: Points deduction (immediate or suspended). Financial penalties (immediate or suspended). Removal from the Premier League. Being removed from the Premier League would mean City lose their membership and are demoted to a lower division from the end of the season. That could also happen through a points penalty so severe they would effectively be relegated. This video can not be played 'I don't really know how to feel' - Man City fan on charges The Premier League declined to comment on the case when approached on Friday. City issued a statement that showed frustration news of the verdict had leaked. It read: "The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. "As such Manchester City FC's position remains consistent with the club's statement of February 2023. "The club has diligently respected due process for eig

title: Sir David Beckham nets £38.5m after World Cup ad deals
description: His stake in DRJB Holdings has entitled him to almost half of its £85.5m in dividend payments.
body: Sir David Beckham has netted a £38.5m payout from his sports, fashion, and media business after the 2026 Men's Football World Cup helped it bring in record profits. The former England star's DRJB Holdings, which includes the Beckham brand, reported an almost £50m profit in 2025, a 46% jump compared to a year earlier. Sales rose from £72.2m to £84m. The rise was driven by a slew of advertising partnerships struck in the runup to the tournament, including with Bank of America, McDonald's, Verizon, and PepsiCo Lay's. Sir David, Britain's first billionaire sportsman, was commonly seen in adverts during the summer's World Cup. In the US, it was difficult for fans to watch a game without coming across Beckham in adverts for Stella Artois, Home Depot and Lay's crisps - known as Walkers in the UK. Sir David also launched menswear collections for Hugo Boss last year, as well as a pair of Adidas Predator football boots and an eyewear range with Italian glasses maker Safilo. Revenues at DRJB, of which Beckham owns almost half, were boosted by growth in Beckham's health supplements business too. DRJB paid its shareholders £38.9m, followed by a special £46.6m payment after the end of the financial year. Sir David's share of those dividends would have been around £38.5m due to how much of the company he owns. The remainder of DRJB is owned by New York-based Authentic Brands Group, which also owns Reebok, as well as the rights to other celebrity brands such as comedian and actor Kevin Hart. Authentic's entertainment chief executive Corey Salter said the performance showed Sir David's name is "one of the most powerful global brands in sport, lifestyle, entertainment and much more". "It's been an outstanding year, from new partnerships to important philanthropic campaigns and overall brand growth," he said. Sir David previously drew criticism for associating himself with a country where same-sex relationships are illegal by acting as an ambassador for the 2022 Men's Football World Cup in Qatar. "It was an important competition and one I was proud to be part of," he said at the time, adding that he had engaged with the LGBTQ community during the tournament. title: Discovery of 97 million files related to SAS inquiry 'regrettable', MoD says
description: It comes after the inquiry's chair called the disclosure - three years into the investigation - "troubling".
body: The SAS carried out night raids with Afghan special forces during the conflict The discovery of 97 million documents more than three years into an inquiry investigating allegations that UK special forces committed war crimes in Afghanistan was a "regrettable failure", the Ministry of Defence has said. The admission comes after the inquiry's chair, Lord Justice Haddon-Cave, called the discovery "troubling" and "extraordinary news". The independent inquiry was established in 2022 to investigate alleged executions by members of the Special Air Service between 2010 and 2013, during so-called night raids targeting the Taliban. It has yet to produce any findings. MoD lawyers were called to a hearing on Friday to explain why the documents from the period in question were not found sooner. Haddon-Cave said he had taken the "exceptional step" of calling the hearing because of the disclosure and the "somewhat casual way" the MoD had informed his team. Steven Gray KC, representing the MoD, said the ministry "apologises that it fell short". The "failure was one of communication, not application", he said, adding that the ministry was working hard to search through documents across multiple IT systems and classifications at "huge expense". Gray added that the department was taking steps to avoid any similar revelations happening in the future. Lawyers acting for the bereaved families said it was "staggering" the documents came to light at such a late stage in the inquiry's work. Within the new files, the MoD says it has identified thousands of potentially relevant documents, including images that appear to have been taken during a number of special forces operations under investigation by the inquiry. However, it stressed that much of the material found would be unrelated to the inquiry's terms of reference. The Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan (IIA) told the BBC it was yet to receive any of the new material. How a British special forces raid went fatally wrong Afghan inquiry into alleged SAS war crimes has already cost £58m, MoD figures show Ex-UK Special Forces break silence on 'war crimes' by colleagues SAS war crime evidence suppressed, inquiry hears SAS troops carried out night-time arrest raids across Afghanistan during the conflict there, called Deliberate Detention Operations (DDOs), which were meant to target Taliban commanders and bombmakers, and collect material that could provide further intelligence about insurgent networks. Following a night raid, members of the SAS and their support staff took photos of anyone killed, and collected mobile phones and other devices for intelligence purposes. Forensic experts are examining these images to see whether the SAS's account of what took place during the operations fits with the ballistic evidence visible in the photographs. The inquiry follows years of reporting by BBC Panorama, which revealed evidence that the SAS deliberately killed people who posed no threat, including children and handcuffed detainees during raids. It has already heard evidence from senior UK military personnel who have said they believed the SAS carried out extrajudicial killings of Afghan civilians. It has also heard concerns about the secrecy under which the SAS operated and that previous investigations into the allegations were ended prematurely. Edward Craven KC, acting on behalf of the bereaved families, echoed the chair's comments on the newly discovered documents, saying the disclosure represented yet another example of the MoD frustrating the justice process. Craven said that what mattered most to the bereaved families was getting the truth about the deaths of their loved ones. Haddon-Cave said it was crucial that "any material of real relevance is quickly identified and disclosed", adding that he intended to call another hearing next month to question the MoD on its progress. The MoD said it was fully committed to supporting the inquiry and that it regretted that it was "not as prompt or consistent as it should have been" in disclosing the documents. Set up by the then-Defence Secretary Ben Wallace following the publication of the evidence by the BBC in 2022, the IIA has come under criticism over delays and mounting costs. It had stated that it would provide an interim or final report 12-18 months after it was established in 2022. After almost four years, it has yet to publish any findings. The BBC revealed earlier this month that it has already cost the public purse £58m. Around half of that cost is understood to have been money spent by the MoD and the wider government in responding to the inquiry, including lawyers representing former SAS officers and senior military figures. Public inquiries are rarely quick or cheap. The inquiry into the fire at Grenfell Tower, which claimed 72 lives and was found to be entirely avoidable, took more than seven years to complete and cost more than £170m. Haddon-Cave said he had set a deadline to hear all evidence by 30 April 2027 and that he was seeking assurances that the new discovery would not delay the work of the inquiry further. Or use the Signal messaging app, an end-to-end encrypted message service designed to protect your data. Signal: 0044 7714 956 936 Note: The SecureDrop link will only work in a Tor browser. title: Palmer misses too many opportunities to play for England - Tuchel
description: Thomas Tuchel has said that Cole Palmer "misses too many opportunities" to play for England after the Chelsea forward pulled out of the latest squad.
body: England will play four matches during this international window. Cole Palmer "misses too many opportunities" to play for England after the Chelsea forward pulled out of the latest squad, says manager Thomas Tuchel. The withdrawal of Palmer came as a surprise as he has started all five of Chelsea's matches in the Premier League so far this season, though Tuchel says he had been playing with "discomfort and pain". The 24-year-old was left out of the World Cup squad by Tuchel and has featured just three times since the German took charge of the Three Lions in January 2025. "My understanding is that he is playing with discomfort and pain, and he cannot compete at the highest level with discomfort and pain. So he withdrew and informed us, and Chelsea informed us." Tuchel said. "For sure. It is a missed opportunity. He misses too many opportunities. I don't blame him for it. It is just a fact. "He misses way too many camps with injuries, and I only want to rely on what I witness and see within in my team, and for that you have to be in camp. "And if you're not in camp, there is a next level to impress that you cannot achieve because you can only do it when you are actually on the pitch with me. So yes, it is a missed opportunity." It is understood Palmer is currently abroad completing an injury-specific training plan. Chelsea's non international players have been given days off and have been permitted to travel if they so wish. Palmer has been accompanied by a Chelsea rehabilitation coach on his overseas trip. Declan Rice, Tino Livramento, Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo are the other players who pulled out with injury. Tuchel said he was not worried that players may put their clubs above playing for their country. "We are not managing load. When I was in club football, I used the term 'international break' and, when you hear it from the other side, it is a totally different picture," he said. "It is a competitive environment, but it is also an environment that the players love to be a part of. "That is what togetherness and brotherhood look like, and that is what we have created since last September in qualifying. We will never compromise on that. "We will never let it creep in that we have a feeling players do not want to come. We focus on the guys who absolutely want to play for England." The match against world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday is England's first game since the end of the World Cup. The Three Lions ended the tournament with a 6-4 win in the Bronze medal match against France, but were criticised for the way they lost 2-1 to Argentina in the semi-final. England led 1-0 going into the final 15 minutes but dropped deep and conceded possession, with Argentina scoring two goals in the final minutes to reach the final. Tuchel does not think there will be a negative reaction from the fans because of the result. "I would be very surprised if the atmosphere would hold a third place or an accident in the 85th minute of a semi-final against us and against our team, that would surprise me a lot." Tuchel said. "The time and how and how fast it sold out shows me how excited everyone is to come and watch. "That's the reality of it, Spain make it hard for you to play a high intensity game. They are happy to control the ball and the rhythm. "There can be spells when we will suffer and have to suffer, but there can be spells where we dominate and can bring the attributes that make us strong, so let's see how it plays out." title: Ed Sheeran's next US concerts cancelled due to storm warning
description: The star's concerts in Massachusetts on Friday and Saturday are cancelled after severe weather warnings.
body: Ed Sheeran's concerts in Massachusetts on Friday and Saturday have been cancelled because of severe weather warnings in the area. The singer had been scheduled to perform two shows at the Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, near Boston, as part of his current US tour. The tour has been in the headlines because of a row over a decision to drop Sheeran's support act Macklemore for making pro-Palestinian comments on stage. Stadium owners including the Gillette Stadium's Robert Kraft lobbied for his removal. A statement from the venue, external said: "Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, the promoter and tour have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium." It added: "The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority. "Refunds are available now at the point of purchase. Ticketholders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded." Weather warnings for high winds are in force in the area until the early hours of Sunday, and officials have told drivers to minimise travel. Sheeran was at the eye of a very different storm last week after the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour. The decision came after the rapper made on-stage comments at earlier concerts including calling for "free Palestine" and referring to "genocide" in Gaza, as well as showing images of Gaza. Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the US rapper of hate speech and said Macklemore would not be allowed to appear at the Gillette Stadium, the home of his New England Patriots American football team. Sheeran said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoter, not by him. The promoter said venue owners including Kraft would have refused to let the concerts take place if Macklemore was on the bill. Macklemore's removal from the tour led Sheeran's other support and backing artists to pull out in protest, and sparked a heated debate over free speech and the role of politics in music. Returning to the stage last weekend, Sheeran told fans he "had to take and make difficult decisions - and I am making mistakes - and I'm so, so sorry". title: Students strike across Germany in protest against military service
description: A law establishing voluntary military service came into effect in January, but protest organisers fear compulsory service could follow.
body: School strikes are taking place across Germany to protest against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service. One of the organisers of the strike, Bela Breitner, from School Strike Against Compulsory Military Service said the federal government was "serious about gradually reintroducing compulsory military service". At one protest in Hamburg, demonstrators waved flags and held up banners emblazoned with the words "We won't take part in your wars". German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made boosting Germany's military a priority following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. A new law introducing voluntary military service came into force in January, with the aim of recruiting volunteers to increase the number of soldiers. However, if the security situation worsens or if too few volunteers come forward, a form of compulsory military service could be considered by Germany's Parliament, the Bundestag. Under the law, all 18-year-olds in Germany are being sent a questionnaire asking if they are interested and willing to join the armed forces. One protester, 16-year-old Elias Bernhard, from Hamburg, said that the responses to the questionnaires "show that young people do not want to join the Bundeswehr [Germany's armed forces]". "That is why I am out on the streets today. That is why we are serious about striking until compulsory military service is off the table. We will carry on." The questionnaire is mandatory for men and voluntary for women. All 18-year-old men will have to take a medical exam to assess their fitness for possible military service. The organisers of the protests, say the trigger came after some 18-year-olds in the northern German towns of Kiel and Flensburg, were sent official invitations for medical exams, even though they expressed no interest in joining the army on their registration forms. The group says over a hundred demonstrations are planned across Germany, including in Kiel, Hamburg, Berlin and Frankfurt. A spokesperson for the Defence Ministry told the BBC that under the law, the obligation to undergo a medical examination applies "to all men liable for military service who were born after 31 December 2007". This also applies to people who have stated that they have no interest in compulsory military service. The spokesperson said that since July around 1,000 18-year-old men, who showed no interest in the army, have had the medical exam. During the Cold War, Germany, like many other European countries, had a large army. But it reduced its armed forces during the 1990s after the fall of the Iron Curtain. Germany's former Chancellor, Angela Merkel, ended compulsory military service in 2011. But now, in the face of perceived threats from Russia and heavy pressure from Germany's traditional ally, the US, Merz has vowed to transform the Bundeswehr into Europe's strongest conventional army. The Bundeswehr currently has around 186,700 troops. By the early 2030s, Germany wants to raise the number to 260,000, supplemented by around 200,000 reservists, in order to meet new Nato force targets and strengthen Germany's defences. title: Senior Kazakh officials detained after 14 service members swept out to sea
description: Seventeen service members were swept out to the Caspian Sea during military exercises.
body: The investigation is looking into decision-making by senior military officials Five senior military officials have been detained in Kazakhstan following the death of 14 service members who were taking part in military exercises. Those who died were among a total of 17 who were swept into the Caspian Sea as they were disembarking from a boat on Thursday. Officials say the incident occurred "during a combat training mission due to a sharp deterioration in meteorological conditions and increasing winds". Those detained include the chief of staff and first deputy commander of Kazakhstan's Naval Forces, two military unit commanders, and the commanders of a marine company and a boat. They are suspected of criminal negligence. An interior ministry committee has been set up to investigate the incident, which occurred some 43km (27 miles) from the city of Aktau in south-western Kazakstan. Deputy Interior Minister Sanzhar Adilov said a pretrial investigation into the deaths was being conducted. The investigation was looking into the decisions made during the organisation and execution of the military training exercise, whether safety requirements had been observed, and weather conditions had been taken into account - in addition to technical specifications of the boat. More than 500 military personnel, warships and coastal units were participating in the Caspian Defense 2026 military exercise, according to the Kazakh ministry of defence. title: Man City found guilty of breaking financial rules, sources tell BBC
description: Manchester City are found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching, sources tell BBC Sport.
body: Manchester City have won the Premier League eight times Manchester City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching, sources have told BBC Sport. The Athletic, external is reporting that the sanctions have not been decided but that the independent panel has reached its decision, finding the club guilty of all but one count. Sources have also told BBC Sport a decision has been made in the case, and City have been found guilty of the majority of breaches. The Premier League declined to comment. Asked if the report was correct, City did not comment either way. Instead they released a statement saying the "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality". "The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence," it added. BBC Sport has also been told that, in the event of being found guilty, City will appeal against the findings. Other Premier League clubs are believed to have been informed about the panel's decision.
