title: Met should probe handling of 'Putney Pusher' case, police watchdog says
description: Nicholas Brandram's family say he took his own life due to the "pressure" of a police investigation.
body: Nicholas Brandram was under police investigation over the 2017 incident The police watchdog has said the Metropolitan Police's professional standards unit should investigate the force's handling of a case after the death of a man suspected of being the "Putney Pusher". Nicholas Brandram was found dead at his London home on 15 September. His family said he took his own life after the "immense pressure" of a police investigation. The 44-year-old was under suspicion of being the jogger who pushed a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in May 2017. The Met police made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) following the banker's death. The family of Nicholas Brandram said a Metropolitan Police investigation into its handling of the case should be "thorough, independent and unflinching in establishing what went wrong". His sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker said in a statement: "We have been clear about the litany of failings that need to be examined, and we expect those questions to be answered." They called for the investigation to be a "priority", adding that they wanted no other family "to endure what ours is going through". In a statement, the IOPC said: "After carefully considering the referral, we have decided that an investigation is required and that the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards should conduct it. "We have recommended the review considers matters including the necessity and proportionality of arrest, what engagement was there with the media and considerations made in relation to Mr Brandram's welfare and the relevant policy." This video can not be played Jogger 'pushed' woman in front of bus The police watchdog added that if the Met's investigation did not find "any potential misconduct", the final report must be submitted to the IOPC for review. Brandram's family insisted in an interview with the BBC that he was not the so-called "Putney pusher". Inquest opens into 'Putney Pusher' suspect's death Family blame police for 'Putney pusher' suspect's death 'Putney pusher' suspect found dead at home Brandram had been arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm in relation to the incident in May 2017. He was linked to the incident in April this year when a person contacted officers with information that opened new lines of inquiry, according to the Met. His family has since claimed there is no forensic evidence linking him to the case. The Met said that it had not named Brandram publicly when he was arrested or at any point before his death. Ch Sup Dan Knowles said he recognised the "strain that being subject to a police investigation" could cause to individuals and their families. He confirmed that the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards would carry out the investigation. Video footage from May 2017 appeared to show a jogger pushing a woman into the road as a bus approached. The woman narrowly avoided being hit. Bus driver Oliver Salbris told the Sunday Times at the time: "If I hadn't swerved, I would have smashed her head." Detectives identified more than 50 people of interest following the incident. The Met had initially closed its investigation in 2018 after three men had been arrested and released without charge. The force said the investigation into the incident remained ongoing. title: Jeffrey Donaldson victim describes 'profound impact' of child sex abuse
description: The former DUP leader was found guilty of 18 counts of child sex abuse, including one of rape, in June.
body: Jeffrey Donaldson, pictured in May during his trial, was convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse The victims of child sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson have described the impact the abuse had on them. Donaldson was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children. The former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader appeared at Newry Crown Court for a hearing prior to his sentencing in October. He is seeking to appeal his convictions. The prosecution barrister told the court that one of the women said her childhood had been stolen, while the second said the abuse affected her every day. In her submission to the pre-sentencing hearing, Rosemary Walsh KC outlined what she described as the "salient facts" that were heard during the course of the trial. She also described the impact the offending had on both victims, whom were described during the trial as Complainants A and B. She said both complainants often wondered what life would have been like if they hadn't experienced the abuse. In her victim impact statement, Complainant A described the "profound impact" the abuse had on her. Walsh said the complainant believed her childhood had been "stolen" and that she felt an "enormous amount of anger that is always simmering away under the surface". Walsh said the abuse Complainant B had suffered affected her "every day and every relationship", and that she had to fight on a daily basis the wish that she would die. The prosecution barrister also outlined further aggravating and mitigating factors. She said, in sentencing, the youth of the victims had to be taken account, as well as the "multitude of offences", which "spanned a considerable period of time", and the fact there were two victims. Donaldson's defence barrister Keiron Vaughan KC told the court that the 63-year-old was "of previous good character" and that there had been no offending of this type over the last 18 years. "In that period of time, Mr Donaldson has or did achieve significant things in his life," he said. "I readily accept that these convictions obliterate all those achievements that he has made in his life, and that's certainly something he will have to live with." Vaughan said he acknowledged the court would impose a "lengthy custodial sentence", but that he had complete confidence that the court would treat Donaldson in the same way it would any other defendant of a similar age and in similar circumstances. Addressing Donaldson directly, Judge Paul Ramsey said: "Mr Donaldson, I will be sentencing you as soon as I can next month." His wife, Eleanor Donaldson, 60, faced a trial of the facts on mental health grounds, meaning she was not required to participate in the proceedings. She was accused of five related charges, including four counts of aiding and abetting. She was found to have done the acts of which she was accused – a verdict which she is to appeal. Eleanor Donaldson cannot be given a prison sentence, she could, however, be given a treatment order or an absolute discharge. She was not required to participate in the proceedings. However, Judge Ramsey told her defence barrister Ian Turkington KC that in dealing with her, he "would like to be able to speak directly to her" and therefore requested that she appear via video link if she is deemed medically fit to do so. title: Rapist and grooming gang members who preyed on children jailed
description: The court heard the men met in a popular coffee house in Rhyl, with the girls approached on the street.
body: This video can not be played Police release footage of grooming gang members Four men and a woman who preyed on teenage girls in north Wales have been jailed for their roles in a grooming gang. The victims of the group were aged 14, 15 and 16 at the time of the abuse in the seaside town of Rhyl, Denbighshire. The ringleader of the gang Mustafa Iqbal was jailed for 35 years after being convicted of 21 offences, including four rapes and three of sexual assault involving all three of the girls. Three other men and a woman were also jailed for their roles. It followed one of the most complex investigations carried out by North Wales Police into sexual exploitation, much of it in secret with the offenders unaware the case was being built against them. In August 2025 during a series of co-ordinated police raids across Rhyl, the men involved were arrested. During a trial, jurors heard how a popular coffee house was used for the men to meet each other, with the girls approached on the street. They were then given cannabis, and asked to play a game of "spin the bottle" before being abused. "This investigation was really complex," explained Det Ch Insp Richard Sidney, the man leading the inquiry. "First of all we had the challenges of getting the accounts from the victims, they were really difficult accounts to give. "They had to show real strength in doing that." Jailed for their roles in a grooming gang exploiting teenage girls in north Wales: (Clockwise from top left) Mustafa Iqbal, Mohamed Arshad, Jaswinder Singh, Sarah Gray, and Ziaullah Badshah The police team then had to analyse hundreds of hours of CCTV footage, phone records and travel patterns to piece together the true picture of the abuse being carried out. "Our focus as a team was getting justice for the victims and safeguarding the community," said the senior detective. The investigators spent several weeks gaining the trust of the three victims as they slowly revealed what had happened to them. It involved help from social service teams and charities, including the children's charity Barnado's, along with specialist support from the Hydrant Programme - a national police initiative to tackle child abuse, external. The first two victims of the sexual exploitation gang were approached near this Rhyl petrol station by Mustafa Iqbal "I don't think I could articulate how difficult it was for them," said Det Sgt Keira Williams, another key member of the investigation team. "We just made sure we went at their pace, they were allowing us insight into what it was like to be the victim of an incredibly horrendous crime. "The most we could do was be patient and allow them to give us their account in their own time." Det Sgt Keira Williams says patience and expert help was needed to coax the victims' accounts from them over many weeks During a trial over three months, a jury at Caernarfon Crown Court heard how Mustafa Iqbal initially targeted a 14 and 15-year-old he spotted in Rhyl in April 2022. The 43-year-old persuaded them to go back to his home in the town, where they were later joined by local coffee shop owner, Mohamed Usman Arshad and his friend Ziaullah Badshah. The jury heard how the two girls claimed they were 17, smoked cannabis with the men and played a game of "spin the bottle". Badshah, who is 25 and arrived in Rhyl as a refugee from Pakistan when he was 15, admitted kissing 15-year-old Child B and 14-year-old Child C there, and on later occasions having sex with Child B at his own home in the town. Arshad, 36, denied he had ever had a sexual relationship with Child B, but was found guilty of rape, after a sex act in an alleyway outside his former business - Zayn's Coffee House. Iqbal was also found guilty of raping Child B, and also sexually assaulting Child C. This former Rhyl cafe owned at the time by Arshad linked the men in the grooming gang The coffee house was one of the key connections linking the offenders, where the abusers either helped out or met. At the time, it was voted the town's business with the friendliest staff - masking the dark secrets held by owner Arshad and the rest of the grooming gang. It was also there at the coffee shop that the final man in the conspiracy became involved, ultimately leading to it being uncovered. Jaswinder Singh, 61, would let Arshad drive his car, when they would pick up Child B and C, driving them around. Under the pretence of asking 15-year-old Child B to look after his dog, the British-born former builder persuaded her to join him on a trip to London to meet family and friends. But there, an adult raised concerns about Singh's real motive, and alerted the police. Iqbal refused to answer questions when quizzed about abuse by police, stating "no comment" As well as being involved in the Rhyl take-away food scene, he was known as a local drug dealer. It was in that role he began grooming another victim, 16-year-old Child A. He supplied her with crack cocaine and cannabis in return for sex. He roped in the help of 53-year-old Sarah Gray from nearby Gronant with the offer of more drugs if he could use her home to carry out the abuse. But again concerns about the victim were flagged to police, reopening the entire investigation into the gang. Those at the centre of the abuse refused to acknowledge they had been involved. Iqbal gave police a no comment interview, and later during his trial refused to take to the witness stand to defend his actions. Married cafe owner Arshad tried to convince the jury he was an upstanding member of the Rhyl business community who would not risk his reputation by carrying out sexual acts in view of his own premises. Badshah, the youngest of the groomers, insisted he only discovered the victims age when he found himself under arrest. Meanwhile, Singh portrayed himself as nothing more than a jovial friend who liked a drink and talked a lot. The jury did not believe them. "I think all the way through the investigation we saw

title: Internet restricted after fighting breaks out in Ethiopia's Tigray region
description: During the two-year civil war in Tigray, the region was totally cut off from the outside world.
body: The internet was cut in Tigray during the two-year civil war which ended in 2022 (file photo) Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray following the outbreak of fighting this week between regional forces and the national army. Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray. "Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme. The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment. Sources have told the Reuters news agency that the group which controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), ordered the communications blackout, with one suggesting it was to disrupt government drones. The TPLF has not commented. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. Even before the current disruption, finding video and images to establish what is happening on the ground has been a challenge. So far, other than footage from Mekelle, most of what has been shared online has been from outside the region. The young women who fought in Ethiopia's last civil war and don't want to see another one Burbridge said there had been a scarcity of cash in Tigray for the past eight months, with people unable to access ATMs so the lack of internet services would be "devastating for everybody". Many people rely on banking and mobile money applications for transactions, with the majority using Ethio Telecom and Safaricom's networks to access these services. On Thursday a Mekelle resident who we are only identifying as Fitsum made a similar point. He told the BBC "there is almost no cash" in the city. With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he said. This video can not be played Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting fears of a return to a full scale civil war and reports of panic buying. A humanitarian source in the neighbouring region of Afar told the AFP news agency there was "heavy fighting overnight", including drone strikes, around the town of Abala in the mountains between Afar and Tigray, as "federal forces pushed the rebels from entering the town". During the two-year conflict which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world. Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions. It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - with estimates that some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government. On Wednesday, its forces seized control of three airports from federal police. There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in Amhara, as well as Afar. Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray. title: From shaky start to statement wins - 100 days of McInnes at Rangers
description: BBC Scotland charts the first tumultuous 100 days of Derek McInnes' tenure as Rangers manager.
body: Derek McInnes goes into the international break in a good place with Rangers following two wins over great rivals Celtic Derek McInnes has been in charge for 100 days at Rangers - the club he grew up supporting, played for and previously turned down the opportunity to manage. In his brief but busy tenure, there has been a huge squad overhaul, while a sluggish start led to Ibrox jeers and the failure to qualify for European football for the first time in a decade. Then came September. A golden start to autumn quietened talk of crisis as a winning streak extended to six games, including two Old Firm derby victories. BBC Sport Scotland charts the key moments of McInnes' reign. Penrice focuses on Rangers as Scotland remains a target How derby masterclasses provide stark Rangers contrast I wasn't good enough for Rangers - Ure One month and one day after his Heart of Midlothian side were pipped to the title by Celtic on the final day of last season, McInnes is announced as Rangers manager, replacing the departed Danny Rohl. It is 26 years since his days as a Rangers player ended with a move to West Bromwich Albion and eight-and-a-half years since he turned down the chance to become boss under the chairmanship of Dave King. "It is no secret that I grew up a Rangers supporter and I am convinced this is the right time to take on this prestigious role," McInnes says. "There is a lot of hard work ahead." The new era begins at Tannadice with a whimper rather than a bang as Thelo Aasgaard scores a second-half equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Dundee United. "We worked hard to get back into it, but I don't think we were good enough to win the game," McInnes says. "I thought the point was the right scoreline and we're disappointed with that first half. "We wasted a lot, we didn't create too much and it was a bit too frantic." Curtain up on Rangers European campaign - and it does not start well. A trip to eastern Poland in the first leg of their Europa League third qualifying round tie ends in a 2-1 defeat by Jagellonia Bialystok. McInnes notes: "I just felt we beat ourselves, to be honest. We got off to a good start, being patient with what we were trying to do. We made two mistakes for the two goals." Callum Wright's late goal gave Hibernian victory at Ibrox Rangers' first home match of the season ends also ends in a 2-1 defeat, this time by Hibernian. A late Callum Wright goal seals victory for the Edinburgh side and, to make matters worse, striker Youseff Chermitti suffers an ACL injury that scuppers any potential big-money sale amid reports of interest from Galatasaray. "There are little things going against us at the minute, but we have to stay strong - we're not as bad as people think," McInnes insists. "At the minute, we are trying to work boys back to the same level of fitness and trying to manage that situation. "I understand the fan frustration. They want and expect to see their team win. I share the frustration." Another below-par performance has supporters up in arms. Shankland scores from the penalty spot, but a second-half goal from Nik Prelec earns Jagellonia a draw on the night and progress on aggregate. McInnes confesses: "It is not great to watch. My team go from some good highs in the first half to being as poor as we were in the second half and you have to say we didn't do enough. We should be winning this game." Five games into the new season and Rangers record their first win under McInnes - an emphatic 5-1 thumping of holders St Mirren in the Premier Sports Cup. "We gave up a couple of chances, which we weren't too pleased about, but there was a good attacking threat from the team," McInnes concludes. "The players deserved that moment today against a St Mirren team who have been doing well." Derek McInnes' side bowed out of Europe, beaten by Lubos Kozel's Jablonec A penalty shoot-out defeat by the unfancied Czechs eliminates Rangers from Europe altogether. Missed spot kicks by Findlay Curtis and James Penrice hand victory to Jablonec after a 1-0 defeat. A bitter blow for the balance sheet too as the Ibrox club face up to life without European football proper for the first time in 10 years. "I'm embarrassed with the performance," McInnes says. "I think the only people who represented the club well tonight were my support staff and the supporters who, to a man, were outstanding, getting behind the team despite watching what we all watched." McInnes registers his first Scottish Premiership win as Rangers manager at his old stamping ground of Pittodrie. A Shankland penalty gets the job done, much to McInnes' relief as he praises Kim Min-Su as evidence that the summer recruitment is beginning to bear fruit. "It was a tough few days for us all," he says. "I thought we were far more like the Rangers team I want us to be." After a 2-1 success at Falkirk, a third successive Premiership win, but it comes at a cost as Shankland tears a hamstring against Motherwell at Ibrox and will be sidelined for months. Ryan Nederi replaces the captain and scores the only goal. "We'd have taken any sort of win because we're up against a good team, but I really enjoyed how many chances we created," McInnes says. It looks like Rangers' winning run is coming to an end until Bojan Miovski comes off the bench to score a stoppage-time winner at home to St Mirren to spark wild celebrations. Rangers move into second place in the Premiership, five points behind leaders Celtic. With four wins on the bounce, McInnes is sounding more optimistic. "There are obviously loads we have to improve on, but we have to keep winning while we are looking for those improvements," he says. McInnes demanded a big performance from his players in his Old Firm managerial debut - and he got it. He pulled a few tactical surprises and they paid off as Rangers power into the Premier Sports Cup semi-finals. Two goals from the inspired Dan Neill and a first for

title: Giant veg records smashed despite 'bonkers' summer
description: Seven records are thought to have been broken at the National Giant Vegetables Championship.
body: Ian Paton has won the largest pumpkin category, after growing the second largest pumpkin in world Seven giant vegetables are believed to have smashed Guinness World Records as competitive growers showed off their supersized produce at competition. The provisional records were set on Friday at the National Giant Vegetables Championship, part of the Malvern Autumn Show at the Three Counties Showground in Worcestershire. Among the potential record holders was a 26.02kg (4st 1.8lb) beetroot, a 7.808kg (1st 3.2lb) sunflower head and a cucumber plant measuring more than 7.5m (24.6ft). The achievements came despite a challenging summer for growers, with record-breaker Graham Barratt - who presented the giant cucumber plant - describing the weather as "bonkers". Organisers said the seven records would need to be verified, with confirmation expected on Saturday. Vincent Sjodin may have broken the world record for the heaviest sunflower head There are awards for heaviest watermelon, cantaloupe melon and rhubarb Winner of the heaviest aubergine was Maggie Walters from Berkshire Tim Saint, from Reading, Berkshire, has been growing vegetables since he was nine years old Steve Harris said he was proud of his giant marrow, which weighed in at 23.5kg (3st 7lb) Any new world records are expected to be confirmed on Saturday Barrett said his success had come down to feeding the vegetable the "right things at the right time", but this year's hot and dry weather had made growing more difficult. "This year, only one word can describe it - bonkers," he said. "You've had to look after your plants more, you've had to keep them watered, fed... most things have finished too early for the show, so next year I think we have to learn to start the plants a bit later." According to the provisional results, the record breakers are: Peter Glazebrook - heaviest sweetcorn kernel - 0.408kg (0.8 lb) Graham Barratt - tallest cucumber plant - 7.598m (24.6 feet) Terry King - dandelion/weed with the longest root - 1.127m (3ft 7in) Vincent Sjodin - heaviest beetroot - 26.02kg (4st 1.8lb) Vincent Sjodin - heaviest sunflower head - 7.808kg (1st 3.2lb) Kevin Fortey - longest tromboncino - 1.486m (4ft 8ins) Kevin Fortey - heaviest luffa - 5.014kg (11.1lb) 'Why we flushed away Dragons' Den investment' Why council plans to offer buildings to advertisers Growers have faced unusually difficult conditions this year following a hot and dry summer, with many having to provide significantly more water to their crops. Steve Harris, who grew a 23.5kg (3st 7lb) marrow, described the process as a "balancing act". "Giant marrows need about 20 litres (5.2 gallons) a day to help them grow - so it's been a real balancing act to make sure they have enough to continue to thrive, but not so much they actually split," he said. Gloucester's Graham Barratt was the winner of the longest cucumber category, setting a provisional world record Derek Hulme, 65, from Stoke-on-Trent, said some giant pumpkin and marrow growers had seen their vegetables split because of the conditions. "The conditions have been so dry, we're watering more. But then the vegetables soak up more than it can actually cope with and then they split wide open." Neil Hands, who won the heaviest red cabbage category with an 18kg (2st 12lb) entry, said the heat had also caused problems. "It's too hot for my cabbages," he said. "They need it to be cooler. I've just been watering and watering." David Hulme said growers need pay extra attention to their produce to succeed Despite those conditions, some enormous entries made it to Malvern. Ian Paton won the heaviest pumpkin category, while Jack Baggs took the heaviest marrow title with a 107kg (16st 12lb) entry and Curtis Leach won the squash category with one weighing 279.5kg (44 st). Maggie Walter, from Plymouth, took home a £1,000 prize after her 3.95kg (8.7lb) aubergine was judged the heaviest. She said she "never expected" to win and described the victory as a "nice surprise all round". Walter grew eight aubergine plants in a polytunnel using irrigation from a borehole, but said several had gone soft when they came to harvest them. "We parted the foliage a bit more and at the back there was this bad boy," she said of her winning vegetable. All entries must have been grown in the UK, Channel Islands, Northern Ireland or Republic of Ireland, within the current growing season Other winners included Derek Richardson, whose 45.5kg (7st 2lb) swede topped its category, while Sjodin also produced the heaviest kohlrabi at 31.5kg (4st 13lb). Joe Atherton dominated several categories, growing the heaviest cantaloupe melon and onion, as well as the longest beetroot, carrot and parsnip. This year's championship attracted 597 entries from 169 growers competing across 33 categories. Tim Saint, from Reading, Berkshire, entered eight different types of giant vegetable, including a 304kg (47st 12lb) pumpkin. "I get up at 05:30 in the morning before work and as soon as I get home at 17:00 I'm out again until it's virtually dark," he said. Despite the work involved, Saint said meeting other growers at Malvern made the effort worthwhile. "Its like a gathering of the clan really," he said. "Everyone is so nice - it's like meeting your family." title: Special agents' blood and urine test results stolen in FBI hack
description: Experts say the hack could leave agents vulnerable to scams, blackmail and targeted attacks.
body: Cyber-criminals who hacked the FBI say they have extremely sensitive medical data for thousands of its special agents. BBC News has seen samples of the stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations, which contain information such as blood and urine test results, and doctors' notes mentioning conditions such as a "shellfish and banana allergy". The records include agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical concerns including 'blood in the urine' and 'high cholesterol'. Experts say the hack - which the FBI is investigating - could leave agents vulnerable to scams, blackmail and targeted attacks, as well as help criminals impersonate law enforcement officers. "The list maps thousands of agents against their medical and fitness records," said Etay Maor, vice-president of threat intelligence at Cato Networks. "Passwords can be reset if stolen, but medical records cannot, so once this data is out, it stays compromised for good. That permanence, applied across an entire workforce, is what makes this leak so serious." The FBI has not responded to requests for comment. However, on Wednesday it acknowledged the breach and said it was "aggressively investigating" how it happened. The cyber-criminal group ShinyHunters claims it breached FBI systems on Monday, and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site. The group also shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand. Unusually, the hackers are not demanding money. Instead, they are seeking a retraction of an FBI advisory published in May, which they claim "offended" them. The samples shared with journalists appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses. The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors. Professor Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, has described the hack - if confirmed - "as serious as it gets when it comes to data breaches." The news agency Reuters reports that some of the data includes information on agents, external involved in investigations relating to Russia, China and drug cartels. Reporting by 404 Media suggests details of a previously little-known FBI hacking unit may also have been exposed, external. It was initially thought the breach affected the FBI's 38,000 current employees, but the hackers now claim the number could be far higher. The group says it underestimated the scale of the data theft and now claims to hold sensitive information on around 60,000 current and former FBI staff. Jamie Akhtar, chief executive and co-founder of CyberSmart, said the hackers' claims should be treated with caution but that the breach appeared to be extremely concerning. "Such data could be used for highly convincing phishing, impersonation, identity fraud, blackmail or even operations targeting law-enforcement personnel, making the potential implications particularly serious," he said. The hackers, who communicate with reporters in English via the messaging service, Telegram, say they will publish the full dataset in five days unless the FBI meets their demands. ShinyHunters is an international hacking collective that has been active since 2019 and has been linked to a number of high-profile cyber-attacks, including incidents affecting Rockstar Games and the education platform Canvas. The group claims it exploited a vulnerability in an Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI, gaining access to multiple platforms including FBIJobs, FBI BEAST, which handles background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which stores medical records, and FBI BICS, which contains investigative information. In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was still trying to determine whether the hackers had breached its systems directly or compromised a third-party provider. "We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk," the statement said. title: Russell takes pole in Baku as Antonelli hits wall
description: George Russell takes pole position for Mercedes at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix as his team-mate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli crashes out.
body: George Russell beat Ferrari's Charles Leclerc by a massive 0.837 seconds George Russell took an imperious pole position for Mercedes at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix as his team-mate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli crashed out. Russell beat Ferrari's Charles Leclerc by a massive 0.837 seconds while Antonelli, who leads the Britain by 81 points in the championship, will start in 16th. The Italian hit the inside wall at Turn One in the first session and was knocked out. McLaren's Oscar Piastri was third ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar and McLaren's Lando Norris. Lewis Hamilton, compromised by running without a tow from another car, was sixth, ahead of the Alpine of Pierre Gasly and Red Bull's Max Verstappen. With a tow or slipstream worth as much as 0.5 seconds, Verstappen was following Norris on their final laps when the Briton made a mistake and went off track. That scuppered Verstappen's chances of competing closer to the front. But although the four-time champion said he believed he could have been on the front row, he acknolweged that he could not have beaten Russell. On a weekend in which Antonelli's running has been compromised by reliability problems that meant he missed out on half the possible running on Thursday, Russell absolutely delivered on Mercedes' dominant position on this unique track. Russell has looked comfortable all weekend and never looked in danger of being beaten for pole, his first since the Austrian Grand Prix at the end of June. "That's probably the biggest margin I've had in my whole career," Russell said. "The lap felt really sweet and the car has been feeling great all weekend." Kimi Antonelli's qualifying ended early when he hit the wall and broke the suspension on his Mercedes Leclerc was somewhat taken aback by Mercedes' superiority, saying that the position was what he expected but the gap most definitely was not. At the bottom of the top 10, there was finally some good news for Williams, for whom Carlos Sainz achieved the team's first top 10 qualifying performance of the year. Williams have introduced a new chassis this weekend which has brought them down to the weight limit for the first time this season, after being as much as 25kg over at the start of the year. Along with some additional developments, it appears to have produced a big step forwards, although the caveat is that Baku is a track that suits the characteristics of the Williams car and does not expose its weaknesses. Team-mate Alex Albon did not manage to secure a tow in the second part of qualifying, and was "anyway struggling with straight-line speed all session", and was 13th, just under 0.4secs behind the Spaniard. Antonelli's error came on his second lap of the first session. He turned into the first corner too early, and the left front wheel clouted the inside wall, breaking the suspension. He initially tried to get the car back to the pits but was told by engineer Peter Bonnington to park up. "Let me try," Antonelli pleaded, before Bonnington told him that either the track rod or upright was broken and there was no way Mercedes could fix that in the time they had to turn the car around before the next session. Antonelli had been on the back foot all Friday trying to catch up time lost to a hydraulic problem that had stopped his car on track halfway through first practice, and was not repaired until halfway into the second. It was Antonelli's first major mistake of the season since he crashed heavily in final practice at the first race of the season in Australia. title: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies
description: A gunman shot Jim Copenhaver twice while also killing another man and grazing Trump's ear with a bullet.
body: Copenhaver was one of three Trump rally attendees who was shot, as well as Trump, whose ear was grazed by a bullet One of the three attendees who was shot at Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has passed away from complications stemming from his injuries, according to the Pennsylvania attorney general. Jim Copenhaver, 76, was struck twice when a gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop. Another attendee, Corey Comperatore, was killed in the shooting and Trump's ear was grazed by a bullet. Copenhaver died on Wednesday at a hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, according to a statement from the Allegheny County medical examiner shared with local media. The gunman, 20-year-old Thomas Crooks, was killed by Secret Service after he opened fire. This video can not be played Months on, Trump shooting witness still stunned by security lapse In a post on his social media site Truth Social, Trump called Copenhaver a "true American patriot". "More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice," Trump said. "Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne." An attorney for Copenhaver's family said his dedication to the US was a "defining part of his life". "As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered," the lawyer said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News. In an interview with CBS a year after the Butler rally, Copenhaver and David Dutch, the third attendee who was shot, said they had been through infections and surgeries after being wounded. Copenhaver was shot in the arm and the abdomen. A year later, the bullet was still lodged in his body next to his spine, he told CBS, causing him to walk with a cane. Both Dutch and Copenhaver sued the federal government for damages in June, arguing the Secret Service failed to ensure their safety and was therefore liable for their injuries. Republicans in the US House of Representatives also paid tribute to Copenhaver on Friday, saying in a social media post: "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance." title: New-look squad, but how will Pocognoli's Scotland line-up?
description: Former Scotland forwards James McFadden and Pat Nevin try to guess who new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli will pick to start in Slovenia on Saturday.
body: Scotland have been training in La Manga, Spain Nations League: Slovenia v Scotland Saturday 26 September, 14:00 BST Showtime is fast approaching for Sebastien Pocognoli's Scotland. The Tartan Army are taking over the Slovenian capital of Ljubljana and their heroes will join them later on Friday when they fly in from La Manga for Saturday's opening Nations League game. Scotland's new head coach took a fair few fresh faces out to Spain, something that earned him early kudos from supporters who were calling for a bit of shake-up in the squad - but how does that translate to his team? Adding eight uncapped players to a 27-man squad - before releasing Findlay Curtis and James Wilson to the under-21s - is one thing, but will the line-up reflect such a shift when it drops on the national team's social media channels on Saturday afternoon? Former Scotland winger Pat Nevin thinks it would be "slightly bizarre" to see any more than two uncapped starters, while his fellow ex-international, James McFadden, insists the team will look "pretty similar" without any "big surprises". So is it a case of the more things change, the more they stay the same for Scotland? This video can not be played Bonus preview of Slovenia v Scotland with former internationals James McFadden and Pat Nevin Going by what we know of Pocognoli's past, many are leading with the assumption he will play a back-three in defence. The addition of Stephen Welsh, Luke Graham and Luis Binks - all new to the Scotland set-up - perhaps offers a sneak-peak as to what could come further down the line, but for now, will it be a more tried and trusted trio? Jack Hendry and Scott McKenna - although the latter now does have left-footed competition in Graham and Binks - appear to be favoured by most, but what of the the right centre-back? McFadden thinks pushing Brentford right-back Aaron Hickey there will help "drive" the team forward. "I hope the centre-backs aren't the players on the team who have the ball the most," the former Scotland forward said on the BBC's Scottish Football Podcast. "I don't want to see this centre-back to centre-back play. If they're getting it, I want them to drive and I think, if you had Hickey as a right-centre-back, he'd be driving into the play and trying to commit to going forward. "I don't want them just sitting in a safe position, playing around the back. I don't want to see that, it's boring." You are the new Scotland boss - what would you do? Pocognoli has 'positive nervousness' for Scotland debut Wilson & Curtis leave Scotland squad to join U-21s One player who is seldom boring for Scotland is Billy Gilmour. The midfielder's presence was missed at the World Cup, but after signing off from Serie A at the weekend with a goal for Napoli, he is returning ready to go. Nevin will be making a swift exit from the Stozice Stadium if Gilmour is not starting - where he will surely be beside Lewis Ferguson. "One of, if not the best player for us at the World Cup," McFadden said of the Bologna captain, who will surely look to his left and find captain Andy Robertson at wing-back. "You're not going to go and change the midfield up. I don't think there's a need for a change for change's sake. "I think that the freshness was needed, but I'm just looking forward to seeing them actually play and see if there's any difference in how they approach it - if they are more aggressive in a press and more dominant with possession." Central to that will be John McGinn. At times, Scotland have struggled to get the Aston Villa captain in his best position in midfield - and yet he still never fails to perform. With Scott McTominay missing from the squad as he recovers from successful minor heart surgery, Nevin suggested: "We need his explosiveness in the final third, so I would like to see him a little bit further forward." It is the same old names so far - with Bournemouth winger Ben Gannon-Doak operating somewhere down the right, dependent on Hickey's position - but we do know there will need to be a new-ish name up top of sorts. Even still, the favourite to lead the line is 16-time capped, Oli McBurnie. His exile from international football does mean he feels like a new addition - as does his words about his desire to perform on his long-awaited return. "He's coming back with a point to prove, which I like," McFadden said. "You've got someone who will give their all, which is how Oli plays anyway, and he'll feel privileged that he's got the opportunity to play again. "It's a big opportunity, because over the last couple of years we've been so used to seeing Che Adams, Lyndon Dykes and Lawrence Shankland, so it'll be nice to see a bit of freshness up there." That all leaves one spot up for grabs and, in this case, it's on the left of the front three. And Bournemouth's Ryan Christie is familiar with that responsibility. title: NHS to suspend staff suspected of snooping on patient records
description: There have been too many cases of staff abusing patient trust, and enough is enough, the head of the NHS in England says.
body: NHS staff in England suspected of looking at patient records without a valid reason will be immediately suspended as part of a "zero-tolerance crackdown" on snooping. Those under suspicion will also be locked out of NHS computer systems, preventing any further viewing of confidential records, including from home. NHS England chief executive Sir Jim Mackey has written to every trust, ordering the measures to be introduced immediately to strengthen protection against data breaches. The move follows a series of high-profile incidents involving the records of Nottingham and Southport attack victims and a child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire. This week, Bristol Foundation NHS Trust said it had launched an internal investigation after it emerged the medical records of an 18-year-old had been accessed years after his death. The boy's mother, Paula McGowan, told the BBC she was "deeply concerned and hurt" and called for the NHS to do more to deal with the problem. Oliver McGowan, pictured here with his mother Paula, died in 2016 after being prescribed anti-psychotic medication at Southmead Hospital in Bristol The NHS said the "hardline" approach is part of a wider crackdown, including the launch of a national campaign to "remind staff of their responsibilities and the serious consequences of unlawful access". "Patient records contain some of the most private information people will ever share," said NHS England's chief executive Sir Jim Mackey. "We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust, and enough is enough. "Anyone who thinks they can satisfy their curiosity by looking at a patient's record should know this: they will be found out, they may lose their career and could end up with a criminal record." This month, an investigation for the Health Services Journal found that at least 214 NHS staff have lost their jobs and around 2,000 been sanctioned for snooping on sensitive patient data over the past five years. In some cases, it emerged staff were curious about a high-profile patient and wanted to know more about their condition or care. Other staff have been struck off after looking up the medical records of relations, acquaintances and ex-partners without authorisation. In 2023 an NHS consultant in Cambridgeshire was investigated by the General Medical Council (GMC) after accessing the health history of a woman who had started dating the doctor's ex-boyfriend. There is no single NHS-wide electronic record system that every member of staff can access. Instead, organisations including GP practices, hospitals and specialist clinics maintain their own records and determine who can view particular information. IT systems keep an audit trail that should be able to show exactly who accessed a patient's records and when. Paula McGowan, whose autistic son Oliver died in 2016, was told that at least five members of staff at Southmead Hospital may have accessed his records without permission as recently as this year. Bristol NHS Foundation Trust said it was undertaking a "thorough investigation" and it would be "inappropriate to reach conclusions before those enquiries are complete". McGowan said she welcomed the NHS's commitment to tackling the problem but said it must now be followed by "meaningful action". "Medical records contain deeply personal information about people and their families," she said. "Accessing them without a legitimate clinical or professional reason is a serious breach of trust and must have consequences." title: FA Cup tie to be replayed after ref's error - will it set a precedent?
description: Mulbarton Wanderers are "deeply upset" after being told they must replay their FA Cup qualifying tie with Woodford Town because of a referee's error.
body: This season's FA Cup competition began on Friday, 7 August An FA Cup tie between Mulbarton Wanderers and Woodford Town is making the headlines because of a refereeing error which has caused a replay. So what sets this apart from other matches impacted by an error from officials? And could we see it happen in leagues which have the video assistant referee (VAR)? For example, there were 25 VAR errors last season. This season an error has already been publicly acknowledged after Manchester United lost 1-0 at home to Manchester City. Mulbarton, who won the tie 2-1 on the day, say they are "deeply upset" after their opponents lodged a protest because a goal scored from a penalty was ruled out. The referee disallowed Woodford's goal for encroachment by a number of attacking players and awarded Mulbarton an indirect free-kick. Law 14 states, external that the referee should have ordered the penalty to be retaken. A Football Association sub-committee found there had been a technical error by the referee and ordered the match to be replayed on Tuesday. So deciding if a game should be replayed comes down to whether a referee has made a simple subjective judgement call, or whether the decision should not have been given because it is not part of the laws of the game. Mulbarton, who play in the Isthmian League North, claim the decision to replay the game could lead to "wider implications regarding the finality of results" and the "integrity of the game as a whole". Yet matches being replayed because of a misapplication of the laws is more common than you might think, and it can happen for a variety of reasons. A Spartan South Midlands League fixture between Edgware Town and Harefield United in 2006 is thought to be the first in English football to be ordered to be replayed, external because of a referee's error. It was a carbon copy of the Mulbarton-Woodford situation. Edgware scored a penalty, the referee spotted encroachment by the attacking team and gave an indirect free-kick to Harefield. It should have been a retake. Ordering a replay is far more likely to happen in a cup game, as the incorrect decision is considered to have had a direct impact on the outcome of a competition tie. In the league, it is just one match of a season-long tournament. Uefa made such a judgment for the first time in 2015 following a European Championship qualifier between England Under-19 women's team and Norway. Trailing 2-1, Leah Williamson scored England's stoppage time spot-kick, but the goal was disallowed because of attacking encroachment. Again, it should have been a retake. Uefa ordered the match to be restarted from the moment of the penalty, and the players reconvened five days later. Williamson scored from the spot, the game finished 2-2 and it took England to the Euros. There are other recent examples in England, too. An FA Vase tie was replayed last season after a referee's error over a penalty shootout. Last year, Bridlington Town were forced to replay their 2-1 FA Cup win against Knaresborough through no fault of their own. The refereeing team was wrong in law to refuse Knaresborough a fifth substitute during extra time. Crucially, it cannot just be a matter of subjective opinion or judgement - like getting a corner wrong, or awarding a disputed penalty. With the laws on encroachment relaxed in recent years, now requiring it to cause clear impact on an opponent, there was little case for an offence by Woodford. With the goal being scored, the only offence possible would be the encroaching attackers having put off the goalkeeper. It would be a stretch but still subjective. But even if you could justify the decision to disallow the goal, the restart should have been a retake. Other than the kicker committing illegal feinting, there was nothing in the laws about giving an indirect free-kick. Redbridge-based Woodford said the decision "ensures the tie can be concluded in accordance with FA Cup rules". The winners will host Gloucester City of the Southern League Premier Division South in the third qualifying round on Saturday, 3 October. Manchester City won 1-0 at Old Trafford after a VAR mistake handed them the only goal of the game The International Football Association Board is clear when it comes to mistakes by the video official. It states a match is not invalidated because of "wrong decision(s) involving the VAR". Let's take the goal in the Manchester derby. The VAR, Matt Donohue, did not make a judgement on the potential offside offence by Fernandez. Even then, this would still be a subjective assessment of Fernandez's impact on United's Lisandro Martinez and goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Even if Donohue had properly looked at it, this would not be considered a misapplication of the law, but just a mistake. The same would apply to Luis Diaz's disallowed 'offside goal' for Liverpool at Tottenham three years ago. The VAR, Darren England, came to the correct decision in law, but communicated this to the referee incorrectly. This is not considered an error of the laws of the game. In July 2020, the operator of the Premier League's goalline technology system had to apologise after an error denied Sheffield United a goal in their 0-0 draw at Aston Villa. Villa goalkeeper Orjan Nyland carried Oliver Norwood's 42nd-minute free-kick over the line but referee Michael Oliver did not receive a signal to indicate a goal. Also buried within VAR protocol is a clause which states "malfunction(s) of the VAR technology" cannot invalidate a result. 'Let's go, let's go' - inside catastrophic derby VAR mistake VAR did not even consider if Fernandez was offside - Webb Left in the dark - will fans ever get to hear live VAR audio? There was a fascinating case in the Eredivisie in December 2024. PEC Zwolle's late winner against RKC Waalwijk was ruled out for offside. The problem? title: Some BBC channels and radio stations 'may well' have to close, director general says
description: The BBC's financial situation "may well mean" some channels and stations close, Matt Brittin says.
body: This video can not be played 'We can't guarantee any programme or channel forever' - BBC Director General Matt Brittin The BBC's financial situation and changing audience habits "may well mean" some channels and radio stations have to close so resources can be invested in on-demand services, its director general has said. As the BBC seeks £500m savings, Matt Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever". He said: "The tight financial situation means that we're having to look at some of those decisions a bit sooner than we might like." Audience behaviour is also rapidly changing, he said. "If most of an audience is getting things on demand, we have to look the value and the cost of all of those different services." Brittin said his focus when making savings was to "minimise the impact on audience". He explained: "We might have some channels and services where maybe 100,000 people are watching the broadcast service but 500,000 are getting those programmes on iPlayer. "When's the right time to migrate that service fully to being on-demand? And part of my job is to safeguard value for money for the licence fee payer." The BBC should go "in different ways to reach audiences and we're locked into yesterday's model of how people consume content, and actually the audience is always already living in tomorrow's world", he said. In recent months, the BBC has announced a series of closures of jobs and programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live At The Apollo and Football Focus, and further cuts are expected. Laura Kuenssberg's full interview with Matt Brittin can be seen from Sunday Brittin took over as BBC director general in May after a decade as president of Google in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Asked by Kuenssberg if he would allow a programme to be made and presented by AI, Brittin replied: "I would do, within guardrails." He added: "We want to experiment with this technology and understand what it can and can't do, but I'm here because I believe in human creativity. "I don't think anything we do should be replaced by AI. I think there are lots of places where AI can help us make the licence fee go further, but also help us in our decision-making and creativity. But it's not a substitute for humans." He also warned of the danger of a handful of tech companies having too much control over information in the future. "We're also in this moment where AI is in takeoff. So I think there's a danger that six companies will control access to information in future and the creation of information and misinformation," he said. "Six companies, none of them European, let alone British. In that world, here's the BBC. It's the most trusted organisation by over half a billion people." Asked if he trusted big tech companies he replied: "There's a lot of platforms out there, so I wouldn't trust any platform innately. "And I think what you do is you keep under review how those things work and whether your content can show up in the right place and fulfil its mission. "I think the BBC and our apps and services should be the antidote to the algorithm. Everywhere else you go is driven by some commercial interest." The full interview will be broadcast BBC One and iPlayer on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, on 27 September, at 09:00 BST. title: Premier League joins call for Fifa reforms
description: The Premier League joins three of its top European counterparts in calling for "fundamental" reform of the way that world football's governing body Fifa is run.
body: The 2026 World Cup was hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico The Premier League has joined three of its top European counterparts in calling for "fundamental" reform of the way that Fifa is run, claiming its president Gianni Infantino has "actively promoted exploitative ideas". In a joint statement with Spain's La Liga, Germany's Bundesliga, and Italy's Serie A, the English top flight says it is speaking out "because we understand how Fifa's relentless expansionism affects everyone". The four leagues say the shake-up is needed to make world football's governing body "transparent, objective, proportionate and inclusive" and claim that "our sport cannot grow globally if its foundations are undermined". It comes days after Infantino proposed an external review of how Fifa operates amid the ongoing crisis over his failed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors, which sparked a global outcry. Referencing "one of the biggest abuses of power in Fifa's history", the four leagues say that "while football's stakeholders ultimately forced the withdrawal of the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, the conditions that led to FFE remain". The statement added: "The Fifa president has now acknowledged the need for reform, but it is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE – fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within Fifa, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference." That is known to be a reference to the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup after US President Donald Trump called Infantino asking for the striker's ban to be reviewed. "Fifa's governance problem goes far beyond the role of one individual," the leagues added. "The wider question is whether Fifa's president should simultaneously wield such regulatory, commercial and political power without effective checks and balances, including the agreement of affected stakeholders... governance that concentrates unchecked regulatory, commercial and political power in a single office, while relegating affected stakeholders to mere advisory status, is not fit for purpose." Fifa has been approached for comment. This video can not be played Fifa shouldn't be selling stake in World Cup - Masters The four leagues call on Fifa to; establish a permanent body representing key stakeholders, including leagues, clubs, and players from across men's and women's football which has "a meaningful role in [its] decision-making process". ensure "evidence-based decision-making", with any major proposal subject to an independent assessment evaluating the impact on all stakeholders. create a separation between Fifa's regulatory role and its commercial function via "robust institutional safeguards to preserve trust, legitimacy and accountability" with ethics, financial oversight and electoral bodies "that are genuinely independent of the Fifa administration and presidency". Two years ago, Europe's top leagues - along with players' union Fifpro - filed a legal complaint against Fifa with the European Commission over what they claimed was an "abuse of dominance" by world football's governing body over the expansion of the international fixture calendar and an alleged lack of consultation. Fifa denied that, and accused some leagues of "hypocrisy" and acting "without consideration to everyone else in the world". They claim that their legal action "is a consequence of a flawed governance framework in which Fifa can use its regulatory authority to advance its own commercial objectives without accounting for the impact on the economic and social sustainability of national competitions that affect all stakeholders. This must change now for the sake of football". Despite three confederations calling for him to step down, Infantino has said he will stand for re-election in March, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate. The four leagues want candidates to support their proposals and say: "Now is the moment to decide not only who will lead Fifa, but also how Fifa should be led. Leagues have a crucial role to play in this process, and we want to ensure that the voice of every league is heard." The letter is signed by Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League, Marc Lenz, CEO of the Bundesliga, Javier Tebas, president of La Liga, and Luigi De Siervo, CEO of Serie A. Last month Masters told BBC Sport that Infantino had "pressed the self-destruct button" by delivering "a self-inflicted wound" over FFE. title: Daniel Thomas pleads not guilty after dinghy slashed
description: Daniel Thomas is accused of criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy.
body: Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, appeared in court via videolink (file photo) Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has pleaded not guilty to criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the Channel with a knife. The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, was arrested after the livestreamed video on Tuesday. Thomas, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in Hampshire via videolink, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone. He pleaded not guilty to both charges and was remanded in custody until his next court appearance at Portsmouth Crown Court on 29 September. This video can not be played Police had been examining livestream footage appearing to show Daniel Thomas slashing at a migrant boat The court heard a crew member was on the boat while it was heard leaking air. Prosecutor Kevin Lucie, outlining the facts of the criminal damage charge, told the court that Thomas slashed an adrift boat with a knife and said: "You are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more." Deputy Chief Magistrate Tan Ikram said the case could have been heard in the magistrates' court but Mr Thomas elected to be tried at crown court. Far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson, was among those in the public gallery. Some supporters also gathered outside the court. Posting on social media after the hearing, Yaxley-Lennon said: "Danny is being remanded to prison. "His legal team will now prepare to fight at the crown court for his bail." Police were positioned outside the court Hampshire police previously said an arrest had been made after a "boat that had an emergency responder on board" was damaged in the Channel on Tuesday. Several hundred people gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke on Thursday evening, believing that Thomas was inside. The demonstration, which seemed to pass off peacefully, began shortly before 18:30 BST. Protesters stood on the road outside the building and could be heard chanting "free DT". The crowd began to disperse at about 21:45 after they learned of the charges against Thomas. title: Red Roses struggle to meet fans' selfie demands - Hunt
description: England scrum-half Natasha Hunt says it is no longer possible to satisfy fans' post-match requests for selfies and autographs, given the Red Roses' success and growth.
body: Natasha Hunt has won 90 Test caps for England England scrum-half Natasha Hunt says it is no longer possible to satisfy fans' post-match requests for selfies and autographs, given the Red Roses' success and growth over the past decade. Hunt, 37, made her England debut in 2011, when the team were regularly playing in front of three-figure crowds. Even in 2019, an attendance of 4,674 at the Women's Six Nations game against France set a new record for a standalone Red Roses game away from a Rugby World Cup. More than 50,000 tickets have been sold for Saturday's meeting with New Zealand at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium, a year on from a world record sell-out crowd of 81,885 who watched the Red Roses beat Canada to become world champions at the venue. "I didn't think ever in my lifetime I would be in a position where we'd get crowds the size that we do," Hunt told Rugby Union Weekly. "It is unbelievable and we definitely don't take it lightly. "We're so appreciative and we absolutely adore our fans and love them and what they do for us and have done for us. "But I do think we're in a tricky space at the minute where there's that expectation that everyone has to have a photo or a signature or something. "Sometimes you go and you see people and they will say 'can you go get Ellie [Kildunne]? Can you go get Meg [Jones]?' And I really can't because they're probably being bombarded by 700 people over there. "Some of the girls have had DMs saying 'it would have made our day, we're disappointed' and it breaks your heart because you want everyone to have the best time ever." Saturday, 26 September, 15:00 BST Live on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentary The same issue has emerged in women's football, with Women's Super League club Chelsea banning their players from posing for photos and signing autographs after matches - saying that although it was a "tough" decision, it was "no longer safe or sustainable". Former Chelsea and England defender Millie Bright previously expressed concern that players were become "collectibles" to fans, emphasising that "we are humans the same as you" in an Instagram post., external Hunt says players' performances, possible injury concerns, recovery schedule and family commitments can all affect their ability to interact with fans after games. "If one of the girls is injured or they've not had the best game, their capacity and energy to come to you and give back might be a little bit less than others on that day," she added. "I'm not saying we don't want to have the photos and autographs, but there is a cap on the time where we have to be back in the changing rooms doing the recovery. "And family is huge for us, let us see our families first. "We'll do everything we can to make your day, but just be aware we're doing our best so please just bear with us." The Red Roses have become the biggest draw in women's rugby on the back of thier on-pitch success and Rugby Football Union investment Hunt says that in the early days of her Test career, it wasn't possible to imagine such a problem. "It was everyone's parents at Esher Rugby Club back in the day," she added. "I would have been out there for 20 minutes, signed everything twice over, everyone had a chat with me, then gone in [to the changing room]!" The Red Roses have partly built their relationship with their growing fanbase by engaging as people, as well as players. Captain Jones' openness about her grief for her parents, and star full-back Kildunne's willingness to talk about her body dysmorphia are just two examples. A recent survey,, external carried out by The Good, The Scaz and The Rugby podcast, revealed a difference in what attracted different genders to women's rugby, with 62% of women, compared to 41% of men, saying they "watch women's rugby because I identify with the players' causes, interests or specific challenges that players face". title: Cyber attack on police force may have 'compromised' staff information
description: Dyfed-Powys Police says no personal data relating to the public was believed to have been accessed.
body: Dyfed-Powys Police say an investigation has been going on into the circumstances surrounding the incident, which was identified on 14 September A cyber attack on a police force in Wales may have resulted in staff information being "accessed or compromised". Dyfed-Powys Police said the hack had caused disruption to some non-emergency systems but no personal data relating to members of the public was believed to have been accessed. The force said the incident was identified on 14 September, and an investigation is under way. The Information Commissioner's Office, external (ICO) has been notified, with a spokesperson saying: "We can confirm we have received a breach report from Dyfed-Powys Police and we are assessing the information provided." Dyfed-Powys Police said it remained fully operational and its response to emergency incidents had not been affected. It said online and email contact services were unavailable for a period following the attack, but these had now been restored and 999 and 101 service had not been affected. The force said it was receiving support from cyber-security specialists and its systems had been subject to "precautionary measures" while specialist teams investigated the incident and worked to restore services safely. A spokesperson said: "At this stage, our investigation has found no evidence that members of the public's personal data has been accessed or compromised as a result of this incident. "We are, however, continuing to investigate whether any information relating to our staff may have been accessed or compromised, and are taking all appropriate steps to protect that information, and will provide appropriate advice to colleagues if required." They added they "understood the potential concern this may cause" and wanted to "reassure the public that we have and will continue to take all necessary steps to protect our information and maintain the security of our systems". The force said it would provide further updates when it was in a position to do so. The ongoing investigation is being managed by Tarian, the Regional Organised Crime Unit (ROCU) for southern Wales, and force systems are being monitored. The IOC spokesperson said anyone worried about their personal information can visit the ICO website for advice and support. "We advise checking regularly for updates from the organisation impacted and following their advice if they confirm that an individual's personal information has been compromised," they added. The area served by Dyfed-Powys Police includes Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion, Pembrokeshire and Powys, and equates to more than 500,000 people - a number that rises significantly with tourists each year. The force has 1,349 police officers, as well as 1,063 police staff, police community support officers (PCSO) and special constables, according to an information request in March 2026. title: Council is letting staff down with fire and rehire plans, says worker
description: Glasgow City Council announced the move after a stalemate in talks over a new salary structure to address equal pay issues.
body: Unison members during a previous strike outside Glasgow City Chambers A council worker has accused Glasgow City Council of letting staff down after it announced fire and rehire plans due to a stalemate over equal pay proposals. The council has threatened to sack more than 23,000 members of staff and then rehire them on new contracts after negotiations broke down with unions. The talks were about the council's plans to replace a pay system found to discriminate against mostly women workers. The changes would see the majority of staff unaffected or better off but they would cut pay for 11% of staff. Speaking on the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast one worker described the situation as "heart breaking". Joanne, a support for learning worker from Glasgow, said the local authority "had a cheek to say they care about their employees" after she read the council's message saying it was dismissing all staff. She was told two weeks ago she would be one of the workers facing a pay cut under the new system, leaving her "distraught". She will lost about £300 per year. She said: "I came away from my work crying, really, really upset. I couldn't believe that after 25 years service to Glasgow City Council I am getting let down yet again." She continued: "I am working with the most vulnerable children in society. I would put it to Glasgow City Council, please come and do my job for one day, one day only and tell me that I am a detriment in my wages. "It is so wrong and I can't afford to lose money." Glasgow City Council to fire and rehire over 23,000 employees Hundreds of council workers face wages cut in end to equal pay row At a meeting last month, the council agreed to an overhaul of its pay and grading structure after eight years of negotiations. The council has previously paid over £770m to 19,000 claimants after it emerged that female workers in roles such as catering or cleaning were paid less than those in male-dominated areas such as refuse collection. The new system would see 63% of those affected gain financially while 11% would have their wages reduced. It was calculated after a job evaluation that looked at each role within the local authority. This saw staff being given questionnaires to fill out, and in some cases interviewed about their job. Each evaluation was based around 13 different factors. Categories included physical effort, mental skills, concentration and physical co-ordination. The job evaluation then provided a score for each role within the council, with those scores used to establish which pay grade - out of a possible 12 - each job should sit in. However, this has resulted in some roles being moved onto lower salaries than they were previously on, with the highest drop in wages expected to be around £11,500. Are you a Glasgow City Council employee? How have you been affected by the fire-and-rehire decision? Every member of non-teaching staff employed by the council will be issued with a letter of dismissal, including chief executive Susanne Millar, nursery staff and refuse collectors. They would then be offered new contracts set to begin on 1 January. Changes to UK-wide employment law will come in effect on the same date which would make dismissing an employee for refusing to accept contract changes automatically become an unfair dismissal. Glasgow City Council says it will fire around 23,000 workers and then rehire them Talks earlier this week between the council and the GMB, Unison and Unite unions fell apart on Wednesday when Unison said it would not ballot its members on a proposed new pay offer. The council said its new proposals would protect those workers who set to lose out for an extra six months, and it accused Unison of "betraying" members by not giving them the chance to vote on it. In response, Unison's education convener Sylvia Haughey told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast the council was using "bullying tactics". She said: "We haven't betrayed anyone, we certainly haven't betrayed our members. We are out fighting for our members. "We are fighting for the members who are in detriment who are losing big financial amounts, whether its £200 or £12,000. "We have not walked away from anything. We are willing to speak to the council at any time." In a statement on Wednesday, the council's director of communications and corporate governance Colin Edgar said the breakdown of talks meant there was now "no agreed way forward between the council and the joint trade unions". "The council has gone as far as it can," said Edgar. "The new pay and grading scheme removes unequal pay and sees pay rise or stay the same for 90% of staff – the council's total pay bill will be substantially higher. "For those staff who are in detriment our joint trade unions negotiated an increase in pay protection from six months to 12 months." The Scottish government's health secretary Neil Gray told BBC Scotland: "I would encourage all those involved, all partners, Glasgow City Council and the trade unions involved to get round the table and to negotiate. "This government supports fair work principles, and we would want fair work principles driving the employment of workers." Both the GMB and Unite unions were in favour of balloting their members over the proposed pay structure. Before the council announcement both unions said they had secured an extra £110m to be added into the salary structure. However, Unison said the extra funding was for "assimilation and arrears", and would not help the staff facing wage cuts. The GMB and Unite unions both criticised the decision to go ahead with fire and re-hire, with Unite calling it a "scandalous threat". Scottish Secretary, Douglas Alexander, said the council's action comes just months before UK government legislation will make fire and rehire schemes illegal, a move he called "the biggest upgrade to workers' rights in a generation." title: Strategy will safeguard nature for generations
description: Local Nature Recovery Strategy is approved for one of England's "most nature-depleted areas".
body: The first Local Nature Recovery Strategy for West Northamptonshire has been approved More tree planting, wetland restoration and drainage work could take place in parts of Northamptonshire to "safeguard nature for generations to come". West Northamptonshire Council has approved its first Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) which was required by the Environment Act 2021 and is the responsibility of all authorities. It said the area was one of England's "most nature-depleted areas" and its wildlife sites "are often small, in poor condition, and isolated from one another". Working with a range of partners the council hopes to improve landscapes that are "under unprecedented pressure" with some species in decline. A spokesperson for the council said: "A healthy natural environment is essential for tackling climate change and wider environmental challenges. "The diversity of habitats and species provide essentials such as clean and plentiful water, food, clean air, productive soil, flood protection, shading and cooling, as well as benefits like space for recreation, exercise and wellbeing." Nigel Stansfield, Reform UK's cabinet member for environment, recycling and waste, said: "Our aim is to safeguard nature for generations to come, and create cleaner, greener spaces that meet the needs of local communities and offer them an opportunity to connect with nature." He said it was vital to have a workable strategy that sets out "how we intend to safeguard nature for generations to come." Stansfield added he hoped the strategy would get organisations, landowners and local people to take action "to ensure our natural environment becomes more robust and resilient to provide the benefits we often take for granted".
