title: Noah Woods left playground through gap in fence, inquest hears
description: Noah's mother tells parents to "hold their children a little tighter and cherish every moment".
body: Noah's family said he was a "happy, cheeky, playful" boy Three-year-old Noah Woods, who was found dead in a pond following a huge search in Suffolk, had left a play area "through a gap in the fence", an inquest has heard. A major search was carried out in the village of Brantham after the toddler went missing on 15 September. His body was found the next day in nearby water by police divers. Assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said it was a "very sad and tragic death" as she opened and adjourned the inquest in Ipswich. A tribute issued by Noah's family called him a "happy, cheeky, playful" boy who loved to laugh, with his mother urging other parents to "hold their children a little tighter and cherish every moment". Suffolk Coroner's Court heard from police that Noah had left the playground, walked into a memorial garden and left that through an open gate. He then ran down a path on a new housing estate towards nearby Decoy Pond. Det Ch Insp Matt Connick from Suffolk Police told the court that CCTV showed Noah in the play area being looked after by a relative, which was "part of a normal routine". The detective said Noah "left through a gap in the fence leading to the memorial garden where he left through an open gate". After he had left the play area, he was closely followed by the relative trying to catch up with him, Connick added. The inquest heard the relative had shouted out to Noah, who lived in neighbouring East Bergholt, but he went out of sight shortly afterwards. Another man was said to have joined the search and then police were called. The written tribute from Noah's family said he was at the centre of their world. "He was part of a loving and caring family, living with his mummy, daddy and his little baby brother," it said. "Every Tuesday since the day he was born Noah went to the park with a treasured relative. They had the most wonderful relationship, they loved playing chase together, running around, and exploring the play equipment. "Those moments were filled with laughter and happiness and are memories our family will treasure forever. "Noah was being assessed for autism, although he had not received a diagnosis. He also had mild hearing loss and was speech delayed. "Despite the challenges he faced, he was learning every day. He was saying new words all the time and had only just started finding and using his little voice." Part of the tribute, from Noah's mother Charlie, said: "If there is one thing we could ask of people, it is to hold their children a little tighter, cherish every moment, and never take those precious memories for granted." Brantham is on the north bank of the River Stour estuary, beyond the railway line at the top of this picture At least 1,300 people helped to try to find Noah in the following 24 hours. Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border. Divers from the Metropolitan Police went into Decoy Pond on 16 September in an area where Noah was last seen. His body was found five metres from the edge within submerged tree roots, at a depth of 1.8 metres. Connick told the court that Noah's death was confirmed at 16:31 BST by paramedics and his identity was formally confirmed by his mother at Ipswich Hospital that evening. A post-mortem examination was carried out at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge, which the court was told "requires further investigation" before a final conclusion on the cause of death could be made. Noah's death was not being treated as suspicious by police. At the outset of the hearing, which was not attended by family, the coroner said: "I would like to express my deepest condolences to Noah's family and friends and all those affected by Noah's death." A date for the full inquest has not been set. Do you have a story suggestion for Suffolk? Contact us below. Follow Suffolk news on BBC Sounds, Facebook, external, Instagram, external and X, external. title: Back and loving it - Pietersen on his history, Brook & helping win the Ashes
description: Former batter turned specialist mentor Kevin Pietersen talks about his new role with England, his past history with the ECB and working with Harry Brook and Brendon McCullum.
body: Pietersen was dropped after the 2013-14 Ashes defeat and director of cricket Andrew Strauss later said there was a "massive trust issue" between the two Kevin Pietersen is asked, after everything that came before, what he would have said if told he would work for the England and Wales Cricket board again one day. In 2014, he was sacked by the ECB in one of most ugly and acrimonious periods in English cricketing history – a period that brought one of the most exciting but divisive international careers to an end. "What do you think I'd have said," Pietersen says with a smile. Bigger stars in English cricket are harder to find. This is the man who had a brief but high-profile relationship with American celebrity Caprice, married a pop star, Jessica from Liberty X, and once tried to explain cricket to Taylor Swift on The Graham Norton Show. Back in the dressing room as a mentor, he is speaking to the media at Headingley - the location of his famous "it's tough being me" press conference. The hair is greyer, but he still carries all of that aura. "I'm 46, man," he says, asked whether animosity remains. "That stuff is so long gone. I am a completely different person. "I live in South Africa. I love doing what I do. I am just here to help Brendon first and foremost, help the players try and become the best versions of themselves." Listen to Pietersen's interview with Test Match Special Pietersen was the most intriguing of appointments to England's dressing room staff because of his own history, but also what he has said before. While commentating on England's white-ball tour of India last year, he suggested the Brendon McCullum outfit were not training enough. "Clearly the perceptions I had before being asked to do the job were completely different to what I feel now," he says. "It is nice to being part of an England team and set-up that is actually really, really driven." Pietersen answers every question with poise. Almost all are given and lengthy, considered responses. His only terse response comes when pushed on what exactly those preconceptions were - and how quickly they took to disappear. "You know what the preconceptions were," he says. "I am not going near it." Pietersen played 104 Tests, 136 ODIs and 37 T20s Despite that, he appears to be loving his return. Pietersen is "not sitting here wanting to be the coach of England" but wants to help McCullum and the players, many of whom grew up idolising him. One of those, Tom Banton, said last week he is still in awe of the four-time Ashes-winner, so much so he was struggling to build up the courage to speak to him. "He wants a YouTube channel," Pietersen laughs. Pietersen, a 50-over great who played in a way ahead of his time, can also help him there. His official title is "specialist mentor" and he will dip in and out to work with the white-ball teams through to the 50-over World Cup next autumn. Before the first ODI in Durham, England posted a clip on social media of Pietersen leading a batting session. Holding court, he had Joe Root and Rehan Ahmed alike involved in a batting drill on how to rotate the strike against spin. "All I want to be is a great person to these guys," Pietersen says. "I want to be the best guy in the room, so that they come to me, and they ask me for information, and if I've got stuff for them, I'll give it to them. "I am lucky to have worn every T-shirt an England cricketer can wear – the good, the bad the ugly. "I can potentially help them to stay away from the ugly." Pietersen's eyes roll slightly when he is asked about Ben Stokes' recent comments comparing Harry Brook's talents to his. Pietersen, like Brook, was a maverick – a batter capable of incredible highs. Those highs mean the lows come with a disproportionate level of criticism. "Where I can help him is playing situations, because there was a lot of method in my madness," Pietersen says. "Yes, occasionally, I got out to reckless shots and crazy shots in the '80s and '90s but there was a lot of structure to the way that I batted. "I've still got notes on my phone on how I played in T20 cricket, one-day cricket, Test match cricket, and about hitting straight back at the stumps, and the techniques, and how I did it, and don't play certain shots. "That all-round structure is something I could potentially help him with because he's so flipping good. "It's actually frightening how good he is and how good he can be." And Pietersen says he will not limit himself to working purely on white-ball cricket. He has already spoken to new Test coach Stephen Fleming about how he can help the Test batters during his time with the white-ball squads. Though he said he would not have time for a full-time role, he suggested he is open to working with the Test side before next summer's home Ashes series. "I have got a pretty mad schedule," he says. "I wouldn't say no. "I don't think that necessarily means I need to be in a dressing room. "There is a lot of time in the lead up to an Ashes series and a tour of South Africa, when I will be with the Test batters. "There are conversations I can have there." Who knows how long this will last. England may as well make the most of this second chance. title: Israel game should not go ahead - Republic of Ireland's Knight
description: Jason Knight has become the first Republic of Ireland player to publicly voice his opposition to playing Israel on Sunday.
body: Jason Knight made his Republic of Ireland debut in 2020 and has won 44 caps Jason Knight has become the first Republic of Ireland player to publicly voice his opposition to playing Israel on Sunday. The sides are due to meet in Debrecen, Hungary at 19:45 BST, with the return fixture in Backa Topola, Serbia on 4 October. Since the sides were drawn together in Group B3, there has been increasing calls in Ireland to withdraw from the games due to the ongoing war in Gaza with a 'Stop The Game' campaign gathering pace. Speaking before Thursday's 1-0 defeat by Kosovo in Pristina, Republic stand-in skipper Dara O'Shea confirmed the players would meet on Friday to discuss their approach to Sunday's 'home' game against Israel, which will have no Irish fans in attendance, before their behind-closed-doors match the following week. "Look, it's difficult, the manager, and Dara, and Nathan [Collins] spoke well about it, I don't think the game should be going ahead but it is going ahead," Knight said following the Kosovo game. "We'll have a deeper talk about it and what that means, we'll get our thoughts as a group and go from there. "I think it was a difficult one. It's obviously big talk in Ireland. I have been focusing on my football in England in the Championship. But I knew this was coming so I had a think about it." 'Don't put pressure on us' over Israel games - Ogbene Israel player sent off for goal celebration Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN). "We had chats about it with the players, and more senior players on what the step will be," added Bristol City midfielder Knight. "Now we're here, we can have a really in depth talk of what that means and what the consequences are. We'll do that [on Friday] and go from there. "I am quite experienced. None of us have gone through this scenario before but I'd like to think I'm experienced, thick skin and can get through most things and that is what I will try and do. "I'll try and focus on the football as much as I can. I'll give my view and my thoughts on when I see fit, but I'll be trying to focus on the football as much as possible." title: Jay-Z rape accuser says her allegation was false
description: A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 now says she has never met the rap superstar.
body: Jay-Z, pictured at the Met Gala in May 2026, previously hit out at the "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations" A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 has formally said her allegation was untrue. The unnamed woman filed a lawsuit in 2024 claiming she had been drugged and raped by Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, and Sean "Diddy" Combs at a party after the MTV Video Music Awards in 2000. The stars denied the allegation and she dropped the lawsuit last year. Carter then sued her and her lawyers. In a statement filed in that case on Thursday, she wrote: "Shawn 'Jay-Z' Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr. Carter. Mr. Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever." The woman, known in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, also said: "My claims that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me while a third celebrity, [name redacted] watched are false. There is no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter. "I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone." Carter had vehemently denied the accusations, saying they were a "blackmail attempt" and describing them as "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations". When the accuser dropped her case in February 2025, the rapper, who is married to singer Beyoncé, said: "The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed." The woman, from Alabama, has now been removed from Carter's lawsuit. She said she had not received any money from the rap superstar or anyone acting on his behalf, and had not been paid to make her latest declaration. The rapper is still suing the woman's former lawyers, led by Tony Buzbee. In a statement to Rolling Stone, external, which first reported Jane Doe's new declaration, Buzbee said he had not seen it. He said: "We have multiple lawyers (at least four) who dealt with Ms Doe long before she met me. She gave the exact same story to each. If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that's new information." When Carter filed his lawsuit against the woman and her lawyers in February 2025, Buzbee claimed at the time that Carter's investigators had "repeatedly harassed, threatened and harangued this poor woman for weeks, trying to intimidate her and make her recant her story". In her new declaration, the woman said: "I never received any threat from Mr Carter or anyone acting on his behalf." Setting out the events that led to her allegation, the woman said she saw an advert on Facebook in September or October 2024 looking for people who might have sexual assault claims against Combs. "The ad triggered memories of being raped when I was 13 years old," she said. She was contacted by a law firm but was not provided with a draft of the lawsuit containing her allegations and did not authorise it before it was filed in October 2024, she said. She also said Buzbee and other lawyers acting on her behalf filed it "without conducting any independent investigation, background inquiry, or due diligence, and without obtaining any corroboration of the allegations". She said: "The October Complaint alleges that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me when I was a minor while an unnamed celebrity watched. As discussed above, these allegations were false." Buzbee also represents numerous other people who have made allegations against Combs. Combs denied Jane Doe's claims, which his lawyer described at the time as one of a number of civil cases "pushed forward by an attorney more focused on media headlines than legal merit". The BBC has contacted Buzbee for comment. In July 2025, Combs was convicted by a criminal court on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends, and is currently serving a four-year prison sentence. title: No action taken against Iranian man who tried to enter nuclear base
description: The 34-year-old was arrested in March after trying to access the Faslane base in Argyll and Bute, home to the Royal Navy's nuclear submarine fleet.
body: The 34-year-old had been arrested at HM Naval Base Clyde near Helensburgh, in March No action is to be taken against an Iranian man who tried to enter the Faslane nuclear submarine base earlier this year. The 34-year-old was arrested at HM Naval Base Clyde near Helensburgh, Argyll and Bute, on 19 March, along with a 31-year-old Romanian woman. The Crown Office said it had carefully considered the case and decided there should be no further proceedings against the man. It had previously said in March that no proceedings would be brought against the Romanian woman. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland The man had been charged, but was later released pending further inquiries without appearing in court. Faslane, on the Gare Loch about 25 miles (40km) north-west of Glasgow, is the home of the Royal Navy's nuclear-powered submarine fleet. Those include the UK's four Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines which carry Trident nuclear missiles. The March arrests came a few weeks after the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February. The Crown Office said: "The Procurator Fiscal received a report relating to a 34-year-old man and an incident said to have occurred on 19 March 2026. "After careful consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, including the available admissible evidence, the procurator fiscal decided that there should be no proceedings taken at this time. "The Crown reserves the right to proceed in the future should further evidence become available." title: Man in court charged with murder over north Belfast shooting
description: Robbie Lawlor was shot multiple times outside a house in Etna Drive in Ardoyne in April 2020.
body: Robbie Lawlor was 36 and from Dublin A 41-year-old man has appeared in court charged with the murder of Robbie Lawlor, who was shot dead in north Belfast in April 2020. Lawlor, 36, who was from Dublin, was shot multiple times outside a house in Etna Drive in Ardoyne. Paul Drew, with an address in Whitebrook Park, Tallaght, Dublin, has also been charged with possession of a firearm or ammunition with intent to endanger life or cause serious damage to property. He was arrested in Liverpool on Wednesday. At Belfast Magistrates' Court on Friday, Drew spoke only to confirm he understood the charges against him. Robbie Lawlor had been a suspect in the abduction and murder of Drogheda teenager Keane Mulready-Woods. A detective told the court that she would not be making a declaration of evidence against him but added that there was a "correlation of CCTV and telecom enquiries". The officer told the court "work was still ongoing and may take some time" and that another file had been submitted. The defendant's legal team said that they were working on a bail package and "wanted to present it to the court". The court heard that Drew was self-employed and the judge said given the serious charges he would grant legal aid. Drew waved to supporters in the viewing dock as he was taken into custody. The case will be heard again in relation to the proposal for bail on 28 September. title: Ridiculed MSP says chest infection and lack of sleep led to committee blunder
description: Collette Stevenson says she has faced "misogynistic bullying" after asking whether government agency Transport Scotland is a charity.
body: Transport committee member Collette Stevenson says she suffered a momentary lapse of concentration during a meeting earlier this month An MSP who faced ridicule over a blunder at a Holyrood committee has said she suffered a "momentary lapse" brought on by lack of sleep and a chest infection. Collette Stevenson, who has represented East Kilbride for the SNP since 2021 and is a member of the transport committee, was criticised after asking if Transport Scotland was a registered charity. Transport Scotland director Graeme Cook then explained to her that it was a national agency which was part of the Scottish government. Posting on Facebook, Stevenson said her illness had affected her concentration, and said she had been subjected to "misogynistic bullying" following the incident. The 57-year-old added that she later took a week off work, on medical advice, to recuperate. She posted: "During a recent committee evidence session, I experienced a momentary lapse in my questioning regarding the status of Transport Scotland. "I was in the early stages of a severe chest infection, which affected my sleep and, in turn, my concentration. "On medical advice, and following a flare up of asthma, I have taken this week off from Parliament to recuperate and allow the various medications to work, so I can focus on making a full recovery." This video can not be played Transport Scotland director Graeme Cook explained to the MSP that his agency was an integral part of the government Stevenson sits on the equality, human rights and civil justice committee as well as the transport committee, and is a substitute member of the delegated powers and law reform committee. She has previously asked questions during committee meetings about the Clyde Metro development - a key recommendation from Transport Scotland's strategic transport review - and worked with the body on the East Kilbride rail enhancement and electrification project. But earlier this month, after about two hours of evidence on Scotland's rail services, Stevenson asked: "I take it Transport Scotland is a registered charity?" "Transport Scotland is a non-departmental government body," Graeme Cook, director of rail delivery for Transport Scotland, responded. "Transport Scotland is an agency so all of the Transport Scotland staff are already part of the civil service. "Transport Scotland is the same legal entity as the Scottish government." Stevenson said that since her mistake she had been ridiculed and bullied online. She said: "Whilst robust scrutiny is a necessary part of public life, the disproportionate abuse, mockery, and misogynistic bullying directed at me online following an honest mistake demonstrates the toxic culture women in politics still have to endure far too often." The MSP added her focus remained on serving her community, and thanked her friends, colleagues and constituents for their kindness and support. After the incident, SNP minister Stephen Gethins stood up for Stevenson's character, describing her as "a really good colleague and fantastic local advocate". title: Discarded lamp-post flags turned into 'unity' artwork
description: The huge union jack was produced using tattered flags previously hung from lamp-posts.
body: The piece was produced using tattered flags previously hung from lamp-posts A huge union jack artwork has been created by repurposing discarded flags from unauthorised lamp-post displays as a message of "unity". Birmingham textile artist Clare Elisabeth said her work, titled Re-Union Jack, incorporated dozens of worn-out flags and was a response to a flag-raising movement that had "caused division in communities across the country". The names of hundreds of notable figures from across the West Midlands have been added to the piece, with some visiting the project specifically to endorse it by adding their signature. Elisabeth said the work, created as part of the International Day of Birmingham, celebrated the region's heritage as a "magical melting pot". Signatories include a descendant of inventor James Watt, and members of reggae bands Steel Pulse and UB40. The four metre by seven metre artwork was sewn and glued by a small team led by the artist, who usually works with vintage fabrics. The artwork was shown at the city's Council House as part of International Day of Birmingham celebrations on Thursday and Friday Unauthorised displays of union jacks and St George crosses started appearing around the country last year, including the West Midlands, with various groups behind the movement. However, their presence in several suburbs of Birmingham led to angry clashes between opposing groups and residents who claimed their presence was divisive rather than patriotic. Council injunction to ban activists putting flags up Fury, threats and a film crew: How a row over flags reached boiling point Lamp-post flags organiser has 'no regrets' Speaking about the artwork, Elisabeth said the piece was a symbol of "togetherness". "I thought rather than throw them away, there's got to be a way that I can repurpose them into something more positive because they have been causing a lot of division. "We have had dozens and dozens of people join in the project so it's much more than just ours. "It's covered in the names of influential people in the Midlands who mean a lot to people and who make the Midlands this magical melting pot that we have." While some people have come in to sign their names, others have been added to it Names on it include those of Ozzy Osbourne, Duran Duran and Jorja Smith. The artwork was shown at the city's Council House as part of International Day of Birmingham celebrations on Thursday and Friday. title: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
description: The EU had said X "deceives users" by selling blue ticks without "meaningfully verifying" accounts.
body: The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges. In December 2025, the European Commission said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account. But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control. Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies. The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed an application, external with the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss ​the case. It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court". The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law". It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy. In a press briefing on Friday, external, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court. He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act. They are carrying out, of course, the hearing and the ruling, but I can tell you from our side is that we have a very solid case that we have advanced indeed with the €120 million fine against X last year in December, and the Commission is of course absolutely ready to defend its position in court. And a follow up. In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data. Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability". "Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms. "The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X. "The days of censoring Americans online are over." His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely". The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark. The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU. However, the EU is also conducting several other investigations into the platform, including one into its integrated AI assistant Grok over concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people. title: Business Daily
description: Did trade frenemies find common ground at the White House?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·25 Sep 2026,·17 mins Available for over a year What's next for trade, tariffs and AI after Presidents Trump and Xi met at the White House? Vishala Sri-Pathma is joined by Henry Wang from the Center for China and Globalization and the AI researcher and author Stephanie Hare. title: Watch: Robbie Williams' surprise singalong after Peru gig cancelled
description: Robbie Williams gave an impromptu performance outside a hotel in Lima after his stadium concert was cancelled.
body: This video can not be played Robbie Williams gave an impromptu performance outside a hotel in Peru's capital Lima, after his concert at a stadium in the city was cancelled. Authorities announced that the Arena 1 Park gig could not go ahead, citing failures by the venue to comply with safety regulations. Robbie told fans outside his hotel he was "broken-hearted" and held a brief singalong with the cheering crowds. Robbie Williams' surprise singalong after Peru gig cancelled. title: Men charged over £10m village ketamine haul
description: Police say the drugs, with an estimated value of £10m, were found in black bin bags.
body: Police say the drugs were found in black bin bags Three men have been charged after police seized what is believed to be the UK's second-largest haul of ketamine. West Yorkshire Police said 500kg (1,102lb) of the drug, worth an estimated £10m, was found at a property on Rose Avenue in the the Upton area of Pontefract. The largest find was worth an estimated £17m and was found in Merseyside in 2025. The force said 20 black bin bags were found during the West Yorkshire operation, led by the Regional Organised Crime Unit. Curtis Binns, 32, Paul Turner, 40, both from Upton and Christopher Willis, 42, from Wolverhampton, have been charged with drugs offences and are due to appear at Leeds Magistrates' Court later. Police said Binns, 32, of Sunny Avenue, had been charged with possession of a Class B drug with intent to supply and money laundering. Turner, of Common Lane, had been charged with possession of a Class B drug with intent to supply while Willis had been charged with supplying a Class B drug. Ketamine is commonly used as a horse tranquiliser. When abused, the drug can cause serious health problems including permanent bladder damage that can require lifelong treatment. title: Families failed by decision to bail sex offender to flat near playground, victims commissioner says
description: Victims of Zafer Dogan were living close to the 32-year-old who took thousands of pictures of children at a playground from his bedroom window.
body: Zafer Dogan took photographs from his bedroom window Victims and their families were "grossly failed" by the court system that bailed a sex offender and repeatedly allowed him to return to his home overlooking the playground he targeted, London's victims' commissioner said. Zafer Dogan, 32, of Enfield, north London, was jailed on Thursday for two years and four months for taking thousands of pictures of children and using AI software to "nudify" them. Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today, Andrea Simon said the case showed that "the justice system did not centre victims" and called for a multi-agency review. A government spokesperson said the law was clear that bail "should only be used where necessary and proportionate, including to protect victims". Dogan had pleaded guilty to multiple offences, including making indecent images of children. According to the police, he had taken more than 5,000 pictures, many from his bedroom window. Despite protests from the police and prosecutors, he had previously been bailed back to his flat, forcing one family who had fallen victim to his crimes to move into temporary accommodation. Simon said: "I think victims and their families were grossly failed by the decision to allow this paedophile to return to an address where he was overlooking a playground near to his victims. "The case [shows that] the justice system just does not centre victims. To know that the police and prosecutors opposed bail multiple times, but nevertheless, he was returned to the community, is an indication that the capacity pressures on prisons are not being balanced with the impacts that that's having on victims' lives. "We seem to be lurching from one crisis to another, and victim safety and their rights seem to be put to one side, as the justice system struggles." Sir Mark Rowley said one family was left feeling so fearful they moved away Simon's criticism was echoed by Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley who said it was "unfathomable" that Dogan was ever granted bail. Sir Mark said: "Prosecutors rightly opposed bail on multiple occasions, building on officers' clear assessments of the great risk he posed, and yet bail decisions were ultimately made that prioritised the offender's interests over the safety and the peace of mind of the victims. "A victim and their family found themselves living in close proximity to a man who had admitted targeting them. "They were so fearful, they ultimately felt forced to move to distant temporary accommodation, disrupting their lives and disrupting their children's lives, simply to escape being in the neighbourhood of the offender." He also criticised "some grossly irresponsible technology and AI companies". "Dogan voyeuristically photographed children known to him before using an AI photo-editing technology to manipulate those images for his own sexual gratification," he said. "Companies must do more to prevent their platforms and tools from being used to facilitate sexual offending and harm." Dogan, shown in footage recorded by Met Police bodyworn cameras, was arrested in July Remand and bail decisions are made by independent judges or magistrates. According to the prosecutor, Dogan had been on conditional bail "throughout" the proceedings: 16 July 2026: Dogan was arrested on suspicion of offences involving indecent images of children 4 August: He was arrested again and the following day was charged and remanded by police 6 August: Dogan's first appearance at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court where he pleaded guilty to all offences. He was granted conditional bail 7 August: A bail hearing was held at Wood Green Crown Court. The court decided bail conditions would remain with an additional one for Dogan to attend appointment with probation for pre-sentence report 7 September: Bail hearing at Wood Green Crown Court at request of Police and Crown Prosecution Service. Judge brought forward sentencing in an attempt to mitigate 11 September: Snaresbrook Crown Court sentencing - judge sends back to Wood Green Crown Court on 23 September 23 September: Wood Green Crown Court sentencing adjourned 24 September: Sentenced at Wood Green Crown Court Simon said there were parallels to be drawn with the case of serial sex offender and murderer Simon Levy. Levy killed two women and raped a third in 2025 while on bail for other offences, after a series of decisions by authorities that left him free to roam the streets. Levy had been reported to the Metropolitan Police for a sexual assault in 2017. He then assaulted two women in 2018, but was only convicted for those offences in 2021. After being released from prison - where he sexually assaulted a female officer - he committed other assaults before the 2025 murders. He was sentenced to life in prison in August. Sir Mark previously described that case as a "whole system failing", criticising the decision of the courts and Crown Prosecution Service to bail Levy. Simon also raised concerns over the government's early release scheme which is set to see about 2,550 eligible offenders leaving jails in England and Wales by the end of the year. "I hear from victims about what they think they want to do ahead of offenders' early releases from prison," she said, " they feel they may have to install security cameras or change their daily routines, or live in fear." title: 'A tumour the size of a football saved my life'
description: Lisa Carroll, 47, who was diagnosed with rare form of ovarian cancer, urges women to check symptoms.
body: Lisa Carroll was only 41 was she was diagnosed with the rare form of ovarian cancer A mum-of-three who was diagnosed with a rare cancer has urged other women not to dismiss their symptoms. When Lisa Carroll, 47, from Coventry, returned from a family holiday in August 2021, she thought she was suffering from irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), a kidney infection or something minor. Instead, she was told it was mucinous ovarian cancer (MOC), one of the rarest forms of ovarian cancer in the UK. "I thought I had possibly a bit of IBS or a kidney problem or something like that. I was in quite a lot of pain," she said. Next year, Carroll and her husband are looking forward to celebrating their 20th wedding anniversary After calling NHS 111, Carroll was sent to hospital in Coventry where medics discovered a 12cm cyst on her right ovary. She was told it did not appear particularly sinister and was placed on a waiting list for surgery. "Within a month, a cyst the size of a fist had grown to the point that I could feel it like a football in my stomach. Pain and discomfort got worse and I felt shattered emotionally and physically", she said. By December, scans revealed the tumour had grown to 20cm and was beginning to rupture, so three days later she underwent an emergency procedure to remove the tumour, a fallopian tube, her appendix and surrounding tissue. Two weeks later, doctors gave her the diagnosis. Following surgeries and chemotherapy, Carroll is approaching her five-year anniversary of being cancer free The cancer is exceptionally rare, with only around 200 cases diagnosed annually in the UK, said Ovacome, an ovarian cancer charity. "Some ovarian cancers are really sneaky, hang around for years and you've got no sign of any symptoms at all", said Carroll, who works as the CEO of Lifespace Trust, a Warwickshire-based charity for young people. "The fact that mine grew so quickly was what alerted them as early as they did." Yet despite losing her hair and enduring months of treatment, she says the biggest challenge was something she had not been prepared for. "I got chucked into early menopause and that was the bit I massively struggled with. I didn't know what was depression and what was menopause." The Ovacome charity is hosting a fundraising walk in Cannon Hill Park, Birmingham on Saturday "I didn't know what was a cancer symptom and what was a menopause symptom. I couldn't open the washing machine, the dishwasher or the oven. I couldn't cook anything on the hob because I'd just have this awful hot flush. I was forgetting words. I was incredibly emotional." Today, Carroll is cancer-free and approaching the five-year milestone that will see her formally discharged from oncology care. "I do not underestimate how fortunate I am that my long-term outlook is a lot brighter than for many," she said. "That brings with it a kind of survivor's guilt." She has since became involved with Ovacome, which connected her with others facing the same fears. "They became my safe space," she said. "They helped me to connect with other people who understood what I was going through. They made an incredibly scary and isolating time feel far more manageable." Now preparing to take part in the charity's annual fundraising walk, Carroll hopes sharing her story will encourage others to trust their instincts and seek help when something feels wrong. The fundraising walk takes place at Cannon Hill Park in Birmingham on Saturday. title: Africa's richest man helps fund $660m fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and Djibouti
description: The pipeline would strengthen energy security in landlocked Ethiopia, while creating jobs at Djibouti's port.
body: Aliko Dangote made his fortune from cement in Nigeria Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, Ethiopia and Djibouti have agreed to develop a $660m (£500m) petroleum pipeline and storage project linking the two countries. The project will include a 120km- (75 mile-) pipeline connecting Djibouti's Damerjog port to a distribution facility in Dewele, Ethiopia, as well as storage capacity of about 400 million litres. It is expected to begin operations within 18 months. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said the pipeline would reduce the time needed to transport fuel from Djibouti's port to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, from five days to one. The first phase will transport key petroleum products, including jet fuel, diesel and petrol. Speaking at the groundbreaking ceremony, Dangote said the project would strengthen Ethiopia's energy security and make its fuel supply chain more resilient. Landlocked Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti's port for imports, including petroleum products. The new infrastructure is expected to reduce pressure on existing transport systems supporting industries, including transport, aviation, agriculture and construction. Djibouti is also expected to benefit from increased port activity, job creation and higher government revenues. The project is part of Dangote's wider expansion of infrastructure and manufacturing businesses across Africa. Dangote Cement has production capacity of about 55 million tonnes a year, while his oil refinery in Nigeria currently has capacity to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day and is seeking to double that to 1.4 million barrels a day. The refinery recently listed 4.1 billion ordinary shares on the Nigerian stock exchange, aiming to raise about $1.63bn (£1.2bn). In Kenya, the company is due to break ground next week on a proposed 700,000-barrel-a-day crude oil refinery in Lamu. title: Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market
description: BBC Sport explores why clubs at the top of English football are increasingly trading academy players and what the impact is on the youngsters themselves.
body: JJ Gabriel is one of the most highly-rated prospects in English football A 15-year-old growing up in the UK faces many tough personal decisions about their future - which school subjects to study, which social circle suits them, and where their priorities lie in life. But in the past few weeks the choices teenage Manchester United striker JJ Gabriel has been making about his future in football have drawn huge public attention in sports media and online. Gabriel has informed United he wants to leave the club and join another. BBC Sport has reported that he has stayed away from training and begun talking to other clubs because he and his representatives are unhappy with United's handling of the 15-year-old's progress. That a transfer saga involving a footballer so young could generate so much interest highlights a truth that to many is uncomfortable - money is changing how the football transfer market works, and children are increasingly deemed to be among its most valuable commodities. So what is behind the rise in transfers involving boys who in some cases are not even old enough to have taken their GCSEs, what kind of influence can the money on offer have on agents and parents, and what exactly are the country's top football clubs getting out of it? "It's crazy when you think about it," says Ryan Cardwell, former youth scout at Liverpool and Southampton. "In what other kind of world would 15 and 16-year-olds be spoken about in the media like this?" This summer alone, all six of the Premier League's wealthiest clubs either signed a highly-rated academy player from another, or lost a youngster to a direct rival. "It is such a competitive market," Cardwell explains. "There are now tens of transfers between the elite academies every summer, when it used to be the case that if you were already at one of those, you would likely stay the course. "The race for talent is huge – you look at what teams are spending on transfers for senior players and it's enormous, so if you can spot a player earlier and offset some of that financial risk, you're going to do so." Some inside football claim that the transfer of Rio Ngumoha - the now 18-year-old winger who was called up to this month's senior England squad - from Chelsea to Liverpool at the age of 15 in 2024 ushered in a new era of competition for academy players among the nation's elite. One of the major factors is Brexit. Before 2021 English clubs were allowed to sign academy players over the age of 16 who held European Union passports. Since the UK left the EU, foreign players cannot join English clubs until they reach 18. "Heathrow and Gatwick [airports] on a Friday night were inundated with scouts going to other countries to look for young players", says Caldwell. "Belgium and the Netherlands were full of scouts for Premier League clubs. "Now it's the competition between English clubs that has increased, looking at each other's players, including the old-school 'top six' but also the likes of Southampton, Aston Villa, and Fulham." Young players have further added financial value - youth signings don't count towards the Premier League's squad cost ratio rules, and any future sale counts as 'pure profit' in club accounts. Advances in video technology and data analysis mean more young players are being identified, tracked and approached by rival clubs than ever before. Rio Ngumoha was one of the country's highest-rated young prospects at Chelsea, and has now made 22 Premier League appearances for Liverpool Players can de-register from their academy at the end of their under-12, under-14 and under-16 seasons if they wish to explore options elsewhere. They can be offered paid scholarship contracts from the season in which they turn 14, and can sign professional deals from the season in which they turn 16. Some pundits and fans have criticised Gabriel's family over the controversy in recent weeks. Gabriel can potentially join clubs in Europe because he has an Irish passport. "It's a really tough world - players and families want the best for their kids and you can't give them stick without knowing what their motivations are," says Phil Jagielka, whose son Zac left Liverpool in 2024 and signed a scholarship deal at Hull City at 16. "The harsh reality is that if a young player fails to progress, or gets a bad injury, teams will stop being interested in them. So there is an element of strike while the iron's hot." When a club signs a player from a rival academy, they pay a set compensation fee based on how long they had been trained there. Depending on the player's age, the fee can reach millions of pounds. The increasing allure of signing young academy players from rivals means some parents are now compiling data packs on their sons to give to potential clubs, and more and more children are represented by football agents. "There are good agents and bad agents," Cardwell says. "You certainly speak to some and think 'that's completely the wrong idea', or, ' this player is going to be misguided'. Sometimes they push for a move when a player isn't ready. "The contracts can be enormous and [money] can be a huge motivation to move. It could set a young player's family up for life. "I would quite like to see some form of financial cap. My fear for some of the young players is they're on the biggest salaries they'll ever have, because if they don't make it at the top level, they can go from being on tens of thousands (of pounds) a week to one or two thousand lower down the pyramid." Football academies in England are graded between 1 (the highest) and 4 (the lowest). There are 31 Category 1 academies, including Manchester United, and the competition between them is significant In decades gone by, development of academy players would be combined with menial tasks around the training ground. title: Education, Barcelona & Basque culture - why Spain are dominating football
description: Spain go into Saturday's Nations League match against England on a 38-match unbeaten run - and with a host of honours to their name. Why are they so good?
body: Lamine Yamal is just one of Barcelona's academy products playing for Spain World champions. European champions. Olympic champions. Undefeated in two and a half years. Spain are the dominant force in men's world football. Of the past 10 major international tournaments, they have won five. Going into Saturday's Nations League meeting with England at Wembley (19:45 BST), they are on an international record 38-match unbeaten run. They have not lost since a 1-0 defeat by Colombia in a 2024 friendly. And the success does not stop with the senior men's team. During that time, Spain have also won: The Women's World Cup in 2023 At club level, Spanish teams have won half of all available Champions League and Europa League titles since 2009. Spain football expert Guillem Balague told BBC Radio 5 Live there are "three pillars" that explain Spain's coaching culture and its unprecedented success. "The first one was university, and in particular something called the National Institute of Physical Education," he said. "University entered physical education in Spain a long time ago, in the 1990s, and they created physical coaches and football coaches with a deep understanding of learning and training processes. "Some of those fitness coaches became really big managers, like Rafa Benitez or Marcelino Garcia Toral. They came from learning and studying what football was about ahead of anybody else. "The second pillar is the Basque culture. The Basque Country represents historically a special reference within Spanish football because they relate to work ethic, massive work ethic, daily effort. "And the third pillar is what everybody knows: the Barcelona influence, Johan Cruyff and the tactical revolution that followed through him." This video can not be played 'We had a date with history and we got there first' - Spain react to World Cup win Eight players from Barcelona's La Masia academy were in the Spain squad who won the 2010 World Cup under Vicente del Bosque, and another eight were in Luis de la Fuente's group as they lifted the trophy again this summer. Barcelona won their first European Cup in 1992 under Cruyff playing total football - a style pioneered by the Netherlands team of the 1970s in which he played, and later mirrored at the Nou Camp under Pep Guardiola's management between 2008 and 2012. That was a period where Barcelona won three consecutive La Liga titles, while Spain won back-to-back European Championships in 2008 and 2012 either side of their 2010 World Cup triumph. Xavi, Andres Iniesta and Sergio Busquets were brought through in a system where players learn the art of ball possession and positional play in its purest form. Jordi Gratacos, Barcelona's international director of academies from 2009 to 2011, and then from 2016 to 2020, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "The number one thing is to understand the tactical meaning of the technical action. What I mean is to create intelligent players [who are] very good in technical aspects. "In this level, all players are very good in the technical aspects. The most important are these players who always decide the best option inside the field and make others better. "The main objective is to prepare the players to take the position. It's an open education when you create some scenarios, context and ecosystem where the player needs to decide, and the coach needs also to say: 'This was the best option - next time, take the other option.' "The most important thing is that they need to decide inside the game." In his first two seasons as Barcelona manager, Hansi Flick is repeating what Guardiola did - not only in the sense that he has won two La Liga titles in a row and chasing a third. Academy products form the engine of his project, with Lamine Yamal, Dani Olmo and Pau Cubarsi forming key components of success at both club and international level - just as the generation of 2008-12 did. Spain have found the formula to repeat success, and Barcelona are at the heart of it. This video can not be played World Cup winners gifted their weight in tomatoes If Barcelona and Catalonia represents the artistry of Spanish football, the Basque Country represents its character. Five players in the 2026 World Cup squad were from the region and came through at either Athletic Bilbao or Real Sociedad - clubs where eight players were playing at the time Spain won Euro 2024. Then there is Mikel Merino, who scored a quarter-final winner against Germany at Euro 2024, before going on to score six goals in six games in World Cup qualifying, and late winners against Portugal and Belgium over the summer. Although not Basque, Merino is from Pamplona in the autonomous community of Navarre - a region that has a significant influence of both Spanish and Basque culture. Just five kilometres away from Pamplona is Zizur Mayor - the town where former Chelsea captain and Spain international Cesar Azpilicueta grew up. When asked to describe Basque culture, Azpilicueta told BBC Radio 5 Live: "The discipline, the culture of working hard, of not giving up or being resilient, not very flashy. "Normally, people want to display this culture of fight, being tough - like English football - more duels, more physical, less technical. "But also in terms of tactical approach, more compact, great knowledge of knowing where to go, and with the ball keep it simple and try to go forward as quick as possible." The five Basque players from the 2026 squad have formed an important part of Spain's recent success and are an embodiment of what Cruyff thought of players from that region. Cruyff once said: "The first thing I did as a coach, was to sign four players from the Basque region. They are not afraid of anything." For current Spain boss De la Fuente in 2026, Unai Simon played in goal, with former Manchester City defender Aymeric Laporte a key cornerstone of a defence that conceded just one goal in eight matches all tournament.

title: Zidane waited for France - now can he harness their star power?
description: Zinedine Zidane says he waited for the France job, but what will he bring to the role after five years out of management?
body: Zinedine Zidane won the Champions League three times as Real Madrid manager France will have a new face on the touchline for the first time in 14 years when they face Turkey on Friday. Zinedine Zidane replaced Didier Deschamps after France's fourth-place finish at the World Cup, but his appointment had been an open secret long before Les Bleus' third-place play-off loss to England. Talks between the former Real Madrid manager and the French football authorities kicked off as early as February 2025 - after Zidane's former team-mate Deschamps announced a few weeks earlier he would step down following the 2026 World Cup. When he was unveiled in Paris, Zidane was keen to highlight the time he had spent waiting on the sidelines and preparing for the job. "I had several offers in the last four or five years, but I turned them all down," an emotional Zidane said. "The national team is the only thing I wanted." While his enthusiasm at taking the job was the overarching theme of his first news conference in the French capital, the midfield legend offered few clues to France fans as to how he would approach the role. Even a question on Kylian Mbappe's captaincy was bypassed: "The most important thing for him now is to rest, we'll have the chance to speak in September." Mbappe, speaking to Spanish newspaper AS, has since said having the former Real Madrid star as his national team coach was "like a film". When asked about his preferred style of play, Zidane opted against going into tactical detail. "I can't explain to you in just a couple of words how we're going win. I have to arrive, meet with the players, and explain my plans to them. After that, it'll be up to me to keep this team winning." However, Zidane confirmed his intention "to do things differently" and he has called up five uncapped players for this international break. He went on to signal that there would be a degree of "continuation" from the work of his predecessor, which he made sure to praise. "I'm going to try do what I know how to, but it won't be a complete break either." So what will Zidane bring to the France dugout? Zidane, who retired in 2006, was one of the most exciting attacking midfielders of his generation. He won league titles and European trophies with Juventus and Real Madrid, while he helped France to victory at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000. Zidane started his career at Cannes and then moved to Bordeuax. He almost joined Premier League side Blackburn Rovers in 1995, but the move broke down with Rovers owner Jack Walker reportedly asking manager Kenny Dalglish: "Why do you want to sign Zidane when we have Tim Sherwood?" Instead Zidane moved to Juventus, winning six trophies, before he was signed by Real Madrid for a then record £45.8m. For France he was the hero of the home 1998 World Cup, scoring twice in the final, a 3-0 win over Brazil and was named the best player at Euro 2000. He retired after the 2006 World Cup, a campaign full of highs, leading France to the final, and one big low, when his playing career ended after he was sent off in the showpiece match for headbutting Italy defender Marco Materazzi. Zidane and Deschamps - two 1998 World Cup winners - do share a few similar traits in their management, not least in their pragmatism, as well as the laissez-faire approach to attacking phases which Deschamps embraced in the recent World Cup. Given the attacking talent at his disposal, it stands to reason that Zidane would carry on in that vein. "I was a number 10 as a player," he said, hinting he would retain the role Michael Olise thrived in for much of the summer. "What motivates me is the game, it's scoring goals," he added. With the team netting 20 times in North America, Deschamps has arguably laid the foundations for his successor's attacking set-up. Zidane is finding Les Bleus in immeasurably better shape than his predecessor did at the start of his own tenure, at which point the wounds of the 2010 World Cup fiasco were still fresh. The appointment does come with a degree of uncertainty, though. Given that Zidane has spent five years out of management, and the Real Madrid job is the only other senior coaching role of his career, it might seem like a gamble. The 54-year-old himself has acknowledged leading a national team would be an entirely new proposition: "It's new to me, but I'm not scared. This is what I wanted." Predictably, the reaction among players and fans to Zidane's arrival has been almost unanimously positive. He was met with a crowd of supporters carrying flares and banners as he left the French Football Federation's headquarters after his unveiling. "Welcome home," Mbappe wrote on Instagram later in the day. Zidane was met by fans and media after his unveiling as France boss "It's a great day for French football," his former France and Bordeaux team-mate Bixente Lizarazu told France Info later that day. "He is more than fit to manage Les Bleus, given what he did at Real Madrid with great players and big egos." The respect that the former Ballon d'Or winner commands in a dressing room is one of his key strengths. Even more so than Deschamps, a France legend in his own right, Zidane is a figure who can rival - perhaps even overshadow - his own players in terms of star power. In this sense, he may be the ideal manager to get the most out of an attack made up of Mbappe, Ousmane Dembele, Desire Doue and Olise. This international break - lasting four Nations League fixtures over three weeks - will offer the France players a crash-course to the new management style. After facing Turkey, they have two games against Belgium and one against Italy in Paris. Given his iconic status within French football and on the wider national stage, Zidane will invariably enjoy an unprecedented degree of goodwill regardless of his initial results. Whether he uses that leeway to experiment tactically and bring in new faces

title: Trump and Xi toast new chapter in friendship at White House state dinner
description: The lavish state dinner included tech billionaires, red tablecloths, bok choy and festive toasts.
body: Xi thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with "meticulous care and consideration" US President Donald Trump welcomed China President Xi Jinping to the White House for a lavish state dinner where both leaders touted a new chapter in their friendship. The dinner was attended by billionaire business leaders, Trump administration officials, US tech CEOs and others. Their arrival was marked, however, by protesters loudly shouting from just outside the White House gates, some of whom were arrested. Both Trump and Xi praised one another, pledging to continue talks to ensure stability between their two nations. But experts say that not much concrete has been yielded in talks so far. The dinner came on the second day of Xi's three-day trip to Washington. The noise of protests could be heard inside the White House as guests arrived for dinner Trump thanked Xi for making the long trip to the US, and said the relationship between the two men was strong. "We've never gotten along better," Trump said. He praised the long history of US-China relations, although he did take an unscripted detour to praise his ongoing ballroom project. In the off-the-cuff moment, he said as a "special treat" the Chinese leader and his wife could be the first to enter the ballroom, which is still a year away from completion. "Anybody who wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkling, it's our honour to have you do so," he said. He also presented Xi with a sculpture of a bald eagle, America's national symbol, saying it embodied "the free and soaring spirit of America". "We hope it will find a nice, wonderful place in Beijing. It's your honour," he said. Trump added that he and First Lady Melania had participated in the design of the sculpture. This video can not be played Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? Xi thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with "meticulous care and consideration", making them "feel truly at home". He said the two leaders are "making history in our bilateral engagements". "We agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability," Xi said, adding that the two shared "sincere and in-depth exchanges" that will strengthen relations between the two countries. Like Trump's, Xi's remarks were heavy on flattery, focusing on cultural ties and shared history between the US and China. The relationship between the two countries was "forged in blood and fire" during the fight against Japan in the Second World War, before being furthered during the "ping pong" diplomacy of the Nixon administration, he said. Towards the end of his speech, Xi said the US and China's goals can be "mutually reinforcing". He urged both sides to explore a "new approach for major countries to get along". Musk was seen mingling with guests, alongside US Secretary of State Marco Rubio When the BBC entered the dining hall for the dinner, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was standing over a table and appeared to be telling an entertaining story that had two others nearby barreled over with laughter. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was at another table, with a serious look on his face. His wife is sat beside him, with Jared Kushner and White House chief of staff Monica Crowley nearby. The White House invited scores of US officials, as well as conservative broadcasters, tech industry bosses, social media CEOs and other corporate executives. Attendees included members of Trump's cabinet, as well as family members like his children Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany. Bosses from the tech industry in attendance included Apple's Tim Cook, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google's Sundar Pichai, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Both Cook and Huang were seated at the same table as Trump and Xi. As was Musk, who previously worked in Trump's administration leading the effort to shrink government. Other companies whose leaders were in attendance include General Motors, Visa, Paramount Skydance, ExxonMobil and more. Social media mogul Mark Zuckerberg also attended, as well as Jeff Yaas, the American billionaire who owns a share of TikTok. "Everybody wanted to be there," Trump said ahead of the event. "I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world, and a lot more." But one notable absence was Anthropic - one of the biggest and most valuable AI firms in the world. The BBC has asked Anthropic if it was invited, or if they chose not to be there. Business leaders and tech bosses were among those in attendance The office of the First Lady Melania Trump, which planned the event, said the dinner menu would showcase "American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence". For their first course guests enjoyed yellow squash, wild mushrooms and crispy pancetta. The ate off red tablecloths - red being a symbol of luck and good fortune in China. For their main course they dined on a sesame-crusted sea bass, braised bok choy and roasted eggplant. Dessert featured the two leaders and their fellow diners tucking into vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit, with an accompanying ice cream "made with harvested White House honey". The wine chosen by the first lady included Schramsberg Blanc De Noir - a nod to President Nixon's 1972 "Toast to Peace" with former Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai, when they used a bottle from the same vineyard. Trump and Xi will begin their day with tea at the White House's Red Room with their wives. The group then head to the US National Archives for a tour of the building and its exhibits. Formally called the National Archives and Records Administration, the building holds some of the most important documents regarding the founding of the United States - including the US Constitution, the Declaration of Independence and the Bill of Rights. title: Betty the 'cold-stunned' turtle set for Azores release
description: Betty was washed ashore at Dunwich during storms and has been nursed back to health in Hunstanton.
body: Loggerhead turtle Betty was found cold-stunned on Dunwich beach and has spent seven months recovering at Hunstanton Sea Life Centre A rare loggerhead turtle found "cold-stunned" after coastal storms is preparing to return to the sea after seven months of recovery and rehabilitation. Named Betty by her carers, the turtle was mistaken for "debris" on Dunwich beach in Suffolk by a member of the public in February who called the British Divers Marine Life Rescue (BDMLR). She was transferred to Hunstanton Sea Life Centre in Norfolk, where a second loggerhead turtle, called Olive, has been under care since December. Both will travel to the Azores later this month for release. Katie Robertson, display supervisor at the centre, said: "The moment they finally get released is going to be an emotional time for us." Both turtles were found cold-stunned - when temperatures rapidly decline and the struggle to find warmer waters can make them lethargic and experience decreased circulation. The condition can be fatal. Katie Robertson said sea life centres were preparing for a busy winter as loggerhead turtles cold wash ashore more often Robertson added: "With temperatures changing in the waters during the summertime, our temperatures in the sea are increasing and it's getting into the low 20 [degrees] - which is causing them to travel further north than where they would normally travel. "When our temperatures drop drastically compared to the Mediterranean they get cold-stunned, which basically means the surrounding water for them gets too cold." X-rays and CT scans were carried out on Olive (pictured) who was found in Scotland in December, to make sure she no longer had pneumonia Loggerhead turtles, external are the most common turtle in the Mediterranean and typically nest on beaches from Greece and Turkey to Israel and Libya. They weigh up to 400lb (181kg) and can be up to 48 inches (1.2m) in length. The species is named for their large heads that support their powerful jaw muscles, needed for catching prey. Since the turtles have been in the centre's care they have undergone a range of tests, including x-rays and CT scans checking for pneumonia. Betty, who came straight to the team from the beach, underwent more specialist care. Robertson said it was "a step-by-step process" to get Betty ready to return to the water, as they had to work to increase her body temperature very gradually every day. Betty and Olive are due to travel to The Azores in Portugal and will leave Norfolk on 28 September Robertson said visitors had loved seeing the rescued turtles improve and that the two animals had come a long way. She said: "When we got the all clear for both turtles, the whole team, we just had a moment where we were just so proud of all the work we've put into it but also proud of the turtles themselves." The creatures will leave Hunstanton on Monday before travelling to The Azores in Portugal where they will be monitored for up to two weeks before they are released back into the sea. title: Farmers down 240 million litres of milk after heat
description: Milk yield was affected by a series of extreme heatwaves which led to poor grazing conditions, researchers say.
body: Debbie Wilkins is among the farmers in England and Wales who have started giving their cattle winter feed Extreme heat this summer has led to dairy farmers delivering 240 million fewer litres of milk than expected, researchers have said. Farmers delivered four fewer days of milk supply than would be expected between May and August, according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU). With the heat leading to poor grazing conditions, stunted harvests and heat strain on livestock in England and Wales, many farmers have started giving winter feed to cattle, including Debbie Wilkins, a dairy and beef farmer in Gloucestershire. "The costs pile up when you have to bring the cows indoors and the loss of milk production compounds the issue," she said. Council leader voted out after no confidence motion Cotswolds home to UK's first air taxi centre Rare Bronze Age finds unearthed in city dig Wilkins, who farms in Prior's Norton, said it had been a "difficult" summer. In total, the ECIU said dairy farmers lost milk valued at more than £83m - enough milk to fill more than one billion school milk cartons. It follows the UK's hottest summer on record in 2026, with five intense heatwaves and drought declarations. But while farmers delivered significantly less than expected over the summer, the ECIU said UK milk production could still hit near record levels in 2026. It said this was because farmers built up a cushion earlier in 2026 which had partially offset the litres lost over the summer. More shade, trees and water are needed if farmers want to survive future severe weather events, the ECIU said ECIU said the consolidation of dairy farms in recent years had allowed for "economies of scale and mechanisation to increase milk outputs while the herd size reduces". Tom Cantillon, a senior analyst at ECIU, said future heatwaves would become progressively harder to recover from, especially as milk was an "unforgiving product in farming" as it cannot be stockpiled. "The costs don't stop now that the rain has come," Cantillon said. "A second bad year for grass has pushed farmers into their winter forage early, with feed prices to follow." Cantillon said farmers needed help to roll out climate resilience measures such as more shade, trees and water.
