title: Our son's death could have been prevented by FA - Billy Vigar's parents
description: Billy Vigar's parents says the Football Association could have prevented their son's death.
body: This video can not be played Billy Vigar's parents speak about their son "You swing from sadness to anger because you just feel it could have been prevented." That is the view of Camilla Vigar, whose son Billy, a former Arsenal academy player, died a year ago today from a "significant brain injury", five days after colliding with a concrete wall surrounding a pitch. The 21-year-old striker was playing for Chichester City at Wingate and Finchley FC in north London. In their first broadcast interview since their son's passing, the Vigar family accuse the Football Association of doing "nothing" after previous similar incidents. "[Billy] had his whole life ahead of him. He was 21 years old and he lost it playing football when he didn't need to," she told BBC Sport. "I personally feel that the FA could have stopped Billy losing his life because they had so many warnings." They give the example of amateur footballer Ben Hiscox, who died in 2015 after colliding with a clubhouse near Bristol. After the coroner warned the FA about the risk of future deaths, padding was added to Stoke Gifford United's clubhouse and the run-off between it and the pitch was increased. The Vigars also point to the life-changing injuries sustained by Alex Fletcher in 2022. Fletcher fractured his skull when colliding with concrete barriers next to the pitch at Bath City's ground, and was forced to retire in 2024. The FA conducted a review of clubs after that incident. "As far as I'm aware, nothing was done with that information and it just sat there. One of the clubs as far as I'm aware that was highlighted as being one of the high-risk clubs was Wingate [and Finchley], where Billy then lost his life," said Camilla Vigar. When asked by the BBC what was done with the information it had gathered, the FA provided no comment. Vigar, aged 21, died after sustaining a "significant brain injury" on 25 September 2025 At the time of Vigar's accident, the FA's stadium accreditation criteria, which applies to the National League System in men's football and the Women's National League, said clubs needed to have a "permanent" barrier around the pitch "of sound construction (eg concrete and steel)". In light of what happened to Vigar, the FA launched a safety review of more than 900 clubs, which was conducted by independent experts. As a result, the stadium criteria was updated last month and "no longer permits solid brick, breeze block or concrete barriers around pitches". The BBC has been told 169 clubs in the men's National League System and women's National League were notified they would need to make changes "as soon as is reasonably practicable". Where walls are structural, they must be "covered with suitable protection", such as padding. The FA said: "This important work is under way, and we will continue to fully support the clubs involved." Funding is being provided by the FA and the Premier League. BBC Sport approached hundreds of affected clubs in an effort to gauge their views on the changes and understand the status of their remedial work. Bromsgrove Sporting near Birmingham, which has a concrete wall surrounding its pitch, told BBC Sport the changes were "completely understandable and long overdue". It added: "We are fully supportive of this and are grateful for the 100% funding from the FA." The club said it had been given a deadline of the end of this season but "being high risk it would be good to complete this side of Christmas". Sheppey United are one of the 169 clubs who have been advised to modify their stadium Meanwhile, Sheppey United, in Kent, has a concrete supporting wall around two sides of its 3G pitch, which will be covered in padding. Asked for their thoughts on the changes, the club said: "There is always an element of risk in all sports and they can't all be mitigated, unfortunately in this instance the remedial works are more a reactive response rather than a proactive one. If the funding wasn't in place I think it would make it difficult for some clubs to fund this." Bath City, where Fletcher's incident happened, has solid perimeter walls on all sides of its pitch. The club told BBC Sport: "We welcome the ruling as it seeks to improve player safety and recognises that funding needs to be available to support clubs to implement this fundamental change to the ground grading regulations." Keith Vigar, Billy's father, said: "I work in the health and safety industry, and the main thing is you don't go to work and expect to get injured, let alone even die at work in the workplace." The Vigars want the regulations extended above and below the National League. "It needs to change basically at all levels, not just at the levels that have changed," said Keith Vigar. That is a view shared by Fletcher, who said the FA had "ignored" his years of campaigning on the issue of pitch perimeter safety. "It wasn't until Billy's passing that [the FA] came to the table on this issue," he said. "So for me, that is a complete dereliction of duty on their part, and there should be accountability for that failing." Fletcher also said he is worried the ban on concrete, breeze block and brick walls does not cover all levels of the game and wants that explored urgently by the authorities. "There could be still situations where football is being played at some level, to some degree, organised football in this country, with these unsafe pitch perimeters. I would like to see that guidance, or the regulation, extended to consider all of football." Vigar joined Arsenal's academy aged 14 and spent almost seven years at the club Compared to many youngsters, Billy Vigar joined the football system late - and yet his talent was still recognised. He was scouted by Arsenal while playing for local club Hove Rivervale in Sussex, and joined the Premier League side's academy. "It was just an amazing feeling," said his father. "Sort of

title: NI's economic output rises, but businesses warn of rising costs
description: Northern Ireland's economic output, which is broadly equivalent to UK GDP, rose by 2.3% in the year to June.
body: Northern Ireland's economic output rose by 2.3% in the year to June Economic activity in Northern Ireland in the second quarter of this year grew faster than the UK and Republic of Ireland, according to official figures. Northern Ireland's economic output, which is broadly equivalent to UK GDP, rose by 2.3% in the year to June. Comparing economic activity in both NI and UK, NI had stronger growth over the year. Ireland's GDP increased by 10.2% over the latest quarter, but its "Modified Domestic Demand" (MDD), which removes the distorting effects of globalisation, experienced a decline of 0.8% over the quarter. That's compared to quarterly growth of 1% in Northern Ireland. This growth was driven by an increase in the production sector, which includes manufacturing. Greg Bradley's company has secured contracts with high profile customers all over the world Greg Bradley is the founder of BLK BOX, a company that makes gym equipment in Newtownabbey. It has secured contracts with high-profile customers all over the world from sports teams like Manchester United to chains like PureGym. Bradley said Covid had made people realise the importance of their health and "a lot of young people are into going to the gym". "We have won high profile contracts and expanding internationally across France, Spain, Germany and other countries," he told BBC News NI. "When I started the business 14 years ago I remember someone telling me I would never sell outside of the island of Ireland and I remember thinking, 'I'm going to prove you wrong'. Thankfully, we have been able to do that," he added. The company works internationally across the EU and markets like the US, Sri Lanka, Maldives, India, Australia and has grown its workforce to 180 staff. He added that the Windsor Framework had also been advantageous compared to English competitors. "We've been able to win a contract with a large French gym chain, Stade Français rugby team, so it's actually worked out good for us and we are really doubling down on that. "There's still a bit of an education process with it, not everyone knows that we can ship frictionlessly across Europe, they are a bit scared of tariffs but once you explain it, everyone is really interested." Daniel Duckett said rising petrol prices in particular will affect the cost of goods. Output in the services sector, which is the largest part of the Northern Ireland economy, also increased in the last 12 months. While these figures suggest the Northern Ireland economy ended the first half of this year in a position of strength, there are real concerns that rising energy and food costs could put businesses under significant pressure in the months ahead. Pastry chef Daniel Duckett closed his east Belfast patisserie in the last year, but has now re-opened in partnership Knott's bakery chain in Forestside shopping centre. Duckett said that Knott's has the buying power for ingredients so "they can control costs a little bit better than we would have been able to". "They have been able to absorb a lot more of the costs that we would have been paying before," he added. Duckett said rising petrol prices in particular will affect the cost of goods. He added: "We have to think, how much do we deliver to the shops? Because that will also affect our petrol prices that fill up vans that travel across Northern Ireland." "I think a lot of people don't realise that the weather and global warming affect a lot of the products we bring in - tropical fruits, vanilla, cocoa, sugar cane." "Those are things that are definitely affected by storms and El Niño. I would try to brace myself for that as well," he added. Mr Duckett added: "For the second half of the year we will have to be vigilant about where those products that have to travel far come from, as petrol prices will have to factor in to that." title: 'Heartbreaking': The man driven out by the UK's £5bn theme park
description: Ritchie Wood is almost brought to tears at he looks at the empty homes once loved by his neighbours.
body: Seeing his neighbours' homes being demolished has almost brought Ritchie Wood to tears Surrounded by rolling fields and lakes, Ritchie Wood's home of 11 years provided the serene village life he loved. Yet in recent weeks, his neighbours have packed their bags and left - their houses in Kempston Hardwick, Bedfordshire, soon to be reduced to rubble. "It's totally changed to how it used to be - it used to be lovely. We had a nice little community here, lots of wildlife, very quiet," Wood tells the BBC. Now, as the 55-year-old looks around him in Manor Road, all he sees are empty properties. Wood knows his will be next. His rented home lies in the middle of what will be Universal's new £5bn theme park, touted to be the UK's biggest tourist attraction when it opens in 2031. Universal hopes to demolish these 12 homes, which lie at the heart of its planned theme park After a long-running standoff between the developer and the residents, some of whom initially refused to leave their homes, demolition work has now started. "I genuinely have nowhere to go", says Wood, who expects to be homeless within two months when his landlord evicts him. "Unfortunately, I wouldn't be able to afford anywhere in the area for the same sort of rent [I pay now]." Contractors want to raze a terrace of 12 properties in Manor Road, as well as several others, and have closed the road until 28 November to work on it. Large diggers have been used in Manor Road for several days The quiet hum of village life has been replaced by the sound of lorries and generators working on the 476-acre (193ha) theme park, Wood says. "It's very strange and very surreal. When I drive up and down this road, I almost feel I shouldn't be here now." Seeing his neighbours' houses being demolished is a sight that almost brings him to tears. "I came past and saw them being demolished yesterday and it's heartbreaking," Wood adds. "It almost brings tears to my eyes because it's all just going to go." Universal UK Resort is expected to become the country's biggest tourist attraction There are clear benefits to the Universal resort, which is expected to draw 8.5 million visitors a year and contribute £50bn to the UK economy by 2055. A 500-room hotel is planned at the site and shuttle buses from Milton Keynes Central will serve it every seven minutes on average, according to Labour MP Emily Darlington, external. Then there are the adrenaline junkies excited by the prospect of a resort that will rival Disneyland Paris. "Everyone else is doing great out of this," Wood sighs. "I'm in a very unique situation. Out of 70 million people in the country, I'm the only person facing homelessness out of this." Some residents told the BBC they felt forced to leave their homes Residents in Manor Road were not subject to compulsory purchase orders, but, nonetheless, have told the BBC they felt forced to move. Universal bypassed local planning procedures and instead got permission from the government to build the resort in December. Wood says the global brand has not done enough to support him while trying to find a new house. Wood adds: "This has been my home for 11 years and the uncertainty of not knowing where I'm going to be in a few months time is really, really worrying. Genuinely very worrying and scary." Universal has been contacted to respond to his concerns. In a letter to residents, external on 18 September, the theme park developer said it remained "committed to being a good neighbour" during the project. It has previously stressed that 80% of the attraction's workforce will come from Bedfordshire and neighbouring counties, stating "local focus is important". title: Mum's heartbreak over LA killing and granddaughter's location
description: June Bunyan's mother says she has been left in legal limbo over her daughter's death and custody of her granddaughter.
body: This video can not be played Mum's 'heartbreak' over daughter's death in LA The mother of a Scottish law graduate killed in Los Angeles says the lack of information from US authorities since her daughter's death has been heartbreaking. June Bunyan's dismembered body was found in her apartment in September last year. Her husband Jonathan Renteria has been charged with murder, mutilation and child cruelty. He has pleaded not guilty. Jill Bunyan, June's mum, says she is in legal limbo and is still not certain who is caring for her baby granddaughter. June Bunyan was found dead in Los Angeles in September 2025 Jill Bunyan was previously told the court process against Renteria could take two years. The latest of many court hearings was held on 4 September – the first anniversary of June's disappearance. But Jill and her family, from Arran, said they received no official information about that hearing until almost two weeks later. The case has been continued until October. "My health has had an absolute battering, and it's not just with losing June. It's the lack of respect, the lack of communication," she said. "It almost feels like nobody cares. Nobody actually cares, and that is heartbreaking, and that is as bad as losing June because it just plays mind games with you. It is horrendous." The flat in LA where June Bunyan lived with her baby daughter June studied law at Robert Gordon University in Aberdeen and moved to California in 2023. Less than two months before she was killed June had given birth to a baby girl called Regina. Jill thinks she might be in the custody of Jonathan Renteria's parents but does not know for sure. BBC Scotland News has attempted to contact Renteria's parents but has been unable to verify where baby Regina is. If she is with Renteria's parents, Jill has this message for them: "That is my daughter's daughter who I'd seen everyday [over the internet]…pick up the phone, send a picture, just let me know she's all right." Jill is currently crowdfunding to pay for a lawyer to try to track down Regina. Jill Bunyan is trying to find out who is looking after her granddaughter Regina in the United States June's family and friends have just marked a year since she was killed. "Grief controls you, you don't have any control over grief. It points you in a direction and you just have to go with it, " said Jill. She described herself as heartbroken. "That's never going to change," she said. "I'll be heartbroken until I go. Jill says she is grateful for the support she receives from her local MP Irene Campbell, as well as the charity Victim Support Scotland. But she is critical of the level of support she has received from the UK government Foreign Office and hopes to meet the foreign secretary to highlight the challenges of losing a loved one abroad. Jill visits her daughter's grave in a cemetery in Lamlash nearly every day "It doesn't have to be this difficult," she said. "It's difficult enough without having to fight everybody to get answers to simple questions, but I can't get answers." The day after Jill recorded an interview with BBC Scotland News, she received an apology from the prosecution service in Los Angeles for the lack of communication about the court case against Renteria. BBC Scotland News has not received a response from the District Attorney's office to our request for comment. The UK Foreign Office said it was supporting the family of a British woman who has died in the US and is in contact with the local authorities. If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line. title: V&A workers to strike over pay and conditions
description: A limited number of galleries will be open on Friday and Saturday at the museum's South Kensington site.
body: Museum workers at the V&A in London are to stage a two-day strike in a dispute over pay and conditions. Members of Prospect and the Public and Commercial Services union (PCS) will walk out on Friday and Saturday, meaning only a limited number of galleries will be open. Prospect is calling for a minimum 4% pay increase for staff earning above the living wage and other benefits including time-and-a-half for bank holiday working. The strike action will only cover the museum's site in South Kensington but Prospect said it remained in dispute at other V&A sites across the capital. Schiaparelli: Fashion Becomes Art will remain open throughout the strike (as will the cafe) Mike Clancy, general secretary of Prospect, said members had been left with "no choice" but to take action as senior management "continues to not engage seriously on our very reasonable demands". He added: "Directors at V&A continue to demonstrate their lack of respect for the very people who make the museum what it is – its dedicated, highly qualified staff. "The V&A can still avoid this strike, but it needs actual effort to meet our terms and for senior management to demonstrate that they are serious about wanting to find a solution." The V&A said in a statement: "Due to planned industrial action on 25 and 26 September 2026, V&A South Kensington will be operating a reduced visitor offer. "Schiaparelli: Fashion Becomes Art, the café and a limited number of galleries will be open, but we expect the rest of the museum will be closed. "We deeply regret that the Trade Unions have voted for strike action. We have been negotiating with them in good faith since February and have met the majority of their demands with a significantly improved offer, which we believe is fair, competitive and affordable. "We remain available for negotiations with our Trade Union colleagues." Young V&A, V&A East Museum and Storehouse will be open as usual. title: Turner Prize gallery 'centre of creative universe'
description: Work by four artists nominated for the prize will go on display from 26 September.
body: Work by four artists nominated for the Turner Prize will go on display at the Middlesbrough Institute of Modern Art Turner Prize nominated artworks are going on display at a gallery in what its director has called a "prestigious opportunity". Work by four artists in the running for the prize - Simeon Barclay, Kira Freije, Marguerite Humeau and Tanoa Sasraku - will go on display at Teesside University's Middlesbrough Institute of Modern Art (MIMA) from 26 September. Dr Laura Sillars, director of MIMA and dean of culture and creativity at the niversity, said of the exhibition: "While it's here, at a certain level, we are the centre of the creative universe." The Turner Prize is awarded each year to a British artist for an outstanding exhibition or other presentation of their work. Middlesbrough Mayor Chris Cooke said the exhibition, which includes works of mixed media, sculpture and spoken word, would provide residents with an "incredible opportunity" to see cutting-edge art in their home town". He said: "I hope it inspires our young people to dream about what's possible. "Why shouldn't it be them in a few years' time? "Hosting the Turner Prize gives us a chance to show off what we have to offer to people across the country." Established in 1984 and named after English Romantic painter Joseph Mallord William Turner, the prize is one of the most prestigious awards for visual arts. The winner, who will be announced on 10 December, will be awarded £25,000, with £10,000 given to the other shortlisted artists. title: Endangered dormice on farm signal healthy landscape
description: Dormice are detected on a farm near Bridport during surveys by the Countryside Regeneration Trust.
body: Dormice have been detected at Babers Farm following the installation of footprint tunnels Endangered dormice have been found on a farm that has been working to improve biodiversity and nature habitats. Babers Farm in Marshwood, near Bridport, Dorset, is under the stewardship of the Countryside Regeneration Trust (CRT), which seeks to create nature-friendly farms. Hazel dormice are a European Protected Species and are considered vulnerable to extinction, but their presence is a marker of a healthy, well-connected landscape. Since it began surveys in May, the CRT has installed 39 footprint tunnels along hedgerows and woodland edges, with nine of the tunnels recording dormouse footprints. Ruth Moss said survey data helped inform CRT's management of its farms Babers is one of the first CRT farms to return positive dormouse results after a fundraising appeal to fund surveys and habitat improvements across its 16 properties. The survival of dormice is dependent on diverse woodland, species-rich hedgerows and connected habitats that provide year-round food and shelter. CRT conservation officer Ruth Moss said: "It's really encouraging to see evidence of hazel dormouse presence on the farm. "As the survey progresses, the results will build up a more complete picture of where, within the areas surveyed, dormice are present on the farm. "Having a current set of data helps us to manage these areas with dormice in mind." The CRT works with tenant farmers to restore soil health, improve biodiversity and strengthen the natural ecosystem while producing food. Footprint tunnels have also been installed at Bere Marsh Farm in Dorset and at Pierrepont Farm and Green Farm in Surrey. Dormouse footprints were detected on nine footprint tunnels The surveys will continue in Dorset throughout September and into November in Surrey. Dormice have also been detected at Turnastone Court Farm and Awnells Farm in Herefordshire. CRT supporters raised £6,000 to fund dormouse surveys and habitat improvements across the charity's farms. As surveying continues through 2026, the CRT hopes to build a clearer picture of dormouse populations across its farms and use the findings to guide future habitat management. The tiny nocturnal species has disappeared from 20 counties in England since the 19th Century. The loss of traditional skills such as coppicing has led to their habitats being lost, which also makes it more difficult for populations to travel between locations. Climate change has also disrupted their hibernation patterns. title: Cotswolds home to UK's first air taxi centre
description: The futuristic air taxis will be built at a new centre at Cotswolds Airport in Gloucestershire.
body: The Valo aircraft take off and land vertically like helicopters Futuristic air taxis that take off like helicopters will be built at a new facility that is the first of its kind in the UK. Bristol-based company Vertical Aerospace has announced a new aircraft assembly centre at Cotswold Airport, near Kemble in Gloucestershire, describing it as a "once-in-a-generation opportunity". The Valo aircraft currently being developed and tested there are electric, carry four passengers and can fly up to 160km (100 miles) with no operating emissions, the firm said. Minister for Reindustrialisation Blair McDougall said the new facility would "help turn British innovation into British manufacturing". The new centre adds 60,000sq ft (5,574sq m) of space to Vertical's existing flight test centre at Cotswold Airport. Council leader voted out after no confidence motion Rare Bronze Age finds unearthed in city dig Man who used police ruse to assault girls jailed Vertical said construction of the new aircraft would begin in late 2027 with an initial 25 being built every year before the company increases that number to 900 a year by 2035. The company said it had 1,500 orders, many of which were from airlines. It said there were plans to get the planes certified for commercial use by 2029. Vertical's CEO Stuart Simpson said the new centre was an "important step" for the company Vertical's CEO Stuart Simpson said: "We're getting really close to this idea of flying cars, flying taxis. "Opening our aircraft assembly centre is an important step in Vertical's transition from prototype developer to aircraft manufacturer. "Bringing a new category of aircraft to market is a once-in-a-generation opportunity and it is especially rewarding to do that here in Great Britain, drawing on the country's proud aviation heritage." Testing of the new aircraft technology was already under way at Cotswold Airport, a spokesperson for Vertical said McDougall said the assembly centre was "exactly the kind of investment we want to see more of as we work to reindustrialise Britain, creating high-skilled local jobs and strengthening our manufacturing base". Suzannah Harvey, CEO of Cotswold Airport, said she was "delighted" to support the new centre which she said strengthened the airport's "growing role as a hub for aerospace innovation". Plans for a separate full-scale production site, intended to support higher-volume manufacturing, are expected to be announced later this year. title: Scam hotel booking sent family to Wetherspoon pub
description: Which? says staff are turning away up to 20 tourists a day after scammers used the pub's address.
body: Wetherspoon staff have been turning away up to 20 tourists on a daily basis as scammers use the address as a fake Booking.com holiday apartment, Which? has found A theatre-goer fell victim to a "sophisticated phishing attack" after booking a "luxury" London apartment, only to discover the address was a Wetherspoon pub. Paul Dawson, from Loughborough in Leicestershire, paid £73 for a one-night stay for his family via Booking.com at The London Crown apartments to watch the musical Hamilton in the West End. Days later, he said, he discovered the address shown in the listing was actually The Liberty Bounds pub, a Wetherspoon near Tower Bridge. Consumer protection organisation Which? said Wetherspoon staff had been turning away up to 20 tourists a day after scammers used the pub's address as a listing for a "block of luxury apartments". Which? said it was also made aware of a property listed as "Apartments near Big Ben", with the address given as Portcullis House, part of the House of Commons estate, where hundreds of MPs work. Booking.com told Which? that in both cases, listings for legitimate properties had been targeted by a "sophisticated phishing attack, allowing criminals to hijack the listings". Wetherspoon said it had informed Booking.com about this scam "as soon as it came to their attention". Paul Dawson said he had to find alternative accommodation for his family Dawson, 55, made his booking in August. Two days later, he said he received an email from The London Crown containing a link to a fake Booking.com page, which asked for his bank details. Dawson told Which? he contacted Booking.com with his suspicions, but said the platform told him that he would need to visit the "fake apartment" and wait until after 7pm before it would relocate him. This was despite Mr Dawson explaining to them that he had since discovered the address shown in the listing was actually The Liberty Bounds pub. He told Which?: "I explained to the support staff that I had autistic children and the idea of turning up at a clearly non-existent property at 10.30pm would have been catastrophic. "This did not change their response, that I needed to go to the property. They said that if it was not possible to check in then I could contact them again and they would find an alternative." Dawson said the family ended up staying in the Premier Inn in Goodge Street. The Liberty Bounds is in Trinity Square, Tower Hill, and near the Tower of London The listing for the London Crown apartments had 250 negative reviews from August and September along with a handful of, likely fake, positive reviews, Which? said. The BBC checked the listing on Thursday. The information was still visible but the page carried the message: "We're sorry, but this property isn't taking reservations on our site right now". Wetherspoon said the listing was removed only for it to reappear, "though it now appears that the ability to book has been blocked". "We have again notified them [Booking.com], asking for the listing to be permanently removed. "It is clearly unacceptable for people to be defrauded in such a flagrant manner. "This is upsetting for the pub team, as there is little they can do to help, but even more so for the people who have been misled and have lost money as a result. "Booking.com urgently needs to adopt more robust procedures to prevent fraudulent listings like this appearing in the first place." The BBC was able to access the listings page on Thursday for The London Crown, but bookings were frozen Many of the reviews from customers said they told Booking.com that it was a scam but had been ignored. One customer said: "I reported it to Booking.com three days before check-in but they refused to do anything." Another customer, from Spain, complained that she and her friend had been left stranded, writing: "Two girls alone in London at two o'clock in the morning with no accommodation." Booking.com also has an AI trip planner called Dot, which allows users to ask questions. On The London Crown listing page a Which? researcher asked: "Is this a real property, or is it a scam?". It replied: "The London Crown is a legitimate property located in the centre of London. It offers various amenities such as free wifi, free bikes, and free private parking. It is conveniently located near Longleat Safari Park and Longleat House, with London City Airport just 10km away. Based on the detailed description and amenities listed, the London Crown appears to be a real and well-equipped property." Dot failed to recognise that Longleat Safari Park was more than 100 miles (160km) from London, in Wiltshire. An AI trip planner called Dot said The London Crown was conveniently located near Longleat Safari Park and Longleat House "Apartments near Big Ben" and The London Crown apartments were both targeted by the phishing attack, said Booking.com. "The attack affected the properties' own computer systems and gave cybercriminals temporary, unauthorised access to the accommodation's Booking.com account," a spokesperson said. "We take incidents like this extremely seriously, and suspended bookings at both properties, as well as supporting affected customers." An Ofcom spokesperson said: "Fraud online can have serious consequences for victims and platforms have clear legal duties to take down illegal content generated by users once they become aware of it. "More broadly, we've shown that we'll use our enforcement powers against platforms that fail to comply with the Online Safety Act, and have already launched investigations into over 100 sites." title: British rapper Yung Filly to face rape retrial in Australia next June
description: Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos was cleared of several sexual offences in July but a jury was undecided on three rape charges.
body: Yung Filly will face a retrial next June after a jury in Australia failed to reach a verdict on three rape charges British rapper Yung Filly will face a rape retrial in Australia next June after a jury failed to reach a verdict during an earlier trial. In July, a jury acquitted the 31-year-old - whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos - of three counts of rape, one of assault and one of strangulation but found him guilty of two assault charges. No decision was reached for three rape charges, which he has denied. A fan, aged 20 at the time, alleges Barrientos repeatedly raped and assaulted her in his hotel room in Perth, Western Australia, after a 2024 concert. The court previously heard that Barrientos and the woman had consensual sex before she alleged it turned violent and he refused to stop. On Friday, Perth's District Court set 15 June as the start date for the retrial which is expected to last eight days. Barrientos was not required to appear in court and is understood to have returned to the UK after the court granted him permission to leave Australia as part of his bail conditions. Sentencing for the two assault charges that the jury found Barrientos guilty of in July will take place after the retrial. Barrientos, who was born in Colombia and brought up in the UK, is known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad. He has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows. title: Xi got Trump's red carpet welcome - but not everything he wanted
description: China wanted progress on trade, technology and Taiwan - but hasn't got as much as it would have hoped for.
body: This video can not be played Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? President Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim. China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan. On this visit, however, despite Trump rolling out the red carpet for him, the Chinese leader didn't get everything he wanted. The trade truce that saw both countries pause a tit-for-tat tariff war and prevent a further escalation, was extended by only a few months - from November to January. Beijing had hoped for at least a year as Xi looks to ride out the remainder of Trump's presidency. This means key disputes on tariffs, China's dominance on rare earth supplies and access to advanced US chips are being kicked forward into yet another round of negotiations. This suggests the US wants China to do more to fulfil its side of the bargain before offering longer-term concessions. Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White House The uncomfortable truth for Xi is that his domestic economy is in trouble. While the country sells a record number of goods around the world, consumers at home are holding back. Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their own homes. Trade is helping to prop up growth, making access to overseas markets more important than ever. Xi needs to protect those exports from the kind of debilitating tariffs the US imposed last year. On Taiwan, Xi once again made clear that US arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China. The US is bound by law to provide the self-governing island with the means to defend itself. In May, Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict". Trump then delayed the approval of a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, describing it as a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing. Xi may have seized on that opening during the talks and likely argued that restraining support for Taiwan reduces the risk of conflict. On Thursday he reiterated his hope that the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence. However, Trump - who is coming under some bipartisan pressure to continue US support to Taiwan - is yet to make any public response to the Chinese leader's comments. Trade is helping to prop up growth The two leaders did at least discuss artificial intelligence (AI) although it's unclear whether they agreed to any safeguards. All eyes were on whether they would make any concrete decisions on AI - such as an agreement to hold a summit - in the wake of an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the slowing down of AI development to make it safer. That followed a warning by a top safety researcher from the company that there was a "greater than 10% chance" that AI could cause the extinction of humans. But besides Xi talking about the importance of ensuring AI "is always under human control" we didn't get much else. Trump has most recently dismissed fears of human extinction from the technology as a "hoax". And, of course, let's not forget the pandas. The gift of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta was first heralded in April, but Xi has now announced they will arrive in just a few days as China's panda diplomacy resumes. There may be more announcements to come as the two prepare to have tea and visit the national archives on Friday. Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measures But for now, one of the summit's biggest victories for Beijing may have been the optics. The lavish welcome, a personal greeting at the airport and a state banquet featuring sesame crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy have been welcomed by those watching from China. It will have helped cement Xi's image at home as Trump's equal. Memes contrasting the two leaders have spread widely on Chinese social media. One popular image shows Trump grimacing as bomber jets fly overhead, while Xi remained impassive. Xi has found a way to manage one of the world's most unpredictable leaders. But while Trump talks of a "truly great friendship", China's leader is focussed on something bigger: securing China's place alongside the United States as a superpower. The pandas, the pageantry and the warm words may help smooth this relationship. But beneath the spectacle, the competition between the world's two most powerful countries remains as fierce as ever. title: Why Trump gave Xi an ornate bald eagle statue at the state dinner
description: From redwood benches to DVDs, gifts are an important part of the art of diplomacy.
body: President Trump said he and First Lady Melania helped design the statue US President Donald Trump has presented Chinese President Xi Jinping with a sculpture of a bald eagle, a bird native to North America and his country's national symbol, during a lavish state dinner in Washington. The gift, which was unveiled before VIP guests at the Thursday dinner, embodies "the free and soaring spirit of America", said Trump. He said that he and First Lady Melania Trump participated in its design. The statue is part of a valuable - but sometimes tricky - aspect of international diplomacy: gift-giving. Such gifts are a small but meaningful element of the larger aim of Xi and Trump's three-day summit – forging personal relationships between heads of two global superpowers. "They're going to discuss all of these complicated issues," Daniel Kritenbrink, partner at The Asia Group says. "But at the end of the day, these are still two human beings. "So that personal relationship means something," he says. "I think the gift exchange is one key part of that." Kritenbrink, who spent over 30 years as a US diplomat, mostly in Asia, says personal relationships are of particular importance to Xi. He believes the direct Trump-Xi bond is the glue that is holding together "the most complex and the most consequential relationship in the world". He says Trump, too, values what Kritenbrink calls "leader-level diplomacy". Gifts have had a unique presence in the Trump presidency. The US president has received a luxury jumbo jet, an engraved gold bar, a diamond-and-jewel encrusted gold ring, and more. Ole Jacob Sending from the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs says: "You think about the Trump presidency in that way, I think gift giving, certainly broadly defined, is very much part of how he operates." On Thursday morning, Xi announced a gift of two Chinese pandas to a zoo in Atlanta - and a new student exchange programme, which will welcome 100,000 US students to study in China over five years. "The giant panda have been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and the Americans," Xi said. "In a few days, two pandas - Ping Ping and Fu Shuang - will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people." It's unclear if he gave any further presents. The BBC has contacted the White House. This video can not be played Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? Today, the practice of giving lavish gifts mostly exists in Gulf states and autocratic governments. "Autocracies like China give much more expensive gifts," says Morten Skumsrud Anderson, who co-authored a study on diplomacy and gifts with Sending. In the West, Anderson says, the tradition has been watered down by democratic guardrails and restrictions. For example, the US Constitution has an emoluments clause that puts a dollar-value limit on gifts a president can receive from a foreign government. Currently, the limit is $525 (£397). Anything higher and it becomes federal property, unless the president chooses to buy it back with his own money. Also, when giving a gift beyond a certain amount, a US president would have to go through Congress, unless he was paying for it personally. "There are a lot of rules and protocols involved," Sending says, "A lot of thought and process relating to what type of gift to to give, where should the gift exchange happen? How should it happen? When? "All of this is highly scripted, and involves negotiation at lower levels that goes on for weeks and weeks in advance," Sending says. Anderson adds: "This is not a last-minute purchase at the airport." During Xi's state visit to the US in 2013, then-President Barack Obama gifted him an inscribed bench made of redwood, native to California where the two had met. They sat on it together afterwards, smiling for cameras. It was a more shining example than in 2009, when then-British Prime Minister Gordon Brown gifted Obama an ornamental desk pen holder made from the timbers of a historic anti-slave ship; while Obama gave Brown a set of DVDs, which reportedly were not formatted for UK DVD players. "That's one example of a kind of an embarrassing exchange," Sending says. Fortunately, Brown and Obama were allied leaders and not deep rivals looking to resolve seemingly intractable differences. "You don't want to mess up," Sending says, adding that the wrong gift could potentially derail any larger objectives. In this case, there is potentially a lot at stake between Trump and Xi. Their third face-to-face encounter since the start of Trump's second term, this summit is happening amid growing fears of an AI-led apocalypse as both countries race for dominance in the quickly growing industry. It's also taking place in the wake of a bitter US-China trade war that has only been resolved by a temporary truce, extended on this trip. So, do the military plane flyovers, cue the performances, fill the wine the glasses, Kritenbrink says. Exchange the gifts. "It's protocol and it's optics and it's gift giving all as a means to an end, which is stable US-China relations," Kritenbrink says. "I'll take a fragile truce over a white-hot trade war any day of the week." title: Miliband tells Iran minister UK will not tolerate 'hostile activity' on British soil
description: The foreign secretary stresses "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community".
body: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi that the UK will "not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil". The ministers met face-to-face at the UN General Assembly in New York City. The Foreign Office said Miliband spoke to his counterpart about "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community", and discussed war in the Middle East and a British couple detained in Iran. There was no immediate comment from Araghchi. The Islamic Republic News Agency reported the men met and "discussed bilateral ties and international developments during their talks". Miliband's comments follow an arson attack on four Jewish community ambulances in Golders Green in March and other incidents. The BBC understands that British intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it had a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026. They later concluded that secret intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack. In July, a small power plant in the UK was also shut down due to a cyber attack, which the Telegraph reported , externalwas carried out by hackers affiliated to the Iranian regime. The Foreign Office said Miliband also spoke to his counterpart about the country's war with the US, telling Araghchi that Iran should choose "de-escalation and diplomacy instead of prolonging the war" and stressing the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz. In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran, killing the country's supreme leader. Iran responded by launching strikes on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases. It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, impacting the global economy. On Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly that any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade stopping Iranian ships from using the waterway. Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, Pezeshkian said his country will never "bend the knee". "The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying," he said. There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address. The Foreign Office said Miliband also used Thursday's meeting to raise the detention of British couple Lindsay and Craig Foreman in Iran. The couple, who are from East Sussex, have been detained for more than 20 months after being arrested while passing through the country on a motorcycle journey. In February, the Foremans were each sentenced to 10 years in jail on espionage charges, which they deny. In Miliband's discussion with the Iranian foreign minister, he reiterated the call for them to be immediately released and stressed that their welfare remains a priority for the government, the Foreign Office said. title: Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?
description: The BBC’s China correspondent Laura Bicker unpacks how the trip panned out for Beijing and Washington.
body: This video can not be played The world’s two most powerful men – Xi Jinping and Donald Trump – have just met in Washington after days of pomp and pageantry. While there were many symbolic gestures, including Chinese pandas from President Xi, there were few big movements – although they committed to a six month extension of the tariff truce. title: The Papers: 'Xi urges rivals to coexist in peace' and 'It's on at last'
description: Many of the papers include photographs of Chinese President Xi Jinping's historic visit to the White House.
body: Many of the papers on Friday include photographs of Chinese President Xi Jinping's historic visit to the White House. The Financial Times leads on quotes from his address, where Xi said the US and China should "coexist in peace" and avoid being drawn into conflict. US President Donald Trump and his wife Melania are pictured alongside Xi on the front page of the Times, standing on the White House balcony after a military show. The main story for the paper focuses on a sex offender who was repeatedly allowed to return to his home overlooking the playground he targeted. It leads on a statement from the Metropolitan Police commissioner, who said police officers felt "hamstrung" by a system that he said results in "seemingly unfathomable decisions". Sir Mark Rowley told reporters that "the children should be put first, not the paedophile". The Sun says Sarah Ferguson has received offers of up to seven figures for an autobiography, and is just "days away" from a book deal. The paper adds that the Royal Family are still reeling from the revelations in Earl Spencer's memoir about his sister, Princess Diana. The paper's front page also includes a nod to the upcoming fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. The headline reads "It's on at last". People who believe they have ADHD or autism must wait two years before they can be assessed, according to the Guardian. The paper reports that the decision to delay assessments is because the NHS is struggling to meet the "surging demand", and cannot afford the cost of the number of assessments people are seeking. It adds that the NHS disclosure of this approach precedes a major government-commissioned review of the "colossal increases" in diagnoses of ADHD, autism and mental illness. The NHS is also the focus for the i Paper, which reports that overcrowding in A&E has been linked to more than 500 deaths a week across the UK. It says that, on average, emergency rooms are operating at 175% capacity. The Daily Telegraph carries a series of allegations regarding the care of celebrated explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, who has been open about his battle with Parkinson's disease. "Labour's army of migrants", reads the Daily Mail, which says that the number of small boat migrants who have reached the UK under the Labour government is "larger than the entire British Army". The paper says that 83,279 migrants have reached British shores since the last general election, according to figures quoted by Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp. A photograph of migrants in the English Channel leads the Daily Express under the headline: "Desperate to reach Britain". Former England striker Andy Carroll is pictured on the front page of the Mirror, after he revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021. The paper reports the incident took place at Carroll's home, with the unnamed attacker set to stay over after arriving to watch a boxing match. Carroll is also the leading story for the Star, which says the perpetrator assaulted the former footballer while he slept. His attacker was jailed for three years following the incident, the paper adds. The UK has launched its first retail facial recognition system in a London coffee shop, which the Metro claims "endangers civil liberties" and "risks unleashing fraud on a dangerous new level". The paper explains that when a customer goes to pay, the system, which is powered by online bank Revolut, checks their biometrics against those provided when they first signed up. title: 'I was living out my dream career in football – tumours mean I need to leave'
description: After years of dismissing health issues, Dan Robathan is now unable to return to the pitch.
body: Dan Robathan spent years climbing the football ladder as an assistant referee It was May 2025 and life was good for Premier League and Fifa assistant referee Dan Robathan. In fact, he was flying high. Years of climbing the football ladder had paid off and he was running the line at the FA Cup final between Crystal Palace and Manchester City. But just months after this career highlight, symptoms Dan thought were sciatic nerve pain and wear and tear were revealed to be benign tumours in his spine, which needed to be operated on immediately. "I saw a neurosurgeon who told me I had two tumours, initially I thought it was one, but it was two," Dan tells BBC Newsbeat. "It was compressing nerves, there was a chance it could affect a motor nerve which means it could affect function in my leg. "I needed to go home, lay down and not move. I did that for 15 days, my life turned upside down overnight." BBC Newsbeat met Dan at a football pitch in Norwich, close to where he lives, where he revealed the struggles he has had in trying to regain his fitness and mobility. Dan Robathan (centre) worked his way up to top flight football Dan picked up his first flag at 10 years old, working his way up from grassroots football to the lines at more than 200 Premier League clashes and World Cup qualifiers. Speaking at the time of the FA Cup final, Dan said it was "a privilege to stand there on behalf of over 37,000 referees across the country". The chances of becoming an elite level referee are low. The FA describes Fifa match officials, external as the "pinnacle of the officiating ladder". Photos of Dan over the last few years show him doing everything from embracing then Liverpool manager Arne Slot to explaining a decision to Emiliano Martinez, and officiating games without fans due to the Covid pandemic. And in his social media posts, Dan gives a glimpse of everything you would expect from an official at elite level - from the roar of fans to sprinting to be in the right place during split second decisions. To the outside world, all looked well. "I started having quite bad problems with sexual dysfunction or bladder issues where I'd have to sit down to urinate and I couldn't stand up," he explains. "It got to a point in September [2025] where something's not right at all." A neurosurgeon confirmed to Dan he had two tumours in his spine – and his life ground to a halt. "It was fear, anxiety, not knowing how long it will take me to get back. "What would my life look like? Will I be a normal man? Will I walk again?" Surgeons removed one tumour and left one alone, which was deemed safe. Dan says he needs time to "grieve" his career - but has hope for the future The tumours were non-cancerous, but have caused significant damage to Dan, who describes his post-operation recovery as "brutal". Yet there was "no doubt" in his mind that he would return. But by Christmas 2025, Dan was still feeling fatigued and struggling to lift his heel, walk, or feel his calf. "The surgeon said I had under a 10% chance of ever getting back on the field but even then I was like I don't care I will prove everyone wrong," Dan recalls. Yet despite fighting "like mad", he was unable to regain his fitness levels. This week, Dan was forced to medically retire, saying in effect "the decision was made for me". Dan says he wants to help other men speak up about health problems The 38-year-old says he still has days where he struggles to walk, or where his back feels "on fire". "My body just can't do what I want it to do," he says. Dan underwent testing to confirm his tumours weren't linked to genetics, which was reassuring, but still leaves him facing the unknown. "It's a loss of identity. I've been 'Dan the ref' since I was 10 years old. "It's 28 years of being who I am, it's my personality. "When you have the recognition that that sort of life is over, psychologically it is really tough." Dan is now working with a psychologist to decide the path forward. "I feel like a 16-year-old who's just left school and trying to work out what I want to do with my life," he jokes. "I have a few options, staying in football. "[But] I don't know if I will be able to with the mental health problems I've had. "Can I stay involved in a sport that I loved but can't do myself?" One thing he is certain of, is going into the future with his family. "I want to put my son, fiancée, my stepchildren first. I want to try and advocate for men's mental health, for men speaking about health issues. "If I can help one or two men in the process, I've done my job." And Dan accepts that if he gets back into football it would need to be for the right reasons. "I need to get that fire my belly." title: Treadmills to deadlifts: Why Gen Z are swapping cardio for strength training
description: Gyms are booming, solitary cardio is out - how workouts are changing.
body: When Antonia Duffin, 34, started going to the gym, she wanted to lose weight and tone up. It became such a big part of her life that she decided to become a personal trainer alongside her day job in operations for a supermarket chain - and now runs her own women's gym in Manchester. "Some of my clients want to feel stronger, some want to get in shape for a baby and some are struggling with other conditions like endometriosis and want to feel better," she says. Hybrid training, like Hyrox, which is sociable and competitive, seems to have taken over from running on a treadmill or general cardio on a bike, she explains. Antonia also notes an appetite for more strength training workouts among younger clients, adding: "I think people are now realising the importance of it - we're preventing osteoporosis and things like that." Do numbers bear that out? And how are workouts across the UK changing? This video can not be played Why more young people are switching from cardio to weights According to Sport England, more young adults are going to the gym, using exercise machines and weights to keep fit compared to nine years ago. "Gyms offer broader types of exercise, like resistance training, which can improve body composition and shape more quickly than aerobic exercise training," explains exercise expert Dr Andrew Scott, from the University of Portsmouth. He says social media is having an impact too. "Lots of people are largely learning from influencers, suggesting 'I can do it, this is what I did and so can you'." Student Will Seward, 19, started going to the gym when he was at secondary school because he wanted to "get stronger and build up his physique". His workouts - usually three a week - have changed over time, from using running machines and exercise bikes initially to more explosive training using weights, to help build athleticism. "It's had a real impact on my day to day life," he says, "improving my mood and making me feel generally healthier." Barbells, kettlebells, dumbbells and cable machines are all part of the strength training Antonia offers in her gym space, located in a shipping container. Recent research suggests doing the recommended two hours of strength training each week may offer many of the same benefits as regular aerobic exercise, such as lowering the risk of dying from heart disease or stroke while also protecting the brain and boosting self-esteem. These benefits are not the only appeal of exercise though. Many say they feel a sense of connection when exercising with other people. Dr Hussain Al-Zubaidi, a GP, personal trainer and triathlete, says there is now "an enormous ecosystem" for those who are already active, featuring gyms, running clubs, fitness apps, social media and wearable tech. How different age groups meet overall exercise targets varies. Among nearly 2 million participants in Our Future Health - a health and lifestyle questionnaire - younger age groups were more likely to do shorter bursts of vigorous activity every week like fitness classes, aerobics or football. While running has fallen in popularity overall, it is still the most common form of exercise for young men and women - and in the top two activities for adults overall. And organised, social running is thriving, with children, 20-somethings and over 50s accounting for a growing share of participants in parkruns, which are free to everyone and have over 1,400 events taking place across the UK every weekend. Prof Esther van Sluijs, professor of behavioural epidemiology from Loughborough University, says community exercise offers social connection. When working from home is so common, particularly for young people, "easy access to community clubs close to home is very important", she adds. So how much is keeping active costing exercise goers, at a time when budgeting is tight? More than a quarter of 16-34 year olds say paying for gym membership and keeping fit is a top spending priority, over holidays and eating out, data from UK Active shows - up from a fifth in 2024. A 2026 survey by the Gym Group found a third of Gen Z spent £26-50 per month on health and fitness, with a quarter spending more than £50. Events manager Cordelia Sheridan, 27, who exercises four to five times a week at her gym in Battersea, says she treats her £45 gym membership "like an essential utility bill". "If you go to the pub and you're with a group of mates, you can buy a few pints and easily spend that on a night out," she says. Living just five minutes walk from her gym makes it easy to get there for 6.30am and exercise before work. At the gym, she spends 10 minutes on a stair-climbing machine then 35 minutes using weights and machines to strengthen the thighs, hips and lower back. Before, her routine was all about cardio - but she didn't feel she was getting better or stronger. Now, she says, it's really nice being able to hit targets and lift heavier weights. "I want to go into my 30s being strong." "And it's also weirdly more sociable," she says. Persuading people to exercise is about making it the easy, social and enjoyable thing to do, even if it costs, says Dr Al-Zubaidi. "I think that's why activities like the gym, running clubs and padel have been successful - not because they prevent disease but because they are fun and sociable." title: Just how hot and dry was your summer? Use our postcode lookup to find out
description: Most of us experienced drought and heatwaves - but temperatures and rainfall were not the same everywhere.
body: The UK faced its hottest summer on record this year, with much of the country experiencing drought and repeated heatwaves. But temperatures and rainfall were not the same everywhere. Type in your postcode to see what summer 2026 was like in your area. A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive. As a result, we can't show information for your location, but data for the entire UK is available below. Data up to August 2026 In the UK summer temperatures have been above average. The maximum daily temperature was 21.3C on average, which is 2.4C above what it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. Virtually all of the UK experienced above average temperatures, driven by repeated heatwaves. Southern England and Wales saw heat far above usual. Temperatures were closer to normal across Scotland and Northern Ireland. Rainfall in the UK has been below average this summer. Across the country a total of 195mm of rain fell on average, which is 23% below what it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. Summer months tend to be drier, but this year was exceptional. Only north-western Scotland saw more summer rain than usual, as droughts were declared across much of the rest of the UK. This lookup uses data from the HadUK Grid dataset (opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UK’s changing climate. The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically “fill in the gaps” between weather stations. The results displayed for each grid area represents a mean average of that grid cell and its nearest grid cells. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on the primary grid cell. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away. This approach aims to avoid sharp jumps between neighbouring locations which may occasionally arise due to uncertainties in the data, while still making use of the most detailed dataset available to capture local weather conditions across the UK's varied geography. The data for 2026 is provisional, with fewer observations feeding into calculations due to lags in data availability. As such, the precise values could change slightly in future as more data comes available. The historical averages are calculated over a 30-year period from 1991-2020, which matches the standard period used by the UN’s World Meteorological Organization. The average temperature represents the mean average of the selection of grid cells across the month or season. The maximum temperature is the mean average of the daily maximums recorded across all nearest grid cells for the month or season; the minimum temperature is the mean average of the daily minimums. The rainfall is the total amount of rain for the month or season, averaged across the selection of grid cells. Methodology support from Dan Hollis, Amy Doherty and Oli Claydon, UK Met Office. title: New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM
description: Andy Burnham is under pressure to deliver a compelling vision for the country as he steps from the sidelines on to the main stage.
body: Andy Burnham is gearing up to deliver his first conference speech as Labour leader Andy Burnham had plenty to say about where the government - and the country - was going wrong at last year's Labour conference in Liverpool. But that was at a fringe meeting on the sidelines of the main event. Now, as Labour leader and prime minister, he is the main event - and it is down to him to show party members and the wider public that he has some answers. Earlier this week, he said his debut leader's speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role". "People are going to know the direction I want to take this country and I will set it down quite clearly," he told reporters en route to the UN General Assembly in New York. An internal No 10 note has set out the broad themes he will explore when he takes to the stage in Liverpool on Tuesday - including setting out long-term solutions to build a belief that the future can be brighter. The slogan for this year's conference is "Hope Again". So in his speech he is likely to point to his forthcoming 10 Year Plan for the UK – which, he says, will have "making life more affordable" at its core. As for the specifics of what he will say, some of it will be very familiar to anyone who was listening to his conference fringe speech 12 months ago. Back then, he declared then that the country had "lost control" of "the essentials" following the Thatcher-era sell off of utilities and that we were all "overpaying for water, housing energy, transport". He called for a renewed emphasis on technical education and wanted to see a decade of council house building on the scale of the post-war Labour government. For a politician frequently denounced for "flip flopping" he has been remarkably consistent in recent times. He is likely to re-alight on themes from his Labour leadership campaign – saying more about his commitment to greater "public control" – though not necessarily public ownership - of life's necessities; building national resilience in an unstable world; and investing political capital in the reform of social care. A potential crowd pleaser would be to tell Labour activists from the main stage what he told them as Greater Manchester mayor from the fringe last year – that he will set up a commission to examine electoral reform. Such a move would be supported by about a quarter of his own MPs and would tie in with his leadership campaign promise of "a new politics", focused on "problem solving" rather than "point scoring". We are also likely to hear more about getting young people into work or training, with the conclusions of the review by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn likely to be published soon. And there is certain to be plenty about his efforts to devolve power away from Whitehall to England's mayors and the new No 10 North. The task for Burnham is to meld these snapshots into a compelling and coherent narrative, culminating in a vision of the Britain he wants to see a decade from now. But there are already worries that this might become a fictional narrative unless he also focuses even more on the here and now. After all, Sir Keir Starmer's "decade of national renewal" was binned after just two bumpy years in office. Unite's Sharon Graham is calling for more help with the cost of living We are told there will be policy announcements on each day of the conference – starting on Saturday. Each announcement will have to fit in with the PM's priorities – "putting power in people's hands" - in other words more devolved powers; "growth in every postcode" – such as investment decisions around the country; and help with cost of living. Party insiders say measures such as removing VAT from electricity bills are just the start of that assistance. But Labour's biggest union funder, Unite, wants to see much more robust action on living costs sooner rather than later. The union does not want the promise of jam tomorrow, but some instant sweeteners. Its leader, Sharon Graham, has called for a "winter fuel in reverse" – a policy from Burnham next week which would be as popular as Starmer's early removal of payments from many pensioners was unpopular. The union has put forward a motion which gives the PM plenty of options such as a cap on energy prices and unfreezing tax thresholds – an issue Burnham himself said had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to be the MP for Makerfield. The union has said revenue can be raised through a windfall tax on banks. The umbrella body for unions, the TUC, has called for an increase in the bank surcharge to subsidise energy bills. All eyes will be on John Healey's first conference speech as chancellor on Monday. With borrowing costs for last month soaring to their second highest level, his room for manoeuvre is limited and he will not scoop his own Budget next month by announcing what is in it. But Labour activists will be keen to know from his language whether Healey's Treasury will opt for continuity or will represent a break from the past two years under Rachel Reeves, not just in rhetoric but reality. Some in Labour's ranks believe Burnham is planning for an early election, with party HQ recently launching "operation second term", to beef up its campaigning and organising strength. Burnham does not have to call an election until August 2029 - but going to the country early - perhaps as early as next spring - could deliver him a mandate of his own and free him from the constraints of Sir Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto. Recent polling has suggested that a "Burnham bounce" is real, though not dramatic. The party has moved from just under 20% in the polls at the end of the Starmer era to around the mid-twenties now. title: From weeks to hours - the rapid new test transforming brain tumour diagnosis
description: The test means patients can start treatment sooner and are spared weeks of uncertainty.
body: The test means patients can be diagnosed within hours rather than weeks, like Steve Palmer whose case the BBC followed A rapid new test for brain tumours that the NHS has started using can slash the time it takes for an accurate diagnosis from up to eight weeks to two hours. The test, which is used by doctors to diagnose which type of tumour a patient has, should mean patients can start treatment including radiotherapy and chemotherapy sooner, and are spared weeks of uncertainty. Steve Palmer, 55, from Nottingham, is among those to benefit from the new technology - and it meant surgeons were able to get his result while they were still operating to remove his tumour. "Getting that quick diagnosis removed weeks of anxiety," he told the BBC. NHS England said that the genomic test, which works by quickly analysing the genetic code of a sample of the tumour, will be piloted in specialist centres around England. There are around 150 different types of brain tumour ranging from slow-growing to aggressive cancers, each of which can respond differently to treatment. Steve was diagnosed with a brain tumour after he collapsed at the gym, and the test revealed it to be a grade 4 glioblastoma. "It wasn't the result I wanted to hear but it means I can get on with the next phase of treatment and recovery, and get on with fighting whatever it is I've got to fight," he told the BBC. Consultant neurosurgeon Stuart Smith, who led Steve's operation at Queens Medical Centre, part of Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, told the BBC the test "seems almost magical." "The diagnosis of brain tumours relies on molecular and genetic analysis but it can take up to six to eight weeks to get the full information back. Here it is done while we are still operating." Diagnosing the type of tumour while the patient is still on the operating table could impact how surgeons operate. Smith explained: "For some tumour types, which are curable, surgery needs to be as radical as possible to remove every last bit of tumour that we can find. "Other types, sadly, are too aggressive, and beyond what surgery can remove, so we would be more cautious in order to lower the risk of causing damage to the brain." Neurosurgeon Stuart Smith, who points to a screen during Steve's surgery, says it means patients will also have quicker access to clinical trials The test works by sending small tissue samples taken from the tumour to the pathology lab. The samples are prepared for loading into a shoebox-sized sequencing machine made by Oxford Nanopore, which uses specialist software developed at the University of Nottingham, in partnership with hospital clinicians. The molecules of DNA pass through a nanopore - a tiny hole - which reveals the tumour's unique genomic fingerprint. In Steve's case, after the nanopore machine was running for 20 minutes, the neuropathology team called the theatre to tell them that the tumour was likely to be a glioblastoma. Dr Simon Paine, consultant neuropathologist at Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, explained that the genomic test was transformative in comparison to what he could determine by looking at tumour cells down a microscope. "I'm crystal ball gazing and can do it reasonably well on a good day, but nowhere near with the clarity of the nanopore, which gives a comprehensive molecular classification," he said. More than 12,000 people in the UK are diagnosed with a primary brain tumour each year. It is the biggest cancer killer of children and adults under 40. Prof Frankie Swords, NHS medical director, said: "For people with suspected brain tumours, getting the right diagnosis quickly can feel like a race against time, while waiting weeks for answers can be agonising for them and their families. "This remarkable rapid test has the potential to completely transform how we diagnose brain tumours, with results reaching patients in a matter of days rather than weeks. "This is a huge leap forward for patients - a faster diagnosis means they can start the right treatment or access clinical trials sooner, while for some patients it could mean surgeons can make potentially life-changing decisions about their surgery while on the operating table." The NHS England pilot will involve five specialist centres in Nottingham, Birmingham, London and Newcastle - they are Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, Great Ormond Street Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, King's College Hospital and Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. It will later be extended to sites in Bristol, Oxford, Leeds and Manchester. The pilot builds on an earlier project already under way in Nottingham and Birmingham. The BBC watched the surgery to remove Steve's tumour, shown here on the scan, at Queens Medical Centre, Nottingham Prof Dame Sue Hill, chief scientific officer for England and senior responsible officer for genomics in the NHS, said: "This is another world-leading development for NHS genomics, taking pioneering science and testing how we can use it safely and consistently in patient care. "Rapid genomic testing could dramatically shorten the wait for answers for brain tumour patients and, in some cases, give surgeons vital information before an operation is even over. "Our ambition is to build the evidence for this testing to become part of routine NHS care, so patients across the country can benefit equally from faster, more precise diagnosis." Smith added: "For patients it will mean not only mean quicker access to results and treatment, but because we have a full genetic profile of the tumour, more rapid access to clinical trials."
