title: Smart beds and motion sensors - is this the future of dementia care?
description: Jyoti and Bharat Patel are testing dementia technology including sensors in socks, their bed and around the house.
body: Jyoti and Bharat Patel are "super testers" of dementia technology in an NHS trial There are sensors in every room of Jyoti and Bharat Patel's home. Their movements and habits are monitored constantly. But this doesn't worry them, in fact it gives them peace of mind. Jyoti was diagnosed with dementia five years ago, and they are now part of an NHS trial using high-tech devices to help patients live at home safely. The couple, who are in their 70s, are one of more than 250 families participating in the project by the UK Dementia Research Institute (UK DRI). The hope is that the technology could be extended more widely across the health service, to reduce preventable trips to hospital and give families peace of mind. Bharat and Jyoti travelled all over the world as professional magicians Bharat and Jyoti met at a magic show in 1977 and became a double act, with their career leading them to meet King Charles and Princess Anne as well as a host of celebrities. In 2019, Bharat started noticing that Jyoti was making uncharacteristic mistakes on stage. "Normally she used to set my stage up and everything was perfect, but I saw something I was looking for and it wasn't there, so I thought something is wrong," he said. They went to a private health specialist who diagnosed Jyoti with Alzheimer's in 2021. Jyoti says when she went out, if she did not look around her, she would find that she was lost. "I didn't know it [was] dementia but I knew it was something which [was] unusual," Bharat says. The couple sleep on a smart mattress that tracks Jyoti's heart rate and breathing In 2023, they were approached by the team at UK Dementia Research Institute and Imperial College London to take part in the trial, which is funded by the medical research charity LifeArc. Their house in west London is now fitted with different sensors, which are connected via the internet, that send data back to a dedicated team of doctors, nurses and other clinical specialists. The team then uses the information to better understand how the person is managing their daily routine, identify early signs of changing health and care needs with the hope that they can maintain independence for longer. Door sensors detect if someone leaves in the middle of the night, movement is monitored to check for signs of a fall, while kitchen appliances are fitted with sensors to check whether Jyoti has eaten and is sticking to her daily routine. The couple sleep on a "smart mattress" to track sleep disturbances and Jyoti's heart and breathing rates, which can spot early signs of an infection. Alongside this trial, Jyoti is also testing out smart socks and a special watch that also contain sensors to monitor her body temperature and keep track of any long-term changes in her gait - indicating frailty. Costs are expected to be about £2,000 a year, mainly to cover the monitoring and paying healthcare staff to analyse the data. If rolled out more widely that could be a significant amount of money with almost a million people living with dementia in the UK. But Sarah Daniels, health and social care lead at the UK Dementia Research Institute, says the cost is no more than a couple of weeks in a care home. The main aim, she says, is to give earlier signals to health and social care professionals. "Earlier signals means earlier intervention, which means we can head potential complications of an infection, potential challenges around care, we can head that off before it becomes a crisis," says Daniels. Devices around the home pick up movement and alert care staff if needed None of the devices record sound or video, protecting the individual's privacy, however, some people may feel nervous about the amount of data they are allowing other people to access. Daniels argues that by enhancing the level of information you provide to your GP, it enables them to make better decisions about your care. The number of people with dementia in the UK is expected to climb by another 40% by 2040, so the hope is to extend it more widely across the health service. Dr Jeremy Isaacs, national clinical director for dementia and older people's mental health at NHS England, said the health service would be closely monitoring the trial and said the research built on NHS programmes which were already supporting people to remain more independent in their own homes. While some people might feel uneasy about having all these sensors in their home, Bharat says they give him greater "peace of mind". "Even if it can cut down my worries by 5 or 10%, then it helps me and it will help other people too," he says. title: Will you get £13,000 a year when you stop working? Here's how to check
description: How to find out how much state pension you're likely to receive - and what you can do about it now.
body: It may well be decades away, but do you know how much money you will get when you stop working? The current state pension is soon likely to top £13,000 a year. Yet one in eight people surveyed by the UK tax authority have never checked how much money they are forecast to receive. Here's how to find out, and what you can do now to boost it. If you're working, it is highly likely you're contributing to the state pension - paid by the government when you hit pension age in your late 60s. the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 - is £241.30 a week (£12,547.60 a year) the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 - is £184.90 a week (£9,614.80 a year) Many people on the old basic state pension may receive a top-up called the additional state pension. Most pensioners have other income, primarily from pension savings built up over their career. The state pension goes up each year in line with the highest of either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5%. So next April, the flat-rate state pension is expected to go above £13,000. Workers pay National Insurance (NI) contributions. In general, you need 35 years of qualifying contributions to get a full state pension. You may have gaps in your NI record if, for example, you have lived abroad. If you've taken time away from work to care for children or family members, then you get NI credits if you receive child benefit or carer's allowance. It's possible to boost your contribution history with voluntary payments. Since April 2025, you have only been able to make payments for the previous six years. That's one reason why it is important to check your state pension forecast well before you retire, experts say. You can see what you are forecast to receive: By downloading the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) app, external Using the official online state pension forecast webpage, external To get a state pension, you will need to prove your identity using official photo ID. Importantly, never click on a link sent in an unsolicited email or text message, even if it looks official, as it could be a scam. For more general information about tax and pensions, HMRC has launched a Tax Confident website, external. And the government-funded, independent Money Helper website has a free retirement guidance tool, external to walk you through the options. The most common reason for not checking a state pension forecast was feeling that retirement was still too far away to think about, a recent survey of 5,000 consumers by HMRC found. Losing track of pension pots from previous jobs, and concerns about how career breaks might affect their entitlement, were also frequent responses. People aged 45-54 were the most likely to have never checked. "Whether retirement is decades away or just around the corner, I'd encourage everyone to check their forecast and see if there's anything they can do now to boost their entitlement later," says Myrtle Lloyd, HMRC's chief customer officer. title: What food items should you stock up on in case of an emergency?
description: Extreme weather may be changing the way we need to shop, with the UK government urging people to stock up on canned goods.
body: Extreme weather may be changing the way we need to shop. Earlier this month, the UK government urged people to add a few more long-life products into their food basket - just in case the food supply chain is interrupted. Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon El Niño would lead to "more extreme storms in this country". Climate change, along with cyber-attacks, disease outbreaks and conflicts can all put a strain on the process that eventually gets food into our shops and homes. This video can not be played Watch: The food items to keep in your cupboard Prof Richard Wilding, an expert in supply chain strategy, tells me not to be "overly worried" as global shipping professionals are adapting all the time but to be prepared to buy different products if needed. "Things that were in supermarkets and seen as relatively abundant may all of a sudden be in shortage," he adds. So how easy is it to stock up and what are the things to avoid? A staple item for those looking to stock up on supplies is tinned oily fish - including salmon, mackerel and brine Senior nutrition scientist Dr Sammie Gill, from British Nutrition Foundation, says you should prioritise certain food groups: Complex carbohydrates such as wheat biscuits, wholegrain cereals, crackers and breads plus oats, rice and pasta Proteins such as canned chickpeas, lentils, kidney beans, unsalted nuts, peanut butter and canned oily fish such as tuna, mackerel and sardines Rebecca McManamon, a consultant dietitian, lists the following essentials: Tinned fruit as you can drink its juice for added fluids, vitamins and fibre Pickled foods such as vegetables and eggs Both experts also recommend keeping long-life milk found in the non-refridgerated aisle for protein, calcium and as a source of fluid Gill says look out for salt and sugar content when buying tinned items: Avoid items tinned in brine or syrups, water is the healthiest option Avoid instant noodles and tinned soup due to high salt content Avoid breakfast cereals and snack bars with added sugars and limited nutrients Choose tinned fish over tinned meats such as sausages, hot dogs or corned beef as they are often processed and high in salt and saturated fat Limit sweet treats such as biscuits and chocolates as they have a high sugar content And what about making the essentials taste nice? McManamon says stock up on nuts as a sweet alternative but be aware that they may have a shorter shelf life. She also recommends keeping dried herbs, spices and salt available as, she says, tinned food can be slightly bland. Make basics taste a bit nicer with peanut butter and pickled veg, say experts You should aim to take in about 1,500-2,500ml of fluid a day, whatever the weather, says McManamon. This can obviously come from bottled water, but also from what she describes as fluid rich tinned foods if supplies are short. For those worried about whether tinned food is as nutritious as fresh food, Dr Gill says it absolutely can be used as part of a healthy diet. "There is little difference nutritionally between canned and fresh food in terms of macronutrients, like carbohydrates, protein, fats, and fibre, as well as fat-soluble vitamins, like vitamin A and E, and minerals," she says. It may not be as good for other vitamins, such as B and C, because the canning process has been found to decrease vitamin levels, but Gill offers assurances that these foods can still be a "useful source" of vitamins. title: Union calls for halt to graded Ofsted inspections over health concerns
description: The National Association of Head Teachers says inspections in England may pose a "risk to life" for school leaders.
body: England's biggest school leaders' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections, saying they could pose a "risk to life" for school staff. The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said the change to inspections, rolled out nationally just under a year ago, had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare. It said schools should instead be rated using short narrative reports that set out their strengths and areas they could improve. Ofsted said it had worked closely with unions and parents to develop the new report card inspection system, and would continue to grade schools. Ofsted, England's schools' inspectorate, introduced the report card system to replace its previous one or two-word judgements last November, following the death of head teacher Ruth Perry, who took her own life after Ofsted downgraded her school from "outstanding" to "inadequate". An inquest ruled that an Ofsted inspection had contributed to her death in January 2023. That led to a change in how Ofsted assessed schools, bringing in report cards designed to grade schools on several areas, rather than focusing on one overall grade for the whole school. Example of an Ofsted inspection report card But the new system faced criticism from when it was first proposed, with Perry's sister, Prof Julia Waters, saying it appeared to be "a rehash of the discredited and dangerous system it is meant to replace". The NAHT issued a claim with the High Court for a judicial review over the changes, arguing there had not been adequate consultation on the new report cards before they were introduced, but that was rejected. Nearly a year after it was fully rolled out, the NAHT says evidence from its members suggests the new system is having a detrimental impact on school leaders' mental health. Testimonies seen by the BBC suggest head teachers are being left "overwhelmed" and "anxious", with the pressure caused by the inspections described as "intolerable". Although the system had been changed with the intention of lowering the burden on school leaders, the testimonies say the inspection and assessment process had become "higher stakes than ever before". Amanda Hulme, head teacher at Claypool Primary School in Bolton, said a recent inspection at her school had been "easily the most stressful experience" of her career. "It was definitely damaging to my health and really quite distressing," she said. "I couldn't sleep and it led to my blood pressure and pulse rate increasing. "The effect on my team has also been significant, with some colleagues no longer wanting to pursue headship, and another teacher considering leaving the profession entirely." Head teacher Amanda Hulme says she found the new inspection system "much worse" than the previous one The NAHT says it has shared examples with Education Secretary Lucy Powell of some of the "damaging experiences" it says its members have faced. Speaking to LBC earlier this month, Powell said she took head teacher wellbeing "incredibly seriously" and that the system of accountability needed to be "supportive and understanding. "I'll continue the work that I do with head teachers, head teacher representatives and others to make sure that we get this Ofsted framework, but also the culture and the whole regime, right," she added. The NAHT said the results of a recent survey of its members suggested that the majority who responded felt that inspections had worsened in the past 12 months. The union is now calling for inspections to pause to allow for a "fundamental review of how inspection works", drawing on examples from other nations. In Wales, the inspectorate Estyn has removed judgements such as "excellent" and "good" from its reports, instead summarising findings by highlighting a school's strengths and areas for improvement. Northern Ireland's Education and Training Inspectorate (ETI) also uses narrative reports without grades. Scotland's His Majesty's Inspectorate of Education (HIME) does use grades, but there has been a recent consultation on their use. NAHT general secretary Paul Whiteman said: "The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it. "It poses a real and present danger to the well-being and mental health of school leaders and teachers, possibly even a risk to life." He said he welcomed the new education secretary's focus on teacher wellbeing, adding: "Really fundamental changes to inspection are needed, and we stand ready to work with the new government to achieve that." Responding, Ofsted said it has worked closely with teaching unions over the past three years, to deliver significant reforms and reduce unnecessary pressure on teachers. "Ofsted exists to raise standards for children and to provide clear reporting to parents," a spokesperson said. "We will continue to engage closely with trades unions – but we will also continue to grade schools." title: Specialist courts for rape cases to be rolled out across England and Wales
description: Funding will allow victims to view proceedings remotely and give evidence from a separate room via video link, the government says.
body: Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, the prime minister has announced. Each crown court will have at least one courtroom especially set up to hear such cases, while victims will be able to view proceedings remotely and give evidence from a separate room via video link. Victims will also be provided with private entrances and waiting rooms to separate them from defendants, though it is understood this will be dependent on the architecture of each building. Rape Crisis England and Wales said this was a "significant step forward" and addressed several reforms it had been requesting for many years. "Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice," said the charity's chief executive, Ciara Bergman. Under the new measures, expected to cost around £23m from the Ministry of Justice's budget, court staff will be given "trauma-informed training" and a single person of contact will be assigned to each survivor. From next month, trials will be given a fixed date rather than placed on floating lists in what Prime Minister Andy Burnham said was an effort to "rebalance the scales of justice and put victims first". The government said the changes follow Labour MP Charlotte Nichols showing "immense strength and bravery" in speaking publicly about being raped and calling for changes to the justice system. Nichols waived her automatic right to anonymity in March when she made a Commons speech and described having to wait more than 1,000 days to go to court. Earlier this year, the government announced that rape victims would be given access to specialist legal advice throughout the criminal justice process. MP reveals rape ordeal during court reform debate Delays to my rapist's trial left me terrified, survivor tells BBC Rape victims to get specialised legal advice in courts 'Rape victims failed by court delays' say charity Woman dropped sex assault case after court delays Labour promised in its 2024 manifesto to halve violence against women and girls within a decade. "For too long, victims of rape and serious sexual offences have felt let down by our justice system," Burnham said. "Prosecution rates for rape remain shamefully low, with many victims waiting years for justice. This is not good enough." The changes were "long overdue" and would make a "significant difference" but focusing on prosecution alone would not be enough, he added. "So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place," the prime minister said. Nichols spoke publicly for the first time about being raped when she accused the then Justice Secretary, David Lammy, of using crime victims as a "cudgel" to push through his reforms of the legal system. She was criticising the Courts and Tribunals Bill's plans to limit jury trials to cases with a likely prison sentence of three years or more. She said she had waited 1,088 days to go to court, with every day being "agony" and the "trauma" made worse by her role in public life. Her attacker, she said, was acquitted at crown court but subsequently ordered to pay compensation after she won a civil case against him. "It is because I have been raped that I am as passionate as I am about what it means for a justice system to be truly victim-focused," she said. "It is because I have endured every indignity that our broken criminal justice system could mete out that I care what kind of reform will actually deliver justice for survivors and victims of crime more widely." Responding to news of the specialist courts being rolled out, the Conservatives said tackling delays to criminal rape trials was "long overdue" and they pushed Labour to commit to scrapping plans to restrict jury trials. "The fact that victims have been withdrawing their cases because they have taken too long has been a disgrace," said shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy. "Labour need to get courts sitting throughout the year, end the delays and clear the backlog – not undermine our right to a trial by jury." Last year another charity, the Salford Survivor Project, said victims of rape and sexual assault were being "failed by the system" as court backlogs reached a record high. The long delays for cases to go to trial were having a serious impact on victims' mental health, it said. Also last year, a woman who says she was sexually assaulted by a taxi driver on her 21st birthday told BBC News she had dropped the case because of court delays. She reported the alleged incident in early 2022 and gave evidence in court in December 2023 but the case was adjourned until September 2024 when the judge fell ill. "I made the decision, even though I hate the statement, to drop the case," she said. "I couldn't let this hurt me further." The Crown Prosecution Service said that, without her testimony, the case had been dropped because of insufficient evidence. If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website. title: Workers came across human remains – and unearthed a mass grave of 572 people
description: Workers in northern Sri Lanka accidentally uncovered the country's largest mass grave – and reopened wounds from its civil war.
body: Jeyaruby Jeyabalan was 12 when her father, Kandaiah Jayapalan, disappeared When a mass grave was unearthed in northern Sri Lanka last February, it was not by design. Workers were digging to extend a cremation ground in the Chemmani area of the Jaffna region when they suddenly discovered human remains, prompting an investigation. By August, archaeologists had completed the third phase of the excavation at the site, during which they found the skeletal remains of 572 people, including children and infants. Among the dead were artefacts from their lives – bangles, a school bag, a milk bottle. It is believed to be the largest mass grave site ever uncovered in Sri Lanka. There had been whispers of its existence before - a soldier on trial for the rape and murder of a young woman during the country's devastating civil war, had spoken about a mass grave which contained hundreds of bodies. Rights groups said they were disappeared civilians But there was no proof - until now. And while the discovery is devastating, it has offered hope to people like Jeyaruby Jeyabalan, whose father was among thousands of people who disappeared during the decades-long war. Jeyabalan and families like his hope that answers about what happened to their loved ones lie among the bodies. Many Tamils believe the grave holds the victims of extrajudicial killings carried out during the civil war. They are calling for an investigation – and for justice. But the excavation process at Chemmani has moved slowly, testing the patience of families searching for answers about their disappeared loved ones. The discovery of hundreds of remains near a previously identified mass grave has fuelled anger among the Tamils, who have long-demanded a thorough inquiry into disappearances. Many fear the mass grave will eventually fade from public attention because of a lack of political will to pursue the truth – and so the grave has become a rallying point for renewed protests in Sri Lanka's north. Sri Lanka, particularly the Tamil-dominated north and east, suffered decades of conflict. The war, which lasted from 1983 to 2009, divided the island-nation along ethnic lines. Tamil Tiger rebels fought for an independent state in the north-east of the country due to what they called systematic discrimination by the Sinhalese-dominated government. The conflict lasted 26 years and the fighting killed an estimated 100,000 people. It also left about 23,000 – mostly Tamils – missing. Both the security forces and Tamil Tigers are accused of atrocities and crimes. A baby's bottle was among the personal items uncovered at the grave site. In 1995, after a bloody conflict, the Sri Lankan army wrested control of the Jaffna Peninsula from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). It was seen as a key turning point in the war, which ended with the defeat of the Tigers in 2009. As they extended control in the late 1990s, the entire Chemmani region became part of a high-security zone and was dotted with army camps, check points and security posts. There was an army camp in Chemmani close to the cemetery as well. Some at that time described the Jaffna region as an "open prison" - and the security forces were accused of causing the disappearance of thousands of civilians, something Sri Lankan governments have always denied. "I was 12 years old when my father was picked up by the Sri Lankan army at a checkpoint close to Chemmani area in September 1996. We still don't know what happened to him," Jeyaruby Jayapalan, who now lives in Jaffna, tells the BBC. She recalls how, after learning of his disappearance, the family panicked and visited military camps and police stations across Jaffna in a desperate search for information without any luck. He never came back. Her father, Kandaiah Jayapalan, was a government employee who also ran a roadside café not far from Chemmani. "I went to Chemmani mass grave with many others hoping that I will find some answers. But we didn't find any material evidence. We want a detailed forensic analysis of the human remains," says Jeyaruby. Two weeks before Kandaiah Jayapalan vanished, an 18-year-old Tamil school girl, Krishanthi Kumaraswamy, disappeared in the same area. In 1998, a court in Colombo sentenced five soldiers to death for the rape and murder of Kumaraswamy and for killing three of her family members. The case drew global attention at that time. Their bodies were later found buried in Chemmani area. It is among the most infamous cases from the conflict – and the grave currently under investigation is within 100 metres of the remains of Kumaraswamy and others were found. In a startling court testimony, one of the convicted soldiers, Somaratne Rajapakse, alleged that between 300 and 400 people who had been killed in the mid-1990s were buried in Chemmani. His claim led to the first excavation at Chemmani a year later, during which investigators unearthed more than 10 human skeletons. Human rights activists believed those remains were linked to people who had disappeared during the civil war, but there was little judicial follow-up. Activists say that because the war with the Tamil rebels was ongoing, the then government didn't pursue the investigation and did not explain why. The discovery of another mass grave in the same area has revived calls for accountability. Map of Sri Lanka showing location of Chemmani "Preliminary inspections suggest this was not a normal burial site and not consistent with ordinary Hindu burial practices," says Gehan Gunatilleke, a commissioner with Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka, which conducted inspections at Chemmani last year. Activists and experts say that while a few dozen bodies appeared to have been formally buried, the vast majority told a different story. Most of the human remains were found without clothing, packed tightly together and, in some cases, stacked on top of others. title: Man, 82, dies after beach fight with 76-year-old over sunlounger in Greece
description: One eyewitness said the scene was so chaotic that screaming could be heard from the other end of the beach.
body: The incident occurred on in Vouliagmeni beach near Athens on Sunday An 82-year-old man has died after getting into a fight with a man in his 70s over a sunlounger on a beach in Greece, local media is reporting. Witnesses say a disagreement over the use of the loungers at Vouliagmeni beach, near Athens, escalated into a violent fight, which then further spiralled to involve other people. One eyewitness told the Kathimerini newspaper that the scene was so chaotic, the screaming could be heard from the other end of the beach. The younger man, who was 76, has reportedly been arrested. A 21-year-old woman who was with him was also detained but later released. Witnesses told Ta Nea daily newspaper that she had a bloodied and swollen face. During the fight, the 82-year-old collapsed. According to various reports, he received CPR and a defibrillator was used on him before an ambulance arrived. The man was taken to hospital where he later died. Another witness said that the victim seemed to be waiting for other people and had reserved a sunlounger, which appeared to be the cause of the initial disagreement. Authorities are investigating what led to the physical altercation and what caused the man's death. title: Smith wins World Series of Darts Finals as Littler run ends
description: England's Ross Smith shocks Wales' Gerwyn Price to win World Series of Darts Finals as Luke Littler's clean-sweep dream ends in last eight in Amsterdam.
body: Finals winner Smith lost in the first round of his only two other appearances in this season's World Series of Darts Englishman Ross Smith won the final six legs to produce a shock 11-5 victory over two-time former winner Gerwyn Price in the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. It was just a second major title for the 37-year-old, whose only previous success at this level of the PDC World Tour came at the European Championship in 2022. But the world number 14 overpowered his loftier opponent with a barrage of 180s, hitting 11 maximums, compared to Welshman Price's five, to finish a deserved winner. It was a fitting finale to a tournament of shocks that saw world champion Luke Littler lose in the quarter-finals and miss out on his quest to claim a clean sweep of the major PDC titles in 2026. Littler could boycott Dutch events over booing Littler seals dramatic final-leg win over Aspinall Thousands at darts audition to take on Luke Littler "Honestly, I am made up with the win. I am just so happy," said Smith, who suffered first-round exits in New Zealand and Australia in his only two other appearances in the 2026 World Series. "You are playing Gerwyn Price - one of the best players in the world. You have got to up your game." Smith beat Northern Ireland's Josh Rock 10-7 in the last eight and Dutch hope Gian van Veen 11-8 in the semi-finals to give himself a shot at the £100,000 winner's prize. Price, meanwhile, made it past England's James Wade in the quarter-finals before beating compatriot Jonny Clayton - Littler's conqueror - in the last four. The 2020 and 2022 winner won back-to-back legs to make it 5-5 against Smith in the final but was hanging on as his opponent continued to score heavily albeit with a lower checkout success. Smith, however, was far more clinical after the interval, winning the next three legs, including back-to-back checkouts of 127 and 123. The checkouts cooled but Smith won a succession of scrappy legs to seal victory as Price's game deserted him. Earlier, Littler's bid for a clean sweep of all major PDC titles in 2026 was ended by a 10-4 defeat by Clayton in the quarter-finals. The world number one had followed his World Championship triumph at Alexandra Palace in January by winning titles at the World Masters, UK Open, Premier League, World Cup of Darts and World Matchplay. But after threatening to boycott events in the Netherlands after being roundly booed by the crowd during his last-16 win over Nathan Aspinall, the Warrington-based player failed to produce his best darts against Clayton. title: Illegal off-road vehicles to be seized on the spot as police warn of 'long walk home'
description: With damage to protected habitats reportedly rising, police have powers to seize illegal off-roading vehicles on the spot.
body: TikTok accounts linked to one group of off-roaders showed images and videos of damage being caused to ancient peatlands Police say off-road drivers causing anti-social behaviour or damage to protected habitats will have their vehicles seized "on the spot". PC Eryl Lloyd, of North Wales Police's rural crime team, said new powers allowed officers to take vehicles without notice, and warned offending drivers: "It's a long walk home." Both the force and Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said damage caused by off-roading incidents and other anti-social behaviour was on the rise. In August, three men who caused "irreversible" harm to the Berwyn Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) in 4x4s were convicted after videos of them causing the damage were shared on TikTok. Off-roaders caught damaging protected site after posting videos to TikTok John Robinson, Michael Williams and Joseph Hodgson were part of a seven-vehicle convoy which drove from Liverpool to the Berwyn range, an area of moorland in northeast Wales, where they caused "serious damage" to the peat and bog habitat. Robinson and Williams were fined more than £2,000 each and disqualified from driving for two months. Hodgson was ordered to pay £1,000 compensation for damaging the SSSI, as well as costs, and was also banned from entering the Berwyn SSSI for three years. PC Eryl Lloyd – who is seconded to NRW – said his team had "definitely seen an increase in off-roading incidents". As well as 4x4 vehicles and motorbikes, "we're getting a lot more reports about e-bikes, which also cause the same amount of damage as motorbikes" he added. This video can not be played Illegal off roaders, caught by their own footage, were prosecuted in August Under the Crime and Policing Act 2026, introduced earlier this year, police have new powers to tackle the problem. "Previously, we had to give a warning for incidents of anti-social behaviour, careless driving. "Now we can just seize the vehicles there on the spot. "We will use these new powers and we will be seizing vehicles on the spot as well." Although the reason for a rise in off-roading incidents is unknown, Lloyd believed it was "to do with social media" and people sharing locations. He added: "They come from all over the UK. We are very close to the northwest of England. But we've seen people travelling from the Midlands, even London as well." While social media may have contributed to a rise in off-road incidents, Lloyd also said: "We've had incidents over the summer in Newborough Forest, Newborough Beach [Anglesey], where social media has exploded. "And the amount of people coming to wild-camp, and causing anti-social behaviour from that, from illegal fires to barbecues… so it's been a busy summer." Both Kirsty Roberts of NRW and PC Eryl Lloyd are seeing a rise in incidents On the Berwyn Range, damage which led to the convictions of drivers last month included the wearing away of hundreds of years worth of peat growth. Kirsty Roberts, of NRW, said: "On this specific occasion we're talking about peatlands, which are really slow-growing habitats. "So in this particular scenario we had a depth of 40cm (15in) worth of peat, which equates to around 400 years worth of peat depth and peat growth. "And so, to see this area naturally recover, we just wouldn't see it in our lifetime." Damage caused by off-road vehicles to peatlands and vegetation also impact wildlife, including ground-nesting birds, she said. Without intervention to avoid further degradation, she warned: "We're not going to be able to reverse that biodiversity curve." As well as a rise in 4x4 and e-bike incidents, she said "general anti-social behaviour" was also increasing, including use of barbecues and "a lot of waste being dumped on protected sites", adding: "It's happening on areas that are really fragile." Lord Newborough is "gutted" by the damage, and says more resources are needed Lord Newborough, of the Rhug Estate in Denbighshire, owns the Berwyn land damaged by the off-roaders convicted last month. He said areas of the estate had been opened up "for the public to enjoy", but "the mountain is very precious and we've tried to protect that and be good custodians for many years". He agreed that damage to important habitats caused by off-road vehicles was becoming more frequent. "I feel gutted basically because this is damage that has happened in recent years." Under the Countryside and Rights of Way Act, a fifth of Wales is classed as "access land" including areas where land owners have agreed the public have a right of entry on foot. "I'm pretty old myself, so I grew up respecting the mountains and not seeing the encroachment that we've got by the public now. "So, yes it hurts me and it hurts, the fact that the damage has been done. "We monitor the bird life on the mountain every year and we know that certain precious nests are being damaged wilfully, and this isn't really the way ahead." title: Human extinction fears make me want to flee AI and live on an island
description: People share their anxieties following recent headlines over concerns about AI advancement.
body: James Downs is a mental health campaigner who shares his own experience of anorexia, depressions and anxiety to educate others Since headlines broke about claims AI advancement could lead to human extinction, James Downs has felt his anxiety rising. "It makes me almost feel powerless. Like, what can I do as an individual?" said the mental health campaigner from Cardiff. This sense of fear has led him to check his phone for more news. "And the more you look at it the more your attention's drawn to the negative or scary things and the worse and worse it can seem," said the 37-year-old. Earlier this month, a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned AI was advancing so quickly he believed there was a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. Then computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC that the claim was "not unreasonable", external. On Tuesday, amid rising public concerns about the risks, the boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe. James says connecting with friends and doing something positive for the environment helps him feel good during anxious times James, who is in recovery after being diagnosed with anorexia, anxiety and depression as a teenager, said the recent headlines about AI have added another layer of worry to ongoing concerns such as the climate crisis, the cost of living crisis, conflict around the world and nuclear threat. "I can't escape this background anxiety about the future - will I be OK? Will the planet be OK? Will my finances be okay? All of these different, multi-layered things which go from the big existential things, like what if it wipes us all out, to the day-to-day things." He said it could lead to a sense of helplessness. "It kind of makes me want to give up trying to make a positive change in the world, or makes me just want to run away, be a nomad or something, go and live on an island somewhere with no technology, but that's not a sustainable solution either." Psychotherapist Lucy Theo says her clients often bring up their anxieties over AI during therapy Lucy Theo, a psychotherapist from Bonvilston, Vale of Glamorgan, said clients had been bringing up the recent news about AI in therapy. "It's kind of intensifying people's nervous systems which are already kind of stretched post Covid," she said. She said for a long time clients had been talking about their fears over what AI could mean for things like privacy and job security and the latest headlines had advanced that conversation. "It kind of intensifies a general feeling of lack of stability," she said. "Fear of death is a very common fear and it can cross into that sense of 'who am I? What's my path? How are things going to be for me at the end of my life'?" Luke (left) says he treats news about AI advancement with a scepticism On an overcast Friday at Barry Island, Vale of Glamorgan, people's reaction ranged from sceptical to concerned. Chelsea Brown, 31, and her husband Luke Brown, 32, were out for a walk with their newborn. "I'm nervous but also suspicious as leaders of AI companies say things when it suits them," said Luke, who works in tech. "That may be me trying to feel more comfortable about it, but I am sceptical because they do say things that either boost their stock or suit their agenda." But he said by using AI at work he had seen how quickly it had progressed. "It does scare me but the way I cope with it is I look at the news with a sense of scepticism," he said. Chelsea, who works in marketing, said she feared what the speed of progress would mean for their new baby and four-year-old. "I've got quite a lot of anxiety about it, we talk about it quite a lot... it's terrifying," she said. "I really hope regulations come in a lot quicker than they did for social media. I don't know why the regulatory process is so slow." Susan Harvey has found recent reports "quite scary" Susan Harvey, a grandmother to five, said she was out for a walk to clear her head and escape the news. "It is quite scary," she said. "The stories sound extreme and I worry for my grandchildren. I think everything is out of control." She too described feeling powerless, but did have some optimism. "I do think things are changing, people are becoming more 'let's stand up against this and do something'," she said. The Royal College of Psychiatrists said AI's rapid development could "understandably cause anxiety for some people". Its chair Prof Alka Ahuja said: "As with any major technological change, people may feel uncertain about what the future holds and what it could mean for their lives." He advised limiting exposure to alarmist content, discussing any concerns with trusted friends or family and seeking help from a GP if anxiety begins to affect daily life, wellbeing or relationships. Neil Ingham says there are some simple steps that can help top manage anxiety over world events Neil Ingham, executive director for Samaritans Cymru, said: "These headlines affect everybody and they can create anxiety and can make people feel like they don't have control." He said there were steps people could take to reduce their anxiety. Curate your social media feeds: "We can choose who we follow, who we don't follow, what types of trusted news sources we choose to get our news from and who we choose to maybe ignore and mute," said Neil. "We can also choose what alerts pop up on our phone." Think about what time of day you consume news: "If your phone is next to your bed when you wake up you're going to pick up your phone, and if the start of your day is reading about big global news stories or a story about AI you're not really giving yourself a chance to settle into the day," said Neil. title: Mourinho prints out 'red card' incidents after Real lose derby
description: Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho prints out screenshots displaying two incidents he believes should have resulted in Atletico Madrid dismissals.
body: Where did he find a printer? Mourinho arrived at his news conference with screenshots of incidents he believed were red cards for the hosts Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho arrived at his post-match news conference carrying an A4 sheet of printed paper with screenshots displaying two incidents he believed should have resulted in Atletico Madrid dismissals. Mourinho accused the officials of making key errors after Real Madrid were beaten 2-1 by Atletico Madrid, claiming the hosts should have been handed two red cards in the first half. It was Real Madrid's second defeat of the season, having lost 1-0 to Real Betis earlier in September. "We can skip the press conference because the story of the match is right here," Mourinho said as he showed media the printed images. "Those were two clear red cards. Given the difficulties we faced afterwards playing 11 against 10, we can only imagine what 50 minutes of 11 against nine would have been like. "So I'll just have to limit myself to hugging my players, who gave it their all and played a first half, showed great class and character, setting us up perfectly to win the second half." Diego Simeone, in contrast, was ecstatic with the result and when asked to respond to Mourinho's refereeing rant, said he was always respectful of everyone else's opinions. "I understand that we're in a privileged position with a lot of public scrutiny, as coaches, and whether it's Mourinho, [Hansi] Flick, [Manuel] Pellegrini, me, or anyone else, we need to be careful about what we say," he said. "We have to know how to respect others, the referees, our colleagues and we all lose out. And when someone crosses that line of respect, it's not right - you can't cross that line." Mourinho argued the two first-half decisions had a significant impact on the match, insisting his team had shown character despite the circumstances. The first incident Mourinho referenced involved Real's Jude Bellingham and Atleti's Cristian Romero in the 37th minute, when both players challenged for a loose ball and the clash ended with Bellingham being shown a yellow card. At the time, Mourinho pleaded with the referee for a red card to be shown to the Argentina international for dangerous foul play, because replays showed Romero made contact with his studs on Bellingham's knee. Bellingham's yellow card was retracted after a video assistant referee review and Romero was given a yellow. The second was for a challenge by Atletico's Lee Kang-in on Fede Valverde, which Mourinho believed should have been a straight red card. The Portuguese also questioned the appointment of the match officials, saying he wanted to believe the decisions were mistakes rather than deliberate. "I want to believe they are simply mistakes, just as a coach makes mistakes, just as a player makes mistakes," he said. Despite the defeat, Mourinho said he had no complaints about his players' commitment and praised their performance, particularly in the first half. "I liked my team as a unit. Even in the first half I really liked them, and in the second half it was obviously very difficult to get the ball and to stop Atleti's possession. I liked their pride, I liked their determination, and it's a good feeling for me to not be disappointed in my players". Mourinho also addressed the dismissal of Dean Huijsen, which awarded Atletico a penalty, admitting he had not yet watched the VAR replay. The defeat leaves Real Madrid fourth in the league standings, with Atletico second - five points behind league leaders Barcelona. Yet Mourinho was keen to stress that there was still a long way to go in the season. "Under normal circumstances, it's not about how it starts, it's about how it ends," he said. Atletico manager Simeone rejected the suggestion the result would be overshadowed by the refereeing debate, saying his team had controlled the contest. "The match I watched was an intense one, where I think we controlled it at all times," the Argentine said. "We faced an opponent with incredible transitions and extraordinary players who obviously play for their team and do so very well. We controlled almost all the transitions they could have had." Simeone described the derby as an intense match and praised his players' defensive organisation and collective effort against a Real Madrid side featuring several dangerous attacking players. "I think we controlled the match at all times, through our teamwork, our defence, our collective effort, our group dynamics, and our play. Looking for where we could hurt them, which we knew was on the right side." La Liga will resume on Friday 9 October following the international break. title: Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief
description: Gary Neville calls Manchester United "pathetic", but boss Michael Carrick maintains belief after salvaging draw at Fulham.
body: This video can not be played Carrick impressed Man Utd 'kept belief' to earn draw at Fulham Gary Neville took a deep breath after Lisandro Martinez's own goal put Fulham ahead just over an hour into what had been a laboured Manchester United performance, and delivered his verdict. The former United skipper is never short of a scathing word, but even by his standards, this was brutal. "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen," he said. "Absolutely pathetic. "I've never seen such a lack of effort. What must [Michael] Carrick be thinking?" For context, Neville was part of the United side beaten 3-1 by Sunday's opponents Fulham at Old Trafford in October 2003. In recent memory they have also lost 7-0 at Liverpool and 6-1 at home twice, to Tottenham and Manchester City. Neville's words came after a poor quarter of an hour from the start of the second half to Martinez's moment of ill fortune, before United went on to snatch a 1-1 draw thanks to Matheus Cunha's deflected strike in the 89th minute. It seemed an extreme reaction. But in a week when United lost the Manchester derby to a City side reduced to 10 men midway through the first half, then against Brighton for the first time in more than 50 years were beaten at home after giving away a two-goal lead, frustration among the fanbase is high. Questions over fitness were first raised during pre-season when midfielder Youri Tielemans revealed United were not prioritising running. While Cunha did not exactly agree with Neville in his post-match interview with Sky Sports, his comments will have fuelled more debate around the issue. "At the beginning of the second half they put in more energy than us," said the Brazilian. "We cannot accept this." Unsurprisingly, Carrick had a different take. He used the way his side tried to pressure the home team in the latter stages, leading to Cunha's equaliser, as evidence his squad is fit enough. "The way we finished the game, actually, it didn't look like that. We finished the game really strong actually, and kept pushing. I don't think that's an issue, no," he said. This video can not be played Cunha's late strike denies Fulham first league win of the season Cunha also mentioned the "noise" around United when he spoke to BBC Match of the Day. Neville is a significant part of that noise, either directly or through his growing media empire. Carrick has previously said he can shut it out. It cannot be quite so easy though when United fans - who usually back their team through disappointment - followed up chants on Wednesday in disgust at the Brighton debacle by here booing Carrick's decision to take off popular England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo 11 minutes from time. "There's always going to be certain reactions when you're making changes," said Carrick. "I've spoken to Kobbie after the game and he's absolutely fine. "I understand at times when we are chasing the game, everyone's a little bit emotional. The supporters are, as well they should be, desperate for us to do the right thing. "But I don't take any negatives or offence to it. I think we've just got to try and keep doing the right things to get back into the game. "The supporters were unbelievable today, I have to say, all the way through, and stuck with the boys and supported them. At least we've given them something small at the end to take from it, and I'm sure there's more to come." And that is the key point. A draw at Fulham is "something small" considering the home side started the game at the foot of the Premier League - and have now swapped places with Tottenham. Five points from five games leaves United 12th, an incredible 10 points behind pacesetters Manchester City already. Their £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba is still to make his debut, and long-term injury victim Matthijs de Ligt was not involved at all, even though both were part of the squad that travelled south on Saturday. Striker Benjamin Sesko also missed the game after suffering a recurrence of the shin problem against Brighton that he was troubled by for an extended period last season before submitting to a recovery programme that ruled him out for more than three months. Carrick says "at this point" the extent of the damage is unknown. This would all be pretty underwhelming were it not for the ticketing issues instigated by the club's touting crackdown that has annoyed so many in the fanbase. On Wednesday, United will release their full-year financial results to 30 June, around which the full extent of their current debt will be revealed. Then there is the general debate about the wisdom of new stadium, which is set to cost in excess of £2bn, with planning permission potentially submitted with the main Old Trafford masterplan, which is earmarked for late 2027 or early 2028. Little wonder, after leading United back to the Champions League so unexpectedly last season, Carrick is presiding over a club whose supporters feel deflated, even if he does not recognise that. "It's still a big season ahead," he said. "It's a long season and you're going to have spells through a season. That's part of the journey. "It's not a sprint, it's a long effort. "I'm not playing it down, you know. We wanted more points, so I'm not saying everything's great. I understand the frustration. We wanted to be better and we wanted to do other things. "But deflation is certainly not what we have within the club and within the group. The players didn't have that on the pitch today and that's what will carry us through the season without a doubt." title: What have we learned from the Premier League so far?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the opening weeks of the Premier League season as a long international break arrives.
body: Brighton's 3-0 win over Arsenal could have a big impact on both teams' seasons The Premier League takes a near three-week break as we enter a four-game international window. So, what have we learned from the opening five matches of the season? BBC Sport takes a look. This video can not be played Highlights: Brilliant Brighton batter Arsenal in shock first defeat as champions Premier League champions Arsenal were looking fairly unstoppable in the opening weeks of the season. A win over Brighton on Saturday would have given the Gunners a club-record equalling eighth consecutive win in all competitions to start the season. But that all ended with a 3-0 loss at Amex Stadium on Saturday. The Gunners had not lost a league game by more than one goal, let alone three, since October 2024. It was their heaviest defeat in the league since May 2023 when they lost 3-0 to the same opposition. "That's not going to take away what the team has done and the boys have done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup," said boss Mikel Arteta. "What we've done, the way we've competed and the amount of games we've won has been remarkable - but this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level." Brighton humbling 'a big lesson' for Arsenal - Arteta This video can not be played Man City come out on top in eight goal thriller against Sunderland Many wondered if Manchester City would experience a post-Pep Guardiola slump when the legendary boss left after a decade. Things did not start too well under Enzo Maresca, with the Community Shield defeat by Arsenal. But they have won all five games in the Premier League - and seven in a row in all competitions - after Sunday's entertaining 5-3 win over Sunderland. That takes them three points clear of Arsenal. "In the press conference before the game, I said I expect a very tough game," said Maresca. "Then we also conceded two or three goals but we have learned a lot in these eight weeks and this is good." Perfect 24 hours as Man City put pressure on Arsenal This video can not be played Brentford stay unbeaten as they put three past Chelsea Brighton and Brentford, two clubs who have never won a major trophy, have continued to impress this season. Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton enjoyed that 3-0 win over Arsenal to see them sit third in the table, only two points behind the Gunners. Brighton have won at home against the reigning Premier League champions in each of the last three seasons. Star player Pascal Gross laughed and said "no" when BBC Sport asked him if Albion were in the title race. But stranger things have happened... Meanwhile, just one point below them in the table are Keith Andrews' Brentford. Many tipped the Bees to struggle after the departure of Thomas Frank last summer but if anything they improved under their former set-piece coach Andrews. And their start to this season - unbeaten after five games and fourth in the table - is showing he is no one-season wonder as a manager. They go into the break on the back of their most impressive result, a 3-0 home win over Chelsea. Leeds, impressing again under boss Daniel Farke, are also on nine points and in a potential Champions League place. Andoni Iraola's Liverpool and Everton are just below them on goal difference. From near oblivion to Europe - Brighton celebrate 125th anniversary in style This video can not be played Cunha's late strike denies Fulham first league win of the season Seven years apart, United did the same thing twice hoping for different results - appointing a club legend who last managed in Britain in the Championship after a good start as caretaker boss. In 2019 it was Ole Gunnar Solskjaer and this time it was Michael Carrick. But this season, after Carrick having a summer to work on his team, the Red Devils have only won once in the league. Their five points after five league games is their joint fewest at this stage of a Premier League season. They go into the international break on the back of a 1-1 draw against Fulham, and even needed a late deflected Matheus Cunha strike to stop the Cottagers winning their first game all season. After the Lisandro Martinez own goal that give Fulham the lead, ex-United captain Gary Neville said on Sky Sports: "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. "Absolutely pathetic. I've never seen such a lack of effort." United's owners will have almost three weeks to stew on this before they host fellow underachievers Tottenham (more on them soon) on 10 October. This video can not be played Coventry defeat Forest for first win since Prem return In 2024 and 2025, the three promoted teams went straight back down - mostly with really low points tallies too. But that streak came to an end last year when Sunderland finished seventh to qualify for Europe and Leeds came 14th. Only Burnley went down. And the early weeks of this season indicate we could be in for a similar situation. Hull City are eighth after five games, with their 2-1 loss to Newcastle their first defeat. Ipswich are 11th. And Coventry, after losing the first four games without scoring, beat Nottingham Forest 1-0 and only sit in the drop zone on goal difference. But expectations were raised after a summer of big spending - with Spurs splashing out £302m as well as making two high-profile loan signings. Defence and midfield in particular were overhauled, with new wingers too. But they are left with one senior striker in Dominic Solanke, who has only scored 12 Premier League goals in over two years at the club. "I feel they have overpaid for every player

title: Sister of Pakistan's ex-PM Imran Khan arrested
description: Aleema Khanum is accused of mobilising her brother’s supporters ahead of country-wide protests.
body: Aleema Khanum, pictured in January 2025 outside Adiala jail, speaking to the media after her brother's jail sentence The sister of Pakistan's imprisoned former prime minister, Imran Khan, has been arrested ahead of next week's protests held in his support, his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has said. Aleema Khanum was detained in the eastern city of Lahore on Sunday afternoon, PTI officials said, calling it an "illegal detention". Her son is demanding her return. The order for Khanum's arrest, which came from Lahore's deputy commissioner, alleged that she was mobilising Imran Khan's supporters "through social media and public meetings". It added that she will be detained for 30 days. Khanum is a vocal critic of her brother's detention, regularly speaking to his supporters and the media. A police official confirmed Khanum's arrest to the BBC. According to the order, she will be taken to Kot Lakhpat jail in Lahore. Earlier in the day, her family said they had had "no contact or news of her whereabouts". "We demand the government immediately disclose her whereabouts and ensure her safe return," Khanum's son Shahrez Khan wrote on X. Many have linked her arrest to the protests that have been organised across the country on 27 September, when demonstrators plan to march to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad. The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government." Streets in Islamabad are already lined with shipping containers, ready to safeguard the city's government buildings. Local media has reported Pakistan's interior minister as saying that the protests harm the country and that the government will do everything they can to stop them. Khan has been detained since 2023, when he was sentenced to three years in prison for not declaring money earned from selling gifts he had received while in office. He has faced charges in over 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts - all of which he has decried as politically motivated. Last year, the cricket star-turned-politician was jailed for 14 years in a land corruption case - the longest sentence he has received. While in prison, his health has being deteriorating, and last month Khan had to visit a hospital for an examination. title: Middlesex beat Leicestershire to win One-Day Cup
description: Middlesex claim their first silverware in a decade as they beat Leicestershire in a thrilling One-Day Cup final.
body: Middlesex lifted their first white-ball trophy since 2008 Metro Bank Men's One-Day Cup final, Trent Bridge Middlesex 231 (49.5 overs): Higgins 100, Duke 55; Holland 5-36 Leicestershire 200 (44.2 overs): Kelly 103; Roland-Jones 3-27, Helm 3-32 Middlesex win by 31 runs Middlesex claimed their first silverware in a decade as they fought back from a tricky start to beat Leicestershire in a thrilling One-Day Cup final at Trent Bridge. Having been put into bat by Leicestershire captain Stephen Eskinazi, Ryan Higgins' magnificent hundred dug Middlesex out of a hole and helped them reach 231 before being bowled out in the final over of their innings. Higgins, 31, struck nine fours in his 115-ball knock after his team had slumped to 71-5 in the 22nd over, putting on 135 with on-loan Yorkshire wicketkeeper Harry Duke (55) for the sixth wicket. Ian Holland returned his second-best List-A figures of 5-36 for the Foxes, while England all-rounder Rehan Ahmed took 3-55. In reply, Leicestershire too lost early wickets as former England seamer Toby Roland-Jones bowled 10 overs straight through in a fine opening spell of 3-27. Leicestershire were indebted to the efforts of New Zealand international Nick Kelly, who reached a glorious century of his own off 103 deliveries and appeared to be taking his side to victory. However, the game swung again in the over after Kelly reached his hundred as the left-hander heaved Tom Helm to Higgins on the mid-wicket fence to leave Leicestershire eight down. And that proved the decisive moment as Helm dismissed Ajaz Patel and Tom Scriven skied Naavya Sharma straight up, with captain Ben Geddes taking the winning catch. Middlesex's most recent success was the County Championship in 2016, and they had not won a white-ball trophy since lifting the T20 Blast in 2008. Ryan Higgins' hundred was crucial in Middlesex's total of 231 Middlesex had to overcome adversity more than once in Nottingham as they ended their long wait for a trophy. They faced the most difficult batting conditions of the day in the opening hour and many teams would have crumbled at 71-5. The sixth-wicket partnership between Higgins and Duke was a game-defining one as they fought back and gave their bowlers something to work with. It was Higgins' first List-A hundred and it will live long in the memory for Middlesex supporters fortunate enough to watch it as he displayed character, graft and no shortage of skill. Roland-Jones is a legendary figure at the club and he showed exactly why with a near-immaculate spell, taking the key scalps of Rishi Patel and Ahmed. Sharma is Middlesex's leading wicket-taker in this competition and the 21-year-old too impressed with the ball, making the breakthrough as he found Eskinazi's outside edge, pinning Hamza Shaikh lbw and then returning to take the final wicket. With Kelly in full flow, heads never went down and they showed all the composure of a team that have only lost once in this format all season. The wicket of Nick Kelly (right) was the decisive moment for Middlesex Off the back of their 27-point deduction in the County Championship, Leicestershire's team talk is more than likely to have been straightforward. And they started like a team with a point to prove after Eskinazi won the toss, backed by a vocal travelling support. Holland set the tone with the new ball, nicking off Nathan Fernandes and Max Holden cheaply before Tom Scriven took two wickets of his own, including a fine catch by wicketkeeper Ben Cox to remove Josh De Caires (26). Incredibly Cox caught the first five wickets to fall. Middlesex fought back through Higgins and Duke, and the Foxes will perhaps look back on that partnership as an opportunity that slipped away. Rishi Patel and Eskinazi got the chase off to a bright start, but three wickets for just three runs stalled their momentum and similarly to Middlesex's innings, Leicestershire found themselves five wickets down in the 70s. Ahmed will regret his decision not to review after being given out lbw off Roland-Jones, with replays showing it would have missed leg stump. Much as Higgins revived Middlesex, Kelly breathed new life into the Leicestershire chase with his defiant knock, which featured 10 fours and three sixes. The Kiwi left-hander was being serenaded from the stands as the runs required ticked away, but he had to drag himself from the middle with 44 runs still needed. Those fans continued to sing until the end, but were left disappointed as their team fell short. title: German Chancellor Merz calls state election a 'disaster' for his party but vows to stay on
description: Exit polls show damaging losses for Merz's centre-right CDU party in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
body: Merz delivered a statement shortly after exit polls were announced from Berlin and Mecklenburg- Vorpommern Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party. In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was projected to only just scrape into parliament, while the AfD was on track to win the most votes. Merz called the result "a disaster" for his party. In Berlin, the ruling CDU was also expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left). Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap. Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. Echoing comments he made after that defeat, Merz told reporters on Sunday that he would forge ahead with his coalition government's plans to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms. "The reforms have to come," he insisted. "I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward". "I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society," Merz added. As the projected results came up on the screen at the CDU's election night gathering in Berlin, there were no cheers or celebration. This is a party that knows it's in trouble. Friedrich Merz is going on the offensive, quickly declaring he is going nowhere. He has long coveted the top job in German politics and likely won't give it up easily. Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected in the coming hours. According to public broadcaster ZDF, the AfD was projected to take 38% of the vote share in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It was followed in second place by the centre-left SPD, on 36%. However, the AfD is unlikely to govern in the state as other parties refuse to work with it. For Berlin, the broadcaster put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke on nearly 26%. Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved. Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months. While his backers have argued that many of the problems the nation faces are inherited, Merz himself is deeply unpopular. The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left. title: Last-minute Cunha goal saves Man Utd from another defeat - who rated highest at Fulham?
description: Last minute Cunha goal saves Man Utd from another defeat - who rated highest at Fulham?
body: Manchester United's Marcus Rashford tries to beat Fulham pair Timothy Castagne and Josh King at Craven Cottage Matheus Cunha's deflected last-minute equaliser spared Manchester United more misery after Lisandro Martinez's own goal had threatened to give Fulham victory at Craven Cottage. Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below. What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? Cunha rescues point for Man Utd at Fulham Bernd Leno: On his toes to make an early save from Lisandro Martinez and scrambling when Matheus Cunha's effort looped on to a post. Denied Bryan Mbeumo with full-length save. 7 Timothy Castagne: Booked for bringing Marcus Rashford down as Manchester United broke in the second half. 6 David Affengruber: Excellent defence-splitting pass to release Josh King, but he couldn't finish. Exceptionally fortunate to escape after being outwitted by Cunha close to the goalline but stepped in to take the ball off Mbeumo as he looked to counter. 7 Calvin Bassey: Not the easiest game positionally as Manchester United played without an orthodox centre-forward. Got forward to create Fulham's goal. 7 Antonee Robinson: Pushed into advanced areas in the inside forward position, which caused the visitors a defensive issue. 7 Sander Berge (Off, Larsson 76): Shot from the edge of the area turned away by Senne Lammens. 7 Shea Charles: Midfield partnership with Berge was key in protecting the Fulham defence when the visitors had extended spells of possession around the home area. Passing let him down on occasion. 6 Oscar Bobb (off Kevin, 70): Rolled an effort just wide of the post and probably should have done better. 6 Josh King (off Andersen, 79): Always looking to get on the ball and threaten. Took a good save from Lammens to deny him at the far post and his shot across goal was going in without the visitors' keeper kicking it away. Blotted his copybook by getting booked for diving. 8 Alex Iwobi (off Palacios, 70): Also tried to exploit the inside left channel when Fulham went forward. Low cross almost created a chance for Gonzalo Garcia and another deep one did for King. 7 Gonzalo Garcia (off Muniz, 79): Half a stride away from having a tap-in from an Iwobi cross from the left. 6 Palacios (on 70, Iwobi): Kept Fulham ticking over. 6 Kevin (on 70, Bobb): Settled in well. 6 Larsson (on 76, Berge): 6 Muniz (on 79, Garcia): 6 Andersen (on 79, King): 6 Subs not used: Lecomte, Manuel Angel, Sessegnon, Smith Rowe. Senne Lammens: Key first-half saves to keep Manchester United level and came out bravely at Iwobi's feet to prevent another Fulham chance. Distribution could have been better and he didn't cover himself in glory with the Fulham goal. 6 Diogo Dalot: Tidy spin and dash into space to create a chance for Rashford but had too much work to do defensively as he lacked cover far too often. 6 Harry Maguire: Used his experience to draw a foul out of King as United tried to deal with Fulham pressure near their own goal. 7 Lisandro Martinez: Well-struck half-volley drew an excellent save out of Leno. He did eventually find the net - at the wrong end. 5 Luke Shaw (off Dorgu, 83): Returned from a three-match absence. Carrick's side are far more balanced when he is there. 7 Youri Tielemans: Wasted an excellent opportunity when he got no power behind his effort as he ran on to Rashford's short pass. 5 Kobbie Mainoo (off 79, Mount): Usual tidy game in possession without making the key passes. Never looks flustered. 7 Bryan Mbeumo: A lot of strong runs but, like many Man Utd forwards, nowhere near his best. Tough ask, but did he give Dalot enough defensive support? 6 Bruno Fernandes: Low shot against the post from Cunha cut-back but once more not at last season's levels. 6 Marcus Rashford (off 76, Zirkzee): Tried to set up Tielemans with a short pass but the Belgian couldn't finish. An attempt of his own before the break was saved by Leno and another, better opportunity flew way over the bar. 6 Matheus Cunha: Again started in the number nine role he doesn't seem suited to but created an excellent opportunity for Fernandes. Deflected shot hit the post and spun wide. Probably the visitors' most dangerous forward. 7 Zirkzee (on 76, Rashford): 6 Mount (on 79, Mainoo): 6 Dorgu (on 83, Shaw): 7 Subs not used: Darlow, Mazraoui, Mount, Yoro, Andrey Santos, Baleba, Lacey. title: Danny Dyer and Becky Hill join water industry protest
description: Activists are calling for the water industry to be returned to public ownership.
body: Danny Dyer and his daughter Dani Dyer joined a protest calling for public ownership of water companies in Leysdown Actor Danny Dyer, his daughter Dani Dyer and singer Becky Hill have attended a protest in Kent demanding public ownership of the water industry. Activists from Surfers Against Sewage descended on Leysdown on Sunday after 315,000 signed a petition calling for the water industry to be returned to public ownership. Rivals and EastEnders star Dyer, who has been running a caravan park on Isle of Sheppey as part of a new TV series, told the BBC: "Sometimes when you look out to the sea, you can smell the twang in the air." Water UK said that "no sewage spill is ever acceptable", while Southern Water said it was committed to reducing storm overflows. Dyer said that the quality of the water was "a disgrace". "It's a very dangerous thing," he told the BBC. Meanwhile Hill said that she loved swimming in the open water but found it "disgusting" to find human waste in the sea. She said that she was campaigning for her family and other families for a cleaner sea. "We can stand up and make a difference," she added. Singer Becky Hill said that she would like to see improved water quality in the sea Ed Acteson, co-founder of the protest organisers SOS Whitstable, said: "The public has had enough of being asked to accept polluted waterways, failing infrastructure and rising bills. "Water is an essential public service, not a vehicle for private profit. "We want an industry run in the interests of people and the environment, with its income reinvested in the system rather than extracted from it." Meanwhile Cliff Roney, a GMB activist who has worked in the water industry for more than 40 years, said: "I have seen this industry at its very best and now at its very worst. "If the industry is not brought back into public ownership quickly, we are heading towards a national catastrophe." Water UK said it was working to end sewage spills "as fast as we physically can". "That's why we are tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works," a spokesperson said. "This is part of a record £104bn investment programme – the largest in the industry's history – to stop sewage entering our rivers and seas, secure our water supplies and support economic growth." Southern Water's director for environment and innovation, Nick Mills, said its 10-year, £1.5bn Clean Rivers and Seas Plan was "already starting to make a difference". "In Whitstable, we're harnessing both AI and nature-based solutions, and we're investing £90m in improvements to Swalecliffe Wastewater Treatment Works. Together, these measures will dramatically reduce storm overflows in the area." According to Defra's Bathing Water Quality site, the most recent classification for Leysdown is rated good, based on samples taken from 2022 to 2025. There have been no pollution incidents reported there, the website states. Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds.
