title: Charles 'sounded giddily elated' after Diana died, Earl Spencer claims
description: Buckingham Palace has strongly pushed back against claims in a new book by the late Princess of Wales's brother.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Royal row intensifies after fresh claims in Diana's brother book Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after her death in 1997. In a controversial book about Diana, he alleged the then-Prince Charles sounded like a "lottery winner" after the news. Buckingham Palace strongly pushed back on Wednesday against the credibility of the book, after an initial extract claimed Charles had said of Diana: "We'll forget her soon enough." A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss." The latest claims are once again highly personal in their attacks on King Charles and the royals, interpreting their motives in a very harsh light. The evidence is Earl Spencer's own recollection of conversations about that emotional time around his sister's death, almost 30 years ago. What remains to be seen is how the public might respond to the allegations, whether they might support this book as a new and different Spencer perspective, or whether they might feel it to be inappropriate to be sharing such private disputes. Representatives of Prince Harry have said they do not want to comment on the book and Buckingham Palace has pointed back to its response from Wednesday, when it rejected the account of Prince Charles in the wake of Diana's death in Paris. Buckingham Palace has strongly pushed back against claims in a book by the late princess's brother In excerpts from Earl Spencer's memoir published in the Daily Mail, external, he recounts being alerted to the car crash on 31 August, 1997, by a phone call from his sister Jane in the middle of the night at his home in Cape Town, South Africa. During the calls that followed, which confirmed the death, the then-Prince Charles telephoned him, he writes. The book alleges: "Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated - like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time." According to Earl Spencer, Charles informed him he had told Princes William and Harry of their mother's death first thing that morning, in their bedrooms at Balmoral. The royal couple had divorced in August 1996. Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week. BBC News has not seen the book in full. The then-Prince of Wales and Earl Spencer were photographed speaking at a banquet in Cape Town around two months after Princess Diana's death In the memoir, Earl Spencer writes of his sister's troubled marriage - claiming a friend of Diana's had told him that on the eve of their wedding in July 1981, Prince Charles had told her he was "very happy to marry her, but… not actually in love with her". Things became "very difficult indeed" in the marriage early on, Earl Spencer writes, adding that he is "sure that both spouses despaired of the other at times". He now believes his sister had attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, external (ADHD), and as part of her condition suffered from Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria - describing the latter as an "intense emotional pain in the face of others' rejection or criticism". In her later years, he writes, Princess Diana considered taking her own life on more than one occasion but love for her sons "stopped her from going further". title: Marooned Lord Byron statue returns to Hyde Park
description: The statue was left isolated on a Park Lane traffic island after new roads were built in the 1960s.
body: The Duke of Gloucester unveiled the freshly restored statue A statue of the 19th-century poet Lord Byron has been returned to Hyde Park, nearly 70 years after it was isolated on a traffic island when new roads were built through the area in the early 1960s. The Grade II-listed statue was erected as a national memorial in 1880 after receiving special permission from Queen Victoria. Changes to the Park Lane road layout 80 years later left it inaccessible, leading it to become isolated, neglected and dirty. The Lord Byron Society launched a campaign to relocate the statue six years ago, arguing it had become neglected. The move cost more than £400,000, funded by a £230,000 grant from The National Lottery Heritage Fund and additional donations. "We are all extremely grateful that our plea to rescue Byron and put him back into full public view was met with so much support by everyone involved," said Lord Robin Byron, the president of the society. Lord Byron's statue was marooned in the middle of a traffic island in Park Lane and became neglected over the years The campaign to have the statue moved back into the park faced a number of administrative hurdles, and required permission from the Royal Parks and Westminster City Council. Once granted, a large-scale project,, external involving conservation specialists, stone masons and architects, was initiated to restore and then move the statue. At the statue's final unveiling this month, Lord Robin Byron said: "Our sincere hope is that the statue will encourage people to explore Byron's poetry and also his letters, which are so accessible and give a brilliant insight into his engaging personality and fascinating inner life." Byron was one of the most popular figures of the Romantic movement The poet was a popular Romantic figure in Victorian Britain, described as "mad, bad and dangerous to know" by one of his lovers, Lady Caroline Lamb. He was born in London's Holles Street, off Oxford Street, in 1788. He died from a fever in 1824 in Missolonghi, in modern day Greece, after joining Greek insurgents the year prior to fight a war of independence against the Ottoman Empire. title: 'Built differently' - Hodgkinson reveals hamstring abnormality
description: Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson says she is "built differently" after an MRI scan uncovered an "abnormality" in her hamstring.
body: Keely Hodgkinson is part of the leading trio of women's 800m runners, alongside Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson says an MRI scan has uncovered an "abnormality" in her hamstring. Following a suspected tear last year, Hodgkinson had a scan which revealed she has a "split" hamstring, giving her two tendons instead of one. The 24-year-old is still learning how to manage the anomaly, which allows her to continue running when one of the tendons is torn but may also make her more susceptible to breakdowns. Following her second-place finish to Swiss Audrey Werro in the 800m final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest in September, Hodgkinson announced she had sustained another hamstring tear at the European Championships in Birmingham a few weeks earlier. "My body is quite literally built differently," said Hodgkinson. "Where most people have one tendon, mine is split - I have two - and we're trying to figure out if it's a strength or a weakness. "So when one of them tore, I still had another one because it's split. In Birmingham, it didn't affect me during the race, but I could feel something wasn't quite right. "It's a weird one. You can still run on them. I haven't missed any training the last three weeks. But I've just had to alter my approach. I've had to take my foot off the speed [training], because that's when it's most risky." The 'F1 of athletics'? Athlos set for London debut Hodgkinson second to Werro after hamstring tear Hodgkinson has endured two injury-plagued seasons since winning Olympic gold in Paris in 2024, waiting for more than a year to race again after suffering a hamstring injury the following February. Impressing on her return in August 2025 with back-to-back Diamond League wins, she went on to set a new indoor 800m world record in February 2026 before winning gold at the World Indoor Championships a month later. However, she has been unable to replicate that form outdoors, suffering three defeats by Werro, including losing her European crown to the 22-year-old. Hodgkinson has since said she suffered a freak injury while jogging along a canal during a warm-down session, sustaining cuts to both knees and whiplash-like jarring in her back which have made the past few months a "battle". But, while acknowledging that the fall could have contributed to her injury at the European Championships - which ruled her out of Diamond League meets in Zurich and Brussels - she stressed she is not making excuses. "Part of me wants to talk about it and then part of me doesn't, because I feel like my words get twisted or people are like 'oh, she's making excuses'," Hodgkinson said. "Going into the Europeans, I thought I was in the best shape ever. But when I fell over, that kind of messed me up way more than I thought it did. I think that's what contributed to my hamstring, because I couldn't really use my quad for a while." Speaking after her defeat by Werro at the Ultimate Championship, Hodgkinson described 2026 as "frustrating" but remained optimistic: "Overall, I'm finishing second in the world and I can't really be too hard on myself for that." Hodgkinson will end her 2026 season in London at the all-female Athlos event, launched by Reddit founder Alexis Ohanian, on Friday. title: UK needs 'credible path' on defence spending, says Nato chief
description: Mark Rutte tells the BBC that UK ministers accept the need to make yearly steps to up spending.
body: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said he is confident the UK government understands the need for a "credible path" to increase defence spending. The alliance's secretary general told the BBC he was "absolutely confident" in the UK's commitment to hit a Nato-wide spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035. Speaking after meetings in London, he said British ministers accepted the need to make yearly steps towards hitting the target. But he accepted that the exact "pathway" towards the goal would not be set out until next year. Andy Burnham has followed predecessor Sir Keir Starmer in committing to reach Nato's 3.5% spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year. He has said date for reaching a planned 3% interim target will come next spring, when the long-term budgets of government departments are due to be set. But he has faced pressure to immediately commit to reaching the milestone by the end of the decade. His chancellor and ex-defence secretary John Healey has previously argued this would show Britain was serious about the Nato goal. Former Dutch PM Rutte has been encouraging members of the alliance not to pencil in large spending increases shortly before the deadline. Speaking to BBC political editor Chris Mason after meeting Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in London, Rutte said he was confident British ministers understood the 2035 target could not be met "in one go in 2034". "I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the 3.5[%] they are there," he said. "I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there. "There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year," he added. Rutte also said that defence spending should be separated out from the issue of welfare, adding that economic growth was the key to ensuring military commitments could be met alongside spending in other areas. The Conservatives have been pushing for hikes in defence spending to be funded through cuts to benefits, and have criticised Burnham for saying last week that national security "can't come at the expense of social security". Rutte added: "I don't know all the details of the UK economy, I think this is something this government is now navigating," he added. "But I would say these are two separate issues." "One is, indeed, spending on defence, but the other is of course making sure that the economy is growing enough, so you can distribute the success of a growing economy amongst various income groups, various issues in the Budget, for example welfare and healthcare and the pensions." "You have to do it all, and if you want to do it successfully, you need economic growth," he added. "Of course there are issues. I've been prime minister myself for 14 years. You have to take tough decisions, and it's not always easy." This video can not be played “Let’s not be naive about what Putin could do”, Nato chief tells BBC Elsewhere in his interview, Rutte said recent Russian military activity in western Ukraine which saw Poland close two of its airports on Thursday showed Vladimir Putin was "increasingly desperate" over his prospects for the war. Asked about the possibility of a Russian attack that could demand a Nato response, he replied: "If you are willing to sacrifice 1.2 million of your own people in this crazy unprovoked fight, let's not be naïve about what Putin could do." He also said there would be discussions among Nato allies over how to respond to the situation in the Red Sea, where Iran-aligned Houthis recently seized control of parts of Yemen's coast along the important shipping route. Saudi Arabia has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. "I would not be surprised if some phone calls were taking place between European allies, 'hey, how are we going to deal with this?'" he added. "Let's see what happens, and if Nato can help, we will always be helpful". title: Man, 29, jailed for raping two 14-year-old girls
description: One victim escaped and told a neighbour her friend was being raped by the Afghan national, the court heard.
body: Sultani Bakatash, 29, was jailed for 14 years after being convicted of offences against two 14-year-old girls A man has been jailed for 14 years for raping two teenage girls after encouraging them to drink alcohol at his flat. Sultani Bakatash, 29, an Afghan, met one of the girls on Snapchat before inviting her and her friend to his home in Georgina Court, Bolton, Greater Manchester, on 6 December. Bolton Crown Court heard the 14-year-old girls drank vodka and Coke and became so intoxicated they were passing in and out of consciousness before Bakatash raped and sexually assaulted them. Following a four-week trial, he was convicted of two counts of rape, one of sexual assault and one of assault by penetration. The judge said his work with the British Army in Afghanistan might mean he was not deported. One of the girls managed to escape from the flat and knocked on a neighbour's door, the court heard. She said: "He's trying to rape my friend. She's locked in. He's raping her." The court heard Bakatash encouraged the girls to keep drinking while taking only a sip himself and complimenting them on their appearance. Charlotte Rimmer, prosecuting, said he had arranged to meet the girls, encouraged them to drink and then seized the opportunity to rape them. She described him as "a man, intent on sexual gratification, regardless of what they wanted". The court heard both girls became so drunk they passed out and each witnessed the other being raped and sexually assaulted. Bakatash was sentenced at Bolton Crown Court following a four-week trial Sentencing Bakatash, Judge Kenderik Horne said he was sure the defendant had used force to overcome physical resistance. "You encouraged them to keep drinking," he said. "You did that so they would become so drunk they would not be able to stop you having sex with them." Bakatash initially claimed the teenagers had initiated and consented to sex. He then said he could not remember what had happened before later denying any sexual activity had taken place. The judge told him: "You told the jury you had not engaged in any sexual activity. That was a lie, the jury saw through your lie." The court heard one of the girls had suffered severe psychological harm, while the effects of the sexual assault on the other would stay with her for life. A probation report said Bakatash did not acknowledge his offending and assessed him as posing a continued high risk to women and girls. Bakatash fled the property after the offences and was arrested two days later at his brother's house. The court heard he had been in the UK for two years and had indefinite leave to remain, with his mother, two brothers and two sisters also lived in the country. Umar Shehzad, defending, said Bakatash had been shot and injured while working with the British Army in Afghanistan. He said Bakatash had left Afghanistan out of fear following the Taliban takeover in 2021 and had felt "overwhelmed" by living in a foreign country. The judge said Bakatash could be deported after serving two-thirds of his sentence, but added this might not happen because he had worked with the British Army and fled Afghanistan in fear following the Taliban takeover. title: UK Youth Parliament looks set to be axed
description: Some say scrapping the parliament for 11 to 18-year-olds would be a blow for democracy, while others say it is overdue.
body: Members of Youth Parliament pictured in the House of Commons chamber in February 2025 The UK Youth Parliament is at risk of being axed within months, BBC News has learned, as the government is not committing to funding it any longer. The parliament was launched in 2000 to boost interest in politics among young people and has more than 300 elected members aged between 11 and 18. Once a year, the young politicians are allowed to hold debates in the House of Commons chamber, on a day when MPs are not sitting. Some MPs and young people say axing it would be a blow for youth democracy, while others say it is not providing value for money. The Department of Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), which funds the parliament each year with taxpayer cash, is not committing to giving any more grants to it. A spokesperson for the DCMS praised the youth parliament's "important legacy... giving elected young people a national platform to represent their peers, engage with decision-makers and develop confidence, leadership and skills for life and work". It received £453,000 in taxpayer funding in the last year alone with about £2.4m public money spent on it among other youth initiatives between 2017 and 2024. While no final decision has been made on funding beyond March 2027, a government source said: "The government has not committed to continuing the programme in its current form." UK Youth Parliament insiders told the BBC that without government funding, it is likely to close. It follows a government review, external published in October last year, which concluded that while the parliament was delivering on its intended goals, only a quarter of young people know about it - and some schools felt "excluded from the process." The government says it is working with young people and youth organisations to design a new scheme that increases their involvement in democracy and decision-making, with further announcements to be made this autumn. Any new scheme will have a "particular focus on under-represented groups", a government source said. Bobby Forbes, the recently departed chair of the UK Youth Parliament's Youth Select Committee, which works with officials in Westminster, said it gives teenagers "a direct way to scrutinise government and hold decision-makers to account". Bobby Forbes, 18, was a member of the UK Youth Parliament until recently The 18-year-old said scrapping it "would be a huge mistake and detrimental to youth voice across the UK," and it should be allowed to evolve within its current format. But Jack Rankin, the Conservative MP for Windsor, said last year it "should not receive taxpayers' money and should not sit in the Chamber of the House of Commons". He has said it should be funded by voluntary donations rather than public money. It is understood the funding is spent on the UK Youth Parliament's annual conference, held in Brighton last year, plus travel, communication and support staff. The youth parliament is run by the National Youth Agency, but was previously under the British Youth Council which closed amid financial challenges in 2024. Members are elected every one to two years by voters aged 11 to 18 who live, work or go to school in local authorities. Similar schemes are held for the devolved Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish parliaments. Some politicians started their careers in the UK Youth Parliament, including Labour minister Keir Mather who was became the younges MP in 2023 - known as the "baby of the House" - when elected aged 25. Peter Swallow, the Labour MP for Bracknell in Berkshire who ran for UK Youth Parliament aged 14, told the BBC the organisation has campaigned successfully on issues such as votes for 16-year-olds. A Bill to lower the voting age from 18 to 16 for all UK elections is currently making its way through Parliament. It would be "short-sighted to cut off funding to a scheme" given these developments, Swallow said. "As we face a world where trust in politics is low and young people in particular are doubting the value of democratic institutions, I cannot imagine a more important time for young people to be invited into the heart of our democracy through programmes like UK Youth Parliament." title: Former MI6 spy takes Trump to Scottish court for £800,000 legal payout
description: Christopher Steele was the author of a salacious "dossier" linking Trump to Russia during his 2016 election campaign.
body: Donald Trump was named in a hearing at Ayr Sheriff Court A company founded by a former spy is pursuing Donald Trump at a small Scottish court for more than £800,000 in unpaid legal costs. The US president was named in a hearing at Ayr Sheriff Court as Orbis Business Intelligence seeks funds from the Trump Turnberry golf resort. The case concerns legal costs owed by Trump from a 2024 English data protection case against Orbis's director Christopher Steele - a former MI6 agent. But SLC Turnberry Limited - which owns the course - is disputing Trump's role as the "ultimate owner", arguing that his stake in the course is held by a trust. Steele was the author of a salacious "dossier" linking Trump to Russia during his 2016 election campaign. London's High Court of Justice ruled Trump's action out of time and a judge ordered him to pay Orbis £680,000 in legal costs. Orbis is targeting the president's financial interests at Turnberry in order to claim the funds. The case called at Ayr Sheriff Court because the resort falls within its jurisdiction, while Steele and Orbis have no connections there. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland Sheriff officers served papers at the Trump Turnberry resort last September. Court documents named Trump as a "debtor" and reveal that, due to interest, the amount sought by two applications brought by Orbis totals £789,812. In an online procedural hearing Orbis's advocate Duncan Hamilton KC stated that, despite an English court ordering the president to pay money to Orbis, "over the last 18 months since the last judgement, he has refused or failed to do so". Due to interest accruing, he said, the costs now claimed by his client were now "north of £800,000" and that the applicant had spent "a great deal of time and money chasing president Trump in various jurisdictions." Hamilton continued: "President Trump has stated emphatically that he owns Turnberry. "He has committed that to federal filings of assets... He has made that clear in a witness statement to the High Court." Stating that Turnberry said the president was not the owner, the KC said Trump was "being put in a degree of legal and reputational jeopardy by the position adopted by Turnberry" as it implies his previous assertions were false. Turnberry's advocate David Massaro told the court that the company was not claiming that president's statements were false. Massaro said Trump's stake at the course "ultimately rests in a trust in the US, and as they have averred, the president is the beneficiary". He stated that it was his client's position that shares are held by trustees and that this is not a "sufficient link" to the company. Sheriff Millar ordered a further hearing to take place in November and that the president be informed of the updated amount claimed by Orbis. Christopher Steele compiled a dossier on Donald Trump that included uncorroborated intelligence claims Steele is a director of Orbis and a former head of MI6's Russia desk. In 2016, he was hired by a law firm linked to the Hillary Clinton presidential campaign to gather information on then-Republican nominee Trump's alleged links to Russia. The so-called Steele dossier included a series of uncorroborated intelligence claims, including that the US president had been cultivated by Russia, that he had taken part in sex parties and had been "compromised" by the Russian security services. The dossier was later published without permission by the website Buzzfeed in 2017. Trump denies all the claims and launched legal action against Orbis through English courts. In February 2024 the case brought by Trump against Orbis was thrown out. Last April, a court ordered the president to pay Orbis more than £600,000 in legal costs. Ayr Sheriff Court documents reveal that, due to interest, the amount sought by two applications brought by Orbis now totals £789,812.91. Donald Trump has visited the Ayrshire golf course on several occasions The Trump family acquired the Turnberry resort in Ayrshire in June 2014. Donald Trump was a director at the company SLC Turnberry Ltd until he resigned the position in January 2017 - a day before he was inaugurated as US president. His sons, Don Jr and Eric, remain directors at the company. Information held by Companies House states that Donald Trump Snr has significant control of a company called Golf Recreation Scotland, which in turn has significant control at SLC Turnberry. A person with significant control is usually someone who has more than 25% shares or voting rights in a company, can appoint or remove a majority of directors, or can influence or control the company. In September last year, the Daily Mail reported that sheriff officers had served legal papers at the Trump Turnberry resort. At the time, a spokesperson for Orbis told the newspaper it was "concerned that Donald Trump continues to be in breach of the English High Court and are alarmed by the outrageous costs of this vexatious case in wasted time and money". In court documents, Donald Trump is named as a "debtor" while it lists SLC Turnberry Limited - the company that runs the resort - is named as an "arrestee". title: £2k pay rise for MLAs is 'grotesque', says first minister
description: The proposals follow MLAs being awarded an almost 27% uplift in their annual wages in April - a rise of more than £14,000.
body: The increase will take effect from the first sitting day of the new assembly mandate next May A pay rise of more than £2,000 for Northern Ireland Assembly members (MLAs) is "grotesque", the first minister has said. The proposals planned for next year would bring MLAs annual salary to £69,216. The increase will take effect from the first sitting day of the new assembly mandate next May, under draft proposals by Stormont's Independent Remuneration Board. Speaking to the media at Stormont, she said: "This issue of wages is not in my agenda. It's not something we've pushed for." "It's not something we've asked for and actually I think it looks quite grotesque in the climate that we're in." The proposals follow MLAs being awarded an almost 27% uplift in their annual wages in April - a rise of more than £14,000. The first minister said Sinn Féin did not "push" for the pay rise A spokesman for the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) said the party has "no input" in setting MLA salaries. "At the present time we are focused on the need for a fair and stable funding settlement for Northern Ireland so that hardworking nurses, doctors and other frontline workers are properly rewarded for their work," they added. Alliance MLA Eóin Tennyson told the media on Thursday that the pay rise "smacks of being completely out of touch with where the public are". "We are more than adequately paid," Tennyson said, adding that he sees no "coherent" argument for the rise. The leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, Jon Burrows, said "our nurses need their pay rise before our politicians". He added that, while he respects the independence of the remuneration board, he feels there is a sense of "unease" around MLAs' value for money. "We haven't set a multi-year budget, we haven't got a budget of any sort, and people think that Stormont is under-performing." Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna said a pay rise is "going to be impossible for people to stomach". "Those who are doing their job and trying to do their job should be properly remunerated for it but unfortunately some are prevented from doing that by the dysfunction". Alan Lowry, chair of the board, said the 27% rise was a "corrective measure" after years of no substantial rises - but future increases would be expected to "reflect inflationary and other pay trends". "MLAs carry out a wide range of important duties, from representing constituents and scrutinising legislation to holding ministers and departments to account," he said. He said it was "right that their remuneration recognises the complexity and importance of those responsibilities, while ensuring that financial considerations do not discourage people from seeking elected office". He added: "As we look ahead to the assembly election next year and the start of a new mandate, it is important that we put in place a structured and transparent mechanism that links MLA pay to changes in earnings in Northern Ireland. "This approach ensures that pay remains aligned with wider developments in society, while providing certainty and maintaining public confidence in the process." Alan Lowry, chair of the board, said that was a "corrective measure" after years of no substantial rises Under the proposals, while the basic MLA salary will increase in line with earnings growth, payments for different office holders will remain unchanged throughout the 2027-32 mandate. Lowry said: "In making this draft determination, we are increasing the transparency of our decision-making and making it easier for the public to understand how remuneration is structured. "The board will now consult with our statutory consultees - MLAs, the Assembly Commission and the Assembly Members' Pension Trustees, over a four-week period. "It is also inviting views from members of the public during this same timeframe. "After that, we will take some time to reflect on the responses received and present a final determination to the Assembly Commission for publication and implementation." The proposals come as Stormont ministers face pressure from trade unions over public sector pay, with some health workers taking part in strike action in recent months. The health minister at the time said he was unable to implement pay awards in the absence of an agreed Stormont budget. Northern Ireland's four-party devolved government has yet to set a budget five months into the financial year. Stormont departments are facing a shortfall of up to £1.6bn,, external according to a spending watchdog. With no agreed plan, public services have been operating under contingency arrangements. The parties have been holding talks with the UK government and Treasury in recent months in a bid secure additional funding. Maria Morgan NIPSA Deputy General Secretary said it doesn't "land well" Maria Morgan NIPSA Deputy General Secretary said it was surprising in the context of the rise of the 27% and the £14,000. "I think it will go down very badly with our members," she said. "I think it will go down very badly with the public given we've just been announced significant cuts in the health service, significant cuts in education...right across the public sector our members are waiting for their pay." Members of the Scottish Parliament receive £77,711, external while members of the Welsh Parliament earn £79,817 a year., external At Westminster, MPs earn £98,599 a year, external while members of the Dáil (lower house of the Irish parliament) earn €119,467 (£102,334)., external The three-member panel, external was set up with the sole remit of setting MLAs' pay and pension entitlements. It was established under legislation passed last year. The body replaced the Independent Financial Review Panel (IFRP), which had made decisions on both the wages and expenses provisions for MLAs. title: Ukrainian guilty of vandalism at mosques linked to Russian network behind Starmer arson attack
description: Illia Bilyk, a 21-year-old Ukrainian man, has pleaded guilty to targeting five locations in east London.
body: Ukrainian Illia Bilyk, 21, pleaded guilty to carrying out a string of vandalism attacks in London A Ukrainian man has pleaded guilty to spraying abusive graffiti on mosques in east London, in a case linked to the Russian state network behind arson attacks against the former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer. Illia Bilyk, 21, entered guilty pleas at Thames Magistrates' Court to five counts of racially and religiously aggravated criminal damage. Bilyk sprayed graffiti on the Stratford Islamic Association, Al-Birr Mosque and Leyton Jamia Masjid on 23 January 2025. Two days later he targeted Noor Ul Islam Primary School and the Islamic Shariah Council. The BBC has learned that Bilyk told police he was recruited into spraying the graffiti by a Russian speaker after being approached on the messaging app Telegram. Bilyk said the Russian speaker told him where to target and paid him afterwards. In June this year two Ukrainians - Roman Lavrynovych and Stanislav Carpiuc - were jailed for conspiring to carry out arson attacks targeting a property and a car connected to prime minister Sir Keir Starmer. An investigation by the BBC and Hope not Hate revealed that Russia was behind the arson attacks and had also generated Islamophobic vandalism throughout London, including on the east London venues which Biluyk has now admitted vandalising. Bilyk (bottom right corner) spraying graffiti on Leyton Jamia Masjid in January 2025 Lavrynovych, who personally started the fires targeting Sir Keir's property, also admitted spraying Islamophobic graffiti on an Islamic building in south London. He was recruited on Telegram and offered money by an anonymous handler, known by the initials EL, for the graffiti and the arson attacks. EL was a Russian operative who organised a widespread sabotage and provocation campaign remotely through social media and Telegram. EL was centrally involved in running a fake far-right group called Direct Action UK, which was created by Russian operatives to provoke acts of vandalism on British streets, including the graffiti attacks on mosques. After Bilyk sprayed his abusive graffiti in east London in January 2025, images of the attacks were shared in a Direct Action Telegram group. A Russia-linked group tied to the arson attack against the former UK prime minister shared images of graffiti sprayed by Ukrainian man Illia Bilyk Hours after two of his attacks, EL posted in a jobs group for Ukrainian people offering money for pictures of buildings in the area. The BBC investigation named a Russian diplomat, Evgeny Lyukshin, who was part of the Direct Action UK chat group. Lyukshin was trained in "information warfare" by senior Russian spies and his details matched those of EL. He did not respond to the BBC. Bilyk will be sentenced on 19 October at Stratford Magistrates' Court. Chief Superintendent Rhona Hunt, from the Met Police, said: "We recognise that these incidents caused significant distress within Muslim communities across east London last year and that they continue to cause concern. "Anti-Muslim hate crime and Islamophobia have absolutely no place in London. We are committed to tackling hate crime while supporting and reassuring our communities." title: Wife of US scholar jailed in China asks Trump to raise arrest at Xi meeting
description: Sylvia Zin is among the family members of people imprisoned in China who are seeking Trump's help when he hosts the country's leader next week.
body: The wife of a US scholar imprisoned in China on charges of spying and endangering national security has asked President Donald Trump to secure his release when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House next week. U Min Zin, the director at a think tank focused on Myanmar, was arrested on 3 June after travelling to the Chinese city of Kunming for an academic conference. "I'm deeply hopeful that President Trump will raise my husband's case with President Xi Jinping at the summit next week," his wife, Sylvia Zin, testified to Congress on Wednesday. Xi is due to arrive for a state visit to Washington DC on Wednesday. It comes after Xi hosted Trump for a visit to Beijing in May. Ahead of the meeting, families of prisoners being held in China have travelled to the US capital to advocate for their release. Sylvia Zin appeared before the House Foreign Affairs Committee East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee on Wednesday for a hearing titled Lives, Not Leverage: The Long Arm of China and North Korea's Repression. In her remarks, Zin said she believed Trump would also be able to secure the release of Chen Youlin, a US seismologist who tracks nuclear tests that has been held in prison in China for two years. "Knowing the president's historic record on bringing wrongfully detained Americans home has reassured me that he will also be able to secure the swift release of Min Zin and other wrongfully detained citizens," she said. Congresswoman Young Kim, the chairwoman of the subcommittee, opened the hearing by warning Americans: "If you travel to China, Beijing may take you hostage as leverage in diplomatic negotiation." Speaking about Zin's arrest, she added: "Beijing wanted to send a message to those whose research inconvenienced it, and detained Mr Zin ahead of the upcoming Trump-Xi summit." Min Zin, a student activist during Myanmar's 1988 pro-democracy movement, directs the Myanmar Institute for Strategic and Policy Studies (ISP-Myanmar), a think tank that studies China's role in Myanmar, including Chinese interests, relations, and regional influence. The son of Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai also appeared on Capitol Hill to call on Trump to secure his father's release. The US president previously raised the case with Xi, telling reporters that his Chinese counterpart "told me that would be a tough one". Asked for comment on Thursday, a senior White House official, speaking anonymously, told the BBC: "Resolving the wrongful detentions of US citizens is always a top priority for the President." China detains US scientist who studied North Korea nuclear tests China arrests US scholar suspected of spying Last month, the US State Department said that two Americans - U Min Zin and Chen Youlin - were being "wrongfully detained" in China. This designation in the US allows the cases to be transferred to the office of the Special Envoy for Hostage Affairs - raising the profile of each case and allowing the US government to allocate more resources to securing their release. Zin, who lives in Thailand, told the committee on Wednesday that she has not yet been able to speak to her husband in jail, "so every month, we anxiously await his consular visits because they reassure us that he is alive". Zin said US officials had told her that Min Zin was being subjected to up to six hours of interrogations each day when he first arrived in jail. "I'm trying to be strong for our daughter, but I'm constantly wondering if he's OK and how to get him back home to us," she said. Last time Trump and Xi formally met, Trump pressed for the return of another American in jail. Underground church leader Jin Mingri was freed two months after Trump's request. title: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees
description: There is no certainty that the idea will ever get off the ground, let alone become a blueprint for other countries, writes Katya Adler.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Is Canada about to join the EU? Is Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot of confusion right now. The EU constitution rules that possibility out as Canada is geographically outside Europe. But in a speech on Thursday to the European Parliament, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities." Mark Carney was responding – extremely warmly – to an invitation by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become the EU's first associate member. The EU and Canada already have a far-reaching trade deal (Ceta) in place but Carney insisted additional cooperation on energy and economic security, on critical and raw materials, education, tech and AI innovation, and defence would help safeguard all countries involved. Canada and the EU feel increasingly squeezed by the superpowers USA on the one side and China on the other – and by tech giants, too, that seem to operate supranationally. The idea of associate EU membership, Carney emphasised, would not be to form a third superpower or to create a bloc against anyone else. "We do not pursue zero sum deals," he said. Instead he suggested like-minded nations should club together to create a new form of multilateral global governance in an increasingly turbulent world where – in the minds of some others - might is right. Only by countries joining forces and shunning isolationism, Carney suggested, could they close key capability gaps, build strength and ensure national sovereignty. This last may have been a nod to upcoming elections across Europe and the continent's increasingly powerful nationalist politicians. Their slogans – whether "Italy First" or "France for the French" or "Make Poland Great Again" – echo Donald Trump's call to Make America Great Again. Carney's words were hopeful and warm; the applause in the European Parliament rapturous and apparently heartfelt. What could EU associate member status mean for Canada? Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member' Not so across the Atlantic. On Wednesday, Donald Trump dismissed the EU associate membership proposal out of hand, threatened to impose "very heavy tariffs" if the agreement came to fruition and warned he may view it as a "hostile act". But the US president is the unintentional matchmaker for this EU-Canada love-in. Traditionally, America is trade partner and defence ally number one for Canada and the EU. But Ottawa is currently embroiled in what it calls an escalating trade "war" with the White House. Both Canada and the EU have been stung by what they view as Washington's weaponisation of trade tariffs. They also fear they can no longer fully rely on the US to have their back in terms of security and defence. Canada is not alone among Europe's far-flung allies, now seeking to cosy closer to the EU, as they worry the US is becoming too unpredictable a partner. Japan and South Korea show an interest in sheltering under the EU umbrella too. For its part, the EU has recently hastened to secure a list of trade deals – with India, Indonesia and Japan for example – to intentionally diversify relationships. But there is no guarantee Canada's associate membership of the EU will ever get off the ground, never mind become a blueprint for other countries, like the UK wanting closer relations stopping short of full EU membership. Any deal would have to be approved by each one of the EU's 27 countries. No legal precedent exists, negotiations would be lengthy and potential conflicts of interest loom, over steel tariffs for example. A suggestion in May by Germany to make Ukraine – a country desperate for full membership of the European Union as soon as possible – an associate member was rejected by others in the EU. Some, including France's government, want to avoid EU non-members securing "too good" a deal. They fear eurosceptic forces at home and abroad could then encourage voters to clamour to leave the bloc. In the end, "associate membership" is just a label. Buffeted by adverse winds – from China, the US and Russia, the normally rigid rules-based EU is coming under serious pressure to show more flexibility in accommodating countries wanting to stand by its side. title: The big questions for Tuchel's first England squad since World Cup
description: Before Thomas Tuchel names his first squad since the World Cup on Friday, BBC Sport looks at the big questions facing the England boss.
body: Thomas Tuchel led England to third place at the 2026 World Cup Sixty-five days after England's semi-final defeat by Argentina, Thomas Tuchel will name his first squad since the World Cup on Friday. While the tournament ultimately ended with a spectacular 6-4 win over France in the bronze-medal match, the Three Lions left the United States with a long list of what ifs. Now, with four games in the space of 11 days coming up during the extended international break, fans will get a glimpse of what Tuchel's next England side might look like. Could players like Trent Alexander-Arnold be recalled? Will others like Alex Scott make their debut? And how might we expect them to play? BBC Sport senior football correspondent Sami Mokbel, journalist Jess Anderson and BBC Radio 5 Live's John Murray go through the big questions facing Tuchel. Sami Mokbel: Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Hall are among the players to have been named in England manager Thomas Tuchel's provisional squad for the forthcoming Nations League internationals, though it remains to be seen whether they make the final cut. Liverpool winger Ngumoha was part of a contingent of young players that flew with the England senior squad for their pre-World Cup training camp in Palm Beach. He was unexpectedly handed his debut in the warm-up game against New Zealand, impressing in a second-half cameo. But the 18-year-old is yet to be picked in a full senior England squad - although he is in with a chance of being selected by Tuchel for the forthcoming games against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia. Hall's World Cup omission raised eyebrows given England entered the tournament without a natural left-back. Before naming his full squad on Friday, Tuchel is required to submit a preliminary squad of players from which he will name his final party. It is understood Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly and Everton's Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall are also among the names selected in Tuchel's extended list. Attacking duo Cole Palmer and Phil Foden are on there too, after being two of the biggest omissions from Tuchel's squad for the World Cup. That decision was deemed a mistake from certain circles, given they are two of English football's most creative players. Meanwhile, Tuchel is expected to omit Jordan Henderson, Dean Henderson and John Stones because of injury. Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico FA to canvass England players in World Cup review Jess Anderson: One of the most talked-about issues surrounding England is who they turn to in the absence of captain and star striker Harry Kane. At the World Cup, Tuchel simply did not turn to anyone. Kane started all seven of England's matches up to the semi-final and was substituted only twice - both times late on with the game already won. Kane was rested for the bronze-medal match, with Ivan Toney the preferred option, although the Al-Ahli striker did not score in the 6-4 win over France. Toney will not be an option this international break as he has since been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear in court later this month. Ollie Watkins' shock summer move to Saudi Arabia puts his England future into question, while Dominic Calvert-Lewin is the man in form with four goals in four games for Leeds United. This could be the moment for Tuchel to start to further integrate Liam Delap, who is improving at new club Nottingham Forest and has yet to make a senior England appearance. He scored his first goal for Forest in last weekend's win at Aston Villa. This video can not be played What would you change about England's squad? John Murray: In the immediate aftermath of the semi-final in Atlanta, Tuchel and the players spoke of being too passive. At the squad announcement it will be interesting to hear what conclusions Tuchel has reached on why that was the case, and how they came to surrender the initiative to Argentina from 1-0 up with just over half an hour to play. Head of the queue for a recall is Cole Palmer, who seems to have recaptured the form he was missing last season, which resulted in his omission from the World Cup squad. What England fans will want to see against Spain at Wembley, is Palmer and his like taking the initiative and imposing themselves on their opponents in a way that was so lacking in the latter stages against Argentina in July. John Murray: Happy or not, that's what they've got - but this has to be better than another group of qualifiers such as the one they had for the World Cup, against teams way below them in the world rankings. In those matches last autumn England played some of the best football they have so far produced under Tuchel. But, while that helped establish patterns of play and build confidence, you never really know until you face the best. That clearly will be the case from the outset in the Nations League, with this opening match against the new world champions. These matches will also provide preparation for the next Euros in 2028 when, assuming they qualify, England will be playing opponents like this at Wembley. And, lest you forget, this tournament does provide an opportunity to win a trophy which would be the best possible way for Tuchel and his team to step on from their third place at the World Cup. This video can not be played 'This player should be in the next England squad...' Sami Mokbel: This will be a key theme to watch over the next three weeks. The spirit was high in the England camp during the World Cup - as evidenced by their brilliant victory against Mexico in the last 16 with 10 men. But the devastating semi-final defeat by Argentina, and questions over England's approach as a 1-0 lead became a 2-1 loss late on, led to some form of an inquest in the England camp into what was to blame. title: Ed Sheeran's tour in 'damage control mode' after Macklemore backlash
description: US stadium owner Robert Kraft says Sheeran asked him to match his own $2m (£1.5m) donation for "aid in the region".
body: This video can not be played Robert Kraft, the US stadium owner who had pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore removed as Ed Sheeran's opening act, says Sheeran asked him to match his own $2m (£1.5m) donation for "aid in the region". It came after Macklemore said he would donate $1m (£750,000) to Palestinian organisations, challenging Kraft to match him. Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots, wrote on Wednesday: "Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis. "Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges." The BBC's Mark Savage looks at the controversy over Sheeran's US tour and why it is in "damage control mode". Ed Sheeran's tour in 'damage control mode' after Macklemore backlash. title: Is Canada about to join the EU?
description: Ties between Canada and the European Union have been getting closer as trade dispute with the US continue.
body: This video can not be played Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed European Parliament on Thursday as discussions continue to swirl about Canada's relationship with the European Union. Both sides seem to be seeking closer ties, and in his speech today, Carney said he welcomed the EU's "ambition" for Canada to become an "associate member". The president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors. US President Donald Trump has threatened to take action against the EU if it makes Canada its first "associate member". The BBC's Europe editor Katya Alder looks at the EU's future relationship with Canada and what it really means. Is Canada about to join the EU? Video, 00:01:28Is Canada about to join the EU? Up Next. title: Repeat offender fined for searching for gold in protected river
description: Brian Wright, 68, from Henley-upon-Thames, was caught gold panning on a protected river in north Wales.
body: Brian Wright was caught panning at Afon Wen river near Dolgellau, Gwynedd A gold panner caught illegally searching for gold in a protected river has been ordered to pay fines and costs totalling more than £4,700, a regulator has said. Brian Wright, 68, had been caught panning at Afon Wen river near Dolgellau, Gwynedd, in October and December 2024. He was found guilty of environmental offences at Llandudno Magistrate's Court on Monday. Environment body Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said Wright had been caught disturbing the "protected and valued environment" of Coed y Brenin Forest, which the river runs through, and was a repeat offender. "Activities such as illegal gold panning can cause significant damage to river habitats and wildlife," said NRW's Richard Berry. "This case should serve as a reminder that illegal gold panning is not permitted on NRW-managed land and those who ignore the rules may face prosecution." Gold panning is not permitted on NRW-managed land because of the potential damage to river ecosystems. The environment body said the excavation of gravel and the removal of minerals could disturb riverbeds, impacting habitats that wildlife rely on. It said that although many were unaware of the repercussions, gold panning could lead to prosecution and sentencing "where it risks disturbing spawning fish and impacting river habitats". It also said Wright, from Henley On Thames, Oxfordshire, had been sentenced for similar offences in May 2022. NRW manager for north-west Wales, Euros Jones, told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast that gold panning was "damaging" and could lead to a "concerning environmental cost". Jones said Dolgellau "has a history of gold mining" and very small specks of gold could be found among "a lot of gravel". "There is a romance around the gold, and it does attract people to the river because it is known for this," he said. title: BBC Inside Science
description: Might the UK and US joining their AI forces help solve nuclear fusion?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·17 Sep 2026,·28 mins Nuclear fusion energy, the idea of copying the sun’s heat source on earth to make limitless commercial energy is famously always 30 years away. This month, the UK and US have agreed to combine the brains of their nuclear fusion supercomputers in an attempt to improve models of plasma behaviour using AI. Tom Whipple is joined by interim CEO of UKAEA Tim Bestwick to understand what challenges must be overcome to make commercialised nuclear fusion a reality. With under a fortnight to go before the winner of the coveted Royal Society's Trivedi Book Prize is announced, we are marking its imminent arrival by interviewing two shortlisted authors. Deborah Cohen, author of Bad Influence, warns how the internet can influence our health. Plus, Steve Ramirez, author of How to Change a Memory, reflects on a career studying the mechanisms of memory and how grief changed his perspective on its purpose. Also on the show, have researchers finally found Nefertiti's tomb? Nature Reporter Lizzie Gibney answers one of the most exciting questions in science news this week. To discover more fascinating science content, head to bbc.co.uk, search for BBC Inside Science and follow the links to The Open University. title: Police hold press conference in search for girl, 13, missing for six days
description: Lillia went missing from Bolton, Greater Manchester, on Friday and was last seen boarding a bus on Saturday.
body: Lillia was last seen at the Trafford Centre in Greater Manchester on Saturday after first being reported missing on Friday The mother of a 13-year-old girl who has been missing from home for six days has made an emotional plea for her safe return. Lillia, from Bolton, Greater Manchester, was last seen on Saturday at the Trafford Centre shopping mall wearing a small black backpack. Police said they believe she then boarded a bus to nearby Altrincham at about 13:50 BST, but it is not known where she got off. In a statement read out by an officer during a police press conference earlier, her mother Jessica said: "Lil, I love you so much. My heart is breaking without you here. I need to know you are safe. We all need you back home safe and well." Ch Supt Helen Critchley, of Greater Manchester Police, said: "Lillia, if you see this appeal, please know your family love you, miss you and just want to know that you are safe. "You are not in any trouble, they simply want you to come home." Lillia's mother Jessica sat beside police as her statement was read out Lillia was reported missing on Friday and was seen in Manchester's Piccadilly Gardens shortly before 23:00 that night. The Trafford Centre sighting was later confirmed on Saturday. Ch Supt Critchley, district commander for Bolton, said the shopping centre sighting formed an important part of the investigation. Police describe Lillia as about 5ft 5in tall with light brown hair and glasses Officers have appealed for anyone who was on the 247 bus from 13:50 on Saturday and remembers seeing Lillia to contact them. They also want to hear from anyone who may have relevant CCTV or doorbell footage, or who has had any contact with Lillia since she was reported missing. The teenager is described as slim, about 5ft 5in (1.67m) with light brown hair and glasses, and was last seen wearing a black zip-up hooded top, light blue baggy jeans, and a black Nike backpack. Lillia was reported missing from Bolton on Friday 11 September. title: Sutton's predictions v legendary guitarist Johnny Marr
description: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on legendary guitarist and Man City fan Johnny Marr, plus the BBC readers and AI with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
body: The pressure is growing on Manchester United boss Michael Carrick, but can his side sign off for the three-week international break by beating Fulham on Sunday? "For teams who have had a bad start to the season, United being one of them, it could be a horrible few weeks," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton. "Any negativity is going to just fester, really. There will be speculation about his future, along with all the talk about whether this is a good time to replace your manager. "United are not the only team to have made a bad start, but there is a lot to ponder on for them at the moment. It makes this weekend even more important." Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests. For week four, he takes on legendary guitarist and Manchester City fan, Johnny Marr. Marr's new album, The Age Of Everything, is out on 2 October. Do you agree with their scores? You can pick your own below. The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page. A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points. Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions. Marr first had success with Manchester band The Smiths in the 1980s. The Age of Everything is his fifth full-length solo studio record - his previous four have all reached the top 10 in the UK album chart Marr has enjoyed City's 100% start to the new Premier League season, with Sunday's win at Old Trafford continuing their impressive start under new boss Enzo Maresca. "I think that derby will be remembered by City fans for a long time," Marr told BBC Sport. "We all feared the worst when Phil Foden was sent off so early, because you don't know what could happen. It should have been a yellow card for him and Bruno Fernandes anyway. "It's all a bit of a learning curve for the fans and the club with a new manager and so many new players, so to see how the team dug in and won was so great for City fans. "No-one expected Maresca to win his first four games... but then again, why not? He's shown that he's his own man with his own philosophy. I like him." Chris Sutton and Johnny Marr were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan. The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'. Gtech Community Stadium, 20:00 BST Chelsea are free-scoring and their front-line is so dynamic - but they are leaking goals left, right and centre and they are a bit of a rabble at the back. I do think Chelsea will stop conceding eventually, but finding the right balance between defence and attack is Xabi Alonso's big problem at the moment because it is far too easy to create chances against his side. Brentford boss Keith Andrews has got that balance in his team. They are very dangerous on the counter-attack, so you have to think they will hurt Chelsea too. This fixture finished in a 2-2 draw in September last year, and I can see it going the same way this time. Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi has this reputation of being a great coach, and we saw what a good job he did at Brighton. But we have not seen any improvement from Spurs yet, despite the big money they have spent, and he is surely going to come under pressure soon if their poor results continue. They are not the only ones to revamp their squad but if you listen to De Zerbi, after about five years they might come good. He keeps saying they need time, but he has had long enough for their results to be much better already. Other clubs, like Hull and Ipswich, have brought plenty of players in and are doing well enough - so why aren't Spurs? I think De Zerbi has to come under scrutiny, but it is different with Unai Emery at Aston Villa. They are also without a league win, but they look more likely to score goals, as they showed against Coventry in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday. I am expecting Villa to improve the same way they did after not winning any of their first five games last season, and I can see them edging this. Do I give Spurs their first league goal of the season? Yes, but only one. They are due a deflection, or Villa will score an own goal. Something will go for them, but not the result. There might be a bit of an edge to this one after Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler had a pop at Arsenal over their time-wasting when they beat the Seagulls near the end of last season. I love the way Brighton play and I was at Old Trafford to watch their comeback to beat Manchester United in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday. It doesn't seem to matter who they are missing from their team, Brighton are just bold as brass with the way they press and get men forward. Luka Vuskovic, who they got from Spurs for £46m in the summer, is only 19 but he strolled through the game against United. What a player he looks. The issue I have with Brighton in this game, however, is that Arsenal are not Manchester United. They are a cut above that. Arsenal are the real deal and I don't see any weaknesses in their team, as their impressive win at Sunderland underlined. They are brave going forward, but they are also street-wise defensively and can see out a game when they have to, time-wasting or not. They have that steel about them but I also think they could expose Brighton if Hurzeler's side go toe-to-toe with them, which is what I am expecting. I nearly went for an Ipswich draw last week but changed my mind and went for Crystal Palace to win. title: Remains found after wildfire identified as mother-of-three missing since 2019
description: A 56-year-old man is arrested after the remains of Joanne Sheen were found in London almost seven years after she went missing.
body: Joanne Sheen was last seen in December 2019 Human remains discovered in woodland in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as a woman who has been missing since 2019. Mother-of-three Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019. Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham on 12 August after bones were discovered in an area of shrubland damaged by a fire the previous week. A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and he remains in police custody. Detectives in London have now handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen. Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force described as "long and complex". The human remains were found after a wildfire in south-west London Police said they had followed more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, taken more than 300 statements and carried out detailed searches at more than 10 addresses and on numerous vessels. Det Ch Insp Toby Elcock, from the Major Crime Team, said: "While this tragic discovery is not the outcome Joanne's family, or any of us, had hoped for, we hope the identification of her remains can at least begin to provide some answers after many years of uncertainty. "Throughout this investigation, Joanne's family have shown tremendous strength and dignity in the face of unimaginable circumstances, and our thoughts remain with them at this incredibly difficult time. "As our investigation progresses, we remain committed to establishing exactly what happened to Joanne and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable." He stressed that the police would still like to hear from anyone with information about Sheen's disappearance. The area damaged by the fire was cordoned off after the remains were found by a member of the public London Fire Brigade was called on 5 August to a blaze that damaged about two hectares of shrubland in an area known as Bedfont Pits. The human remains were discovered a week later, and a post-mortem examination suggested they had come from a woman aged between 25 and 45. A Metropolitan Police spokesman confirmed the remains were found by a member of the public at the site close to Bedfont Lakes Country Park. Crimestoppers has agreed to reinstate a £20,000 reward for information that supports the investigation. Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020 - two months after she was last seen. Several people were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no charges were brought and the investigation remained unresolved. Police previously said she did not have a permanent place of address, a vehicle or a bank account. title: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes
description: The US has not acknowledged carrying out February's deadly strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd.
body: At least 156 people, including 120 children, were killed in February's strike on the primary school in Minab UN human rights experts say there are reasonable grounds to believe the US committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran that killed at least 177 civilians. A new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, external said February's missile strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd constituted indiscriminate attacks causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure. There was no immediate comment from the US. It has previously denied striking Lamerd and said it is investigating what happened in Minab. The experts also found Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during a crackdown on mass anti-government protests in January. They said killings by security forces occurred on "a staggering and unprecedented scale" across all 31 provinces. Iran has also not yet commented on the findings, but it has previously rejected allegations of systematic violations of human rights. 'What was their crime?': BBC visits Iran school where strike killed 120 children Experts dispute US account of deadly Iran sports hall strike in Lamerd Video shows US missile likely used in deadly strike on Iranian town, experts say US missile hit military base near Iran school, video analysis shows "Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel," the fact-finding mission warned in a statement on Thursday. For their latest report to the UN Human Rights Council, the mission's three independent experts investigated two of the deadliest attacks on civilians during the conflict. On 28 February, when the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, Tomahawk missiles struck Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the southern town of Minab, killing at least 156 people, including 120 children, according to local authorities. The fact-finding mission's experts said the school was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) naval complex also attacked that day, but that the school was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated that it was used for military purposes. The experts said that, based on the evidence gathered - including media reports indicating that a preliminary US military inquiry found US forces responsible, and the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses Tomahawk missiles - they had reasonable grounds to believe that the strike on the school was carried out by the US. They also concluded that the school was "the intended point of impact and that the damage did not result from an errant strike or collateral damage" from the attack on the IRGC complex, citing survivors as saying the school was struck twice. The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets". Also on 28 February, Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) dispersed clouds of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in the town of Lamerd, killing at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to local authorities. Again, the fact-finding mission's experts said the sports complex was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated it was used for military purposes. They concluded by saying there were reasonable grounds to believe that the strike was carried out by the US, citing evidence including the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses PrSM missiles. The US military has said it carried no strikes on Lamerd that day and disputed reports identifying the weapon used as a PrSM. In both incidents, the fact-finding mission's experts said there were "reasonable grounds to believe that the US committed the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects". Anita Ghasemi was wounded in the strike on the sports complex in Lamerd The fact-finding mission's report also covers the Iranian authorities' violent repression of the mass protests that took place across Iran in December 2025 and January 2026. The experts said it was an unprecedented escalation from past crackdowns, marked by the widespread use of lethal force resulting in mass killings and injuries, and extensive arrests. They cited witnesses, health workers and victims' families as saying that security personnel positioned themselves on rooftops and other elevated positions, firing their assault rifles into crowds. Protesters also sustained severe wounds to the head, chest and eyes from metal shotgun pellets, causing permanent blindness. As the crackdown escalated, security forces attacked healthcare facilities, beating and arresting wounded demonstrators and arresting some healthcare workers, which deterred victims from seeking life-saving care, according to the experts. They also found that the tens of thousands of people detained during the protests faced torture, solitary confinement and denial of legal counsel. The experts warned that the government had since intensified its use of the death penalty against protesters, with at least 29 men executed following expedited trials on charges connected to the unrest. The fact-finding mission's report noted that it was not possible to independently verify the death toll from the crackdown, but said there were strong grounds to believe that it was significantly higher than the official figure of 3,000, the majority of whom the government identified as members of the security forces or bystanders. The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) has said it has confirmed the killing of more than 7,000 people, almost all of them protesters. The fact-finding mi

title: Hyrox athlete apologises for continuing race after soiling herself
description: Joanna Wietrzyk has also forfeited her win in the fitness competition after competing last week.
body: Joanna Wietrzyk said she was "genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected" An athlete who faced criticism for continuing to compete in a Hyrox event after soiling herself has apologised and said she will retroactively withdraw from the race. Joanna Wietrzyk offered her "sincere apology" for the incident during the indoor fitness competition in Beijing on Saturday, saying she should have "made a different choice" and exited the event. Footage of Wietrzyk competing after soiling herself raised concerns about hygiene, leading Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste to apologise for the handling of the situation. In a statement shared on social media on Thursday, Wietrzyk said: "I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected." Hyrox apologises for allowing race to continue after athlete soils herself How Hyrox became the latest sporting craze After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win. Wietrzyk said: "I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing." She wrote in a social media post, external that she was "completely fit and healthy" at the start of the race, and had "no reason" to expect any illness. "Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused," Wietrzyk continued. Hyrox insisted it had "clear biocontaminant and medical procedures in place". It said "an unforeseen situation arose" during which protocols became blurred, "creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood". In a statement posted on Instagram, Fürste committed to "improving event processes" to "prevent situations like this from happening again". Hyrox was founded in Germany in 2017 and has become a global sensation in recent years After Wietrzyk's identity was shared online, Hyrox said anyone sending abuse or threats to the athlete would be banned from any future events. It said on Monday: "There is no place in our community for threats of violence or encouragement to harm an athlete." In each Hyrox race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag. The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, Germany, and is now held across the world. The sport debuted in mainland China in late 2024. Some have questioned why those officiating the competition in Beijing last weekend did not intervene when the athlete soiled herself, given that Hyrox penalises acts including "spitting, nostril clearing, littering, and water abuse".
