title: Plaid warned not to cut help for poorer children if it wants Labour to back budget
description: Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates makes early years programme Flying Start a red line in negotiations.
body: Ken Skates makes early years programme Flying Start a red line in negotiations with Plaid Cymru's Welsh government Welsh Labour has said it will not support the Welsh government's budget if cuts are made to a flagship early years programme. The party's leader, Ken Skates, said the future of the Flying Start scheme "has to be a red line" in his party's ongoing budget talks with the government. A Plaid Cymru government minister praised aspects of the scheme but did not say whether it would continue in its current form. The Welsh government said support for "disadvantaged children will be enhanced" as it expands its free childcare policy. Plaid Cymru is running the Welsh government without a majority of seats in the Senedd, meaning that it has to strike deals with other political parties in Cardiff Bay in order to pass budgets or new laws. First launched in 2007, the Flying Start scheme was primarily designed to help children in the poorer areas of the country with their language, social and physical development before starting school. It also includes 12.5 hours of free childcare for two-year-olds, and is being expanded Wales-wide as part of the Welsh government's ultimate policy aim of providing free childcare 20 hours a week to all children between nine months and four years. £55m to boost childcare for two-year-olds, Welsh government says Plan to expand free childcare in Wales faces serious challenges, figures show Since May's election, the new government has been under pressure to explain how it was going to fund its flagship childcare policy. The Welsh government's latest estimate, external is that it would require between £250m and £500m of extra funding a year, depending on how many parents make use of the scheme. Speaking at an event held by the Senedd Sources podcast, external on Tuesday, Plaid's Minister for Government Effectiveness, Dafydd Trystan Davies, did not rule out cutting or changing the Flying Start programme. Asked if he could guarantee that the scheme would still be available by the time of the next Senedd election, he replied: "I don't think I can guarantee that any single programme will be in its current form." Davies said: "What is really strong and important with Flying Start is those areas around speech and language therapy, is around the health aspect. "So, can you guarantee that those provisions of Flying Start will be there as part of the [childcare] offer? Clearly, it has to be. "What I've seen with Flying Start is the budget allocated to different councils. Some councils have been far more effective at delivering to a large number of poor and disadvantaged children and therefore, what I'm keen to see there, is that all councils adopt the best practice. "As has been done in various contexts, you can target that provision." The Welsh Labour leader says he would be "deeply disappointed if Plaid didn't commit to the future of Flying Start" Back in July, the government lost a Senedd vote on extra spending plans after failing to strike a deal with Welsh Labour. Plaid and Welsh Labour are currently holding fresh budget negotiations around this year's supplementary budget and next year's full budget. In an interview with BBC Walescast, Welsh Labour Leader Ken Skates said: "It appears they're looking at using Flying Start money to pay for something they never costed during the election or in their manifesto, the childcare offer, which will benefit a lot of middle class and upper class families. "But it's going to be people and children who benefit from Flying Start who will pay the price. "I would be deeply disappointed if Plaid didn't commit to the future of Flying Start." Asked if any change to Flying Start would rule his party out of supporting the budget, Skates replied: "For us as a party, I think it has to be a red line. "If Plaid Cymru think they can take the best of Flying Start and apply it in different areas, I'm afraid they're going to let people down badly. "So, I'm afraid, if they're talking about Flying Start, then they're going to have to do it by themselves, without our consent or support and they won't be getting a budget approval from us." Steffan Evans, head of the Bevan Foundation, said: "The majority of children living in poverty are not in Flying Start areas. "So, if we want to get a childcare system that helps child development in terms of the education and parents back into work and gets to those children in poverty, you do have to strike a compromise, I think, in terms of how that operates. "And that might mean going towards something more universal to get to more children, rather than something that's perfect, but only answers part of the problem." Reform's minister for fairness, families and communities, Cristiana Emsley, said: "Plaid Cymru are raising the prospect of cutting funding for vulnerable children while continuing to spend money on overseas embassies, its Nation of Sanctuary programme and tree planting in Uganda. "At a time when families across Wales are struggling with the cost of living and children are in need of support, it is clear Plaid have the wrong priorities." A Welsh government spokesperson said: "Our offer means that childcare will be more accessible and affordable to all families. "The current phase of delivery which will provide funded childcare for all two-year-olds is being delivered through the Flying Start model. "At the same time, the support available to disadvantaged children will be enhanced as a result of our offer. "We will need to substantially increase the number of providers to ensure that families have childcare options that work for them. "These are all matters under discussion by the Expert Group on Childcare as we work on rolling out the next phase of this ambitious policy." title: Delay to neonatal reform is putting babies at risk, warn doctors
description: The plan to cut the number of neonatal intensive care units from eight to three was announced in 2017.
body: Kelly Dalley's baby Annabel was admitted to Neonatal Intensive Care at Ninewells Hospital The lives of some of the smallest and sickest babies in Scotland are being put at risk because of delays in reorganising neonatal care, doctors have warned. The Scottish government's controversial plan to cut the number of neonatal intensive care units from eight to three was announced in 2017, but has not yet been implemented. Doctors and charities who support the proposals say they would save lives – but have accused ministers of failing to ensure there are enough cots or staff to safely implement the move. Health Secretary Angela Constance admitted that the government could not continue to delay the move and promised: "These changes will be made." Under the plans, neonatal care will be centralised for babies who: Are born at less than 27 weeks Are lighter than 800g (1lb 12oz) Or need specialist complex care The three national neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) will be based at Aberdeen Maternity Unit, Edinburgh Royal Infirmary and Royal Hospital for Children in Glasgow. The five other units - in Dundee, Wishaw, Kirkcaldy, Kilmarnock and at the Princess Royal Maternity Hospital in Glasgow - will become local neonatal units (LNUs), providing a limited amount of intensive care to other babies. A similar move was carried out in England in 2003. The new model in Scotland was due to be implemented by 2026, but there is still no date for when it will be introduced. Health Secretary Angela Constance says the changes will be implemented The British Association of Perinatal Medicine (BAPM) said there had been a lack of progress and that Scotland was "lagging behind England". BAPM president Dr Stephen Wardle said the evidence firmly supported centralisation of services. He said larger centres improved survival chances for the sickest babies, who would have access to highly trained specialist staff, equipment and surgery. Wardle said not implementing the new model was putting some lives at risk and that additional resources should be made available as soon as possible. "Delays in making progress with these proposals will be affecting the outcome for some of these babies", he said. "Ten years is an awfully long time to wait for these changes". Lauren Bruce's baby Grace was admitted to neonatal intensive care at Ninewells hospital in March 2026 He said that the delays were related to a lack of capacity of both cots and staff, alongside the extra space required to adapt these larger centres. BBC Scotland News also spoke to Professor James Boardman, a consultant neonatologist with the NHS and University of Edinburgh. He said the evidence to support centralisation was "unequivocal" and a "matter of life and death" for the most vulnerable, low-weight babies. BBC News has learned that the number of cots in the units earmarked for intensive care has not yet increased as planned. The number of births have been falling in Scotland over the last 20 years, as have the number of babies who need intensive care, according to the available NHS data. The government says only 50-60 of the most premature and fragile babies will be affected by the reorganisation. But there has been significant opposition from some parents. A parliamentary committee is currently considering a petition by campaigners to have the move scrapped entirely. The scrutiny of the petition has descended into a war of words, with the government accusing campaigners and the media of presenting "repeated misinformation". Petitioner Lynne McRitchie says there are "outstanding questions" over the published documents and clinical evidence, including conflicting figures about the number of babies affected. Particular concerns have surfaced around the neonatal unit in Wishaw, with clinicians writing to the committee with their doubts about the new model and its impact on families in Lanarkshire. Lauren Bruce and Kelly Dalley are campaigning for plans to centralise neonatal services to be halted Lauren Bruce from Blairgowrie is one of those who fears any reduction in local intensive care provision will be unsafe because of existing capacity issues across Scotland. Her daughter Grace was born at 37 weeks at Ninewells Hospital in Dundee in March. Moments after the birth Grace became extremely ill and was admitted to one of four NICU cots at the unit. Under the plans, the number of cots will be reduced to one or two. Lauren says three other babies needed intensive care on the night Grace was born, but she was told there was no capacity anywhere in Scotland. "I think that really highlights the pressure that these hospitals are already facing with four intensive care cots there," she said. "What's it going to be like when it's only one?" Kelly Dalley knew her baby had a heart condition and was expecting to travel from Dundee to Glasgow for surgery after she was born. However, Annabel was delivered prematurely at 32 weeks. When she was 12 days old she became seriously unwell. "At that point there was no space in Glasgow, Edinburgh and Aberdeen and staff at Ninewells kept her alive until she was stable," said Kelly. She is also concerned that any reduction in intensive care cot numbers at Ninewells would be unsafe. "I dread to think what the outcome would have been if that capacity at Ninewells wasn't there," she added. Nula Duff needed NICU care in Aberdeen after birth BBC Scotland News has also spoken to parents who are in favour of centralisation. Euan Duff's daughter Nula was born prematurely and stopped breathing shortly after birth. She spent six weeks in the neonatal unit at Aberdeen Maternity Hospital, which is where one of the proposed neonatal intensive care units would be located. He said: "Even though it was a really traumatic experience with Nula, I would want my baby taken care of in the best place. "You can't expect to have all of the most specialised staff in every unit. We would have gone to London if we had to.

title: 'My rent was higher than my student loan' - the booming cost of private halls
description: Private student halls are springing up in Scotland's cities in ever increasing numbers yet rents continue to soar.
body: Lara Reader says her monthly rent was £200 higher than her student maintenance loan You don't have to walk far in any university city before spotting some form of private Purpose-Built Student Accommodation (PBSA). These large blocks of student housing are springing up in cities across the UK, yet rents continue to soar and young people studying at university say they're still finding it difficult to secure a place to live. The increase in PBSA has predominantly been driven by private companies, with many developments targeting more affluent international and postgraduate students, who industry experts say are becoming increasingly important to the sector. Developers say they are meeting a market demand but campaigners argue that they are too expensive for most Scottish students and more affordable housing should be being built instead. Lara, from Kelso in the Scottish Borders, was given accommodation in Brae House Twenty-year-old Lara Reader told the BBC that when she applied for student accommodation at Edinburgh University she did not expect to be allocated the most expensive option on her list. Like many first-year students, Lara selected from a mix of university-owned and privately-operated halls which cater solely to the city's huge student population. She was given a room in Brae House, one of the many private PBSAs in the city. PBSAs typically offer en-suite bedrooms and studio apartments alongside premium facilities such as gyms, study areas and social spaces - but they also come at a higher price point than traditional student halls. The rent for Lara's room was £1,022 per month, more than £200 higher than her monthly student maintenance loan. In case you missed it Why is there so much student accommodation? Despite it being beyond her budget, Lara accepted the offer because of the difficulty of finding student housing in Edinburgh. She said the cost hung over much of her first year at university and she was "constantly stressing" about how much money she was having to put towards rent. To cover the shortfall, she worked 20 hours per week alongside her studies, a decision she says contributed to her failing her first-year exams. "I was exhausted all the time," she said. "I just didn't have enough time to study." "I think when pricing student housing they need to be more realistic. "It makes it so difficult for students like me who don't come from a super wealthy background to find an affordable place to live." The University of Edinburgh said it offered students good value, across a broad range of price points, with entry-level rents being well below the average. A spokesperson said: "We encourage students to select accommodation that aligns with their lifestyle preferences and budget throughout the application process." Across the UK, a total of 206,005 students told the Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA) they lived in private-sector halls in 2024/25. This is up from 117,995 a decade earlier. The rate of increase is higher in Scotland, up from 5,500 in 2014/15 to 14,640 last year. The growth of PBSA has been particularly visible in Scotland's two largest cities. As of August 2026, Glasgow has 21,655 student beds with a further 18,213 in the development pipeline, meaning the city could host almost 40,000 student beds if all proposed schemes go ahead. Edinburgh has also seen rapid growth, with the supply of PBSA increasing by almost 60% over the past decade. A further 5,917 beds were in the development pipeline as of December 2025. Richard Ward, the head of research at student accommodation marketing website StuRents, said the average cost of privately-operated PBSA in Edinburgh and Glasgow is £268 and £243 per person per week (pppw) respectively. The national average (excluding London) is £191pppw. He said: "The rents you're having to charge are about £250 to £300 per week to make a scheme financially viable "The challenge for the sector is, at that price point, a lot of domestic students cannot afford that." According to industry experts, international students, who are often better able to afford higher rents, are a key part of the PBSA market. It's something Lara, from Kelso in the Borders, noticed in her accommodation too. "A lot of people I was friends with through my accommodation were international students, so funding is very different," she said. "I think for the most part, a lot of people didn't have as much of a struggle paying the rent, but I definitely know a few people who were in the same boat as I was." Saba said PBSAs felt safer than trying to organise a private rental from the other side of the world For many international students, however, PBSA offers reassurance that can be difficult to find in the private rental market. Saba, an international student from Pakistan who had planned to study in Glasgow, said they felt safer than trying to organise a flat from the other side of the world. "I didn't really know where to start," she said. "Every country has different laws when it comes to properties and renting places." After missing out on university accommodation, she considered trying to find a property through a private landlord, however, she says she "encountered a bunch of scammers" during her search, including one man who asked for £500 upfront before sending videos of the property. "As an international student, I feel like you're vulnerable" she said "There are good and bad people everywhere and the bad lot try to take advantage of that." John Boyle said developers were often able to achieve higher returns from PBSAs John Boyle, director of research and strategy at estate agency Rettie, said purpose-built student accommodation had become one of the most "financially viable" forms of city-centre development, with developers often able to achieve higher returns than from conventional residential schemes, making projects easier to fund and deliver. title: Mum's Facebook kidney plea prompts 'mind-blowing' gift from total stranger
description: A woman has undergone a lifesaving transplant after receiving a kidney from a stranger who saw her post on social media.
body: Gary Summerfield told his family "this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them" A woman who shared a desperate plea for a kidney on Facebook has undergone a lifesaving transplant after a stranger offered to be her donor. Karen Davey, 41, had exhausted every avenue before turning to social media, where she said she did not "want to leave her family without a mother". Gary Summerfield saw the mum-of-four's post and, after learning he was a match, donated one of his kidneys via an operation in July. "I thought this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them," said Gary. Karen's family said they would never be able to repay Gary for his generosity, adding that it had given her "another chance to be a mum". The average wait for a deceased donor kidney transplant in the UK is two to three years, according to NHS Blood and Transplant, but if you have a living donor it can be about three to six months. Karen says she feels "100 times better" following the transplant in July This was Karen's second lifesaving transplant. She underwent a heart transplant 10 years ago, after having a heart attack aged 31 while watching her son play football. A transplant increases the risk of infection because of the medication patients need to take following the procedure, and complications led to Karen developing kidney failure. "I knew the tablets I was taking following the heart transplant would damage the kidneys so they try and keep the dose as low as possible, but we always knew when I had the heart transplant that I would probably need a kidney transplant at some point, and that is hard to deal with mentally." Karen, from Brynna, Rhondda Cynon Taf, was in stage three kidney failure when she discovered her friends and family were not matches and decided to put a plea on Facebook. She explained in her post that she has a relatively rare blood type and described the kidney failure as putting her life on hold. "My main thing is the kids, I want to be around for them." Karen's eldest is now 22, and she is also grandmother to a one-year-old. "The kids were 10 years younger when I had the heart transplant, and they've been through a lot since then and the kidney was just the next hurdle," she added. Gary seeing Karen for the first time after he donated his kidney to the mother-of-four Gary, a security guard from Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, stumbled upon Karen's post by chance and felt he had to help. "I saw Karen's appeal and she mentioned the children, and I thought 'Karen's a similar age to my daughter and her youngest child is the same age as my grandson', and I just thought it's terrible for the children. "If It was my daughter, I would be searching everywhere if we had exhausted all avenues through the family and friends, I would want a stranger to come forward. And I thought it would be selfish not to." He added: "I thought this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them." Although, Gary, 60, had never met Karen, he immediately volunteered to be tested. He underwent extensive assessments, including compatibility testing, psychological evaluations, blood tests, cholesterol checks and other medical examinations. The pair then underwent the six-hour procedure on 15 July at the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff. Gary said he never had any second thoughts. "It's amazing seeing Karen today, the first time since the transplant and looking so well. "For me, donating a kidney is simply up there with getting married and having my children, it's one of the top three things in my life. "And she's a very deserving lady and a deserving family." Karen, pictured with husband Matthew and son Brandon, who say Gary has given her the "gift of life" Karen said she felt "100 times better" and her husband Matthew said they would always be grateful to Gary. "Everyone knows what's going on in the world at the moment, it's a horrible place at times, but it really does give you hope that there is kindness in the world. "We'll never, ever be able to repay Gary and the family for what they've done, and to give Karen another chance, another chance of being able to be the mother to our children and just live a life that she deserves. "He has given that gift of life." Karen added: "The fact that somebody came forward and has gone through all the testing, because it's a lot of testing. For somebody to put their body through that and having a kidney taken out for somebody that they don't know, it's mind-blowing, I'm just so grateful." The couple's son Brandon, 17, said it was "amazing" to see his mum on the road to recovery after the transplant. "She's looked better now than she has in a long while. "It can be scary, obviously, when she's going into surgeries, but you just have to have hope. It's just amazing there's still good people out there." title: League Two Fleetwood host Arsenal in EFL Cup - full fourth-round draw
description: League Two side Fleetwood Town will host Premier League champions Arsenal in the fourth round of the EFL Cup.
body: Fleetwood reached the fourth round after an own goal by Sheffield United's Rhys Norrington-Davies settled their tie League Two Fleetwood Town will host Premier League champions Arsenal in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup. The Lancashire side reached this stage for the first time in their history with a 1-0 win over Sheffield United on Wednesday night. And their reward was a plum home tie against Mikel Arteta's men, who beat Ipswich Town 4-2 on Tuesday. Holders Manchester City will welcome Brighton to Etihad Stadium if they beat Norwich in Thursday's remaining tie, while Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso will visit his former side Liverpool after the Premier League rivals were drawn together. League One sides Bradford and Peterborough will play for a place in the quarter-finals after they defeated Leyton Orient and Barnsley respectively in the third round. The remaining fixtures are all Premier League affairs with Fulham hosting Crystal Palace, Bournemouth at home to Aston Villa, Brentford travelling to Sunderland and Everton welcoming Newcastle United The fourth round will take place during the week commencing 26 October. title: Watch: Leaked photos reveal extensive damage at US bases in Gulf
description: The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings as a result of Iranian strikes.
body: This video can not be played The BBC's US partner CBS obtained photos showing widespread damage to multiple US military sites in the Middle East as a result of Iranian strikes. The photos came from an unnamed member of the military, who said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public". They images show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings. The BBC's State Department correspondent Tom Bateman talks through what the photos show. title: US interest rates raised for first time in three years
description: The Federal Reserve unanimously voted to increase interest rates to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% on Wednesday.
body: US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices. Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision on Wednesday despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision". However, Trump said rates "should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World - BY FAR". Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings. Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises. But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth. Global oil prices have surged since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, driving up the price of car fuel as well as the cost of goods and services generally. Yet, despite this, Warsh said the US economy was in a strong position and this was one of the things which encouraged the Fed to cut rates. Ahead of the mid-term elections in November, affordability is one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen diesel prices hit an all-time high and petrol rise above $4 (£2.99) a gallon on average. The price of oil is also key in to the costs businesses face in transporting goods across the country and around the world to sell. The higher costs can result in companies increasing prices, hitting the pockets of households. Warsh told a press conference following the decision to raise interest rates that the Fed "cannot effect any individual price whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", but could ensure price rises do not broaden across the economy. He added that those least well off had most to gain from lower inflation. Asked about the message the decision sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president," as he batted away similar questions with the same response. The Federal Reserve is independent of the government, but has faced sharp criticism from Trump over its decisions on rates in recent years. Trump was heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell, who stepped down at the end of his term earlier this year, for not cutting rates. Following Wednesday's announcement, Trump said rates should be cut to "1%, or less". "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!", he posted on social media. Earlier a White House press secretary Kush Desai told Fox News the president and White House had "reiterated our commitment to the independence of the Federal Reserve on numerous occasions" but added it did not prevent Trump being able to voice his opinions. Warsh said at the press conference that "part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane". This hike by the Fed is the first move rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023. A 0.25pp increase will likely add to increasing mortgage rates for homebuyers, as the rates set by banks and other lenders are heavily influenced by the Fed's policy rate. Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp and BNY raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75% in response, which will rates charged on credit cards and personal loans. Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac. Due to many US homeowners having 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, changes to interest rates will not impact monthly repayments, though they could affect those looking to secure a loan for a home or refinance. Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw interest rates going into the future, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%. A small majority said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029. The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's 2% target by 2029. The US is not alone in tackling the inflation impact from the conflict in the Middle East, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday. title: Painful endgame for Gray as stale Hibs slump
description: A club hero, David Gray ends his time as Hibs head coach not to the sound of euphoria from fans, but to the sound of a support collectively exhaling in relief, writes Tom English.
body: Hibernian have sacked David Gray six league games into his third season as head coach It was the strangest kind of farewell; more sadness than satisfaction, more 'thanks for the memories' than 'never darken our door again'. After a dozen years as a player, a goalscoring and Scottish Cup-winning icon, a coach, an interim manager and, for the last two-and-a-bit seasons, the first team manager, David Gray exited Hibernian on Wednesday evening. He left, not to the sound of euphoria from the fans, but to the sound of a support collectively exhaling in relief. Given what he did on an immortal day at Hampden in 2016, no Hibs supporter wanted to boo the man they called Sir David Gray, nobody wanted to call for his head. It was a painful endgame, for everybody. Hibs have sacked many managers in recent seasons, but this was no Nick Montgomery, no Lee Johnson, no Shaun Maloney. Gray was altogether different. Driven, passionate, honest as the day is long, brutally so when talking about how things were going wrong, which he had been doing too much of lately. Gray's big picture tells us this: he was the first manager at Easter Road to qualify for European football in consecutive seasons since the great Eddie Turnbull in the early 1970s. The kind of slump that Hibs are in right now is entirely in keeping with what's happened at Hibs over the last half century. He's the only Hibs manager to win at Ibrox in three consecutive seasons. He won at Celtic Park last season, too. The flipside is also clear. Six successive home defeats in the league equals a grim club record dating back to 1920. Two shots at European Conference League play-offs - and the finance that would have come had they completed the task - were wasted in the most self-harming way. Six points from six games, ninth in the table, an awful loss to lowly Kilmarnock on Tuesday and a sense of drift did for him. Making the League Cup semi-final, against Hearts, wasn't enough to save him. Gray sacked by Hibs after six league games The style of football wasn't easy on the eye, the lack of energy and entertainment was a problem that was only growing. Hibs just look a bit stale, a bit rudderless. Occasionally they can spark into life and show what they are capable of, but those moments have been too fleeting. Jens Berthel Askou brought zest and enjoyment to Fir Park last season and Alfred Johansson, his successor, is trying to build on that. They both had bad nights on Tuesday but Johansson and Wouter Vrancken at Hearts are attempting to create something compelling and their fans are on board with them all the way. Maybe Hibs fans want something similar, something shinier, something more exotic. There is the feeling that they have a decent enough squad of players but also a belief that these players should be delivering more than they are. If there was a table for under-performance, Hibs would be challenging at the top. Some of those same players must shoulder a chunk of the blame for Gray's demise, but they are a largely protected species, even if a number of them, weak-willed and unreliable, have no right to be protected. You can't sack a dressing room in one day, though. A manager and his assistants? Now that's different. Gray goes but others must look in the mirror; the players, a sporting director in Malky Mackay, a chairman in Ian Gordon, a chief executive in Dan Barnett who could scarcely be more low-key if he lived in a bunker under Easter Road. Gordon, presumably, will lead the search for another manager. It would be interesting to do a poll on the level of trust fans have in him and others to land the right man. David Gray after scoring his famous late goal at Hampden in 2016 Gray took them to third in the league in his first season and fifth last season. There is an argument to be made that on the back of those bottom lines he deserved more time, but he hasn't got it. He had a tumultuous beginning as Hibs manager; one league win in his first 14 games. In November he was bottom of the league. Hearts were second bottom. More than once Gray seemed to be in trouble only to pull out a series of wins that made him safe. That first season was a prime example. From bottom of the table, he got them to third by the end. It was a fine achievement. Fifth last season was reasonable, but it must have felt nightmarish to Hibs fans as Hearts roared on and threatened to win the league. The rise of Hearts adds significant pressure on whoever's managing Hibs. It's just the way it is. Throughout his time, Hibs had a ruinous capacity to concede late goals that checked momentum and made the search for the holy grail of consistency all the harder. In 2024-25 Hibs conceded late goals that cost them points against Kilmarnock, Ross County, Hearts, Dundee twice and Dundee United twice in minutes 88, 90, 90, 90, 86, 90, 87 and 90. Last season that unfortunate habit of caving late on continued too often. They conceded damaging goals against Midtjylland, Legia Warsaw, Livingston, Dunfermline, Dundee and Hearts three times in minutes 119, 90, 98, 90, 90, 90, 88, 90 and 86. This season they lost to Motherwell in the 85th minute and shipped goals in the 84th and 90th minute against Gent to exit the Conference League. They salvaged a point, or three, on other days, but they were on the wrong side of the ledger on so many occasions. Gray will have regrets about that. What-might-have-beens. Plenty of 'if onlys' mark his time in the job. His players have cause for reflection, too. They have no shortage of decent-to-good players at Hibs, but there is something missing, some steel, perhaps, some mentality, some leadership, some coaching nous. Gray did his utmost to improve things. He always struck you as a manager who lived and breathed the job, who was terribly cut up by it when it didn't go to plan. Most sacked managers think they could have improved things if they were given time. The be

title: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt
description: Black - who had business ties to Epstein - declined to appear and provide documents related to the convicted sex offender.
body: The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying a legal summons related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Black, who had business ties to Epstein, did not comply with a subpoena ordering him to appear before the House Oversight Committee earlier this month and share documents related to Epstein. Lawyers for Black, who has sued over the summons, called the contempt move "outrageous". After passage of the measure holding Black in contempt, Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said: "No-one is above the law. We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors." In a statement shared with US media, lawyers for Black called the House move an "outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr Black". "The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer," they said. The measure, which passed by unanimous consent, means the matter will be referred to the US justice department, which will decide whether to criminally prosecute Black. In a written statement, the committee's top Democrat, congressman Robert Garcia, called the contempt vote "an important step towards justice and accountability". "We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," he said. The private equity tycoon walked out of voluntary testimony before the House Oversight Committee in June after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time. Black left Apollo Global Management, which he co-founded, amid scrutiny in 2021 over his Epstein ties. He has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein. The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June. Black has said he hired Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling lawmakers in June that he gave Epstein $158m (£118m) for legitimate reasons. The billionaire has said he did not know about Epstein's crimes until he was charged with sex trafficking in July 2019. title: Police boss cancels 'ridiculous' theatre tour
description: Colin Sutton tells a meeting that he has pulled out of a 127-date tour due to residents' reaction.
body: Promoters of Colin Sutton's show claimed it would offer "an unforgettable evening of real-life detective work" An under-fire £79,000-a-year police commissioner said he had cancelled heavily criticised plans to take part in a 127-date national theatre tour. Opposition parties had questioned how Reform UK's Colin Sutton would be able to oversee Norfolk Police while also presenting a live true crime stage show across the UK. Sutton told a council meeting that the number of dates was "ridiculous" and that he had pulled out of the "Makings of a Murderer" tour after being contacted by residents. Conservative Matthew Taylor, who stood against Sutton in the police and crime commissioner election in July, said it had been "a sorry saga". Conservative councillor Matthew Taylor said many people in Norfolk had been left "deeply disappointed by this episode" A high profile former detective who led the investigation to catch Levi Bellfield, the murderer of Milly Dowler, Marsha McDonnell and Amelie Delagrange, Sutton comfortably won the election to become Norfolk's commissioner two months ago. A regular on TV documentaries, he has previously carried out a long national theatre tour talking about his career. Last week, promoters announced his follow-up series of shows would take place next year and Sutton initially said it "wouldn't impinge" on his day job. But on Tuesday, he admitted to the BBC that he was considering cancelling the tour and on Wednesday he told councillors he had now scrapped it. "What surprised me and what made me reflect and think again was the reaction that I got personally from a number of residents," he told North Norfolk District Council's scrutiny committee. "I'm not sure I could do 127 dates because it was ridiculous, but I could have done some. What I don't want to do is to give the impression to anybody that I don't take this role seriously and I'm not going to do a good job on this. "So that's why my decision has been: OK, I'm not legally obliged to do this, I'm not going to do it." Colin Sutton was heavily criticised for his plan to go on tour Taylor, a county councillor who came second to Sutton in the commissioner election, said it had "been a sorry saga, one that erodes public confidence in those who are supposed to represent them". "I know many people across Norfolk have been deeply disappointed by this episode," he added. South Norfolk Labour MP Ben Goldsborough also said it was "good" that Sutton had pulled out. "But the fact it took a huge public backlash to make him realise that being Norfolk's police and crime commissioner should come before his career as a touring personality tells its own story," he said. The promoters of the show, Entertainers, have been contacted for comment. Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below. title: Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free
description: The 69-year-old White House chief of staff is a powerful figure and particularly close to the US president.
body: Susie Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House Chief of Staff. White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis. In a post on X, Wiles said her pathology tests "came back clear" after a visit to the Mayo Clinic earlier this week. Wiles, 69, is considered among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president. In her post, Wiles thanked Trump for his "unwavering support" and vowed to continue working to "advance his America First Agenda". Wiles continued working virtually at the White House during the six months of treatment following her diagnosis. In a March statement, Wiles said that one in eight women are diagnosed with breast cancer. "Every day, these women continue to raise their families, go to work and serve their communities with strength and determination," she said. "I now join their ranks." Her post on Wednesday did not reveal any more details about her treatment. Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff - widely considered to be the most important role in the White House. In her position, Wiles works to keep the president's agenda on track and serves as a gatekeeper to President Trump, as well as a policy coordinator and political advisor. Before taking the job, Wiles played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 presidential campaign. Her tenure, however, has not been without controversy. In December, Vanity Fair published interviews with Wiles in which she gave a blunt - and occasionally unflattering - assessment of her time working in the Trump White House. For example, she described the famously teetotaling president as having an "alcoholic's personality" but added that there's "nothing he can't do. Nothing, zero, nothing." She also provided candid thoughts about other figures close to the US president, describing Vice-President JD Vance as a "conspiracy theorist" and Elon Musk as an "odd, odd duck." The US president, however, swiftly came to her defence and Wiles described Vanity Fair's reporting as having omitted "significant context" to create a "chaotic and negative narrative" about the administration. President Trump and the White House have yet to comment on Wiles' announcement. title: Verstappen passes 100 amateur karters in 14 laps in exhibition race
description: Four-time F1 world champion Max Verstappen passes 100 amateur drivers in just 14 laps in an exhibition go-kart race at Silverstone.
body: Max Verstappen has won 71 grands prix in Formula 1 Max Verstappen needed just 14 laps and 35 minutes to overtake 100 amateur drivers in an exhibition go-kart race at Silverstone. The four-time Formula 1 world champion had a maximum of 35 laps and 75 minutes to pass everyone on an adapted track at the grand prix circuit in Northamptonshire. Red Bull's Verstappen, 28, was up to 37th by the end of a chaotic first lap in which many drivers crashed or span out, resulting in racing being briefly suspended. The ruthless Dutchman, who warned participants "it's not a charity event" on race radio, moved into 10th by the start of lap six and was in fourth by lap 10, with each driver who he passed having to retire. At that stage, the field - made up of TV, sport and social media personalities, with no professional racing drivers - consisted of just Dutch F1 journalist Jacky Martens, Red Bull engine builder Lewis Osler and YouTuber Zac Alsop. All three were given an extra 'fast lap' where they could cut a corner of the track to try to hold off Verstappen for longer, but he inevitably reeled them in. Martens, who was on pole position after qualifying, was the final driver to be passed as Verstappen completed his challenge with 40 minutes and 21 laps to spare. Verstappen began his racing career as a junior in karting and won four consecutive F1 titles between 2021 and 2024. title: Police officer guilty of series of rapes and sex attacks over 17 years
description: Campbell Petrie, 50, was convicted of nine charges while he was a Police Scotland officer from 2006 until 2023.
body: Campbell Petrie was found guilty of nine charges at the High Court in Glasgow A former Police Scotland officer has been convicted of a catalogue of sex crimes, including two counts of rape, over a 17-year period. Campbell Petrie was found guilty of nine charges at the High Court in Glasgow which took place between 2006 and 2023. Petrie, 50, was a serving officer at the time of the offences, which included indecent assault, assault with intent to rape and assault to injury and danger of life. The force confirmed he was arrested, charged and suspended from duty in December 2023. He retired from the force in December last year. Petrie was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced next month. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland Det Supt Adam Brown, of Police Scotland's public protection unit, said: "Our thoughts are very much with the victims in this case and I commend their strength in reporting these crimes and bringing Campbell Petrie to justice." Brown acknowledged how difficult it could be to report such offences "particularly when the perpetrator is a police officer". He added: "I want to reassure the public we will identify and investigate these officers whether they are serving or retired, or whether their crimes are committed on duty or, as in this instance, off duty. "Petrie will now face the consequences of his actions." title: Body found in search for missing Noah Woods, 3
description: About 1,300 volunteers joined police in searching for Noah, who went missing from a playground.
body: Noah Woods was described as looking "happy and healthy" by one of the last people to see him A body has been found in the search for missing three-year-old boy Noah Woods, police have confirmed. Noah disappeared at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk. Supt Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police said dive teams recovered the body of a child from a nearby pond. He said the death was being treated as unexplained but not suspicious. This video can not be played CCTV footage shows the last sighting of Noah at the playground Supt Pearse said formal identification had yet to take place, but Noah's family had been informed. "Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him," he said. "We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support and people putting on their boots to help." Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had helped in the search for the missing boy, who was non-verbal and partially deaf. People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire had turned up to help. Supt Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police said: "Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him" Searches had widened to include East Bergholt and Manningtree, over the Essex border, on Wednesday. Divers from the Metropolitan Police were called in to search Decoy Pond, a nearby fishing lake. The pond is about 350 yds (320m) away from the playground where Noah was last seen. Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had helped in the search for the missing boy Supt Pearse continued: "Since Noah was reported as missing, a vast number of our officers and staff have been deployed in numerous functions in the search for Noah and support for his family. "We've been supported by Suffolk HART (Hazardous Area Response Team), SULSAR (Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue), Environment Agency, HM Coastguard, Fire and Rescue Service and the ambulance service. "As a parent myself, I completely understand why people would want to help and such a response is one that typifies the strong sense of community and the heart-warming nature of Suffolk people that make the county such a special place. "I am sure you appreciate the family now need time, space and privacy and I thank you for your understanding in this." title: Ex-BBC presenter questions role of Royal Family in new documentary
description: John Humphrys, who presented Today and the Nine O'Clock News, heads a new Channel 4 documentary on the topic.
body: Humphrys met Queen Elizabeth II alongside other BBC figures at Broadcasting House in 2006 Veteran broadcaster John Humphrys has said the people of the United Kingdom should "be able to choose our leaders" as he releases a documentary exploring the role of the Royal Family. Humphrys, who for decades was one of the most prominent faces on the BBC, is presenting a new Channel 4 documentary called The Royals: Time to Go? Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, the Cardiff-born presenter said he "admires" King Charles III in many ways, but said it was a "matter of choice". Buckingham Palace has been approached for comment. In the documentary, Humphrys speaks to both critics and supporters of the monarchy, and makes the case for electing a president as the head of state. He recalled seeing the late Queen Elizabeth III visiting Cardiff when he was growing up, watching her being driven down Newport Road. "My father didn't attend and said he would never bend the knee to anyone. I guess that rubbed off on me," he said. Humphrys asked why it was seen as such a taboo to call for an alternative to the Royal Family, saying that "we can because it's a democracy". "I know the monarch is not a political leader, but he is our leader, and we need to bow our knee to him. "That's what I object to. Shouldn't we get a choice?" He met the Queen throughout his career, including at Buckingham Palace where he said he spoke to her "and the corgis of course". Humphrys, who presented the Nine O'Clock News, the Today programme and Mastermind throughout a decades-long career with the corporation, said he took the opportunity to ask her for an interview. "When I'd finished, she looked up at me and said just one word 'no' and I thought I could build on that," he said. title: Charles said Diana would be forgotten 'soon enough', Earl Spencer claims in book
description: Buckingham Palace has pushed back against the claim, saying grief can "colour memory" of events.
body: Earl Spencer (second from the left) said he disagreed with Charles over whether William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" days after her death, in an extract from his upcoming memoir published by the Daily Mail. He claimed the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to have to walk in her funeral procession. Buckingham Palace has strongly pushed back against the claim. A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss." Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. BBC News has not seen the book in full. In the first extract, external from it to be made public, Earl Spencer claims to have been informed by a senior Palace aide that the young princes would walk alongside Princess Diana's coffin, which he objected to. He claims to have received a phone call from Charles shortly after. Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'." Earl Spencer's book about his sister seems set to open a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family. The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, in a car crash in 1997, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood. Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's untimely death. Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do". In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day. Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands. BBC News understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse. title: British soldier who died in Ukraine road accident named by MoD
description: Tributes have been paid to Major Paul Wilks, who was described as a "gifted leader".
body: Major Paul Wilks, 40, died in a road traffic accident in Ukraine last week The member of the UK armed forces who died in a road traffic accident in Ukraine last week has been named as Major Paul Wilks. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) described the 40-year-old as a "gifted leader who earned the admiration and respect of all those fortunate enough to have served alongside him". The incident on Saturday was not the result of hostile action, the BBC understands, with the MoD stating that the accident happened "away from the front lines". Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Major Wilks served this country with pride and dedication. His loss will be deeply felt by those around him." He said: "The tributes paid by those who worked with Paul illustrate his exceptional talent and ability, underscored by genuine warmth, compassion and a desire to support others. "His loss is a poignant reminder of the enormous sacrifice that our armed forces and their families make in the service of our country." Major Wilks, described by the MoD as a "proud family man", is survived by his wife and two sons. He joined the Intelligence Corps in 2012 and was deployed on multiple operational tours, including to Afghanistan. Major Wilks was the recipient of two operational service medals and a long service and good conduct medal. His commanding officer praised Major Wilks as "a man of great intellect, yet he remained a mate to those he served with". They added: "He spoke often of his love for his wife and two sons, expressing his deep gratitude for the support they provided, which allowed him to serve with such distinction. "It is because of that foundation that he was able to meet the challenges of his role, and it is in the course of his devotion to duty that he made the ultimate sacrifice."
