title: Trump says Kennedy Center will shutter 'immediately', as judge rules his name must stay off building
description: The ruling came as the centre's Trump-appointed board was reportedly scheduled to vote on closing it for two years.
body: This video can not be played Watch: President Trump's name added to facade of Kennedy Center The Kennedy Center board has voted to close the performing arts centre for two years, just as a US judge blocked it from adding President Donald Trump's name back to the building. In May, the same judge ordered the removal of Trump's name and blocked its temporary closure for proposed renovations The board, which is chaired by Trump and comprises his cabinet members and allies, approved a resolution in August that called for the inscription "Renovated and Restored by President Donald J. Trump" to be added to the venue. Trump announced the addition of his name to the institution, among other rebranding measures across the nation's capital, last year. The judge's written order came less than an hour before the centre's board voted on the closure. This was the third time it has approved closing the centre since February, amid legal challenges to Trump's work to take greater control of the institution, and there is a chance the centre's doors could stay open despite Tuesday's vote. Trump wrote on Truth Social that the board voted "almost unanimously" to close the storied venue "for safety reasons" and to begin the process of reconstruction. While the closing "will take place immediately", Trump said renovations cannot begin until the court "rules on the Board's approved name" and vowed to take the case to the Supreme Court if it is a "negative" ruling. He added that the US Department of Justice will ask for an expedited appeal and that he had raised $17m for the centre to "keep it afloat". Also in August, the board approved a resolution to rename the campus the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza" if $100m was raised for the renovations. Congress approved more than $250m for renovations in Trump's massive spending legislation known as "The Big Beautiful Bill". However, the centre cannot close unless the federal judge, Christopher Cooper, lifts a temporary block that he put in place in May requiring it to stay open while a lawsuit brought by board member Joyce Beatty goes ahead. When he put the block in place, Cooper said the board could return and request it be lifted, provided it had come to the decision to close "in a prudent manner". The justice department is expected to make that request by Friday, CNN reported. Beatty, an Ohio congresswoman and Democrat, said on Tuesday that the centre had planned to undergo phased renovations for years while still putting on some performances, instead of fully shuttering. She blamed Trump's attempt to rename the centre for the departure of donors, patrons, and artists. "Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity," she said in a statement to the BBC. "That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee. Congress established the Kennedy Center as a living memorial to President Kennedy, and I am proud to defend this cherished institution." In February 2025, Trump replaced several trustees on the board, which then decided in December to rename the institution. New lettering bearing Trump's full name was affixed to the centre's front portico the following day. The changes, including the re-naming, were followed by cancellations by artists booked at the venue and a drop in ticket sales. Most of the legal challenges to Trump's changes focus on the fact that Congress established the centre as a memorial to President John F Kennedy, who was assassinated in 1963. While detractors say that means Congress must approve changes to the memorial, Trump has argued that he has the power to act. "Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing," Judge Cooper said in a written order issued on Tuesday. The judge said the board's proposal to add language to the existing name of the centre and its surrounding campus "bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted". That statute was a decision by the US legislative body to memorialise Kennedy, "and no one else, at the Center bearing his name", the order said. On Sunday, the Kennedy Center administration told its board that the arts institution was on the brink of bankruptcy, the Washington Post, external reported. The administration said it was in a "precarious fiscal position" and would not be able to support its payroll obligations and routine maintenance contracts "within a matter of weeks". The current leadership at the centre has said the building is unsafe for continued occupancy, pointing to part of the ceiling falling in earlier this month. But others close to the centre dispute that it must be closed. The Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment. Earlier on Tuesday, Trump said on Truth Social that the Kennedy Center is "in a virtual state of collapse". He described dire conditions and railed against the "hostile and conflicted" judge for keeping it open despite not having performances scheduled or "people that would have the Courage to even go in". description: The BBC's North America editor Sarah Smith looks at why the US president is contradicting AI leaders, who are calling for the technology's development to be slowed down.

But US President Donald Trump is opposing calls to regulate the technology. The BBC's North America editor Sarah Smith explains the two reasons that are keeping the US president from regulating AI. title: Thirteenth Met Police officer sacked after Charing Cross Panorama film
description: PC Mason O'Connor is dismissed after a hearing found he had breached standards of professional behaviour, the Met said.
body: A Panorama journalist spent seven months filming undercover at the central London police station last year. Another Metropolitan Police officer has been dismissed following BBC Panorama's undercover investigation into the force's Charing Cross station. PC Mason O'Connor was sacked after a hearing found he had breached standards of professional behaviour, relating to a comment he made to a female colleague, the Met said. O'Connor was reported to a "proactive wider investigation" following the broadcast of the programme in October 2025 and he has become the 13th officer to be sacked since then, the force added. Other officers who were covertly filmed for the documentary were seen calling for immigrants to be shot, boasting about excessive use of force and joking about rape and sexual assault. Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said at the time that this behaviour was "totally unacceptable". A disciplinary panel on Tuesday heard that O'Connor had, while off-duty at a pub, told a female colleague that he hoped she would be raped on her way home. He was found to have breached standards of professional behaviour for authority, respect and courtesy, equality and diversity, and discreditable conduct, the Met said. As well as the 13 officers the Met has sacked, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said another two men, both former officers, had also been found to have committed gross misconduct. The policing watchdog added it was still investigating the conduct of a further 15 officers or police staff in the wake of the Panorama film. "This is one of our largest ever investigations in terms of the number of officers investigated," said the IOPC's Amanda Rowe. "The sheer number of fast-tracked disciplinary proceedings show how seriously the IOPC and the Met, who held the misconduct hearings, are treating this matter," she added. Panorama: Undercover in the Police Secret filming by Panorama reveals evidence of racism, misogyny and officers revelling in the use of force at one of London’s busiest police stations, Charing Cross. O'Connor's dismissal comes weeks after his colleague, PC Lloyd Hunter, was also dismissed from the force. In unaired footage from Panorama which was shared with the IOPC, Hunter was seen saying he enjoyed "Tasering people" and that he hated homeless people. Met Cmdr Simon Messinger said the pair had been fired for their "appalling comments and attitudes", adding that the force would continue to support the IOPC investigation. "I hope this sends a very clear message about the standards we expect from all our officers and the Met's determination to improve our culture across the organisation," he said. title: Southport attack victims, survivors and families hit by data breach
description: The Ministry of Justice says sensitive and personal data was accessed in a limited number of cases.
body: The MoJ says sensitive and personal data was accessed in a limited number of cases An investigation is under way after a data breach involving court files relating to victims, survivors and families of the Southport attack, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has said. The unauthorised access by courts staff was identified during a review of the department's digital systems. For a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data, but the MOJ did not state how many people were affected. An spokesperson said the MOJ was "appalled", but there was no evidence personal data had been shared with third parties and the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) had been told. The prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee the matter. An MOJ source said its independent Data Protection Officer had assessed the matter and found that, for a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. Those affected are being notified directly, the department said. An MOJ spokesperson said: "We are appalled that this happened and recognise the distress it will have caused victims, survivors, and their families. "We apologise to those affected - unauthorised access to court files is completely unacceptable. "This is now being investigated urgently, and the prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee this. "All wrongdoing will be met with extremely firm action." The department said it was also reviewing policies and frameworks covering staff conduct, acceptable use and its fraud response plan. HM Courts and Tribunals Service and HM Prison and Probation Service are also investigating. Bebe King, six, Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, were murdered during the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport on 29 July 2024. Ten others were physically injured. The data breach disclosure follows separate cases involving inappropriate or potentially inappropriate access to the medical records of people involved in the attack. In May, a Liverpool hospital trust admitted nearly 50 staff had inappropriately accessed the records of some victims treated at Aintree Hospital. North West Ambulance Service later began investigating potential inappropriate access to patient records by some of its staff. title: US borrowing costs hit highest level since 2007
description: The effective interest rate on US government bonds over 10 years, known as the 10-year Treasury yield, has risen as high as 5.04% but has eased back since.
body: US government borrowing costs climbed to their highest level since 2007 after a jump in oil prices further fuelled concerns about inflation. The effective interest rate on US government bonds over 10 years, known as the 10-year Treasury yield, rose as high as 5.04% but has eased back since. Government bond yields have been rising globally for months, driven by worries that inflation caused by the oil price surge since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran will lead to higher interest rates. The US has been buying back bonds back in a bid to drive the Treasury yield down, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling the intervention "successful". The global benchmark wholesale oil price rose to over $109 a barrel on Tuesday, up from around $86 at the end of August, after renewed concerns about Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil following rising tensions in the region. Investors are anticipating the US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will raise interest rates to combat the inflation caused by higher oil prices. However, US President Donald Trump opposes a rate hike, having long argued lower rates are great for boosting the economy. He fell out with Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell over his decision not to cut rates. Higher interest rates and inflation tend to drive up the yields bond investors demand on government borrowing. Bond yields can also be a sign of how much faith investors have in a given government, with a higher yield reflecting less confidence. Competition for debt from artificial intelligence (AI) firms is also driving up yields. Tech giants are borrowing massive piles of cash to build huge data centres. This raises interest rates on tech firm's debt which increases government bond yields in response. Carol Schleif, chief market strategist at BMO Wealth Management, said bond markets had been signalling for weeks that higher interest rates may be needed. While the rise in borrowing costs has been "orderly" this year, rather than sudden, she said rates could remain elevated if geopolitical tensions and high energy prices remain "front and center". title: Tech Life
description: What should children learn in a world transformed by artificial intelligence?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·15 Sep 2026,·26 mins Available for over a year AI is developing rapidly. What should parents and children make of it all? And how can young people navigate school and future careers when AI is becoming increasingly important? We speak to an expert who has written a new book about these issues. Also this week: we find out how one piece of health tech is helping scientists uncover disease-fighting data in menstrual blood. And satellite imaging is used by conservationists in Indonesia to protect the habitat of a rare species of orangutan. title: Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico
description: Thomas Tuchel regrets not eating any of the grass at the Azteca Stadium after England's epic World Cup win against Mexico.
body: Tuchel led England to the semi-finals in his first major tournament in charge Thomas Tuchel regrets not eating any of the grass at the Azteca Stadium after England's World Cup win against Mexico. His Three Lions beat the co-hosts 3-2 in the last-16 tie in July, despite playing much of the second half with 10 men following Jarell Quansah's red card. England went on to reach the semi-finals, where they lost to Argentina, before beating France in the Bronze medal match for third place. Tuchel, though, made a bizarre admission during an interview with Daniel Sturridge for the FA's forthcoming feature 'Reflections: England's World Cup Journey'. He said: "I texted a friend after the match and I just wrote, 'I regret that I didn't eat some grass after the match to keep something from this in my body forever'. That was the feeling. That was the moment. This video can not be played England win thriller against Mexico to reach quarter-finals England's victory was only the third time Mexico had tasted defeat at the stadium in 90 competitive matches. Tuchel described it as one of the highlights of the campaign and hailed the "huge bond" within the camp, especially the reaction to Jordan Henderson's tournament-ending injury after falling over an advertising hoarding while celebrating the Azteca success. "This game had so much of what you could wish for," added the German. "If you needed any proof of what it meant to these players and how they were with each other, it was the moment Jordan fell over and broke his arm. "Within a second, the players were there. Every single player was there stopping the celebrations, building a shield, protecting Jordan, not going anywhere, in full empathy. It was so special." England are next in action against World Cup winners Spain on 26 September in their 2026-27 Uefa Nations League opener, with the 2028 European Championships also on Tuchel's radar. Confident of ending England's wait for a first senior men's trophy since 1966, he believed their World Cup run not only cemented his relationship with the squad - "it feels like they are my players now" - but also represented "something to build on". Tuchel added: "I'm very excited. I think we got another step closer and I think we're there." title: Turner Prize winner's new vision for hometown
description: Keith Tyson said he hopes to create a space for exhibitions, education and community engagement.
body: The former Mercedes-Benz garage is to be converted into a space for exhibitions, education and community engagement A Turner Prize-winning artist has revealed plans to transform a former car showroom near where he grew up, into a centre for art and learning. Keith Tyson has bought the former Mercedes-Benz garage on Princes Street in Ulverston, where he said he hopes to create a space for exhibitions, education and community engagement. The privately funded project aims to give young people opportunities to experience art after Tyson's own artistic education was shaped by local libraries growing up. He said "there were no galleries for miles around" so he thought this could be a chance to "give young people in the community an opportunity to see and learn about art" in a way that he never had. Tyson said the project had potential to become an arts destination for the north Tyson said the project was still in its early stages but he was "excited by the building's potential to become an arts destination" for the north. The artist, who won the Turner Prize in 2002, said he hoped the centre would include exhibition space, a reference library and programmes for schools and the wider community. "We're still in the very early stages of the project, but I'm really excited about this beautiful building's potential to become an arts destination, celebrating creativity, especially in the north, and supporting learning and engagement through exhibitions, education, and other resources," he said. Among those pleased to see the plans come forward is Adrian Newnham, Tyson's former art teacher at George Romney School in Dalton. Newnham said: "I was Keith's art teacher when he was 10-years-old. I told him he had a talent and I kept his artwork. "When he won the Turner Prize I showed him the artwork I'd kept. He thanked me in the programme when he won. He was a highly talented lad." Newham said Ulverston already had a strong cultural identity and believed the project could strengthen it further. "Ulverston is a festival town with a cultural buzz. Hopefully, his venture will raise the artistic status of the town even more," he added. Tyson became known for work combining art, science and technology across a range of media, including painting, sculpture and installation. title: Nigeria arrests alleged Mexican drug kingpin at international airport
description: Arturo Carrera Loaiza denies allegations he was involved in meth production, the Nigerian authorities say.
body: Arturo Carrera Loaiza has denied allegations that he was involved in methamphetamine production, Nigeria's drugs control authority says An alleged Mexican drug kingpin was arrested in Nigeria last month as he tried to leave the country, the drug enforcement authority has just revealed. That arrest resulted in the discovery of a suspected industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory - the third such find allegedly linked to Mexicans in four months. When Arturo Carrera Loaiza, 40, was detained at Lagos international airport, officials allegedly found digital images of him wearing what they believed to be a laboratory coat alongside equipment consistent with meth production. The pictures' location data led officers to a property in Ebonyi state, where they said chemicals and drug-making equipment were found. Loaiza has denied involvement in methamphetamine production and said he had been invited to Nigeria by a local contact for a restaurant business venture, according to a statement from the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA). How Mexican drug cartels have outsourced meth labs to Nigeria The agency's investigators found a CCTV memory card at the suspected laboratory in Ebonyi with footage from the property showing someone who looked like Loaiza wearing a blue laboratory coat. A Nigerian man was also identified directing people as they removed chemicals and equipment from the site. NDLEA chairman Gen Mohamed Buba Marwa said further intelligence led officers to an isolated house in a neighbouring community, where they recovered chemicals, dehydrators, condensers, a reaction pot, weighing scales, mixers, drums, gas burners and a sieve containing traces of methamphetamine. No estimate has yet been given for how much methamphetamine the alleged laboratory was capable of producing. The NDLEA released pictures of some of the things investigators found after raiding a suspected laboratory Investigators have alleged that Loaiza had recruited and brought a fellow Mexican to work at another suspected methamphetamine laboratory hidden in a forest in Oyo state, which was raided in June. Four Nigerians were also arrested after the raid. A month earlier, NDLEA officers arrested three Mexican nationals and seven Nigerians at what the agency described as an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory hidden in a forest in another part of the country. Marwa said the operations showed international criminal groups were attempting to establish drug-production facilities in Nigeria's forests and rural communities. "Nigeria will not be allowed to become a haven for transnational drug cartels seeking to relocate their laboratories from other jurisdictions into our forests and rural communities", he said. The NDLEA said its investigation into the network is ongoing, including into those it believes financed or helped facilitate the operations in Nigeria. Unlike plant-based drugs, such as cocaine or heroin, which can only be grown and processed in certain places, a synthetic drug like meth can be produced anywhere with the right chemicals and expertise, making it easier for organised crime groups to quickly scale up production. West Africa poses numerous attractive benefits to Mexican syndicates, starting with swathes of forested land which serves well for secluded production sites. title: South African president vows justice as more women's bodies found near Johannesburg
description: Police have not linked the deaths to a serial killer but are investigating this possibility.
body: Elizabeth Moselakgomo's body was found on Saturday three days after she went missing during a routine jog South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings of several women in and around the town of Kempton Park, north-east of Johannesburg, over the last two months. Another body was discovered on Tuesday morning and police say their investigation now includes the deaths of seven women most of whom have been found either partially or fully naked. "These incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women," the president said. Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings. "[It] could be that it's a copycat crime that is happening right here but so far, no linkages as yet," police spokesperson Brig Athlenda Mathe said. One arrest has been made in connection with the discovery of the first body. The person is still in police custody. So far only two of the seven women have been identified. South Africa calls gender violence a national disaster after protests I built this 'AI aunt' for women after family tragedy in South Africa On Monday, police said that one of them was Elizabeth Moselakgomo, a runner whose disappearance last week sparked a frantic and public search for her. President Ramaphosa said he had directed that the cases be prioritised: "Our law enforcement agencies are working urgently to establish the facts, keep communities safe and bring the perpetrator or perpetrators to justice." South Africa experiences some of the world's highest levels of gender-based violence (GBV), with the rate at which women are killed five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women. The discoveries of the bodies have sparked outrage and fear across the country, with many criticising the authorities for failing to adequately protect women. Moselakgomo was identified by her relatives on Monday after her body was discovered on Saturday. It was the 38-year-old's young daughter who raised the alarm about her disappearance after she failed to return from her daily run last Wednesday. The body of the first woman was found in mid-July, the second in late August - the others were discovered this month, two in the last two days. On Tuesday, police said that the body of woman found on 7 September in a town nearby Kempton Park was also being included - bringing the total number of bodies being investigated to seven. "After noticing that there are bodies being picked up, we went back to our police stations… and unfortunately it came to light that a body of a female in her late 20s was observed in a river next to a mall," Maj-Gen Fred Kekana, acting police chief for Gauteng province, said at a briefing. Police have urged women in the Kempton Park area - which is by South Africa's main international airport - to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas". South Africa's Commission for Gender Equality urged residents of Kempton Park to work with the police to find the perpetrators. "These deaths are indicative that women in South Africa continue to face environments in which their ordinary freedom of movement can become a matter of life and death," it said. "Women should be able to run, walk to work, use public transport, return home, visit friends and participate in community life without having to calculate whether an ordinary activity could place their lives at risk." title: Ministers could force phone companies to add 'anti-theft protections'
description: The government could legislate to force firms to act if there is not a drop in phone thefts, the policing minister says.
body: Purple pavement markings in Oxford Street in August 2025 warned pedestrians of mobile phone theives Policing minister Sarah Jones has said that unless there is a drop in the number of mobile phones being stolen, the government could force phone companies to add "anti-theft protections" to their products. Writing to the Science and Technology Committee,, external she said the Home Office had so far chosen to work collaboratively with the tech giants to reduce thefts, but would consider legislation if she did not see progress. Phone thefts have been particularly prevalent in London, but numbers are starting to fall. Samsung said it was "fully committed" to protecting its customers and had "worked quickly to make a significant amount of security enhancements to help address this issue". Apple said it had "led the industry in protections and features to deter theft". Jones' letter comes months after Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley urged the government to compel all phone companies to make stolen devices "unusable bricks". Speaking to the BBC in June, Sir Mark said the market for stolen phones relied "on the fact that security hasn't been good enough on these devices" allowing stolen phones to be reset using "dodgy software" and resold as new. However, he added that Apple - the biggest seller of mobile phones in the UK - had been able to "crack" the engineering problem and since then the "vast majority" of phones stolen in London had not been reset. "That shows they are right and their security is making a difference," he said. In her letter - published last week and first reported by The Times, external - Jones said: "My overriding objective remains to see that the proportion of stolen devices being reused/reactivated reducing, as this should support a reduction in the number of devices being stolen. "If there is no means to reactivate a stolen device, its value is significantly reduced, alongside the incentive to steal it." Make stolen phones unusable, Met Police urges tech giants Met gets more e-motorbikes to fight phone thefts Tech bosses could stop mobile phone theft, say MPs She acknowledged that work between the Met Police and phone companies had been "constructive" and that the results were "promising", pointing to data showing there were 14,700 mobile phone thefts in London in the past year - a fall of 18.7%. Jones said the fall was "welcome" but added that she wanted further reductions and that officials in her department were developing new laws that could introduce a "technical standard for anti-theft protections". She noted the government had so far opted for a collaborative approach with the companies but warned: "If at any point I am not satisfied about the pace of progress in the context of efforts being made, we will legislate." The Science and Technology Committee held an inquiry into mobile phone thefts last year. At one hearing, Conservative MP Kit Malthouse asked if companies were "dragging their feet" due to "a very strong commercial incentive". "The fact that £50m-worth of phones are stolen in London every year means that, if that stopped, £50m of sales would be depressed," he said. The companies giving evidence to the committee rejected the suggestion they were profiting from phone thefts. Responding to Jones' letter, a spokesperson for Samsung said: "We recognise how distressing phone theft can be and have worked quickly to make a significant amount of security enhancements to help address this issue, completing several requests from both the Home Office and the Met Police over the last 18 months to demonstrate how seriously we take this issue. "We have a number of features that would render phones unusable if stolen, including Factory Reset Protection, which restricts a device when a factory reset is attempted and requires authentication with the previous Google account. "Additional One UI anti-theft features include both Identity Check, which requires biometric authentication for any sensitive security setting changes, and Security Delay, which activates a one hour delay if there is an unauthorised attempt to reset biometric data." In a statement, Apple UK said: "We take all threats against our users very seriously and are in close contact with the Met Police and Home Office to ensure they are aware of our initiatives to combat phone theft and are dedicated to supporting their efforts to defeat the criminals targeting our users. "Apple has led the industry in protections and features to deter theft, including Find My, Lost Mode, Stolen Device Protection, Activation Lock, and Activation Lock for parts, which minimise the incentives for thieves to target Apple devices and help protect our users and their data even if their device is stolen, and we are committed to our innovation in this area." title: VAR did not even consider if Fernandez was offside - Webb
description: Referees' chief Howard Webb has admitted that the video assistant referee (VAR) did not even consider whether Enzo Fernandez was offside for Erling Haaland's controversial winner in Sunday's Manchester derby.
body: This video can not be played Refereeing decisions were 'baffling' - Rooney Referees' chief Howard Webb has admitted that the video assistant referee (VAR) did not even consider whether Enzo Fernandez was offside for Erling Haaland's controversial winner in Sunday's Manchester derby. Speaking on the first edition of 'Match Officials Mic'd Up' of the season, Webb said he was "really disappointed" with the error made by the VAR Matt Donohue and his assistant Blake Antrobus. Manchester City striker Haaland thought he had scored the only goal of the game at Old Trafford in the 60th minute, but it was disallowed on the field for offside. A VAR review found Haaland was just onside, and the goal was awarded. But it immediately became apparent that the video officials had made an error in failing to identify an offside offence by Fernandez, diving at the ball in a central position and interfering with opponents. "I was really disappointed with this outcome. We all are," said Webb, Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref's chief refereeing officer. "None more so than the officials themselves. They take a lot of personal pride in what they do and they're obviously hurting now, having fallen short in this situation. "They'll not be officiating again until after the international break." Manchester City won 1-0 at Old Trafford after a VAR mistake handed them the only goal of the game One of the questions which many supporters have asked is how the VAR team could possibly reach the conclusion that Fernandez did not commit an offside offence. Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez initially appeared to be marking Haaland, but then moved over to try and intercept the ball from Fernandez. This left Haaland free at the back post to finish. Former England striker and BBC Sport pundit Wayne Rooney said on Match of the Day that "to not see that and recognise that Enzo Fernandez was in an offside position...anyone who has played the game at any level understands that and to get it so wrong is baffling." The Mic'd Up audio revealed that at no stage did Donohue or Antrobus consider whether Fernandez was offside because, as Webb describes, they got "tunnel vision" over Haaland. The semi-automated offside technology told the VAR that Haaland was three centimetres onside from Josko Gvardiol's cross. But the video officials then only checked for a touch by Fernandez which would have created a new offside phase against the Norway international. This is the transcript, which was dominated by the VAR with the AVAR only making one minor contribution. At the start of the season, video officials were encouraged to be more efficient with their checks and not take an excessive amount of time. Comments made by the technical replay operator have been omitted. VAR: Checking the on-field decision of offside against Haaland. The VAR and the semi-automated offside operator then discuss the decision against Haaland and he is shown to be onside. VAR: Okay, so he's onside. So we now need to check the full APP (attacking phase). VAR speaking to referee Michael Oliver: Michael, Haaland's in an onside position, but I need to check the full APP now. Stand by. VAR: Haaland's clearly onside. Roll it all the way through. Roll it all the way through. VAR: Let's go, let's go, let's go, let's go. VAR: Go back just to check Ndiaye wasn't on offside. Sorry, my apologies. When it's flicked. Quick, quick, quick, quick. Yes, fine. Go, go, go, go, go. VAR: Let's go. It should be a goal. All the way into the back of the net now. VAR: Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go! This is the point at which Gvardiol crosses the ball into the box. VAR: Deflection. Onside. No touch there [by Fernandez]. Confirm, no touch. There wasn't. VAR: Just something [camera angle] tighter. Clear gap. VAR: There's not a touch, is there [by Fernandez]? There's no touch. VAR: Another angle. Roll it through, roll it through, roll it through. VAR to referee: Michael, confirming that you need to change your decision to goal. Haaland is in onside position. Final decision is goal. Check complete. Webb said that the VAR failed to assess how Fernandez found himself in that position, so did not consider the offside offence. "The VAR gets super-focused on Haaland," said Webb, who had already been in contact with Manchester United to share the VAR audio and video. "He establishes he's onside, he thinks that's a good goal. "He doesn't truly evaluate the full impact of Fernandez's position. He has a look to see if he touches the ball, because then that relates to potentially knocking it to Haaland, who goes on to score." Webb highlighted the lack of assistance from Antrobus as the assistant VAR, who did not offer a meaningful contribution during the review. "In that moment, he [Donohue] gets tunnel vision," Webb said. "It's down to the rest of his team to pull him out of that tunnel, and unfortunately, that didn't happen on this occasion. "What looks like a really clear subjective offside, because Fernandez doesn't touch the ball but still clearly impacts [the play but] doesn't get identified, and it's really disappointing. "This goal should've been disallowed. And highly unfortunately, it wasn't, and we'll review it, reflect upon it, and try to take the learning forward to prevent this unusual type of error from happening again." There was also much debate over the red card shown to Phil Foden in the 23th minute for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes, largely because there was no sanction against the Portuguese midfielder for a similar act. Webb backed the decision to dismiss Foden, but said the action by Fernandes did not meet the threshold for violent conduct. "I agree with the red card for Phil Foden," said Webb. title: Warning of space arms race as US confirms weapons in Earth's orbit
description: The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities.
body: This video can not be played The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities. Russia and China responded by warning of an arms race in space. However, according to the BBC's Defence correspondent Jonathan Beale, this is already happening. Details of how the weapon operates have not been disclosed by US officials. Warning of space arms race as US confirms weapons in Earth's orbit. title: 'My son was failed' - Noah Donohoe inquest finds tunnel errors possibly contributed to death
description: The nine jury members, who had 10 questions to answer, returned their verdict on Tuesday at the end of an inquest which began in January.
body: Noah Donohoe was found dead almost a week after he went missing in June 2020 The jury in the Noah Donohoe inquest has found it was possible, but not probable, that failings by the Department of Infrastructure (DfI) over the tunnel in which he was found dead contributed to his death. The jury found that the DfI had failed to identify a hazard at the site, which it maintains, and that there was no warning sign. They also found numerous failings in the Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI's) investigation but that these did not contribute to the 14-year-old's death. Noah's mother, Fiona Donohoe, said he had been failed by both the department and police while the family's solicitor said she had suffered "indignity after indignity". Fiona Donohoe, Noah's mum, outside Belfast Coroner's Court on Tuesday The PSNI said it was a "complex and challenging investigation which garnered huge public and media interest, along with widespread speculation" and the eventual outcome was "devastating". Assistant Chief Constable Davy Beck said there was "no action that police could have taken" that would have prevented Noah Donohoe's death. He added it was important to reflect on any learnings and "ensure they are applied in the future". He said: "Noah was a child with his whole life ahead of him. His death is a tragedy, and our thoughts remain firmly with his family and those who loved him." Infrastructure Minister Liz Kimmins said Fiona and Noah's family are at the forefront of her mind. "As Minister, I will make sure the department does everything it needs to ensure all lessons are learned." As it happened: Noah Donohoe inquest jury finds failings by department officials possibly contributed to death Noah went missing on Sunday, 21 June 2020, after leaving his south Belfast home on his bicycle, sparking a huge search across the city. He was found dead six days later in the water tunnel in the north of the city, which leads into Belfast Lough, with the cause of death found to be drowning. Eyewitnesses, who were the last to see him in the vicinity of the tunnel, reported that he was naked. The incident sparked widespread speculation about what happened to Noah, with his family launching a high-profile campaign. There was no conclusive evidence at the inquest about why Noah was without his possessions and all the clothing he was wearing when he was last seen alive. There was also no evidence about any physical interaction between the schoolboy and anyone else during his journey from his south Belfast to the north. An inquest verdict at last - but many mysteries remain about Noah Donohoe's death Noah Donohoe inquest jury finds failings by department officials possibly contributed to death How the Noah Donohoe inquest came about after six years of delays The inquest began in January, five-and-a-half years after the death of the schoolboy and following numerous delays. Juries do not typically sit for inquests but can be summoned in certain circumstances. Noah's family had requested a jury be used, with a coroner, in 2022, agreeing that it was "desirable". The jury deliberated for five days in total - first, for three days in June and July before the case was adjourned due to the holiday plans of some jurors; and then on Monday and Tuesday when it resumed. The nine members - seven men and two women - had 10 questions to answer and delivered a unanimous verdict, as required by the coroners' court. Those questions included asking the jury to summarise the scenario in which Noah's death occurred; to explain why he behaved how he did after he left the house; to say when and where he died; and whether the Department of Infrastructure's management of the tunnel or the PSNI's investigation contributed to his death. In answering those findings, the jury found: That Noah died between 19:00 BST and midnight on 21 June 2020, the day he disappeared, in the lower reaches of a culvert That there was insufficient evidence to reach a conclusion as to explain why Noah behaved how he did when he left his home That it was possible, but not probable, that any error by the Department of Infrastructure in how it managed the tunnel contributed to his death That it was not possible any PSNI error contributed to his death But there were 13 failings related to the PSNI and DfI that impacted the inquest's ability to reach a conclusion on aspects relevant to his death The finding of the time period of Noah's death means that Noah could have died before his mother raised the alarm with the police at approximately 21.45 on 21 June 2020, or within an approximate two-hour period after he was reported missing. There was no indication at that stage of Noah's precise location, other than he had left his home off the Lower Ormeau Road to travel across the city to Cave Hill. The initial police searches that evening and night covered a wide area of Belfast based on the limed information available at that stage about Noah's intended journey from the south to the north of the city. Noah's presence in the Northwood Road area was not known until the following day. Why was the Noah Donohoe inquest held with a jury? During the inquest, the Department for Infrastructure was criticised about aspects of its maintenance of the tunnel in terms of public access and safety. The PSNI was also strongly criticised by the legal team representing Fiona Donohoe. During the inquest, the police chief in charge of the investigation apologised to the boy's mother for "missed" investigative opportunities. Before the jury resumed their deliberations on Monday 14 September, the coroner Mr Justice Rooney announced that one juror, who had taken part in the previous phase of the deliberations, had been discharged. No reason was given in public for the man's removal from the process. Fiona Donohoe has led a high-profile campaign for answers around her son's deat

title: Baby 'cot cams' plan after inquiry finds Lucy Letby crimes could have been prevented
description: Plans will be "urgently" developed for live-streaming cameras after an inquiry report into Lucy Letby's crimes.
body: Lucy Letby was convicted of the murders of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has said officials will "urgently develop plans" to introduce live-streaming cameras on England's baby wards after an inquiry into Lucy Letby's murders and attempted murders. Inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall called for a series of urgent reforms to neonatal units, including CCTV for all cots and incubators, and restricting access to insulin. Thirlwall said some of the babies Letby killed could have been saved if managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital had taken action earlier. Her report criticises a "complete failure to protect babies" and a "profound failure of management, governance and safeguarding" at the hospital. Thirlwall said this was because "no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt." She said it would never be possible to know exactly how many lives could have been saved if safeguarding procedures had been properly followed. This video can not be played Watch: The key findings and recommendations from the Lucy Letby report Thirlwall added her report described "dysfunctional management and governance, a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians, and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding". Letby was moved on to administrative duties in July 2016 after consultants expressed concerns about her to the hospital's executive team. But the inquiry has found that alarm bells should have been sounded earlier. There were several "missed opportunities" for hospital bosses to intervene, the report said, including when three babies died in one cluster in June 2015. Parents of the babies were "kept in the dark for years" over the concerns that their babies might have been deliberately harmed, the inquiry also found. Thirlwall described the lack of consideration shown to parents as "reprehensible". Repeatedly untruthful, callous and quiet - what we learned about Lucy Letby from inquiry report Key findings from Lucy Letby Thirlwall Inquiry As it happened: Read the live coverage from the Thirlwall Inquiry The report is highly critical of managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital. Hospital bosses carried out a number of internal reviews into increased infant mortality in 2015 and 2016, but did not invite Cheshire Police to investigate until May 2017. Letby remained on site until her arrest more than a year later. Cheshire Police said it would "carefully review" the contents of the report and "fully consider" relevant recommendations. Thirlwall said the hospital's former chief executive Tony Chambers behaved in a "dictatorial manner" and had "intended" to obstruct a police investigation into deaths on the ward. Chambers, along with director of nursing and head of safeguarding Alison Kelly and medical director Ian Harvey, "dismissed the idea that Letby was deliberately harming babies", Thirlwall added. But whether these managers believed Letby was harming babies or not was "irrelevant", Thirlwall said, adding that action should have been taken as soon as concerns were raised. In a joint statement, Chambers, Kelly and Harvey along with the hospital's former HR director Sue Hodkinson said: "We are carefully reviewing the Thirlwall report and its recommendations. "Given that there are a number of investigations under way, and that the work of the Criminal Cases Review Commission has not yet completed, it would be inappropriate for us to offer any further comment at this time. "Our thoughts remain with the families affected by the tragic events that took place at the Countess of Chester Hospital." This video can not be played Letby "should have been removed from the ward," Thirlwall says The inquiry also condemned wider NHS culture, finding evidence of "toxic negativity" that discouraged whistleblowers. The chair of the British Medical Association said on Tuesday that whistleblowers in the NHS "deserve strong protections, and the inquiry makes it clear that these doctors did not get them". Regulator the Care Quality Commission (CQC) was also criticised, with the report saying it did not show enough curiosity to look beyond what it was being told by the Countess of Chester Hospital. Responding to the report, the CQC's chief inspector of hospitals said "crucial information" was not shared by the Countess of Chester, but that the commission as a regulator did not take a "sufficiently investigative and inquiring" approach. Dr Tony Onon said the regulator had since changed its approach to assessments. Lucy Letby has twice been denied permission to appeal against her convictions Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she was "profoundly sorry" on behalf of the government for the failures set out in the report. She said she had asked officials to "urgently develop plans" for cot-cams in neonatal units, and that the government would consider Thirlwall's other recommendations in full. Cooper also said she expected NHS leaders across the country to uphold their safeguarding responsibilities. She plans to meet Thirlwall, who made 17 recommendations including restricting access to insulin, later this week to discuss the inquiry in more detail. Thirlwall was clear that her inquiry was not an investigation into Letby's guilt, which some supporters of the jailed nurse still contest. A number of Letby supporters gathered outside Liverpool Town Hall to voice their concerns over her conviction, calling for her release, before Thirlwall delivered her inquiry findings. Now 36, Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more. She was convicted in 2023 and has been denied permission to appeal against her convictions twice. title: Villagers voting on independence over asylum plans
description: One voter in the symbolic referendum in Piddington, Oxfordshire, calls it the "Battle of Britain".
body: Villagers in Piddington are voting over whether the village should leave the UK Voters in a small village are heading to the polls for an independence vote over government plans to house asylum seekers at a nearby former Ministry of Defence (MoD) site. The residents of Piddington, in Oxfordshire, are voting over Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at MoD Bicester. The symbolic referendum on whether to leave the UK has been organised by the local parish council, with polling taking place between 07:00 and 19:00 BST. Ahead of the vote, council chair Tim McNally said the government "does not want to engage with villagers concerns". "They actually have played every possible trick in the book to avoid engagement," he said. "If we've got to do something, it has to be proportionate, and that is not proportionate - that is us having to assimilate into them, not them assimilating into us." Tim McNally is chair of Piddington Parish Council A spokesperson for the prime minister told the BBC that the government was "working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country". They said the government was "engaging with local authorities to reduce the impact on communities and we've saved taxpayers more than £1bn on asylum support costs since the election". "The Home Office has submitted an application to obtain planning permission to use the Bicester site for asylum accommodation, but it remains the case that no final decision has been taken on the site's future use," the spokesperson added. But speaking outside Piddington village hall on Tuesday, one villager said when it came to holding the vote: "We wouldn't do this lightly." "I think when you see a village like this feeling that they need to hold a referendum it sends a really powerful message to the government that we're being ignored and disenfranchised," he told the BBC. This video can not be played The BBC's Jamie Morris explained in July what the vote is and what it could mean Tuesday's ballot paper asked residents to respond either yes or no to the statement: "I support Piddington seeking to secede from the United Kingdom and pursuing self-determination." The outcome of the referendum, which holds no legal weight and bares a resemblance to the classic Ealing comedy Passport to Pimlico, is expected to be announced on Wednesday morning. Having just cast his vote, Herbert Owen said the referendum was not "just about Piddington". "It means everything our grandparents, our parents fought for – today is the Battle of Britain," he said. His wife, Jennifer Owen, said: "We can't actually leave the United Kingdom, but it just brings things out in the open more for the country as a whole." She added that the proposals would "change our lives forever" if it were to go ahead. The government plans to provide accommodation for up to 1,256 men at the site near Bicester The Home Office first announced its plans for MoD Bicester in June. "We are working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country, moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation," a spokesperson said. This, the spokesperson said, included former military sites that were "designed to be self-contained to reduce impact on the local community". But that is not how many people in Piddington see the proposals, with 96% of voters supporting a referendum on independence from the UK in a vote held on 4 July - a date synonymous with another declaration of independence from the British state. Last week, ahead of Tuesday's vote, 133 women from the village wrote to every female Member of Parliament saying "life as we know it will be destroyed" if the plans succeed. "We will not feel safe walking our streets. We are already living in fear," they wrote. An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence. The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026. About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites. The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029. More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year. Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026. The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa. It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum. In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year. As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year. Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear. Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026. title: Letby failings go beyond one hospital - the whole system has been found lacking
description: Inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall set out how the culture of the health system created the conditions that enabled poor care and criminality.
body: The public inquiry into the Lucy Letby case may have reserved the strongest criticism for the Countess of Chester Hospital and its management, but there are big questions for the wider NHS to answer too. The Thirlwall inquiry's final report said there was a "complete failure" to protect babies on the neonatal unit where Letby murdered seven and attempted to murder seven more. But a third of the report was given over to the wider role played by the health system in England - and make no mistake, it was found lacking. Across more than 200 pages, inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall set out how the culture of the health system created the conditions that enable poor care - or in this case criminality - to go unchecked for so long. The failures encompass everything from regulation and employment practices to the way the NHS and government struggle to learn the lessons of the past. They have prompted Health Secretary Yvette Cooper to say she "will not hesitate" to hold the system to account at every level. She has promised to set up a hub to track the progress on implementing the inquiry's recommendations and pointed to the creation of a new maternity and neonatal commissioner post as a sign of her commitment to improving standards. "This must be a turning point for the NHS," she told the House of Commons when responding to the publication of the report. So what needs to change? The inquiry said NHS managers have become pre-occupied with avoiding blame, leading to an "over-focus on process and reputation management". One witness described this as "blame engineering", with the inquiry concluding this was a key characteristic in the way Countess of Chester bosses approached the Letby case with the report describing it at one point as an "exercise in spin". Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more. She was convicted in 2023 and has twice been denied permission to appeal against her convictions This approach to management means raising the alarm becomes difficult - a concern that has been repeated again and again in inquiries into other scandals. There have been plenty of initiatives to address this over the years. In the last decade, this has taken the form of the Freedom to Speak Up programme with each NHS organisation having a "guardian" whose job is it to support staff who want to issue a concern. But in a number of places the initiative has become a "box ticking" exercise The result? A "toxic negativity" persists around whistleblowing with staff discouraged from speaking out, the inquiry said. This view is supported by the NHS staff survey which showed a declining confidence in speaking out. There is, the Thirlwall inquiry said, a consistent inability within the NHS to deal with poor performance. Failing managers will be moved, often with the active assistance of NHS England, in a process referred to as rehabilitation, the inquiry heard. Countess of Chester chief executive Tony Chambers referred to it as "the donkey sanctuary". The report even noted how some failing managers receive pay offs and move on elsewhere "with few questions asked" as NHS trusts worry about the threat of employment tribunals. While there are many excellent managers in the NHS, profound change is needed in the way the NHS deals with those who fail, the inquiry added. The government wants to bring in a barring service, but the inquiry warned this will be undermined if the system continues to turn a blind eye like it does. In its closing submission to the inquiry, NHS England said it would never "knowingly" move "bad apples" into other jobs, but did believe moving capable senior managers could help improve services where improvement was needed as well as develop individuals. Key findings from Lucy Letby Thirlwall Inquiry Regulation has also been found lacking. The Care Quality Commission (CQC) inspected the Countess of Chester in February 2016 - Letby carried on attacking babies until June of that year. Key information was withheld from inspectors, but the regulator was criticised for not showing enough curiosity to look beyond what they were being told. Only a year before, the CQC had been warned by another inquiry into baby deaths at Morecambe Bay NHS Trust that it needed to take a tougher approach. Weaknesses have persisted since, the Thirwall inquiry said. An independent review in 2024 warned the ability of the CQC to spot poor performance was by that point deteriorating. The CQC has released a statement acknowledging it was not investigative or inquiring enough in 2016, but said it had since strengthened its approach. Meanwhile, the Nursing and Midwifey Council, which regulates nurses, was also told it should have been more curious - it renewed Letby's registration at a time when she was not permitted to work on a ward and a police investigation was taking place. It has offered an apology in response to the criticisms. As part of its work, the inquiry looked at why the lessons of previous inquiries have not been learned. There has been countless inquiries dating back 30 years, with thousands of recommendations made. But the Thirwall inquiry said most of these have not been implemented - and, when they have, it has taken too long or progress has not been tracked. It blamed, among other things, a lack of political will and disruption caused by repeated structural reorganisations. This had a potentially significant impact in the Letby case, the inquiry suggested. It cited the medical examiner system, whereby an independent doctor looks into deaths that are not reviewed by a coroner so that the cause of death is not down to the doctor involved in the patients care to sign off. The move was recommended in 2003 by the inquiry into the Harold Shipman murders and called for again a decade later as part of the inquiry into the failings at Mid Staffordshire NHS Trust. But it took until 2024 for it to be introduced. Former health secretary Sir Je

title: Dan Thomas resigns as Reform Wales leader after arrest on suspicion of assault
description: Thomas said he has done nothing wrong as Gwent Police confirms arrest on suspicion of assault.
body: Reform UK's Dan Thomas has quit as the party's Welsh leader Reform UK's Dan Thomas has quit as the party's Welsh leader, after he was arrested on Sunday of suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Gwent Police confirmed that a 45-year-old man from Aberbargoed, in Caerphilly, was bailed pending further enquiries. In a statement issued by his party, the Member of the Senedd for Casnewydd Islwyn said he was "standing down" from his position due to personal reasons. He said he had been "released without charge" and had "done nothing wrong". Thomas was appointed Welsh party leader by Nigel Farage in February. Plaid Cymru, which runs the Welsh government, said: "Reform UK is descending into chaos." Thomas did not take part in First Minister's Questions earlier today. He was first elected to the Senedd in the elections in May, where his party went from having two politicians in Cardiff Bay to 34. Reform came second behind Plaid Cymru in the vote, with Thomas becoming leader of the opposition in the Senedd. Thomas said: "It has been the honour of my life to have been the leader of Reform Wales and see this party go from zero to 34 elected members and become the largest opposition group in Welsh history. "With deep regret, I am now standing down from this position due to personal reasons. "Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge." He added: "I will continue to serve my constituents in Casnewydd Islwyn and will fully back whoever the group selects as its next leader." The news came on the same day that Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd defected to Plaid Cymru. Who is Reform UK's Welsh leader Dan Thomas? Dan Thomas: The ex-London council leader in charge of big Senedd opposition group Gwent Police said: "On Sunday 13 September a 45-year-old man, from the Aberbargoed area, was arrested on suspicion of assault and engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour. "He has been bailed pending further enquiries." Plaid Cymru Senedd group chair, Marc Jones, said: "Reform UK is descending into chaos." He added: "Sarah Cooper-Lesadd's decision to leave and join Plaid Cymru says it all - Reform is interested in division and headlines, not governing Wales." Ken Skates, leader of Welsh Labour, told the Press Association: "This is quite incredible news and many questions will need to be answered. "Dan Thomas was a personal pick by Nigel Farage and this will surely demonstrate the appalling judgement of the Reform UK leader." Mims Davies, the Conservative Shadow Secretary of State for Wales said: "Reform are hitting the news for all the wrong reasons - massive crypto donations, on top of the jailing of Nathan Gill for pro-Russian bribery. "All this raises serious and deep questions about Reform's judgement and leadership at every level." Welsh Liberal Democrat Leader, Jane Dodds, said: "The wheels are rapidly coming off Reform in Wales and the entire country." Dan Thomas was appointed by Nigel Farage in February, and appeared with him during the Senedd election campaign Thomas grew up in Blackwood in the south Wales valleys. He said in February that both his grandfather and great-grandfather were miners, and he had "fond memories" of growing up in Wales - but left when he became an adult because "good opportunities" there were "few and far between". He worked in financial services in London and became a councillor, and later Conservative leader, at Barnet council in the north of the capital. During this time Thomas stood for the Conservatives in the Islwyn constituency at the 2010 and 2017 general elections, coming second to Labour's Chris Evans on both occasions. Thomas then led Barnet council from 2019 to 2022, eventually becoming opposition leader after Labour won the local election there until May 2024. In June 2025 Thomas defected from the Conservatives to Reform, and at the end of the year resigned from the council. Local media quoted him saying he moved away from Barnet so that he and his wife could raise their young sons in the countryside and live closer to their families in south Wales. title: GPS tracking of bailed suspects to start next year, says Swinney
description: A pilot scheme in Tayside, Central and Fife is expected to start in 2027, the first minister has announced.
body: John Swinney met domestic abuse survivors in Holyrood ahead of a debate on tackling violence against women GPS tracking of people on bail, including those suspected of domestic abuse, is to begin in parts of central Scotland next year, John Swinney has confirmed. The first minister updated parliament on his plans for a pilot scheme in Tayside, Fife and Central during a Scottish Parliament debate on tackling violence against women. It came after he spoke to domestic abuse survivors and relatives of victims at a Holyrood meeting hosted by Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay. The government has been criticised over the slow rollout of GPS equipment, which is used far less in Scotland than in some other countries. Swinney announced plans for the GPS tracking pilot in the annual programme for government, external earlier this month. He confirmed to parliament on Tuesday that regulations to launch the pilot scheme in the Tayside, Central and Fife sheriffdoms - to be led by Sheriff Principal Gillian Anne Wade KC - would be laid before the October recess, and that ministers were aiming to begin the rollout next year. He insisted the pilot would be "subject to robust local arrangements" to ensure public safety. Pilot tracking domestic abuse suspects to begin in 2027 - Swinney tells Holyrood Calls for GPS monitoring of domestic abuse suspects after murder We saw signs of domestic abuse, but we didn't know how to protect Stacy The programme for government also included plans to make permanent a £2m fund providing practical and financial support to women and children escaping abusive partners. The government has further vowed multi-year funding for charities that deliver crisis support to women and girls. And it announced plans to recognise misogyny as a "distinct form of prejudice and abuse", alongside a public health campaign to target toxic male behaviour. However, the brother of a woman murdered by her estranged husband in Renfrewshire this year said previously that the proposals were not "anywhere near good enough". Stacy Hunter, 35, was killed by Jim Mair, 43, at her home near Houston in July while he was on bail for attacking her. His body was found nearby. Sean Hunter - who attended the meeting at Holyrood before the debate - has called for immediate action to prevent further deaths. Sean Hunter has called for immediate action to protect victims following the murder of his sister Stacy Speaking to BBC Scotland News the day after his sister would have celebrated her 36th birthday, he said GPS monitoring would "absolutely make a difference". But he called for authorities to consider more specific offences when making decisions about bailing domestic abuse suspects. "There's so much - strangulation, attempted murder - that's going on that's being overlooked because it's coming under this umbrella of domestic violence," Sean said. "That shouldn't be the case. "When these people commit these crimes they need to be looked at for what they are and kept from harming more people." Liz Shanks, whose former partner Chris Forrest was jailed in 2022 for attacking her over a three-year period, also spoke to the first minister at Holyrood. The campaigner said survivors and victims had been let down by the justice system and that the meeting must not be a "media stunt". She called for reforms to tackle domestic abuse, and warned that victims may be reluctant to come forward if they do not feel the justice system is dealing with the issue robustly. Domestic abuse survivor Liz Shanks says the meeting with the first minister must not be a "media stunt" Opening the debate, Swinney said the so-called "manosphere" and extreme pornography had "warped views and attitudes in disturbing and profoundly harmful ways". He vowed the government would take a "public health preventative approach" to tackle violence against women and push for stronger regulations of social media sites. The first minister told MSPs: "We will work to build a Scotland where everyone is safe, accepted, and respected, where women and girls live free from all forms of violence, abuse and exploitation, and where all are free of the attitudes and stereotypes that perpetuate inequality." However, opposition MSPs noted a 14% annual increase in domestic abuse charges last year. Scottish Labour's Jackie Baillie agreed with Swinney's "sincere" willingness to tackle violence against women, but said a "multi-faceted" approach was required, including a misogyny reduction unit, extra work in schools and investment in police. Conservative MSP Stephen Kerr warned that GPS tracking was a "technology, not necessarily a solution", calling for more investment in community resources. Scottish Tory leader Russell Findlay praised the "extraordinary bravery" of survivors but urged ministers to strengthen bail laws and "robustly enforce breaches". He also called for ministers to scrap "ludicrous" sentencing guidelines that encourage rehabilitation rather than jail terms for under-25s. Scottish Green co-leader Ross Greer said extra measures were required to ensure that education in schools about harmful attitudes was being consistently delivered, and raised concerns about low reporting rates. He also called for men to "contest" harmful views expressed by their peers. Liberal Democrat MSP Yi-pei Chou Turvey called for the government to immediately launch its plans for special sexual offences court. Swinney told MSPs ministers planned to provide funding for the scheme in the next financial year. Reform UK Scotland's Amanda Lindsay questioned whether "some groups" committed more sexual crimes than others, calling for more data on offences against women and girls. In Scotland, electronic tagging has mainly relied on older radio frequency (RF) equipment which is focused on home curfews or detention. These devices are linked to a receiver in the offender's home and cannot track movements away from the property. In 201

title: Ed Sheeran says it was 'not my decision' to drop Macklemore from tour
description: The star says tour promoters took the decision, after Macklemore made pro-Palestinian statements on stage.
body: Ed Sheeran and Macklemore, pictured in 2014, have been friends for 13 years, the rapper said in his statement on Monday Ed Sheeran has posted a long statement on Instagram, saying it was not his decision to drop Macklemore from his current US tour. The US rapper - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - was ejected from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian statements at two dates in New Jersey. His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to have him removed from the line-up. In his statement, external, Sheeran said he had spoken with the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately decided to remove Macklemore from the bill. "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living." The star also attempted to explain his decision not to become embroiled in political issues. "I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care. "Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way." He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds. "Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes. "However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace. "I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change." The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine." He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which is dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors at Columbia University and condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen. Some of the audience cheered - but there was almost immediate criticism online. The Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour; while the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda - a claim that was amplified by the pop star Pink, who reposted it on Instagram. The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience. "Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten. Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law. The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage. During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. After days of press coverage, Macklemore announced on Monday that he had been dropped from the line-up. In a statement on Instagram, he said the boycott had been organised by Robert Kraft - the billionaire owner of the Gilette Stadium in Massachusetts. Kraft - who once hired Ed Sheeran to play at his wedding - confirmed he'd made the decision to bar Macklemore, saying his venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric". "I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said. However, he did not address the claim that he'd asked other venues to put pressure on the tour. Tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone magazine that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans." In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran had been put in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance. "Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote. He also emphasised that, although he was only able to complete two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."
