title: Repeatedly untruthful, callous and quiet: What we learned about Letby from inquiry report
description: The report has shed more details on Lucy Letby - the most prolific child killer in British legal history.
body: Letby was convicted of the murders of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others New details have emerged about Lucy Letby, the killer neonatal nurse whose name can evoke both staunch support and unequivocal disgust. Letby, now 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms after being convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, including one baby whom she tried to murder twice. In a lengthy report, published by Lady Justice Thirlwall earlier, she described how Letby was "repeatedly untruthful in her dealings with friends and colleagues" and "her inappropriate and callous nature was noted by patients and colleagues". The Thirlwall Inquiry was set up to look into what happened at the Countess of Chester Hospital between 2015 and 2016, while Letby was working as a nurse in the neonatal unit. The public inquiry was not tasked with examining Letby's guilt. Instead, it investigated how concerns about the neonatal nurse were handled by the hospital and whether action could have been taken sooner to stop her. Thirlwall found the deaths and near-deaths of some babies who were attacked by Letby could have been prevented if safeguarding practices had been followed. But the inquiry report has also shed more details on Letby herself - the most prolific child killer in British legal history, who has always maintained her innocence. The inquiry looked into the actions of managers at the hospital where Lucy Letby worked Following the death of Baby C, Letby was observed helping to make a memory box with another nurse on the neonatal unit for the infant's parents. However, Letby had not been asked to carry out this task and was "supposed to be somewhere else and was repeatedly told to be looking after a different child," Baby C's mother told the inquiry. Thirlwall noted how "nothing was done about Letby repeatedly ignoring directions from the shift leader and leaving the other child [who she was designated to care for] to intervene with Baby C". She found Letby ignored management instructions when she disliked them and had shouted at her manager. Baby 'cot cams' plan after inquiry finds Lucy Letby crimes could have been prevented Key findings from Lucy Letby Thirlwall Inquiry As it happened: Read the live coverage from the Thirlwall Inquiry Letby was also repeatedly untruthful in her dealing with friends and colleagues, the inquiry found. This included lying about the reaction of the father of Baby A and Baby B, following Baby A's death. In a message to a colleague, Letby said: "Dad was on the floor crying saying please don't take our baby away when I took [Baby A] to the mortuary, it's heart-breaking." Thirlwall said the mother of Baby A and Baby B, who Letby attempted to murder, was clear that this was not true and did not happen. "In her view, Letby's messages were 'attention seeking' and a 'red flag'. I agree," Thirlwall noted in the inquiry report. Throughout her training as a nurse, feedback of Letby's performance in the work place was mixed, the inquiry found. Early assessments pointed out areas for improvements, particularly in relation to enthusiasm, communication with families and drug calculations. But academically her personal tutor reported no concerns. While during her second and third years, she was described by a nurse as "one of the best students she had mentored", however, during her final placement "significant concerns were raised". The deputy ward manager described Letby as "quiet, withdrawn and struggled to build relationships with children, families and colleagues". Letby failed a mid-year assessment and observed structured clinical examination (OSCE). She later passed this examination and qualified as a registered children's nurse in 2011. But Thirlwall outlined how Letby's "inappropriate and callous behaviour" was noted by patients and colleagues. The mother, for example, of Baby E, who Letby murdered, and Baby F, who she attempted to kill, told the inquiry she had had "two thriving little boys" but that "in the space of a couple of hours it had all been taken". After Baby E's death, the mother told the inquiry she found her baby was still in his incubator, and she asked Letby why. "You haven't told us to take him," she says Letby told her. Thirlwall said Letby's remark to a "bereaved mother was shockingly cold and unfeeling." Lady Justice Thirlwall oversaw the inquiry into the Lucy Letby case The inquiry also found how Letby falsified Baby E's medical record. Thirlwall noted how Letby omitted Baby E's distress and the blood on the baby's mouth from her notes. She also failed to record the baby's mother's visit to the neonatal unit. While in Letby's care, Baby J was also found covered in their own faeces, leading to a complaint by the baby's parents. Letby, from Hereford, who maintains her innocence, has twice been denied permission in 2024 to appeal against her convictions. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, is considering evidence presented on her behalf by an international panel of medics, who claim poor medical care and natural causes were the reasons for the babies collapsing. A number of Letby supporters gathered outside Liverpool Town Hall to voice their concerns over her conviction, calling for her release, before Thirlwall delivered her inquiry findings. title: Iran war has led to US munitions shortfalls, Pentagon inspector confirms
description: The inspector also found a bottleneck in resupply, despite President Donald Trump's claims that US supplies are "virtually limitless".
body: US Patriot air defence systems, seen here at Raytheon headquarters in Massachusetts, have been heavily used in the Iran war. The US defence department's inspector general says the war with Iran has led to "shortfalls" in munitions and a bottleneck in resupply, contradicting President Donald Trump who has repeatly denied the US is facing shortages. Trump has claimed US munitions supplies are "virtually unlimited" and said reporting otherwise is "fake news". But the independent watchdog said the US spent more than $22 billion on munitions from February through June, leading to "strategic inventory shortfalls". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment about the discrepancy. The new report provides a first-of-its-kind, independent glimpse into US weapons stockpiles, data that is typically classified. Previous estimates have painted a dire picture of the US shortages. Over the course of the war, US forces have expended vast quantities of both long-range ground attack systems and the air and missile defences used to intercept incoming Iranian attacks. A late July estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, or CSIS, found that stocks of some interceptors - such as the Patriot missile and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD - were significantly depleted, in some cases by more than half. The inspector general's report did not disclose exactly how many of the weapons remain. It did, however, note the inventory shortfalls and reveal "industrial base bottlenecks" for munitions resupply. The report added that the defence department is now working to "streamline procurement processes and production lead times" to address the shortages and "respond rapidly to a contingency". Trump and other administration officials have sought to cast reports of shortages as false and "treasonous". In a 4 August X post, for example, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth described news reporting on the shortages as "not true". And in a lengthy Truth Social post on 3 September, Trump claimed that the US had "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition and is "stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen". The watchdog's report also notes that equipment losses have totaled $3.7bn, with other $7.4bn in other expenditures. Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war from 28 Feb to 30 Jun. Among the losses have been four F-15e fighter jets, a highly advanced F-35 Joint Strike Fighter and 30 MQ-9 drones destroyed in "various circumstances". When US and Israeli strikes began, Trump repeatedly said that the conflict would be over within weeks. More recently, he said the conflict might not end until "right after" the November midterm elections in the US. Polls show that the war is unpopular among Americans. One Reuters/Ipsos poll released in early September found that only 23% of Americans - and only half of Republicans - believe the US to be in a stronger position with Iran compared with before hostilities broke out. As the US pauses the war with Iran, is Trump really running out of weapons? title: The key findings and recommendations from the Lucy Letby inquiry
description: Former nurse Lucy Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more.
body: This video can not be played A report into how serial killer Lucy Letby was able to murder seven babies at the Countess of Chester Hospital has found that some deaths could have been prevented. Letby is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more. She was convicted in 2023 and has twice been denied permission to appeal against her convictions. Responding to the report, the hospital says it is "sorry for the events that occurred in 2015 and 2016", and it's a "different organisation today with new leadership, stronger governance and safety processes". Letby maintains her innocence. Protesters supporting Letby could be seen and heard near Liverpool Town Hall as the report was published. BBC correspondent Judy Moritz reports from Liverpool. title: British woman abducted in Malawi, police say
description: The mother of two young children was kidnapped in the middle of the day in the main city, Blantyre.
body: Police have offered a reward for details that could help find Nusrat Osman Police in Malawi are investigating the kidnapping of a British national who was abducted in the southern African nation's main city, Blantyre. Nusrat Osman, 47, was seized at around 12:30 local time on Friday by four men who had been travelling in a grey Nissan Dualis, according to a police statement. The authorities have offered a reward of more than $17,000 (£12,600) for "credible information" that could lead to the rescue of the mother of two young children and the prosecution of the perpetrators. Osman was reported to have been working for a local auditing firm. A Malawi news outlet reported that Osman's husband was in anguish about the disappearance. "I don't know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor and I have no issues with anyone," he was quoted by Nyasa Times as saying. Police said the motive behind the abduction was unknown and that so far the kidnappers have not contacted the victim's family or the authorities. BBC News has contacted the UK Foreign Office for comment. Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. title: An inquest verdict at last - but many mysteries remain about Noah Donohoe's death
description: After years of delay, the jury has reached a verdict but some questions remain unanswered over what happened to the 14-year-old.
body: It's been more than six years since teenager Noah Donohoe was found dead 600m into a freezing underground water tunnel in Belfast. His death – and the speculation over what happened to him in the week between his daylight disappearance and the discovery of his body – became a huge news story that provoked countless unanswered questions. Now, after an inquest and months of exhaustive hearings and long deliberations by a jury, there is a verdict – but much is still unknown about what happened to Noah. Why, the night before he disappeared, did he leave his home in the middle of the rain-soaked night? Where did he go? Why did he come back 34 minutes later, as documented by CCTV, barefoot? LIVE: Noah Donohoe inquest jury finds failings by department officials possibly contributed to death Hours later, on Sunday 21 June 2020, he left the south Belfast home he shared with his mother for the final time. Why did he leave and go to an unfamiliar part of north Belfast? Why was the teenager naked when he was last seen in the area of the water tunnel entrance? And what might have been if he had seen the social media message sent him by one of two friends he planned to meet in north Belfast telling him their plans were cancelled? An autopsy found Noah had died from drowning, with the tunnel he was found in heading towards Belfast Lough and its tides. Now, after years of delays, a jury has found that it was possible, but not probable, that failings by the Department of Infrastructure over the tunnel in which he was found contribute to his death. They also found 13 failings by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) but that these did not in any way contribute to the 14-year-old's death. Having spent months in court following all the evidence, it was clearly not an easy process for the men and women of the jury. They heard from dozens of witnesses and received voluminous amounts of official and expert documentation. This week they deliberated on Monday and Tuesday. But it came more than two months after the inquest was dramatically adjourned in the early hours after three days of deliberations did not lead to a verdict. While these findings will help his family and the community to understand a little bit more about what happened after Noah went missing, there is no certainty about many of the mysteries surrounding some of the unusual and extraordinary events in the lead-up to his disappearance. It may be that there will never be definitive answers to many of those questions. But one thing was very clear at the inquest – there was no evidence of any physical interaction between Noah and anyone else during his final bicycle ride from his home to north Belfast. During his summing up, the coroner Mr Justice Rooney ruled out several possibilities, including drugs, foul play, suicide, or a psychotic experience. He told the jury before they began deliberations that there was no evidence to support such findings and their verdict had to be based "solely on the evidence you have heard and seen in this court". There was no evidence of drugs in Noah's body during the postmortem. Noah's journey from south to north Belfast was captured on a series of CCTV cameras But the inquest heard expert witness evidence that explained, in some cases, drugs can degrade in a body after a few days, so the possibility of drugs having been in his system "cannot be completely excluded". The inquest also heard no evidence of third-party involvement or any link to loyalist paramilitaries, at odds with years of endless social media speculation that sometimes leaned into conspiracies. Many phases of the inquest focused on next-of-kin concerns about the Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI) investigation into Noah's disappearance, as well as public safety around the tunnel system where Noah's body was found. The tunnel is maintained by Stormont's Department for Infrastructure. The police accepted that they had missed some investigative opportunities and have since apologised to Noah's mum, Fiona Donohoe. And throughout it all, day after day, Fiona Donohoe was a constant, quietly dignified presence, often sitting alone in a corner at the back of the Coroner's Court. Noah's mother Fiona Donohoe attended every day of the inquest The road to the inquest was a long one for Fiona and her family. They mounted a high-profile public campaign around Noah's death, with dozens of supporters soon growing to hundreds and then thousands under the umbrella name of Noah's Army. They took their campaign to the streets in the form of cavalcades around Belfast, as well as protests at Stormont's parliament buildings and at PSNI headquarters. Frustration at the police came to a head in August 2022, when thousands of campaigners protested outside Belfast City Hall over the PSNI's decision to seek a Public Interest Immunity (PII) certificate in relation to the case. As the years went on, the pre-inquest process was plagued by delays. The original coroner in the case stepped aside and the Donohoe family made a request for the inquest to be heard in front of a jury. Finally, five-and-a-half years after he disappeared, the inquest into Noah's death began in January 2026. Questions about Noah's mindset and behavioural changes before he went missing featured prominently at the inquest. The inquest heard how the schoolboy went out onto streets beside his home in the Holylands area of Belfast in the early hours of the day of his disappearance. Shortly after 03:30 BST, Noah walked out of his home into the rain. He was alone and wearing light summer clothing, including shorts and flip flops. He also had a set of headphones. CCTV footage showed Noah leaving his home in the early hours of the day of his disappearance During the following 34 minutes, some of his movements were captured on CCTV as he walked along nearby streets barefoot. title: Former England footballer Raheem Sterling admits dangerous driving on motorway before crash
description: The former England winger crashed a Lamborghini into motorway barriers in May.
body: Sterling made eight appearances for Feyenoord earlier this year Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerous driving on a motorway after he crashed a Lamborghini into a metal gate in May. The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis. Sterling, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of 28 May. Sterling has 82 England caps, the last of which was won at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. The former England winger pleaded guilty to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road before he crashed. The court heard he strayed into the central reservation of the motorway and crashed into a metal gate in a layby on the A327. He was in possession of six canisters of nitrous oxide, a Class C drug. Sterling arrived at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Tuesday afternoon Witnesses described seeing a Lamborghini driver inhaling from a white balloon. Fiona Jennings, who saw the vehicle on the M3 at 8:45 BST, said she looked across and thought that an airbag had inflated, but then realised it was an inflated balloon. She told police she saw "absolutely horrendous driving" as the Lamborghini swerved in and out of lanes. Hampshire Police previously said the charges followed a single-vehicle collision near the M3 southbound, near the Minley interchange. The force said no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported. Sterling most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, having left Chelsea in January, but made just eight appearances in the Netherlands. In four years at Chelsea - including a season-long loan at Arsenal - he made 59 league appearances after signing from Manchester City in 2022. With City he won four Premier League titles, having started his senior career with Liverpool before moving to Manchester in 2015. He is currently without a club. In the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport. Sterling will appear in court on 25 November, and has been disqualified from driving in the interim. title: Ash from Mount Etna grounds flights at Sicily airport
description: All flights are suspended from one of Italy's busiest airports until Tuesday night.
body: All flights have been suspended from one of Italy's busiest airports because of volcanic ash released from nearby Mount Etna. It is the second time in recent months that Catania International Airport, on the island of Sicily, has stopped flights due to emissions from Etna, which is Europe's tallest active volcano and erupts frequently. Airport officials said arrivals and departures, which were first halted on Monday, would be suspended until 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday. Ongoing activity at Etna prompted the INGV Etneo Observatory to issue a red aviation alert on Monday. In a statement on its website on Tuesday, Catania - Italy's fifth-busiest airport by passenger traffic - said further updates would follow. It also advised passengers due to fly from Catania to check with their airline for updates before travelling to the airport. Catania, which usually serves about 12 million passengers each year, was closed for almost a week during the peak summer season last month because of volcanic activity. There have been calls for the airport to shut and other facilities in Sicily to be expanded because of its proximity to Etna. The volcano, which stands at 3,324 metres (10,906ft), is about 40km (25 miles) away from the airport. Despite air traffic disruption, August's eruption drew large crowds of onlookers to Etna's lava flows. About 1.5 million people visit Etna every year. title: Draper decides not to play again this season
description: Former world number four Jack Draper will not play again this season, but says he is aiming to return to the tour at the start of next year.
body: Draper reached the US Open semi-finals in 2024 Former world number four Jack Draper will not play again this season, but says he is aiming to return to the tour at the start of next year. The 24-year-old has been suffering with bone bruising in his serving arm and has only played nine events since last year's Wimbledon. Draper missed the US Open, after losing in the first round in Montreal and Cincinnati last month - and was in tears during his defeat to France's Terence Atmane in Canada. "I am taking this time to reset and heal so when I return I am 100% ready to go," Draper posted on Instagram., external "Tennis is my purpose and passion and so when I step back on court I want to make sure that there's nothing holding me back from where I want to go." Why can't Draper play, and why won't surgery help? Tearful Draper struggles during comeback defeat Draper will not qualify for a protected ranking if he does return in January, as only those who are out for over six months are able to retain the ranking they had when they left the tour. He is currently ranked 155, which means he would require wildcards or have to come through qualifying to play in Grand Slams and ATP Tour events. But none of that will worry him if he is able to play freely and without so much pain. Draper peaked at four in the world last June after winning a first Masters 1000 title in Indian Wells and finishing runner-up at another in Madrid. "Last summer, all the dedication and work I had put into this sport was coming together," Draper added. "It was all going my way and the path seemed so clear. However a complicated injury made things incredibly challenging, and since that moment I've been desperately trying to get back and feel as I once did on the court. "Managing so much change, adversity and pain has helped me to grow massively in many areas of my life but has also made me feel a level of fatigue." Draper has taken a holiday with friends in recent weeks and has been trying to aid his recovery by taking a mental break from the sport. He is expected to make a gradual return to training over the next few weeks, as his team try to work out the principal causes of the injury. Draper used to play with polyester strings, but has been experimenting with natural gut - which is against his instincts, but should ease the burden on his arm. He has also started using a lighter racquet, and is making some changes to his serve. Diet is another area being examined to see if that, too, could be a contributing factor. Andy Murray remains part of his coaching team but will do a limited number of weeks on the road, and so further assistance will be required. Over the summer, Draper benefitted from the help of LTA coaches James Trotman (who was with him full-time as he rose into the world's top five) and Alex Lisiecki. A permanent coach to work alongside Murray will need to be found, however, once Draper returns to the tour. When he does, much thought will go into his schedule. Not just because the bone bruising is unlikely to have healed entirely by January, but also because of the concerns many top players have about the toll the modern game is putting on their bodies. title: Government to end ban on Catholic and Jewish PMs' involvement in Church appointments
description: Andy Burnham, himself a Catholic, says it is "unacceptable for there to be a legislative bar against people of any faith performing all the functions of my office".
body: The government has introduced a bill to end antiquated laws preventing Roman Catholic or Jewish prime ministers from being involved in the process of making Church of England appointments. It was among the first pieces of legislation to be introduced to Parliament under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, himself a Catholic, who has called the current laws "unacceptable". When appointing bishops and archbishops, the Church presents a candidate to the prime minister who then advises the monarch on who to install in the role. Although the involvement of the prime minister in this process has become more of a formality in recent years, legislation still exists that specifically bars Roman Catholics and Jews from exercising this responsibility. That is why earlier this month Burnham, the first Catholic prime minister, transferred the responsibility of advising the King on Church appointments to the Lord Chancellor. But the prime minster said it was "unacceptable for there to be a legislative bar against people of any faith performing all the functions of my office". The Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829 and the Jews Relief Act 1858 are the existing laws in question. When those laws were introduced, they actually eased some of the restrictions on Catholics' and Jews' participation in public life. This included what was, in effect, a prohibition on them becoming MPs. But the law still stipulated that prime ministers of those faiths could not be involved - "directly or indirectly" - in advising during the process of making Church appointments. The appointment of the Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally was approved by then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, a self-proclaimed atheist The Roman Catholic Relief Act, for example, says that a Catholic advising a sovereign on a Church appointment would be "deemed guilty of a high misdemeanour, and disabled for ever from holding any office, civil or military, under the Crown". The law relating to Jews contains a similar threat. These laws and restrictions remain in effect. That is partly because, until now, they have had no practical effect - before Burnham, there has not been a Catholic or Jewish prime minister. Although Benjamin Disraeli - prime minister in the late-1800s - was born to a Jewish family, his father renounced Judaism and had his children baptised into the Church of England. Another former Prime Minister, Tony Blair, is a Roman Catholic, but his conversion formally took place six months after he stepped down. And because the existing laws only discriminate against Jews and Catholics, it meant that Rishi Sunak, a Hindu, and Sir Keir Starmer, an atheist, were not prevented from advising on Church of England appointments in the way that Andy Burnham has been. In practical terms, for nearly 20 years the prime minister has not had much of a role in the selection of Church of England bishops. In 2007, Gordon Brown decided the Church should only present a single candidate to the prime minister, who would then pass it on to the monarch to confirm. Some prime ministers have taken a more interventionist approach. Margaret Thatcher, for example, famously pushed back against candidates who did not align with her political or religious views. Although the archaic laws preventing Jews and Roman Catholics advising on Church appointments technically relates to the Church of Scotland too, in reality the appointment of elders and ministers within the Church of Scotland no longer has any outside involvement. But the bill introduced on Tuesday intends to remove discriminatory laws that mean one aspect of the role of prime minister can now be performed by people of any religious belief that hold the office. It must be approved by the House of Commons and House of Lords before any change would come into practice. title: What weapon could the US have put into space?
description: The announcement by the US points to a developing field of modern warfare in the Earth's orbit.
body: Some types of space weaponry could create a lot of debris and destruction The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena. Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit. So what could this weapon be, and what is wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry? Advanced militaries already deploy satellites in space for range of purposes, from supplying secure communications to reconnaissance, and providing precise location information for targeted strikes and detecting missile launches. As warfare become more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase. Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US. "I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless." Bowen also would not rule out some sort of more disruptive and riskier weaponry, which could create a lot of debris and destruction. "Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile of some sort that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said. "Possibly some sort of close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well." But while the weapon placed in orbit appears to be a first, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time. In fact in the last 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites. "Theoretically, these RPO sats can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC. Bowen adds that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit." This, he says, can be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites. Thornton says that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability. "The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike sats in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he says. "From the Russian point of view they see Nato as having much better and more sats than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat." Thornton adds a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EPM blast would 'fry' any unhardened sats over a wide expanse." He says that, having so few satellites, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, which would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring sats designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers". title: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial oil pipeline
description: Experts tell BBC Verify the pipeline's closure could cut oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day.
body: Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher. The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war. The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen. New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week. The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis. While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks. It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping. The price of a barrel of oil has surged since Saudi Arabia said on Friday it was closing the pipeline as a precaution. Brent crude was trading as high as $108 (£80) a barrel on Tuesday, down slightly from $109.80 on Monday. Experts from trade intelligence firm Kpler said the pipeline's closure could reduce oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day - or about 3.6% of global demand. "Based on new information we've received, damage to the pipeline could take four to six weeks to resolve, given spare-parts availability and impaired supply chains," said Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis. Anne-Sophie Corbeau, from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said pipelines are "like sitting ducks" and recent strikes are a "very important signal" indicating workarounds being used to avoid the Strait of Hormuz "may not be super useful because they can be destroyed". The Houthis have targeted other Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles which has led to some operations being suspended. There have also been attacks on military bases. New satellite images captured on Monday show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait which the Houthis said they had targeted with ballistic missiles and drones last week after it was used to carry out air strikes on Yemen. At least three aircraft hangars or shelters appear to have been damaged at the Royal Saudi Air Force facility where US-made F-15 fighter jets are based. The Saudi-led anti-Houthi military coalition of Arab states said on Tuesday that a Houthi missile and drone attack had injured 13 people in attacks on what the coalition said were "civilian objects". The Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out with more than 50 strikes in western Yemen over the previous 24 hours. The UN Refugee Agency has said that more than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed conflict. title: How city's market became a CBeebies TV set
description: The show, filmed in Coventry, aims to help young children explore food through their senses
body: Aaron Roach Bridgeman and puppet co-host Zesty lead children through food-themed activities Coventry Market's fruit and vegetable stalls, fish counters and busy walkways have become an unlikely TV set. Cameras are rolling among shoppers and traders as local children explore unfamiliar foods for a new CBeebies series. I Can Taste It aims to help three to six-year-olds build confidence in trying different foods through sight, smell, touch, sound and taste. Presented by Aaron Roach Bridgeman and puppet co-host Zesty, the programme is being filmed at the market, which producers say offers children an authentic environment in which to learn about food. "It's important that children see themselves represented in real places with real people," said Dom Sant, founder of Common Story, the Leamington Spa-based company behind the series. He said the market's atmosphere, variety of stalls and sense of community made it the perfect location. Director Jess Matthews with Compost Monster, one of the programme's regular characters Among the young participants is six-year-old Oscar, from Bedworth. His mother, Hannah, said she applied after spotting an advert on social media. "Oscar loves his food and he's very chatty, so when they met him he made a good impression," she said. For Hannah, visiting the market has also brought back childhood memories. "My mum and dad used to bring me here every Saturday morning to do the shopping and I'd always beg to go on the roundabout," she said. "Every time I walk into the market it's nostalgic. I feel like I'm four years old again, holding my dad's hand." Betts and Sons traders are among those taking part in filming for the new CBeebies series Director Jess Matthews described filming as a "glorious chaos", with the production team often responding to children's reactions rather than following a strict script. Alongside Aaron and Zesty, youngsters are also joined by Compost Monster, a character designed to encourage sustainable food habits and reduce food waste. Market trader David Betts said the production had shone a light on one of Coventry's best-known landmarks. "It's one of the iconic places in Coventry and people take it for granted," he said. Fishmonger Clive Miller said the programme introduces children to foods they might not normally encounter Fishmonger Clive Miller, whose stall is due to feature in filming, said the programme would help children discover foods they might not normally encounter. "When children go to the supermarket, they don't get to see fish like this," he said. "It's a chance for them to learn about a wider variety of fish and where food comes from." The series is due to air in spring 2027. Common Story began in a garden shed six years ago with a £10,000 budget. It has since made more than 100 programmes for CBeebies, with a further 30 currently in production. body: This video can not be played The recently released footage shows a helicopter hovering mere feet from a cliff face in the Sierra Nevada mountains in the US state of California while a rescue team secures an injured climber. title: More than 100,000 people in Japan are now aged 100 or older
description: Figures show 88% of the centenarians are women as the population continues to age and shrink.
body: When records began in 1963 there were only 153 centenarians in Japan - now there are 107,677 The number of people aged 100 or more in Japan has exceeded 100,000 for the first time, according to the health ministry. Figures show Japan is now home to 107,677 centenarians, the highest number in the world, of whom 88% are women. The oldest woman is Kishimoto Fuyo, a 114-year-old from Kyoto City and the oldest man is Kato Hikaru, a 112-year-old from Kumamoto. Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno said he was "delighted that so many people are living long, healthy and active lives", citing progress in medicine and technology. But Kenichiri also warned of the challenge the country faces in maintaining a sustainable social security system. Experts put the long lives of the Japanese down to several factors, including a healthy diet and an active lifestyle. The island nation's cuisine predominantly consists of fish, vegetables, and rice - and less saturated fat than many Western diets. Older people also regularly walk, use public transport, cycle and stretch. Japan has been aging for years and sales of adult nappies have been higher than those for babies for more than a decade. Companies have also developed new products for the older population, including a powered exoskeleton to support moving various parts of the body and eyewear that automatically adjusts its focus. Japanese people's diets - largely consisting of fish, vegetables and rice - are thought to contribute to living longer For a population to replace itself, each woman needs to give birth to 2.1 children on average. Last year Japan's total fertility rate dropped to a record low of 1.14. The total population is estimated to drop to 87 million by 2070, representing a 30% decline from its peak of 128 million in 2008, according to data from the National Institute of Population and Social Security research. Residents aged 65 and older currently make up around 30% of the population and are expected to make up nearly 40% by 2070. Japanese authorities have called the trend an "existential crisis" with Prime Minister Sanae Takichi describing the decline as a "quiet emergency". In 2025 Japan's total population decreased in all 47 prefectures but two, and the rate of decline is accelerating. The government's many programmes and subsidies to encourage young people to have more children do not appear to be boosting birth rates. Experts say the reasons are complex, ranging from lower marriage rates and more women joining the workforce to the increased costs of raising children. While immigration has risen in previous years, foreigners only make up around 3% of the population and opposition to accepting more has grown. Migration to Japan has increased in recent years but remains low compared to other major economies When Japan began its centenarian survey in 1963, there were 153 people aged 100 or over. That figure rose to 1,000 in 1981 and stood at 10,000 by 1998. The most recent figures were released ahead of Japan's annual "Respect for the Aged" public holiday, on which the government honours those turning 100 with a personal letter and traditional sake cup. Studies have previously cast doubt on the validity of global centenarian numbers, suggesting data errors, unreliable public records and missing birth certificates may account for elevated figures. A government audit of family registries in Japan in 2010 uncovered more than 230,000 people listed as being aged 100 or older who were unaccounted for, some having died decades previously. The miscounting was attributed to patchy record-keeping and suspicions that some families may have tried to hide the deaths of elderly relatives in order to claim their pensions. title: Canada is a 'safe harbour' for global finance, Carney says
description: The prime minister is hosting a major global investment summit, with the goal of attracting money into the country amid a trade war with the US.
body: This video can not be played Canada's Mark Carney tells a story about Trump gifting him a key to the White House. Prime Minister Mark Carney has pitched Canada as a "safe harbour" for some of the world's largest investors to spend their money in an era of geopolitical and economic uncertainty. The country is "perfectly situated to build in the new global economic order", he told more than 100 global investors and sovereign wealth fund representatives gathered in Toronto for a major investment summit. The group represent more than C$120tn ($86tn; £64tn) of assets. Carney's ambition is that they will invest in sectors like defence, energy, mining, AI and infrastructure. Ottawa hopes they can be sold on more than 160 projects, from data centres to pipelines, and help Canada weather its trade war with the US. Canada's dispute with its largest trade partner has prompted Carney to look to expand economic partnerships with Europe, Asia and the Middle East as he seeks to reduce his country's reliance on its neighbour to the south. "Our goal is simple: to make Canada the most attractive place in the G7 to invest," Carney said on Tuesday morning. As part of that move, Carney announced plans to privatise operations for four of the country's largest airports, saying it would raise billions of dollars that could be reinvested in transport infrastructure. Many of the business leaders attending the event in Toronto received a personal invitation from the prime minister, who worked in the top tiers of global finance and was a central banker before turning to politics. Much of the action will take place in private sessions and bilateral meetings over the course of the day. There will, however, be panels with speakers including Deutsche Bank AG CEO Christian Sewing, Bombardier executive Eric Martel, and BlackRock CEO Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray. Carney gambles on the world's biggest investors betting on Canada Carney eyes 'unique alliance' with EU as trade war with US intensifies The prime minister's office has played down the likelihood of any major announcements coming from the summit, with Carney saying over the weekend it was chance for deep-pocketed financiers to "come to 'peer into our shop window'". The event is also an opportunity for Canada to burnish its reputation as a good place to do business after years of lagging investment performance. Economic analysts say Canada needs to make significant policy changes to help attract investment, including more competitive tax and regulatory systems, and ensuring a supply of skilled labour. Protestors on Monday accused the Carney government of selling off the country For Carney, the event will be a test of whether he can deliver on his promise to strengthen the country's economic resilience. Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed last month and the two countries have since imposed tit-for-tat tariffs. On Tuesday, new US tariffs came into effect on a number of Canadian goods while some others were lifted, and bans on goods like alcohol and motorcycles are due to come into force next week. On Tuesday, Carney addressed the American executives in Toronto directly. "To our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas," he said. "After all, even at times of disagreement during our long history, we have always maintained deep ties." Meanwhile, protestors on Monday accused the Carney government of organising a "great Canadian sell-off" of public resources and infrastructure to corporate interests, and hundreds appeared outside the opening night gala at a downtown museum. "Half the buyers that he has invited here to Toronto are American," said Kai Nagata, with advocacy group Dogwood, on Monday. "Let's be clear, every piece of our country that we sell off to American billionaires brings us closer to becoming the 51st state." title: Number of people claiming key disability benefit hits record high
description: An ongoing review into Personal Independence Payments (Pip) has found the system is "not fit for purpose".
body: The number of people claiming Personal Independence Payments (Pip) in England and Wales has hit a record high, according to new government figures. As of July, just over four million people were entitled to claim the benefit, compared to 3.83 million the previous year, an increase of 7%, data from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) showed. Pip is designed to support people with the extra costs of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions, and eligibility is not affected by a person's income or savings. In July, Sir Stephen Timms, who is leading a review on Pip, said in his interim report that the system was "not fit for purpose". Of the 4.1 million claimants, those aged 50 and above accounted for more than half. Just under three in ten were aged 30 to 49, while 17% of claimants were aged 16 to 29. Pip seeks to offset the extra costs that can occur for those living with certain long-term health conditions. According to the charity Scope, the extra cost of being disabled – known as the disability price tag – has reached more than £1,100 a month. The DWP said the increase in the Pip caseload had actually "slowed", falling from a rise of 400,000 in the 12 months to July 2024, to 260,000 in the 12 months to July 2026. But they agreed the system was "no longer fit for purpose", adding that the Timms review's recommendations would "lay the foundation for sustainable reform". But Helen Whatly, shadow work and pensions secretary, said Labour was "too quick to write people off and too slow to help them into work" - adding that it was "costing us a fortune". Pip has been in the spotlight since the summer of 2025 when the government, led by former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer, proposed reforming and tightening eligibility criteria for the benefit as the cost of running the system increased. Spending on Pip stood at £16.3bn in 2019-20, when adjusted for inflation to today's prices, and had increased to £27.3bn by 2024-25, government figures showed. It is currently forecast to rise to £41.5bn by 2030-31. Reform proposes £50bn welfare bill cut with changes to disability payments for millions Disability benefit not fit for purpose, minister leading review says How a rise in ADHD benefits claims is adding to welfare spending challenge But dozens of Labour MPs expressed concerns about the plans and, fearing its own members would vote down the reforms, the government U-turned. Instead, it commissioned a review into Pip led by Sir Stephen, the minister for social security and disability, to make recommendations that would make it "fit and fair for the future". The interim report published in the summer said the system had become a barrier to work for many, and the process of applying for it was found to be "dehumanising". Under the current assessment system, a health professional scores claimants on everyday tasks such as washing, getting dressed and preparing food using a zero to 12 scale. Earlier this month, the review's "emerging recommendations" suggested more face-to-face assessments would take place, and while cash payments would remain the foundation, there would also be non-cash support available. The Timms review is expected to be published in full later this year. title: Youth star JJ Gabriel, 15, on brink of leaving Man Utd
description: Manchester United's highly-rated 15-year-old forward JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving the club.
body: JJ Gabriel scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut for Manchester United last week Highly-rated 15-year-old striker JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving Manchester United. Even though he was only 14 when the season began, he won the Premier League Under-18 player of the year award last term, in addition to being named United's Under-18 player of the year. He made his senior debut for United in their pre-season game against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm last month, scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut last week and had been expected to make his competitive bow in Wednesday night's Carabao Cup tie with Brighton. The precise issues have not been outlined but it is understood Gabriel did not train with Michael Carrick's squad at the end of last week amid issues in the relationship between the player's family and United. The club have not yet given up hope of resolving the situation given Gabriel has a contract that runs to the end of the season. Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are directly involved in discussions with the player's family, which underlines how seriously the club regard the situation. United sources say they are not sure what has led to the situation developing the way it has. Gabriel has sent a formal notice he wants to cancel his registration with immediate effect. United can challenge the request. Gabriel does not turn 16 until 6 October, when he would be able to sign a scholarship agreement. Born in London, Gabriel scored twice on his debut for United's Under-18 side when he was just 14. He was an integral part of the United side that reached both the FA Youth Cup and Premier League Under-18 finals last season. Gabriel moved into the club's Premier League 2 squad this season and scored sensational goals in his first two games. title: What in the World
description: We look at hacks to help you get around it
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·15 Sep 2026,·9 mins Available for over a year Ever wondered why you might feel a bit unwell after a flight? There are lots of reasons for that - from dehydration, jet lag, cabin pressure and altitude. Last month, a French court recognised that cosmic radiation was a factor in a flight attendant’s breast cancer diagnosis. Studies show that cabin crew and pilots have the highest level of radiation- related cancer deaths compared to more than 500 other jobs. We’re looking at what impacts flying regularly, and for long periods of time, can have on your body. We hear from Savannah, a pilot in the US, about what she does to keep herself healthy when sitting in a cockpit for hours. And Naomi, who is taking a break from being cabin crew, tells us how spending so much time in a plane has affected her. title: Woman jailed for claiming on Facebook her ex-husband was a 'rapist' and 'baby killer'
description: Jennifer Pritchard led a two-month smear campaign against her ex-husband, a South Wales Police officer.
body: Jennifer Pritchard was sentenced to 18 months at Cardiff Crown Court on Friday, 11 September A woman has been jailed for posting a string of lies on social media about her police officer ex-husband, claiming he was a "rapist" and a "baby killer". Jennifer Pritchard, 47, from Tredegar in Blaenau Gwent, created a Facebook page called "Jen's Justice" where she led a two-month smear campaign against Stephen Pritchard, a South Wales Police officer. Sgt Pritchard, who said he had been investigated by his force over the false allegations, said he wanted his "life back". Jennifer Pritchard, who had pleaded guilty on the day of her trial to a malicious communication offence, was sentenced on Friday at Cardiff Crown Court to 18 months in prison. Pamela Kaiga, prosecuting, said Pritchard had previously been prosecuted for perverting the course of justice with lies about her ex-husband. Pritchard had been "persecuting" him with repeated falsehoods about domestic violence, rape and being a baby killer. In a victim impact statement, Sgt Pritchard said: "I was the target of a false and malicious campaign on social media to ruin my career. "I've suffered anxiety, depression and other health issues. I just want my life back. "I don't think she will ever stop," he said. Sgt Pritchard said he had suffered financially because of the legal costs and had been investigated by his own force over the allegations. The judge told Jennifer Pritchard that she presented a "high risk of harm" to her ex-husband and police officers Pritchard has previous convictions for harassment against another ex-husband in January 2025, and later that year was convicted of making a public nuisance or causing annoyance via a telecommunications system to a different police officer. Tabitha Walker, defending, said Pritchard was "remorseful for the distress she has caused", and that there was a "realistic prospect of rehabilitation". But the judge, Recorder Andrew Hammond, said she appeared to "derive satisfaction from the harm you cause". "You say you're sorry for the harm you've caused, but I don't believe you," he said, adding that he had "not seen any evidence of substance to indicate any real remorse". "You have a background of inventing false accusations. You present a high risk of harm to your ex-husbands and police officers," Hammond added. Pritchard was also handed an indefinite restraining order, preventing her from contacting her ex-husband. title: Two sailors missing after tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz, Oman says
description: Iran says El Gaia caught fire after hitting mines, but the US says the oil tanker was struck by a missile and then a drone.
body: Oman's Maritime Security Centre said a fire broke out in El Gaia's engine room following an attack Two sailors are missing and 23 others have been rescued following an attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, Oman says. Oman's Maritime Security Centre said the Panama-flagged El Gaia was being towed to an Omani port on Tuesday after a fire broke out in its engine room, adding that the vessel was targeted 1.3 nautical miles (2.4km) north of the Musandam peninsula. On Monday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the tanker hit naval mines and caught fire while passing through what they described as a restricted and unsafe route. But the US military insisted the Iranian report was false. It said the tanker was struck by an Iranian missile last month and again by a drone over the weekend. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, meanwhile, said it had received a report of a fire breaking out on board a vessel that was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Sunday. Earlier this month, Iran made a similar claim about an incident that killed two Filipino sailors on a Saudi-owned oil supertanker in the crucial waterway. The Revolutionary Guards said the vessel, Sidr, caught fire after hitting a naval mine. But Saudi authorities said it was targeted by Iran and maritime security firms reported that it was hit by projectiles north of Musandam. The International Maritime Organization says at least 22 seafarers have been killed in 79 confirmed incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the Middle East since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran at the end of February. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters. title: Colombian ex-foreign minister charged over nanny's lie detector test
description: Laura Sarabia is accused of ordering police to interrogate her nanny after cash allegedly went missing from her flat.
body: Laura Sarabia was Colombia's foreign minister from January to July 2025 Prosecutors in Colombia have accused former foreign minister Laura Sarabia of abusing her power after she made her nanny take a lie detector test. The scandal erupted in 2023, when Colombian news weekly Semana reported that a woman Sarabia had employed to look after her son had been hooked up to a polygraph and questioned over the alleged disappearance of a case full of cash from Sarabia's flat. Sarabia, who was the chief of staff for President Gustavo Petro at the time, resigned in June 2023 but was later appointed as foreign minister and, following her resignation from that post, as Colombia's ambassador to the United Kingdom. She has denied any wrongdoing. The 32-year-old was one of the closest advisers of Gustavo Petro, Colombia's first left-wing president, who governed from 2022 to August this year. Prosecutors said Sarabia abused her position as his chief of staff by ordering police to question her nanny, Marelbys Meza, over the alleged disappearance of the cash, which was said to amount to several thousands of dollars. Meza told Semana that she was taken by Sarabia's driver to an official building opposite the presidential palace, saying it felt like "a kidnapping". Police officers then attached her to a polygraph machine and questioned her about the alleged disappearance of the money. Meza denied having stolen any money during the test, and has consistently denied any wrongdoing in media interviews since. Prosecutors allege that in ordering police to question Meza, Sarabia improperly used state resources to investigate a matter which was not related to her official post. Sarabia rejected the accusation during a hearing, without going into further details. She had earlier said in a social media post that her lawyers were dealing with the issue and that she respected the judicial authorities and trusted their decisions. title: Data centre could threaten rare species, says charity
description: Incredibly rare habitats would be destroyed, the Essex Wildlife Trust warns.
body: Emily Buttress said the Essex Wildlife Trust was not necessarily against development, but they wanted it to be sustainable Plans to build a new data centre could threaten the habitat of one of Britain's most endangered plants and a rare species of bumblebee, a wildlife trust said. A planning application has already been submitted for the Google data centre at Arena Essex Raceway in Thurrock, which is designated as a local wildlife site. It is home to the rare broad-leaved cudweed and shrill carder bumblebee and the Essex Wildlife Trust fears "incredibly rare" habitats would be "destroyed". A Google spokesperson said it took "our environmental responsibilities very seriously". Data centres are giant warehouses full of powerful computers used to run digital services, such as movie streaming, online banking and artificial intelligence. There are 568 data centres listed in the UK, according to the data centre map., external Emily Buttress, from the Essex Wildlife Trust, said her team was worried about the water and energy usage required, the warming effect on the surrounding land, and a lack of research about the long-term impacts of these buildings. "We are quite worried with the rapid development of data centres," she said. "What would it do for the local community in a water drought county? We are not against development, but it has to happen sustainably." There are hundreds of species that live on the site, the trust has said The Arena Essex Raceway announced in 2018 that it would stop hosting speedway fixtures for the Lakeside Hammers team. Meanwhile, the Essex Wildlife Trust says the surrounding grassland and woodland has become home to 687 invertebrate and 439 plant species. The trust said this included dingy skipper, which is a small moth-like butterfly, and the shrill carder bumblebee, which was only found in two areas in England. It was designated as a local wildlife site in 2006. This does not offer legal protection from development, but it means council planners expect developers to look after the ecology. Nightingale birds, the brown-banded carder bee and the five-banded weevil-wasp have also been recorded at the site. But Global Infrastructure UK Limited bought the 129-acre (52-hectare) site in July 2023 for £47m (exclusive of VAT). It submitted plans for the data centre on behalf of Google last year, and as part of the application, consultancy firm Mallory Land Ltd said the proposals took into account the ecology there. If plans are approved the data centre could bring scores of jobs to the area, Google has said In a statement submitted as part of the plans, Mallory Land Ltd said: "The demand for data centres has expanded significantly in recent years, driven by exponential growth in digital services, the emergence of artificial intelligence, cloud-based technologies, and the increasing adoption of smart infrastructure." Google said data centres were vital to the UK economy and for online services. "We share the Essex Wildlife Trust and Buglife's, external view that development at the former Arena Essex site must be sustainable," a spokesperson said. "Our goal is to regenerate the site, bringing long-term investment and jobs to Thurrock while taking our environmental responsibilities very seriously." The company had worked closely with Natural England and ecologists, they added, to "guarantee a 10% biodiversity net gain", "as well as ensuring a substantial part of the site is preserved for new public open space, green links, retained habitat, and the long-term enhancement of key woodland corridors". title: Unions warn against 'out of control' political spending
description: In a joint statement, unions say donations totalling £72m to Reform UK threaten the "integrity of democracy".
body: Head of the TUC, Paul Nowak, spoke about the recent donations to Reform UK at the TUC congress in Brighton Trade unions have called for "out of control" political spending to be reined in, suggesting that the "health and integrity of democracy" have been threatened by donations totalling £72m to Reform UK. In a joint statement, the TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - called on the government to "protect our democracy from being captured by the super rich". There is no explicit call for a cap on domestic donations to match those the government plans to impose on foreign-based donations. But unions have signalled they are open to discussions with policymakers on any initiatives to "clean up" party funding. The statement, issued at the TUC's annual congress in Brighton, also makes the case that trade union donations should not be treated in the same way as big contributions to parties from rich individuals. The debate over donations to political parties has been reignited after Reform UK received two donations totalling £72m from two British crypto-billionaires who have both recently lived abroad. The government is planning to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British voters living overseas, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March. There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties. Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees. Political donors could face tougher residency rules Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules Many in the trade union movement - especially those with links to Labour - have been wary of a cap on domestic donations in case a future government used this to restrict their donations. But behind the scenes officials recognise the eye-watering donations from Reform UK have changed the game and some form of domestic cap may have to be considered. The leader of the Unite union Sharon Graham told the BBC she favoured a cap of £500,000 to £1m on individual donations from UK-based citizens. But she argued that as union donations are made of lots of individual members making a contribution through a political levy then this should be treated differently. She said: "There is a difference between a crypto-billionaire based in the UK or abroad giving millions and trade union members who are nurses, cleaners, bus drivers giving 10p a week which adds up cumulatively to what we give to Labour." The GMB union has been one of the most wary over the implications of a domestic donations cap. Its general secretary Gary Smith told the BBC: "Whether there will be a cap on political donations, we will wait and see. "We will talk to the government at the appropriate time but we can't have any confusion between the political voice working people have through their unions and crypto-billionaires." What is interesting about Tuesday's union statement is not just what it says but what it doesn't. There has been no consensus on calling for caps on the spending of political parties rather than donations - one option for dealing with the Reform war chest. Another option was to treat big unions donations as a series of donations from individual members. For example a million strong union that donates £1m to Labour would have been regarded as making donations of £1 a member - thus escaping a cap. Some believe this would be politically difficult to argue. Not all unions donate to Labour and those which do not are therefore very relaxed about a cap. One even said the events of the past few days have been helpful in arguing for more restrictions on political donations. But I understand discussions will continue amongst those unions with financial links to Labour - including the three biggest in the UK - to try to reach a common position on Wednesday behind closed doors in Brighton and possibly in days and weeks ahead. title: Pidcock and Backstedt lead GB at Road Worlds
description: Great Britain's best cycling talents including Tom Pidcock and Zoe Backstedt will lead the charge at the Road World Championships - live on the BBC.
body: Pidcock has won several of cycling's biggest races while Backstedt won last year's Under-23 world time trial title Tom Pidcock and Zoe Backstedt will lead Great Britain's challenge at the 2026 Road World Championships. The races for the coveted rainbow jerseys take place in Montreal, Canada, from 20-27 September, live across the BBC. The championships include both the road race and time trial disciplines, with Pinarello Q36.5's Pidcock leading the men's team in the road race, while Ethan Hayter races in the men's time trial. Lauren Dickson and Pfeiffer Georgi will likely lead the women's team in the road race and Zoe Backstedt will be expected to contend for the rainbow bands in the time trial. Not for a long time have GB men a better chance to win in the road race, with double world champion and record-equalling five-time Tour de France winner Tadej Pogacar forced to sit out the rest of the season after suffering multiple injuries in a crash at the Vuelta a Espana. Slovenian Pogacar has dominated the world road race for the past two years, winning in 2024 and 2025 to add to his numerous other honours. The time trials come first in Montreal, with riders setting off at one-minute intervals, racing against the clock. Backstedt steps up to the elite category after winning last year's Under-23 race and is joined by Anna Morris, 31, who has won a number of domestic races in 2026. In the men's time trial Hayter, who came second in the opening time trial of the recent Vuelta a Espana, losing out to Pogacar by just nine hundredths of a second, will be joined by Callum Thornley, while the favourite will be defending champion Remco Evenepoel of Belgium. Performance director for British Cycling Stephen Park said: "The Road World Championships are always one of the standout events in the cycling calendar, and we are excited to return with a highly competitive squad. "This squad showcases the very best of British road racing, at a time when more British riders are making their mark across Europe and on the wider international stage than ever before. "We're proud of the balance in this squad, from established world-class performers to riders taking the next step in their development." title: Building more data centres could push up electricity prices, expert warns
description: Scotland has been identified as a key location for building hyperscale AI data centres because of the high potential for renewable energy.
body: Scotland has been identified as a prime location for building hyperscale AI data centres due to the high potential for renewable energy Building more data centres could push up electricity prices for consumers and challenge climate change targets, MSPs have been told. Scotland has been identified as a key location for building hyperscale AI data centres because of the high potential for renewable energy, principally from wind. But academics have warned that could still result in more gas being used to create electricity at times of low wind and solar power, which has been driving up prices in the Republic of Ireland and the US. The National Energy System Operator (Neso) said plans were in place to decouple the high cost of gas from bills. But it added that building more data centres in Scotland would be an important way of keeping electricity prices lower. Will our peaceful rural life be destroyed by a huge AI data centre? Holyrood's Economy, Tourism and Energy Committee, external is investigating the energy use that will come from placing more data centres in Scotland. Dr Callum MacIver, research fellow at the University of Strathclyde, said data centres in Scotland would mop up excess renewable energy. This would cut the multi-million pound bill for constraint payments, which are made when there is too much wind power being generated. But he warned that the growth was still likely to increase the use of fossil fuels. MacIver said: "Adding demand in general is likely to put pressure on meeting decarbonisation goals. "It's not always windy or sunny so adding new demand to the system is likely to increase the amount of fossil fuel burn you have on it." The academic added that locating data centres in "the most sensible places" could mitigate how big those impacts are by using more wind energy. The inquiry also heard that it was unclear how the increased infrastructure costs, linked to a growth in AI data centres, would be shared between operators and wider consumers as additional costs on their bills. While the tech firms will pay their energy bills, connection costs and their network usage, Dr Wei Sun, from the University of Edinburgh, said it was unclear who would fund broader upgrades required on the transmission network. He added: "It's a concern of a lot of people worldwide. "It's a simple question of whether data centres are going to increase the bill or not. There's no simple answer. "Adding the data centre is probably going to trigger wider system upgrades. "Does the data centre also pay for that? I think that's really the question we need to answer." Scotcast: The Revolt Against Data Centres Matt Magill, from Neso, said modern data centres came with a degree of flexibility which allowed for supply and demand for electricity to be balanced on both sides. Bigger AI operators who use, for example, large language modelling are building in enough internet bandwidth to shift the data handling to different parts of the world when needed. Magill said: "Speaking to some of the large [companies] involved in this, they're looking at some of the [AI] training on a regional basis or even a worldwide basis and can actually move the load around the world depending on what's going on in those places." He said that offered flexibility to those that run the power service. The planned data centres would rely on renewable electricity, which is produced in abundance in Scotland by wind turbines. But turbines are often effectively "turned off" due to lack of capacity in the electricity grid - resulting in substantial "compensation" payments for the wind farm companies. ILI Group CEO Mark Wilson said they wanted to make better use of that surplus energy. He added: "Scotland is in a position not a lot of other countries are and we feel this is an opportunity we cannot afford to miss". Wilson also said the construction of hyperscale data centres across the country could create hundreds of new jobs. The issue was raised at Holyrood in June by the Scottish Greens at the final First Minister's Questions before the summer recess. The party called on First Minister John Swinney to back a moratorium on planning approvals. Swinney said he understood the environmental concerns over hyperscale data centres. He also pledged to give "active consideration" to whether local authorities should be given new national planning guidance. Swinney said such guidance might be a way of balancing the rapid expansion of such centres with national energy and climate goals. Could a huge data centre revitalise Ayrshire - or ruin it?
