title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts
description: Menstrual cycles are highly individual, making blanket advice found on social media difficult to apply, researchers say.
body: Sarah Mackay, known as @fitwsarah online, says her energy levels change through her cycle A woman points to a colour-coded grid dividing the menstrual cycle into four phases, each paired with a different list of exercises. "When you're bleeding, you want to be doing steady-pace jogging, Pilates, barre, walking, resting," she tells viewers. This is one of thousands of videos on TikTok and Instagram suggesting that people change their workouts depending on where they are in their menstrual cycles - something known as 'cycle-syncing'. So-called cycle-syncing workout plans have surged in popularity online, with Google searches for the term rising 740% since 2022 and more than 55,000 TikTok videos now using the #cyclesyncing hashtag. Most of the advice is shared by fitness and wellness creators rather than medical or research experts. They divide the menstrual cycle into phases, recommending: gradually increasing intensity in the follicular phase leading up to ovulation harder strength or high-intensity training around ovulation easing off again during the luteal phase (between ovulation and the start of your period) So what does the science say? Kelly McNulty, a researcher at Leeds Beckett University specialising in menstrual cycles and exercise, says there is evidence that some women experience changes in symptoms, energy or perceived strength across their cycle. But that is different from evidence that all women should train in a particular way at a particular point, she tells the BBC, adding that these videos are "a trend based on marketing rather than any kind of research or evidence". "There isn't any research to support that kind of phase-based prescription," she says. This video can not be played Should you sync your exercise routine with your period? A key issue is that menstrual cycles are highly individual, McNulty adds - they can differ between women, and one woman's experience can also change from one cycle to the next. That makes the blanket advice often found on social media difficult to apply, she explains. Many cycle-tracking apps and programmes are also designed around relatively regular menstrual cycles that are 21 to 35 days, which can make their recommendations less applicable to people with irregular periods, or those using hormonal contraception. "It's not so much about doing certain exercises in certain phases, it's about working with your own individual body and what your needs might be." There are now thousands of videos on Instagram and TikTok recommending women sync their workouts to their menstrual cycles Cesci Burgoyne, a nurse based in Sydney, Australia who is also a qualified personal trainer and nutritionist, adjusts her training depending on how she feels in her cycle. She doesn't follow a prescriptive plan, she says, but instead makes changes intuitively. "In my luteal phase I'll try and ease off in the training," she tells the BBC. "In my follicular phase, I'm so energised, I feel like I can lift so much heavier. I like to try and get my long runs in." Burgoyne also welcomes the growing attention on women's health, and says that exercise and nutrition research has historically focused heavily on male bodies, with findings then often applied to women. Sarah says she has sometimes hit personal records while on her period Fitness creator Sarah Mackay, known as @liftwsarah on Instagram and TikTok, has also noticed her energy, motivation, cramps and mood change through the month. But she deliberately avoids strict plans because, she says, "there are too many variables at play". Some online plans advise women to avoid intense training during their period, she says, yet she has sometimes hit personal records while menstruating. "The problem is not that the menstrual cycle is irrelevant," she says, but that "not everything is predictable". Dr Faye Bate, a trained medical doctor and women's health expert, is also wary of advice suggesting all women should train differently according to their menstrual phase. "A one-size-fits-all model of 'you should be exercising this way in this phase and a different way in a different phase' shouldn't be advice that applies to all women," she says. She is concerned that repeatedly telling women they are likely to be weaker or less capable at particular points in their cycle could create a "nocebo" effect - where negative expectations themselves influence how someone feels or performs. McNulty tells the BBC that routinely easing off resistance training could also limit progress. Strength training is particularly important for women, who face a higher risk of osteoporosis later in life. Building strength requires consistent, progressively challenging training, she says, and "we don't want to create another barrier by suggesting women train less for almost half the month." Dr Bate also warns against normalising severe symptoms: if pain, fatigue or mood changes interfere with exercise or daily life, women should seek medical advice rather than assuming it is an inevitable part of their cycle, she says. While cycle-syncing itself may not be backed by strong evidence, the experts we spoke to did suggest being "cycle-aware". McNulty says tracking your cycle can be a useful way to understand your own patterns, while Dr Bate also encourages women to become more familiar with how they feel at different points in the month. Both welcome the fact that menstrual health is being discussed more openly, but say the focus should be on individual experience, rather than rigid, phase-based rules. In practice, that might mean having painkillers ready before your period, taking a rest day when symptoms are worse, or easing off a workout if you feel unusually fatigued. For Dr Bate, "the most important part is tuning in to how you feel". In other words, use your cycle as information rather than a set of rules. title: How cleaning up the air is speeding up global warming - and revealing a bigger problem
description: A curious online row over this summer's heatwaves points to a wider - and worrying - shift in climate science.
body: How cleaning up the air is speeding up global warming - and revealing a bigger problem This July, during Britain's record-breaking hot summer, a curious row broke out on X over climate science. Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice shared a Telegraph article headlined: "Heatwaves caused by fall in pollution." He said cleaner air, rather than carbon dioxide, was behind higher temperatures and claimed the public had been "gaslit". He was wrong to suggest that carbon dioxide is not the primary driver of global warming. But the science he was distorting is real - and much more interesting than his original claim. The fossil fuels that we've been burning for more than a century produce two very different kinds of pollution. As is well known, carbon dioxide warms the Earth. But less well-known is sulphur pollution, which forms vast numbers of tiny particles in the air and reflects sunlight back into space, partly counteracting the warming effect of carbon. Thanks to clean-air policies around the world - like the US's Acid Rain Program in the early 1990s, that reduced gas pollution from power plants - sulphur emissions are falling sharply while carbon dioxide emissions remain near record highs. Scientists increasingly believe the loss of that cooling effect is slightly speeding up global warming. The past three years were the three warmest ever recorded, and the Met Office says 2027 is "very likely" to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record. And away from social media, the argument over Tice's tweet raised an even more interesting - and worrying - question. Is it possible that our planet is actually more sensitive to greenhouse gases than we imagined? And if so, might the climate be changing more rapidly than we feared? Global temperatures jump around naturally from year to year. El Niño, for example, a natural warming of the Pacific Ocean, can temporarily push them higher. So a run of record hot years does not necessarily mean the underlying rate of global warming has increased. Reto Knutti and his team at ETH Zurich have tried to strip out the effects of El Niño and other natural fluctuations to reveal the underlying trend. "It's pretty clear that the rate of warming has accelerated," says Knutti, a professor of climate physics at the Swiss university and a former co-ordinating lead author for the IPCC - the UN-backed body that produces the world's most authoritative assessments of climate science. A separate study published this year reached a similar conclusion after accounting for several major natural influences. And it seems aerosols are playing a role. Burning coal and oil releases sulphur dioxide, which forms tiny particles known as sulphate aerosols. These particles are bright and reflect some sunlight before it can reach and warm the planet's surface. Pollution from ships can create bright trails through clouds, visible from space You've probably heard the greenhouse analogy used to explain global warming. Gases like carbon dioxide make it harder for heat to escape from the Earth, rather like the glass windows of a greenhouse. Well, sulphur pollution acts a bit like dust on the greenhouse windows. The more dust that gathers on those windows, the less sunlight gets inside, and the slower the greenhouse heats up in the first place. Dr Øivind Hodnebrog, a principal researcher at Cicero, the Norwegian climate research institute, has studied how falling aerosol pollution affects the climate. "Sulphate aerosols, they are really small particles, but they are bright particles," he says. As well as reflecting sunlight, aerosols also cool the planet by changing the formation of clouds. Aerosols act like tiny seeds around which water vapour can condense, making some clouds brighter or longer-lived. Pollution from ships can even create bright trails through marine clouds visible from space. So more aerosols mean brighter clouds and more reflection, and so less warming. Sulphur pollution contributed to acid rain, which destroyed forests, like the one above in what was then Czechoslovakia, pictured in 1990 But sulphur pollution also damages human health (it can get into our lungs and make it harder to breathe), and causes acid rain, which can destroy forests and kill fish - and so countries have spent decades cutting it. Emissions have fallen sharply in Europe, North America and China, while new rules have also reduced sulphur pollution from shipping. In our greenhouse analogy, it's as if we've wiped some of the dust away from the windows of the greenhouse, allowing in more sunlight. And while carbon dioxide remains in the climate system for centuries, sulphate aerosols survive in the atmosphere for just days or weeks. So when sulphur emissions fall, their cooling effect disappears almost immediately. The effect is strongest where sulphur pollution has fallen fastest. One study estimates it has added around half a degree to summer warming in western-central Europe since 1980. Prof Piers Forster, a climate scientist at the University of Leeds and another senior author of the IPCC's most recent assessment, estimates that declining aerosol pollution may now be adding around 0.05C to 0.1C of warming per decade. But aerosols can only explain part of the recent acceleration in warming. Greenhouse gases remain much more important. Forster estimates they are currently adding around 0.2C of warming globally per decade. "It is a very significant contribution," he says of the aerosol effect, "but it is not as important as the greenhouse gas contribution by quite a long way." "The aerosols have masked some of the greenhouse gas warming from earlier," is how Hodnebrog explains it. "Masked" - that's an interesting word he uses. What he means is cleaner air is not causing the underlying warming; it is removing some of the cooling that had been holding that warming back. title: Aviation faces hotter, stormier skies – and passengers might have to accept more disruption
description: Are people going to have to increasingly accept more delays and diversions as the effects of climate change intensify?
body: Aviation faces hotter, stormier skies – and passengers might have to accept more disruption As the country sweltered through one of the many heatwaves of a baking summer in late June, towering thunderclouds were gathering over the south of England and across much of northern Europe. It was a Saturday, and with the holiday season getting under way, thousands of passengers were heading to London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports to catch flights abroad. It was always going to be a very busy day. What followed, however, was chaos for travellers. As air traffic controllers struggled to route aircraft around the storms, airspace became heavily congested and many planes due to fly were simply forced to wait on the ground. In the end, some 900 flights to and from both airports were delayed, some by up to 11 hours. Dozens more were cancelled. At airports across Europe, passengers expecting to fly into London also faced long waits and uncertainty. The weather in the UK may now have cooled, and passengers may soon forget their experiences. But some within the industry believe what happened in June should be seen as a warning. The timing in this case was clearly unlucky. But there are concerns that such incidents are only going to become more common as the effects of climate change mount up around the world and weather systems are likely to become increasingly unstable, making disruption more likely and adding to costs for airlines, airports and travellers. Tim Atkinson, an airline risk consultant and former pilot, says the very crowded skies over the UK and northern Europe mean the region is particularly exposed. He thinks there is a real risk, for example, that all of London's airports could be affected by storms at the same time, potentially with major consequences in the air and on the ground. "What we're seeing now is very rapid climate change," he says. "We're going from the kind of weather activity which takes out an airport, and which the system kind of copes with… to a situation where, with very little predictability, it would be possible to lose all of the London airports from real-time operation quite swiftly and with little notice". Such a scenario, he thinks, would make the disruption for passengers caused by the incident in June seem relatively minor – and could even put lives at risk. But how likely is it? For controllers at National Air Traffic Services's (NATS) main control centre in Swanwick, Hampshire, thunderstorms are a major preoccupation. When I visit, it is a hot and humid day, there are ominous dark clouds in the sky, and heavy, thundery downpours are hitting the surrounding region. In Terminal Control, the part of the building responsible for flights heading to or from airports in London and southern England, those same storm cells are being monitored continuously. Their progress is tracked on large radar screens, while at the same time weather forecasts are carefully scrutinised. Air traffic tends to come in waves during the day. Right now, at lunchtime, it is relatively quiet and the storms have yet to affect major routes. But with activity expected to intensify in the afternoon, staff are already preparing for what could be a tricky few hours. Stormy weather can shrink the available airspace, meaning traffic has to be restricted and rerouted. If planes are unable to land at one airport, for example due to high winds, they may need diverting to another. But that can create its own problems; if too many unscheduled aircraft land at an already busy airport, it might not have sufficient infrastructure to accommodate them all. Heavy rain and storms can make flying harder Planes need fuel and somewhere to park. Passengers need food and facilities. Ultimately, if there isn't space, it can simply refuse to accept all but emergency traffic. This is where the scenario set out by Atkinson comes in. He warns of a situation where traffic is diverted from Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Stansted at the same time, leaving aircraft coming in across the Atlantic and a large number of European flights all looking for somewhere to land at the same time, and some with dwindling fuel reserves. This would at the very least create serious disruption for passengers, who might end up hundreds of miles from their destinations. But it could also, he thinks, create "a very serious risk event, such as an aircraft running out of fuel in the sky". Aircraft are legally required to carry enough fuel to take them to an alternative airport if necessary, and to allow them to fly for an extra 30 minutes on top of that. Not everyone shares Atkinson's concern. Former airline executive Andrew Charlton, who manages the Swiss-based consultancy Aviation Advocacy, thinks the risk is low. "You've always got to imagine the worst-case scenario", he says. "But I also think we need to keep that worst case in context. "Yes, it's possible to imagine it. But I'm also fairly comfortable with the ability of this industry to react well and make good decisions… of all the things that wake me up at 3am…this is not the top of that list." Thunderstorms are caused by what is known as convective activity, where moist air close to the ground warms rapidly and rises quickly. As it rises, it expands and cools, allowing the moisture it carries to condense, forming large clouds. More heat means more convective energy, potentially creating instability. In addition, for every degree the Earth warms, the atmosphere can hold about 7% more moisture, increasing the probability of heavy rainfall. It is not clear whether this means we will actually get more thunderstorms in the UK and across Europe, as so many variables are involved beyond the simple matter of energy and moisture. Some parts of the world may even get fewer. title: Why do ex-MPs join the 'Chiltern Hundreds' list?
description: Sir Keir Starmer is the latest person to take the office as a means of resigning as an MP.
body: Sir Keir Starmer and Boris Johnson are two of hundreds of MPs who resigned by taking the Chiltern Hundreds position Sir Keir Starmer and Boris Johnson have this in common: They both stepped down as Prime Minister before their term was up, and within three years of winning an election. Their subsequent resignation as a sitting MP means they have also shared the unusual office of "Steward and Bailiff of the Three Hundreds of Chiltern". Sir Keir is the latest person to pick up the title after resigning as an MP this week. What is it, and what does it have to do with the Chilterns? MPs across the generations have used the mechanism to resign from their role Thanks to a law dating back to 1624, Members of Parliament (MPs) in the UK are not technically permitted to resign. "Unless they die or are expelled, they must become disqualified if they wish to retire before the end of a Parliament," according to the UK Parliament website. This is because back in the 17th Century, MPs often accepted the role reluctantly, so leaving the job was not to be encouraged. A "parliamentary loophole" was created to get around this, according to the History of Parliament blog, external. "An MP can do this by requesting, and accepting, office as either the Steward and Bailiff of the Chiltern Hundreds, or Steward and Bailiff of the Manor of Northstead," wrote Dr Martin Spychal. "Both offices (or jobs) are nominal. They exist in name only, have no responsibilities and are unpaid." Anyone with these titles is disqualified from being an MP – originally in order to prevent royal influence on politics – but later used by parliamentarians who were unhappy with their lot. High Wycombe is one of the towns in the Chiltern Hundreds region The "hundreds" were areas that belonged to the Crown as far back as the 13th Century. The three Chiltern Hundreds mentioned today refer to Stoke, Desborough and Burnham in Buckinghamshire. The regions include the towns of Amersham, Beaconsfield, High Wycombe, Marlow, Eton and Chesham. Coincidentally, these are near to the prime minister's countryside residence in Buckinghamshire – Chequers. Because a steward of the hundreds might be able to benefit financially from the role, or promote the interests of the crown, it was seen as a conflict of interest. "Resourceful MPs discovered that they could request appointment to these offices, which then disqualified them from sitting in the Commons," wrote Spychal. Nigel Farage and Nadine Dorries are among those to be appointed to the Manor of Northstead or the Chiltern Hundreds The House of Commons Information Office said: "The Stewardship of the Chiltern Hundreds is thought to have been used for the first time as a means of resignation from the House of Commons on 17 January 1751 by John Pitt, who wanted to vacate his seat for Wareham and stand for Dorchester." The Manor of Northstead, in North Yorkshire, is the other remaining office given to resigning MPs. Its most recent recipient was Reform UK's Nigel Farage who resigned in order to stand for re-election in his own constituency. The titles are given out alternately, in case two MPs wish to step down at the same time, and each new appointment replaces the previous one. Spychal said there have been calls to reform the system since 1775 - but in 2026, the peculiar British formality lives on. Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below. title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse
description: The things you're doing to make your sleep better could actually be making your sleep worse.
body: Sleep scores, magnesium, white noise machines - what was once the simple act of sleeping has become a minefield. Trying to optimise sleep in this way is called "sleepmaxxing". Take it too far, and you could end up with "orthosomnia" - the clinical term for an obsession with achieving perfect sleep. While it's not formally recognised as a condition in the UK, doctors tell the BBC they've noticed signs of orthosomnia in their patients, with some bringing their sleep tracker data into appointments convinced, wrongly, that they have a sleep disorder. That fixation is actually making people's sleep worse, they warn. So how and why did sleep become so complicated? And if sleepmaxxing isn't the answer, what is the elusive secret to a good night's sleep? The first commercial fitness tracker to incorporate sleep analysis was the Fitbit Classic in 2009. Since then, many others - including Garmin, Whoop and Apple - have integrated sleep trackers into wrist-worn devices, as have smart rings such as Oura, Ultrahuman and RingConn. These devices vary, but in general they all provide users with a report of their night, broken down by sleep stages - time awake, light sleep, deep sleep, and REM (rapid eye movement). Many also give users a "sleep score". But the concept of a sleep score is "completely made up", according to Dr Alanna Hare, consultant of sleep medicine at the Royal Brompton Hospital in London. "There's nothing recognised in sleep science that is a 'sleep score'," she tells the BBC. "That's just been created by manufacturers." This video can not be played How sleep-tracking can make your sleep worse Hare says she's noticed trackers causing anxiety among her patients. "I've noticed more patients coming to me with data from various trackers, with lots of questions about sleep that... is probably contributing to their sleep difficulties," she says. Even though some have had medical tests with reassuring results, this hasn't allayed their fears, she adds. "It's great that there's more focus on sleep as part of wellness," she adds. "But sleep just does not respond well to attempts to perfect it." One proposed lawsuit against Oura, filed last month in San Francisco, alleges that Oura rings are unable to accurately measure sleep quality and sleep stages, and instead rely on AI-generated estimates that have "a coin flip's chance of being correct". In response, Oura told the BBC that it "stand[s] behind our science, research and accuracy claims". "We're committed to clearly communicating what Oura measures, what it estimates, and how members should use that information," the company added. Studies also show sleep trackers can affect how you function during the day, even if they're not accurate. In one study, external from the University of Oxford, participants were given sleep trackers which assigned them a sleep score. The scores were randomised, however, and had no relation to how the participants had actually slept. The next day participants rated their mood, fatigue levels and alertness, before tests checking their focus and reaction times. Researchers found that the people told they'd slept badly reported feeling more fatigued, and were less mentally alert - even though the sleep scores were all fake. This is something Jess Hill says she noticed in herself after getting a Garmin watch several years ago. "I started to rely on the watch as my Bible for whether I slept well or not," the 32-year-old HR professional from London tells the BBC. "I would think, 'I've had awful sleep so I'm going to really struggle today', even if I actually probably had okay sleep. If I'd slept really well, I'd be convinced I'd have to be on top - even though I was tired, I was pushing through things." Jess Hill was "obsessed" with her Garmin's sleep scores for about three years Her "obsession", as she describes it, with getting a high sleep score lasted three years, until earlier this year, when she started to notice the watch wasn't reflecting how she'd actually slept. "I was awake the other week for four hours in the night, and my watch was like 'wow, great sleep!' - I literally was awake from 01:00 until 05:00," she says. The BBC has approached Garmin for comment. Jess's sleep scores weren't matching how she actually felt Dr Neil Stanley, sleep expert and author of the book How to Sleep Well, argues that gamifying sleep is creating more disordered sleeping. "The thing with tracking your sleep is that it gives you a number, and this means you have a target," he tells the BBC. "So you get into this cycle of worrying about your quality of sleep or the quantity of sleep based on figures." He says he carried out research into actigraphy - wrist-worn sleep trackers - around 40 years ago. Though commercial trackers now are a bit more sophisticated, they work in much the same way - by measuring your movement - and have the same limitations, he says. "If you want to measure sleep, you have to measure the brain," Stanley adds. "Unless you're measuring the brain's activities, you're not measuring sleep." Keeping your bedroom cool, dark and quiet - within reason. "That doesn't mean it needs to be pitch black, exactly 16C or totally silent," she says. "It should be coolish, darkish and quietish." Seeing bright light in the morning, which is good for regulating your circadian rhythm - that is, your body's natural clock. Doing light exercise, and eating a "healthy, Mediterranean-style diet with plenty of plant variability". Above all, keeping it simple - "anything else, you don't need it". title: The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough
description: In an era when reputations can be made or broken with a single post, getting the balance right is tricky.
body: The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough In early 2015, flower crowns started appearing on Ed Miliband's head. Petals and hearts were photoshopped on to the then-Labour leader by the "Milifandom", a movement of young, mostly female, voters sharing romanticised images on Twitter to protest against Miliband's "distorted media portrayal". It was the brainchild of Abby Tomlinson, a 17-year-old sixth-form student, who came to the defence of the man she called "Milibae". The hashtag #Milifandom trended. Then Labour lost the 2015 election. This prompted David Cameron, whose Conservatives increased their number of seats, to boast: "Britain and Twitter are not the same thing." Tomlinson later told me that having her hopes of Milibae in No10 dashed had made her a "political pessimist", after realising winning over voters online "doesn't happen in a day, a week or even months, it's going to take years". More than a decade on and she is again using social media to big up a Labour leader, but this time in the heart of government. She sits in the press office in No 12 Downing Street as head of content for Andy Burnham. The government has spent the last few weeks recruiting producers, videographers and strategists, working out of both Whitehall and No 10 North in Manchester. In his first month as PM, Burnham posted more than 50 times on Instagram, ranging from meetings with world leaders, campaigners, farmers and influencers, to meme-based content like ranking pub snacks with Chancellor John Healey as part of an announcement on business rates. Strategists believe Instagram and TikTok can play to Burnham's communication strengths and sense of humour. The PM's social media game has been a hit with pundits They're all at it, of course. Videos of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch tearing into the budget or mocking ex-PM Sir Keir Starmer have gone viral. Reform UK's Nigel Farage has by far the biggest online audience of any UK party leader, with 7.6 million followers across Facebook, Instagram, X, TikTok and YouTube. In Scotland, the SNP have long mobilised their online army to campaign for independence, building a following larger than that of the Lib Dems, which campaigns across Britain, whose leader Ed Davey has achieved some success with campaign stunts going viral. Restore Britain, founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe, enjoys its highest level of support among users of X. The platform is owned by Elon Musk who has publicly endorsed the party, expanding its reach. Plaid Cymru, newly installed in government in Wales, is still experimenting with its approach, using First Minister Rhun Ap Iorweth in "fun" memes while also posting more serious interview excerpts. The Greens' Zack Polanski has made much of running his own accounts, though as he has found in recent weeks, this comes with risks too. So how much is enough? In a world where reputations can be made (or broken) with one comment or collaboration, getting the balance right is tricky – being accessible, authentic and approachable, without being cringe. And does it make any difference to elections? Cameron's successor, Theresa May, was similarly doubtful about the merits of social media. When she took office she rebuffed aides who suggested she start tweeting: "People don't say 'pass me the hashtag newspaper, or I'd like a hashtag coffee'." Announcements were to be made formally. When cabinet ministers were appointed in May's first reshuffle, it was heralded in press statements beneath the UK government coat of arms. By contrast, this summer, presenting my 5 Live show from Downing Street during Burnham's first reshuffle, I could predict the appearance of another new minister because the two-person social media team from No 10 would move into position to capture the new arrivals on their cameras. Of course, prime ministers (and wannabes) have long adapted to new technology. Winston Churchill harnessed the power of radio, but thought television a vulgar diversion. In the 1960s, Labour's Harold Wilson modelled his TV campaigning on JFK in America. In the 1990s, and 2000s leaders like Tony Blair were just as likely to be found on the chatshow sofa as on the Today programme. Nigel Farage's social media following is larger than that of any other UK leader Now, podcasts give long-form - and less combative - opportunities to connect with voters, while social media gives a quick hit of direct democratic dopamine. Peter Hyman, a former adviser to both Tony Blair and Keir Starmer when in Downing Street, said the success of Burnham's early digital output was about "quantity as well as quality". "You have to narrate the story of what you are doing three or four or five times a day so that you are out there regularly," Hyman said. "Keir Starmer wasn't out there enough and therefore it wasn't landing." There is a causality dilemma here. Is Burnham more popular in the polls because he is racking up the likes on social media, or is he doing better online because people like him? Not everyone is convinced. Cody Dahler, a comedian who posts sweary political explainers to his two million followers, warns voters will become cynical if they sense politicians are just using social media simply "as a comms tool". Burnham, Dahler told me on Newsnight, comes across like a "cool substitute teacher". And after Burnham released a video discussing what a bread roll is called in different parts of the country – barm, cob or bap - to promote his plans for devolution, broadcaster Piers Morgan asked him to "stop wasting your time and ours with these cringe videos". And therein lies the difficulty of striking a balance. title: Inside Health
description: Plus, how much do people really change their habits for a free coffee?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·11 Aug 2026,·27 mins Available for over a year Insulin has been used to treat type 1 diabetes for more than a century but now there is a new treatment being rolled out on the NHS that can delay the onset of the disease for years. Alongside, screening is gathering pace, identifying those that could benefit. So, is this the beginning of a new era for type 1 diabetes treatment? Dima and his mum Elena explain what it was like to be told that he had tested positive for developing type 1 diabetes and what it was like taking part in the trial for this new drug, teplizumab. Parth Narendran, a Professor of Diabetes Medicine at the University of Birmingham, and Consultant Paediatric Endocrinologist Dr Renuka Dias at Birmingham Women's and Children's Hospital, reveal how these changes are transforming treatment. In July, the NHS announced plans to incentivise us to walk a marathon a month by offering vouchers and discounts. But with scant detail on how the plan will actually work, we ask Joan Costa-i-Font, Professor of Health Economics at London School of Economics, what makes schemes like this succeed or fail. Plus, why are horse fly bites so painful? Dr Erica McAlister, an entomologist at the Natural History Museum, explains how the flies break into our skin, while consultant dermatologist Dr Alexandra Banner describes what’s happening in our bodies. Presenter: James Gallagher Producer: Hannah Robins

title: Inside Health
description: Millions of people still have long Covid, yet a cure still isn't quite within reach.
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations Radio 4,·04 Aug 2026,·27 mins Available for over a year More than six years since the start of the Covid pandemic, it might feel like we're pretty over it, yet that's simply not the case for the millions of people who suffer from long Covid. But could there be hope on the horizon? A new clinical trial led by University College London and University College London Hospitals found that over-the-counter antihistamines and a prescription anti-inflammatory drug called colchicine offered a small reduction in fatigue for people with long Covid. But it's still not a cure. Professor Danny Altmann, an immunologist at Imperial College London, joins us to discuss this new research and the problems with understanding long Covid. He also tells us about some of the upcoming studies that might help us better get a handle on the condition. Also this week, did you know that around one in 335 people in the UK are living with a stoma? Yet according to Colostomy UK, more than 60 per cent of those with a stoma say a lack of suitable toilet facilities affects their daily lives. Thanks to a campaign that started in Bristol, B&Q has now made the disabled toilets across its stores stoma-friendly. We pay a visit to B&Q with The Traitors' Mollie Pearce, who has been living with a stoma since she was 18, and colorectal surgeon Ms Caroline Burt from Bristol Foundation Trust to find out more. Finally, many of us have been guzzling ice cream to cool off during the hot weather. But have you seen the social media claims that the frozen treat can reduce your risk of developing type 2 diabetes? We asked nutritional scientist Dr Sarah Berry from King's College London to give us the scoop on the 'ice cream paradox'. Presenter: James Gallagher Producer: Alice Lipscombe-Southwell Production coordinator: Stu Laws Editor: Ilan Goodman

title: Burnham's 'Manchesterism' got him to No 10 - but will it work for the UK?
description: Economics editor Faisal Islam examines whether the north-west city can be a template for the entire country.
body: Burnham's 'Manchesterism' got him to No 10 - but will it work for the UK? It was just five months ago when Andy Burnham retreated to his mayor's office in Manchester, having been blocked by Labour's ruling executive from standing for parliament. When I met him there a few weeks later, he told me he planned to deal with his disappointment with some ambitious plans for his city region. Burnham told me he wanted to appeal directly to Fifa to host the final of the women's football World Cup in 2035 Manchester instead of Wembley. "Imagine how electrifying that is for any girl growing up in the north of England," he said. He said he was also joining forces with other mayors for a "Great Northern" Olympic bid across the north of England, and a plan was also afoot to host the Ryder Cup in Bolton. Sports bodies needed "re-educating" about the rest of the country, he said. Burnham served as Greater Manchester's mayor from 2017 to 2026 Manchester has already poached the Brit Awards from London after half a century in the capital. Big, bold gestures like these tell part of the story of what has happened in the city. Burnham's civic ambition is a byproduct of Manchester's status as the fastest-growing city economy in the country. As Burnham prepares to become prime minister, will he be able to apply the same model to the whole of the nation? Even before Burnham returned to parliament in June, there has been talk of Manchesterism as a political-economic philosophy that offers a programme for national transformation, rooted in a critique of a currently unresponsive, over-centralised British state. The city has a long history of blending the freest of free markets with a strong social spirit. Manchester's cotton traders championed free trade and liberal economics, at the same time as the emergence of the co-operative movement, the trade unions and the Suffragettes. Even the Manchester Ship Canal, the emblem of monopoly-breaking free trade, required local government intervention backed by the workers. But for an understanding of contemporary Manchester, you need to go back to the summer of 1996. Andy Burnham had left the north-west of England by then. He told me how when he first looked for a local media job after graduating in the early 1990s, all he could get was a role as an unpaid reporter on the Middleton Guardian. "I had to do what so many people of my generation, born in the 60s or 70s in the north-west of England had to do to get on in life," he said. "We had to go south." By 1996, Burnham was an MP's researcher. That year, back in Manchester, the IRA detonated the largest bomb in the UK since World War Two, devastating the city centre, The reconstruction in the aftermath of the attack marked the start of Manchester's ascent from the doldrums of de-industrialisation. The essential idea provided by a group of local political, cultural and business leaders, and an architect called Ian Simpson, was that the city centre should be reshaped by demolishing, not repairing, many of the damaged buildings. The bomb caused devastation across the city centre leading to a huge rebuilding project From disaster could then arise a great opportunity to reshape the city's geography and economy. Council leader Sir Richard Leese and his top civil servant, the late Sir Howard Bernstein set the tone for a variety of bold centrally driven strategic plans that were actually largely delivered by private capital and then significant international investment. The council leadership was ruthlessly focused on transforming brownfield industrial sites. The private sector would go nowhere near them, but the council de-risked those investments with public money. It also sometimes stepped in to tide projects over during financial crises. At the end of this process, private capital poured in, lining up the cranes and the hard hats. The council offered a flexible interpretation of requirements to build a proportion of "affordable housing", sometimes effectively waived, sometimes met by funding building in cheaper areas of the city. Paul Thwaite, the chief executive of NatWest, which has funded some of these projects, and who is on the board of the University of Manchester, says Manchester's success story over the past 20 years was "built on there being a clear plan the private sector can get behind". Such a shift would have been unthinkable a generation ago. The model of Manchester's city centre development has succeeded in creating a critical mass of population, housing, jobs and service sector activity that has allowed it to turn its significant undergraduate population into a goldmine. According to the mayor, more people from London had moved to Manchester (13,000) than the other way round (11,800) in the latest set of internal migration figures. He put this down to a flow of young workers into the Manchester city centre service economy. In a reverse from the 1990s, "no-one here has to leave to get on in life", Burnham told me. "And in fact, there's a net inflow of young people from London." Manchester now retains over half its graduates, more than any other city apart from London, according to the Centre for Cities, and Manchester also attracts almost as many young graduates as it produces. Tom Beahon, the CEO of Manchester-based sports brand Castore, who has not been shy about criticising some of the government's business policies, told our Big Boss podcast earlier this year that the mayor had helped "attract inbound investment, making it a place that students want to stay after they graduate from the fantastic universities". That in turn means more businesses want to launch in the city, he added. It is a case study in agglomeration effects - the economic power of locating similar types of jobs close together. And if its infrastructure can keep up, Manchester's economy will continue to fly. Andy Burnham is a product of this Greater Manches

title: Starting uni? What to know about the free NHS meningitis B jab in England
description: It follows the UK's largest and fastest growing meningitis B outbreak to date in Kent earlier this year.
body: A million young people are being offered a free meningitis B vaccine. It comes after concerns over the UK's largest and fastest growing outbreak that happened in Kent earlier this year. Nearly 90,000 doses of the vaccine have already been given, with 135,000 more booked in for the coming weeks. So who needs the vaccine, what's in it and where can you get it for free? The vaccine offers protection against a dangerous strain of meningitis called meningitis B (MenB) that caused the outbreak in Kent. The vaccine does not contain any live bacteria and cannot cause meningitis. It is common to get some swelling, redness or tenderness where you have the injection. You may also get a mild fever, nausea, headache or muscle aches but these symptoms should disappear after one or two days. More serious side effects are rare. Bookings can be made at high street pharmacies across England. Seventeen and 18-year-olds can book via the NHS National Booking Service, external if they are already registered with a GP, external. Other students under the age of 25 who are heading to a residential college or university this autumn for the first time can also contact a participating pharmacy. You can get a walk-in MenB vaccine at a pharmacy if you were born on or after 21 July 2001, and for the first time this autumn you are: starting at a further education college as a residential student International students and students from elsewhere in the UK (Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, the Channel Islands, the Isle of Man) who will be studying in England are also eligible, as well as those who are travelling abroad to study. You do not need to be registered with a GP surgery to use the walk-in service. Find a participating pharmacy here, external. The vaccine, given as two doses and at least 28 days apart, is being offered to 17 and 18-year-olds in sixth form and students under the age of 25 who are heading to a residential college or university this autumn for the first time. Both doses are needed for the fullest protection. A million young people are expected to be eligible for the vaccine in England, including: people born between 1 September 2007 and 31 August 2008 people born on or after 21 July 2001 and starting university for the first time this autumn people born on or after 21 July 2001 who are starting at residential further education colleges for the first time this autumn The meningitis outbreak that happened in Kent in March has been described as unprecedented and explosive. Within weeks, in Kent, there were 29 confirmed or suspected cases and two deaths. That's why the new, one-off campaign is being launched - to help protect those at greatest risk and hopefully prevent something like this from happening again. Students in their first year of university have a risk that is about seven times higher than that of young people of a similar age who do not go to university, says NHS England. Meningitis infections can be spread through close contact - for example through kissing, sharing vapes and drinks or living in close quarters with a person with the bug. UK health officials say the risk to 18-year-olds or those entering university or a residential college for the first time is higher because of increased mixing of social groups and shared accommodation. MenB infection can cause serious, life-threatening problems including inflammation of the lining of the brain (meningitis) and blood poisoning (sepsis). It can lead to life-changing disabilities such as amputations, hearing loss and brain damage, and in some cases can be fatal. The MenB vaccine was added to the UK NHS childhood immunisation programme for babies born on or after 1 July 2015. All babies are now offered it. But it means teenagers and young adults over the age of 11 have not received this jab. Young babies are vaccinated because they are more likely to get invasive infections more often than other age groups, and their bodies are less likely to be able to fight them off. However, research suggests the MenB vaccine doesn't necessarily prevent transmission of the infection from person to person, doesn't target all the different B bacteria strains and doesn't provide long-term protection. But UK vaccine experts now say government should consider routinely offering the vaccine to all teenagers at around age 15. It will be up to ministers in each nation to decide whether to do this. Meanwhile, they do want everyone who is eligible to come forward and get the vaccine because it can prevent serious illness. Around 10,000 people in the Kent region will have already received jabs, as part of the response to the March outbreak. Each nation has its own plans, external, but all are offering the vaccine to most pupils completing Year 13 or S6 in the summer of 2026 - irrespective of their education plans and including people from this age group who are not currently in school. Young people aged 18-25 starting university or moving into residential further education settings for the first time in autumn 2026 are also eligible. In Wales, those aged 17-18 will receive a letter invite, while those aged 18-25 who are entering higher education will need to contact their health board later in July. Meningitis can be caused by many different types of viruses or bacteria, which are spread through close contact with a person who has them. Viral meningitis tends to get better on its own within seven to 10 days. It can often be treated at home with plenty of rest, painkillers and anti-sickness medicine. Bacterial meningitis needs to be treated in hospital. Currently, a separate vaccine covering different strains, the MenACWY vaccine, is offered routinely to 14-year-olds. title: Sir John Curtice: The 'Burnham bounce' is real but it's not massive
description: The governing party's poll ratings have improved but they're only just ahead of Reform.
body: Sir John Curtice: The 'Burnham bounce' is real but it's not massive The consistent message of the opinion polls since the new prime minister walked into Downing Street almost a fortnight ago is that Labour is enjoying a "Burnham bounce". And this has now been confirmed by the party's convincing victory in Thursday's Greater Manchester mayoral by-election. Polls conducted in the last week put Labour on average in the mid 20s. It is the party's highest standing since the beginning of last year and compares to their rating of 19% in late June when Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down. But with Reform polling only narrowly behind Labour, Burnham's party still has a long way to go before it can face the prospect of fighting a general election with confidence. The Burnham boost is far from unprecedented. All but one of the recent mid-term changes of prime minister have been followed by an increase in the popularity of the incumbent government. Support for Labour rose by seven points after Gordon Brown replaced Tony Blair in 2007, while the Conservatives enjoyed a six-point bounce when Boris Johnson took over from Theresa May in 2019. Only Liz Truss' arrival in Downing Street in 2022 – which was overshadowed by the death shortly thereafter of Queen Elizabeth II – failed to give her party a boost. It is not unusual for a new prime minister to enjoy a poll bounce We should also bear in mind the depth of the electoral hole that Burnham has inherited as Labour leader. The 19% at which Labour stood when Sir Keir resigned was the lowest poll rating passed on by any prime minister departing mid-term – even lower than the 23% bequeathed by Liz Truss when she resigned after just 45 days in office. Against that backdrop, it would have been very surprising indeed if the replacement of the deeply unpopular Sir Keir by the relatively popular Burnham had not given Labour a short-term boost. However, even after Burnham's bounce, his party's poll average is still the lowest for any newly minted mid-term PM, while the party is still well adrift in the polls of the (relatively low) 35% it won at the 2024 general election. That said, Labour's victory in Thursday's Manchester mayoral by-election was convincing. True, Labour's 47% share of the first preference vote was well down on the 63% that Burnham secured in the last mayoral contest shortly before the 2024 general election. However, not only did it represent a near doubling of the 24% that Labour registered across the region in May's local elections, but also it was even four points up on Labour's tally locally in the 2024 general election – and thus a much better performance than would have been anticipated from even the latest national polling. But with still no more than a narrow lead over Reform, it is unsurprising Burnham has ruled out an early election. In any event, Reform's displacement from first place in the polls for the first time in over a year appears to owe more to its own difficulties than it does to Labour's new-found popularity. Reform has been dogged in recent weeks by questions about the legality of the source of some of its funding and about whether Farage should have declared to the Commons authorities some of the funding he received before being elected an MP. Following these allegations, Farage announced on 7 July that he was standing down and putting himself again before the voters of his Clacton constituency in a by-election now scheduled for 13 August. This move appears to have backfired. Immediately before Farage's announcement, Reform's average poll rating stood at 27%. In the polls conducted immediately after Farage's announcement, it fell by three points to 24%, the level at which it still stands now, and the lowest it has been for 15 months. At the same time, Farage's personal poll ratings are now the worst they have been since he returned as Reform's leader during the 2024 election campaign. In the Manchester by-election, Reform's share of the first preference vote was nine point down on its tally across the region in May's local elections. As in the Makerfield by-election, the party seemingly suffered from the advance made by Rupert Lowe's breakaway from Reform, Restore Britain, which won nearly 9% of the Manchester vote, outpolling the Conservatives in the process. But for Reform's difficulties, the "Burnham bounce" would probably have been insufficient to put Labour in the lead in the national polls. The principal source of that bounce has been clawing voters back from the Greens and the Liberal Democrats, both of whom have suffered a two-point drop since Burnham's uncontested victory in the Labour leadership contest. For the Greens – much of whose increased support in recent months came from disappointed 2024 Labour voters – the change of prime minister has proven particularly damaging. The Greens' current 11% tally is as much as four points adrift of where it was when Sir Keir announced he was leaving. When he resigned, 14% of Labour's 2024 election voters said they would now back the Greens. That figure is now 9%. Winning back former Labour voters has generally been a key component of the Burnham bounce. Overall, 67% of those who voted Labour in 2024 now say they would vote for the party, compared to 57% when Sir Keir indicated he was leaving Downing Street. Following Farage's difficulties, Labour is also now losing fewer of its 2024 voters to Reform. But the same is true of the Conservatives, whose loss of support to Reform in the polls during this Parliament has always been much greater than that suffered by Labour. Far from suffering from a Burnham bounce, Kemi Badenoch's party has edged up to 20% in the polls for the first time since last spring. Burnham's arrival has given Labour new hope. title: Find out all about the albums up for this year's Mercury Prize
description: This year's best album shortlist includes several returning nominees - but Lily Allen misses out.
body: This video can not be played Who's nominated for this year's Mercury Prize? Olivia Dean's campaign to collect every major music award in existence continues, with a nomination for this year's Mercury Prize. The star is among the favourites to win the £25,000 prize, which recognises outstanding albums, after her second record, The Art of Loving, won album of the year at both the Brits and the Mobo Awards. Sir Paul McCartney also receives his first ever Mercury nomination, aged 84, for the nostalgia-laden The Boys of Dungeon Lane, while Suede, Jade, Raye and Nia Archives are also in contention. But there was a surprise omission for Lily Allen, whose scathing break-up album, West End Girl, was one of the biggest critical and commercial successes of the last 12 months. Olivia Dean and Lily Allen were both expected to feature on the shortlist - but only one made the grade The record examines the collapse of her marriage to actor David Harbour in unvarnished detail. Reviews praised its candour and musical invention, calling Allen's work "breathtaking and heartbreaking", external and "a brutal, tell-all masterpiece", external. Artists submit themselves for the prize, making it impossible to determine whether Allen was snubbed or simply not in contention - but she was previously nominated for her 2018 album No Shame. Other notable omissions include Harry Styles’ Kiss All The Time, Disco Occasionally and Gorillaz’ sweeping meditation on grief, The Mountain. Sir Paul McCartney has released 11 albums since the inception of the Mercury Prize in 1992, but this is his first nomination Dean is also a former nominee, for her 2023 debut album Messy, and returns thanks to the sumptuously singable soul songs on The Art of Loving. Two former winners - Suede and Dave - receive nominations, while Florence + The Machine picks up a fourth citation for her thunderous new album, Everybody Scream. The presence of so many stalwarts largely squeezes out fresh talent, but the mysterious Irish newcomer Dove Ellis stands out as a potential winner, for the otherworldly beauty of his debut album, Blizzard. The shortlisted albums are selected by a panel of 12 jurists, including 6 Music broadcaster Afrodeutsche, musician Jamie Cullum, and The Times' music critic Will Hodgkinson. They'll select an overall winner during the prize ceremony at Newcastle's Utilita Arena on 22 October. Last year's prize went to hometown hero Sam Fender. Other previous winners include Pulp's Different Class (1996), Dizzee Rascal's Boy In Da Corner (2003), Elbow's The Seldom Seen Kid (2008), Wolf Alice's Visions of a Life (2018) and Ezra Collective's Where I'm Meant To Be (2023). Here's all you need to know about the 12 albums selected for the 2026 prize. Introspective and thoughtful, Dave's fourth album drops the bravado of his youth to confront his loss of faith, alcoholism and infidelity. He describes it as a record that "demands focus" and deliberately avoids hit singles - aside from the sensual, Afrobeats-inspired Raindance. Highest chart position: Number one Listen to Raindance: Spotify, external | YouTube, external | Apple Music, external Olivia Dean's second album was born in a rented house in East London, with the singer and her collaborators mixing writing sessions with late night conversations over good food and "lots of red wine". That easy-going approach inspired a soulful collection of love songs whose easy familiarity feels like a best friend spilling their secrets. Highest chart position: Number one Listen to Man I Need: Spotify, external | YouTube, external | Apple Music, external Galway indie-folk musician Thomas O'Donogue only started releasing music under the name Dove Ellis last year, but his soaring vocals immediately sparked a record label bidding war. His debut album has drawn comparisons to Radiohead and Jeff Buckley for its moments of abstract beauty and devastating emotional release. Highest chart position: Number 47 Listen to Pale Song: Spotify, external | YouTube, external | Apple Music, external Florence Welch began working on Everybody Scream after experiencing a life-threatening ectopic pregnancy – and the experience casts a dark shadow over her sixth album. She questions her devotion to her career, worrying about the physical toll it takes, but ultimately finds catharsis in the primal power of her own voice. Highest chart position: Number one Listen to Everybody Scream: Spotify, external | YouTube, external | Apple Music, external Freed from the shackles of girl group conformity, Jade Thirlwall threw everything, including the kitchen sink, at her solo debut. But she romps through the stylistic twists of Angel of my Dreams (electro-dance-opera), Fantasy (sci-fi sex disco) and Midnight Cowboy (catwalk camp) with aplomb, never loosening her grip on a golden vein of pop melody. Highest chart position: Number three Listen to Angel of my Dreams: Spotify, external | Youtube, external | Apple Music, external Kojey Radical's third album was inspired by two separate incidents: A fashion week afterparty where he felt like an outsider, and a birthday bash for a close friend that highlighted a rift in their friendship. Don't Look Down is an album-length interrogation of his motives, insecurities and role as a father, set to a sparkling fusion of hip-hop, gospel and R&B. Listen to Conversation: Spotify, external | YouTube, external | Apple Music, external Like last year's Mercury Prize winner (Sam Fender's People Watching), Knats' latest album is an unflinching portrait of working class life in Northeast England. Their distinctive and gutsy take on jazz is augmented by Geordie poet Cooper Robson, who paints vivid pictures of steel workers whose "sinews punch as pistons" and fist-first troublemakers who are "the type of Billy Elliot to wear a ballet-clava". title: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con
description: Should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences?
body: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con Mandy Bourne lives with her 80-year-old mum in a top-floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves. For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains. Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged-up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool. Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in." Many homes are built to radiate warmth back into rooms That retained warmth can push night-time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths. Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder". Last summer, as the region baked, the residents of Ellum Pointe - a whg scheme for the over-55s - began telling their landlords they simply could not cool their flats. The response was improvised. "We took the community room, closed all the windows and doors, and we put a mobile air-conditioning unit in there," Shields says. "And basically, we created an internal cool room." She likens it to the warm spaces opened during the pandemic for people who couldn't afford to heat their homes. Shields' job has previously focused on decarbonising - reducing the emissions from the housing stock - but she now has to balance those pressures with the need to adapt homes to rising heat. Across the country, landlords are facing similar choices. As Britain enters a new kind of summer, with homes built to trap warmth and heatwaves intensifying, two questions loom: should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon? For 40 years, wealthy countries have focused heavily on cutting the carbon emissions that cause climate change, known as mitigation. Adaptation such as designing housing so it is more resilient to hotter temperatures and installing air conditioning has not always had the same focus. Reducing emissions was seen as morally right because richer nations produced most of the gases that have warmed the planet. And with that focus came a funding imbalance. In 2023, $1.8tn was given to mitigation, while adaptation did not secure even 5% of that – it scraped $65bn globally. Spending too much on adaption was seen by many as giving up on the fight against climate change. But this mainstream view has now been challenged. In a memo published last year, Bill Gates - a man who has poured billions into clean technology - argued that the climate movement's "doomsday" fixation on temperature targets had diverted money from the things that most improve lives in a warming world. Climate change is serious, he wrote, but "will not lead to humanity's demise". Governments, he added, should be investing in cooling for the countries that need it. The publication sparked backlash from climate scientists who accused Gates of making arguments based on "false dichotomies" - pitting mitigation and adaptation against each other. Some, including US President Donald Trump, saw it as sign that the billionaire was "finally" supporting the belief that climate change was a hoax. Gates insisted he was not arguing against cutting emissions, but rather for spending money where it saves the most suffering. The row that followed exposed the real fault line that's coming to the surface this summer: not whether to cut carbon or adapt to the heat – but how much to spend on each. There's another reason that muddies the waters and helps explain why cutting carbon became the prime focus – it was investable. Heat pumps and EVs can be sold. Spending on shade, ventilation and cooler hospitals and homes all produce little in the way of bankable returns - even if it reduces costs of climate change long term. Baroness Brown - also known as the engineer Julia King, who chairs the adaptation committee of the government's Climate Change Committee - argues this imbalance is written into UK law. Under the Climate Change Act, the mitigation half of her committee recommends legally binding carbon budgets that ministers must deliver and are marked on every year. Adaptation has no such teeth: the government writes its own risk assessment and its own plans. "Essentially, the government writes an essay, and our job is to say, is it doing the things it said would do in its essay. It's not actually to say, are these things any good." Her committee has spent, she says, "almost 20 years pulling our hair out" - but this year has been different. With exquisite timing it produced a report just as the first heatwave was striking Britain in May - urging lawmakers to set hard adaptation targets. "We've actually looked at the difference that providing some sort of support with cooling for the 30% of most vulnerable homes, and cooling in our hospitals, [with] preventive care visits. The modelling we've done suggests that that would reduce 40% of the increase in heat-related deaths that are predicted for 2050." "We're saying these are the actions that can make a big difference." title: Who's in Andy Burnham's cabinet?
description: An in-depth look at which Labour MPs have been appointed to cabinet roles by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced his new cabinet after taking office following the resignation of Sir Keir Starmer. Tap or click on a person in our interactive guide below to learn more about them and their role in government. Andy Burnham is the prime minister, after winning the backing of 379 of Labour's 403 MPs as the best person to replace Sir Keir Starmer. He has pledged to shift power away from Whitehall, introduce "greater public control" of the water and energy sectors and to build more council houses - while keeping Labour’s election pledge not to raise the main rates of income tax or National Insurance.He also promised to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living. Born in Aintree in 1970, Burnham was inspired by the miners’ strike to join the Labour Party in his teens and first became an MP in 2001. The former health secretary had twice failed to become party leader - losing to Ed Miliband in 2010 and Jeremy Corbyn in 2015 - and after leaving Parliament, served as Greater Manchester mayor. He returned as Makerfield MP in June and succeeded Sir Keir Starmer a month later. A life-long Everton fan and talented sportsman, he was part of Labour's Demon Eyes FC football team when Tony Blair was PM, and regularly featured in the Labour MPs vs Lobby journalists match while in Parliament. John Healey returned to the cabinet as chancellor of the exchequer, less than two months after quitting as defence secretary. A former Treasury minister, Healey had recently attacked what he called a "Treasury orthodoxy that's a dead hand on dynamic government" that viewed defence as "a drain rather than a driver of growth". Senior figures in government say he shares Burnham's ambitions for reindustrialisation and devolution. He now faces the task of making the government's spending plans add up. It is a surprise appointment for the MP for Rawmarsh and Conisbrough in South Yorkshire, with many speculating the role would go to Ed Miliband or Shabana Mahmood. Healey was parliamentary private secretary to Chancellor Gordon Brown from 1999 to 2001, before serving as adult skills, Treasury, local government and housing minister between 2001 and 2010. Louise Haigh has become chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, first secretary of state and Cabinet Office minister. Haigh, one of Andy Burnham’s closest allies, will run the Cabinet Office, the department that supports the prime minister and co-ordinates the government’s policies to deliver its agenda.Her appointment as first secretary of state underlines her senior status in government and cements her place at the heart of Burnham's administration, after she was among a small group of trusted allies involved in preparations for the transition to power. After entering parliament as MP for Sheffield Heeley in 2015, Haigh was named the hardest-working new MP in 2016 due to the number of her Commons speeches and questions, and praised by then-Speaker John Bercow for her "terrier-like intensity". In 2025, the former special constable and Unite union shop steward became the first person to resign from Sir Keir Starmer’s cabinet as transport secretary after it emerged that she had admitted a fraud offence in 2013. On the backbenches she emerged as a crucial power broker on Labour's "soft left", and was at the heart of the huge rebellion that scuppered the government's welfare cuts in 2025. Ed Miliband is the foreign secretary, after moving from the energy and net zero brief he had held since Labour returned to power. He had been touted as a possible chancellor, but opinion was divided between supporters who pointed to his experience in the Treasury, and opponents who distrusted his views, particularly on energy. Since the election he has spoken out against those urging the government to drop its net zero ambitions and insisted the party's green power transition will help secure social justice and national security. Miliband has been the MP for Doncaster North since 2005 but has been at the centre of Labour politics for even longer - working for Labour MPs before the 1997 election win and as a special adviser to Gordon Brown when he became chancellor. He is best known as a former Labour leader - having beaten his brother David, a former foreign secretary, among others, in the leadership contest that followed the party’s 2010 general election defeat - but also co-hosted the Reasons to be Cheerful podcast for several years. Shabana Mahmood remains home secretary, the position she has held since September 2025. Mahmood, who has a reputation among Labour MPs as a hardliner on immigration, is responsible for that brief in the role, along with national security and for policing in England and Wales. When first appointed as home secretary, she announced sweeping changes to the UK’s asylum system, describing the previous system as "out of control". Her plans include making it harder for migrants already in the UK to settle permanently, which was criticised by more than 100 Labour MPs, peers and union leaders - and former deputy leader Angela Rayner, who is now back in the cabinet, described it as "un-British". The Birmingham Ladywood MP claims to be the first female Muslim MP - although she was elected in 2010 alongside Yasmin Qureshi and Rushanara Ali - because, she says, her count was the first completed on the night. Wes Streeting is the defence secretary, having replaced former soldier Dan Jarvis who had only been in the role for a matter of weeks. Streeting, who resigned as health secretary in May saying he had lost confidence in Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, eventually decided to back Andy Burnham rather than launch his own leadership bid. The former National Union of Students president and London councillor is widely seen as one of the party’s most skilled communicators.
